## अजा क्षयविनिर्मुक्ता मुग्धा क्षिप्रप्रसादिनी । अन्तर्मुखसमाराध्या बहिर्मुखसुदुर्लभा

*ajā kṣayavinirmuktā mugdhā kṣipraprasādinī । antarmukhasamārādhyā bahirmukhasudurlabhā*

Verse 162, namas 866–871.

866. अजा → अ-जा

अ = not (the negative नञ्)
जा = born (from जन् "to be born")
"The Unborn."

Vigraha: न जायते इति अजा।

Bhāskararāya's reason for the nama is that birth entails death — Gītā 2.27, "certain is the death of one who is born, certain also is the birth of him who is dead." To be unborn is therefore to be undying, which is what the next nama says outright. He quotes the Mahābhārata for it: "I was not born, am not born, and will not be born at any time; I am the Kṣetrajña of all beings, hence I am called Aja."

The Śruti he cites is Śvetāśvatara 4.5, the famous अजाम् एकां लोहितशुक्लकृष्णाम् — "the one unborn, red and white and black," the three colours being the guṇas. That verse turns on the double sense of अजा, both unborn and she-goat, and reads Prakṛti as both at once. Bhāskararāya takes only the first sense here.

867. क्षयविनिर्मुक्ता → क्षय-विनिर्मुक्ता

क्षय = decay, wasting, destruction (from क्षि "to waste away"); also, lexically, a house or dwelling (from the other क्षि, "to dwell")
विनिर्मुक्ता = wholly freed, released (वि + निः + मुक्ता, from मुच् "to loose")
"She who is free from decay."

Vigraha: क्षयात् विनिर्मुक्ता।

निर्मुक्ता returns from 862, five namas back, now strengthened with वि — freed from causality there, from decay here. And since 866 has just made Her unborn, this nama is that one's consequence.

Bhāskararāya then takes क्षय in its other lexical sense, a house, and gets a striking doctrine from it: the क्षयविनिर्मुक्त are those freed while still householders. Those who seek liberation elsewhere abandon their homes in fear of worldly objects, but the devotees of Sundarī obtain it without leaving. He quotes his own Śivastuti — "if you desire the supreme abode, do not abandon your own abode; remember in your heart the name of the foe of Kāma, the way to the supreme abode." The pun works because the one root gives both senses: क्षय is what decays and also where one dwells, so freedom from the one becomes freedom within the other.

868. मुग्धा → मुग्धा

मुग्धा = beautiful, charming; and also bewildered, simple, innocent (past participle of मुह् "to be confused")
"The Beautiful One."

Vigraha: मुग्धा सुन्दरी।

The Viśva gives मुग्धा both senses at once — "beautiful and ignorant" — and both descend from मुह्, to be bewildered: the bewildered one is the innocent, and the innocent is the charming.

Bhāskararāya notes that some prefix अ, making अमुग्धा, not-ignorant, and takes it of Her devotees, who are not among the ignorant. This is the third nama in these verses he reads by prefixing a syllable, after अप्रकटा at 830 and अतलोदरी at 847. The device is standing: a nama can be made to say its opposite, and both readings are kept.

869. क्षिप्रप्रसादिनी → क्षिप्र-प्रसादिनी

क्षिप्र = quick, swift (from क्षिप् "to throw")
प्रसादिनी = she who is pleased, who shows favour (प्र + सद् "to settle, to grow clear" — प्रसाद being the clearing of the mind into grace)
"She who is quickly pleased."

Vigraha: क्षिप्रं प्रसीदतीति क्षिप्रप्रसादिनी।

प्रसाद is literally a settling-clear, the mind becoming limpid, and hence favour — so the nama says Her grace comes without delay.

Bhāskararāya then grades the speed, which turns क्षिप्र into a scale rather than a flat claim. The Saura Purāṇa, for those of excessive devotion: "by worshipping other deities salvation is gradually obtained, but by worshipping the Lord of Umā one is freed in the same incarnation." The Śiva Purāṇa, for the ordinary: "though he has only a little faith, that mortal will not surely undergo the pain of the womb after the third birth." The Tantrarāja, for the careless: "prayers, oblations, worship and the rest performed without regularity make one fit for salvation in the next birth." This birth, the third, or the next — quickness measured against the devotee.

870. अन्तर्मुखसमाराध्या → अन्तर्-मुख-सम्-आराध्या

अन्तर् = inward, within (अन्तः, the visarga becoming र् before the voiced म्)
मुख = face, mouth — अन्तर्मुख, inward-faced, hence introspective
सम् = fully, completely
आराध्या = to be worshipped, to be propitiated (आ + राध् "to propitiate, to accomplish," with the gerundive यत्)
"She who is fully worshipped by those whose face is turned inward."

Vigraha: अन्तर्मुखैः समाराध्या।

Bhāskararāya's gloss is brief: अन्तर्मुख is introspection, so She is worshipped by those capable of it. The compound is quite literal — the face turned in rather than out.

सम् is not idle. आराध्या alone would be "to be worshipped"; समाराध्या is to be worshipped completely. So the nama joins fullness of worship to inwardness of attention, and the next nama supplies the contrary term exactly.

871. बहिर्मुखसुदुर्लभा → बहिर्-मुख-सु-दुर्-लभा

बहिर् = outward, outside (बहिः, the visarga becoming र् before the voiced म्)
मुख = face — बहिर्मुख, outward-faced, turned towards external objects
सु = very, exceedingly
दुर् = hard, difficult (दुस्)
लभा = to be obtained (from लभ् "to get")
"She whom the outward-faced find exceedingly hard to attain."

Vigraha: बहिर्मुखैः सुदुर्लभा।

सुदुर्लभा stacks two intensifiers on one root, सु upon दुर्, so the difficulty is emphatic and not merely stated. Bhāskararāya cites Saundaryalaharī 95: "difficult of attainment by those whose senses are wavering."

870 and 871 are a matched pair, the only one in this verse: अन्तर्मुख against बहिर्मुख, समाराध्या against सुदुर्लभा, the same मुख turned two ways. They say one thing twice, once positively and once negatively — the Sahasranāma's usual way of fixing a point it means to insist on.

Note on the verse. Six namas in two unequal halves. The first four concern what She is and what She gives, and they move from negation to gift: unborn, undecaying, lovely, swift to grace. The last two concern the devotee rather than the Goddess, and they state the same condition twice — turned inward, She is fully worshipped; turned outward, She is not to be had.

866 and 867 are joined by the Gītā line: birth entails death, so being unborn is being undecaying, and the second nama follows from the first. निर्मुक्ता in 867 also reaches back to 862.

Bhāskararāya's alternative readings here are unusually practical rather than syllabic. क्षय taken as "house" makes 867 a doctrine about householders liberated where they stand, and the three graded speeds under 869 convert a claim into a scale.

Textual note. This verse is clean — the first in six with no artifact in any of its namas. The next one opens with one, though: nama 872 is त्रयी, recorded as यी with the त्र lost, and the verse text carries the same truncation.

## त्रयी त्रिवर्गनिलया त्रिस्था त्रिपुरमालिनी । निरामया निरालम्बा स्वात्मारामा सुधासृतिः

*trayī trivarganilayā tristhā tripuramālinī । nirāmayā nirālambā svātmārāmā sudhāsṛtiḥ*

Verse 163, namas 872–879.

872. त्रयी → त्रयी

त्रयी = the triad; specifically the three Vedas, Ṛk, Yajus and Sāman (feminine of त्रय, from त्रि "three")
"The Threefold Veda."

Vigraha: त्रयाणां वेदानां समूहः त्रयी।

The dev field in index.html records this nama as यी, the त्र having been lost, and the verse text carries the same truncation. The word is त्रयी, and the file's own gloss says so: "Triple revelation. (Trayī.)"

Bhāskararāya makes त्रयी the three Vedas and quotes the Kūrma Purāṇa, where Devī tells Himavat: "I have another supreme ancient energy called Vedas; at the beginning of creation it appears as Ṛk, Yajus and Sāman." The Padma Purāṇa — "thou art called logic, the three Vedas and ethics." The Devī Purāṇa makes Her present in all three divisions and in the supplementary scriptures besides, hence Trayī.

The Nityā Tantra then gives a phonetic derivation, which is the sharpest thing in the nama. The Sāmaveda begins with अ, the Ṛgveda with अ, the Yajurveda with इ. Joining Ṛk and Yajus by guṇa: अ + इ → ए (Pāṇini 6.1.87 आद्गुणः). Joining the remaining अ to that ए by vṛddhi: अ + ए → ऐ (6.1.88 वृद्धिरेचि). That ऐ is the body of शुचि, and शुचि here means the bīja of the Vāgbhava, the first kūṭa of the Pañcadaśī. So त्रयी also names that bīja, reached by literally performing sandhi on the opening letters of the three Vedas.

873. त्रिवर्गनिलया → त्रिवर्ग-निलया

त्रिवर्ग = a set of three, a triad (त्रि + वर्ग "group, class")
निलया = abode, dwelling, resting place (नि + ली "to settle")
"She who is the abode of the three."

Vigraha: त्रिवर्गस्य निलया।

Bhāskararāya lists what the त्रिवर्ग may be: dharma, artha and kāma; or the three times, past, present and future; or अ, उ and म, the three letters of the praṇava.

निलया returns from 839 मुक्तिनिलया and, further back, from 99 मूलाधारैकनिलया — abode of a cakra, then of liberation, now of the triads.

874. त्रिस्था → त्रि-स्था

त्रि = three
स्था = abiding, standing (from स्था "to stand")
"She who abides in the three."

Vigraha: त्रिषु तिष्ठतीति त्रिस्था।

The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa passage Bhāskararāya quotes is a catalogue, and the accumulation is the point: "there are three worlds, three Vedas, three vidyās, three fires, three lights, three objects of desire, three qualities, three sounds, three sins, three conditions of life, three times, three states of consciousness, three Pitṛs, day and night and twilight, three mātrās — these, O Devī Sarasvatī, are thy form, hence thou art called Tristhā."

स्था for the fourth time in this stretch, after 829 प्रतिष्ठा and 855 गगनान्तस्था. Here the root takes no place at all: She abides not somewhere but in a number.

875. त्रिपुरमालिनी → त्रिपुर-मालिनी

त्रिपुर = the three cities; Tripurā, the Goddess of the three (त्रि + पुर "city, fortress")
मालिनी = garlanded, wearing a mālā; and since माला is also a row or a ring, she who is the ring (माला + इन्, feminine ङीप्)
"Tripuramālinī — she who is garlanded with the three cities."

Vigraha: त्रिपुराणां मालिनी।

Bhāskararāya identifies her by office rather than by etymology: Tripuramālinī is the presiding goddess of the Antardaśāra, the inner ten-cornered enclosure of the Śrīcakra. The second sense of माला, a ring or row, suits that placement. He also drops a counting marker here — the thirtieth verse divides thirty-eight names.

This is the fourth त्रि-nama in succession, and each takes the three differently: the three Vedas, the three ends of life, every triad there is, and now the three cities. With it the त्रि-group closes.

876. निरामया → निर्-आमया

निर् = without, free from (निः, the visarga becoming र् before the vowel)
आमय = disease, sickness (आ + अम् "to be sick, to afflict")
"She who is free from disease."

Vigraha: आमयः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

index.html carries no commentary for this nama at all, only the gloss.

The disease-image has stood before, at 842 भवरोगघ्नी, where saṃsāra was the sickness and She its destroyer. The freedom here is Her own rather than the devotee's: She does not cure the disease so much as stand wholly outside it. रोग there, आमय here, both from roots of affliction.

877. निरालम्बा → निर्-आलम्बा

निर् = without, free from
आलम्ब = support, prop, that on which one leans (आ + लम्ब् "to hang, to depend")
"She who is without support."

Vigraha: आलम्बः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Bhāskararāya's entire gloss is an argument, and a good one: "because there is no support for that which supports all — otherwise we obtain regression to infinity." The nama is not a picture of loneliness but a denial of infinite regress. Whatever holds everything must itself be unheld, or the question simply repeats without end.

Read against 829 प्रतिष्ठा, where She was "that on which all things stand," the two namas complete one thought: She is the foundation precisely because She has none.

878. स्वात्मारामा → स्व-आत्म-आरामा

स्व = one's own
आत्म = self (आत्मन्)
आरामा = delighting, taking pleasure (आ + रम् "to sport, to delight"); and as a noun, a pleasure-garden
"She who delights in her own Self."

Vigraha: स्वात्मनि आरामः यस्याः सा।

Sandhi at both joints, आ by 6.1.101 each time: स्व + आत्म → स्वात्म, आत्म + आराम → आत्माराम.

Bhāskararāya says the nama establishes Her independence, and then explains how self-delight is even possible for one who is alone: She divides herself in two, and the two sport with one another. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.3 is quoted for it — "he was not happy; therefore the lonely one is never happy. He desired a second, and he became thus. He made himself a pair, and they embraced as man and woman; so they became husband and wife." Duality is thus accounted for as the condition of Her pleasure rather than as a fall from unity.

Two further divisions. Taking आराम in its other sense, an artificial garden: the worlds are nothing but Herself laid out as a pleasure-ground, since at creation and dissolution alike She alone remains — the Vāyu Purāṇa, "she, one Lord, through the energy of dominion becomes many; having become many she again becomes one." Or स्व as "hers," the universe being Her possession, with आत्मन् as Brahman and आराम as sporting: She ranges at will in both. The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa — "just as fire is in the fire-stick and atoms in the earth, so remain Brahman and the whole universe in thee."

879. सुधासृतिः → सुधा-सृतिः

सुधा = nectar, ambrosia
सृतिः = a flowing, a stream, a course (from सृ "to flow, to go")
"The Stream of Nectar."

Vigraha: सुधायाः सृतिः।

The dev field reads सृतिः, from सृ, while Sastry transliterates throughout as Sudhāsruti, which points instead to स्रुतिः from स्रु "to flow." Both roots yield the same sense and both readings are current in the editions, so this is a variant rather than a fault like यी at 872.

The stream is located precisely. The nectar in the moon at the pericarp of the sahasrāra flows down through the kuṇḍalinī; the circles of Ḍākinī and the other deities are watered by it, and by that watering the kuṇḍalinī becomes the energy of action. Alternatively it is the stream from the moon's disc which feeds the sun and fire — the Vāyu Purāṇa, "the devas grow fat by drinking the fifteen streams of nectar which flow from the moon in the dark fortnight; all this is the māyā of Śāmbhavī."

The Jñānārṇava adds a practical sense: सुधास्रुति is a particular meditation on Devī which causes nectar to flow and removes poison, used by one aspiring to the Śakti-bīja.

Note on the verse. Eight namas in two clean halves of four. The first four are built on त्रि and widen as they go — the three Vedas, the three ends of life, every triad there is, and the three cities whose inner enclosure She governs. The second four turn to what She lacks and what She is in herself: no disease, no support, delight in her own Self, and the nectar that flows from her.

The hinge is 877, and Bhāskararāya's one-line argument there does real work. What supports all can have no support, or the regress never ends — which answers 829 प्रतिष्ठा, where She was what everything stands on. And 878 follows from 877 rather than merely succeeding it: having nothing outside herself to lean on, her delight too must be in herself, which is exactly why the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's account of the primal pair is quoted at that point and not elsewhere.

The verse also closes a long arc. 879 returns to the nectar of 106 सुधासाराभिवर्षिणी, and the kuṇḍalinī down which it descends was named at 110.

Textual note. 872 त्रयी is recorded as यी, the त्र lost, in both the nama and the verse text — ninth artifact in this run and the first straight truncation. 876 निरामया has no commentary body at all. 879's सृतिः against Sastry's Sudhāsruti is a real variant, not a defect.

## संसारपङ्कनिर्मग्नसमुद्धरणपण्डिता । यज्ञप्रिया यज्ञकर्त्री यजमानस्वरूपिणी

*saṃsārapaṅkanirmagnasamuddharaṇapaṇḍitā । yajñapriyā yajñakartrī yajamānasvarūpiṇī*

Verse 164, namas 880–883.

880. संसारपङ्कनिर्मग्नसमुद्धरणपण्डिता → संसार-पङ्क-निर्मग्न-सम्-उद्धरण-पण्डिता

संसार = the round of worldly existence, transmigration (सम् + सृ "to flow together, to wander through")
पङ्क = mud, mire, slough
निर्मग्न = wholly sunk, submerged (निः + मग्न, from मज्ज् "to sink")
सम् = fully, completely
उद्धरण = lifting up, drawing out, rescue (उत् + हृ "to carry")
पण्डिता = skilled, expert, adept
"She who is skilled at drawing out those sunk in the mire of worldly existence."

Vigraha: संसारपङ्के निर्मग्नानां समुद्धरणे पण्डिता।

पण्डिता is the word to notice. Not willing to rescue, nor able to, but skilled at it as at a craft — so the compound makes the rescue a technique rather than a favour. Bhāskararāya cites the Kūrma Purāṇa: "those who once remember Devī, invoking her protection, do not fall into the endless ocean of saṃsāra which is difficult to be crossed."

संसार is itself सम् + सृ, "flowing together" — the same root सृ that gave सृतिः in the nama immediately preceding, 879 सुधासृतिः. The two stand adjacent and use one root for opposite currents: nectar flowing down, saṃsāra flowing round.

The dev field reads संसारपङ्क निर्मग्न... with a space after पङ्क, and ends पण्डितां with an anusvāra where the nominative पण्डिता is wanted — two faults in the one nama.

881. यज्ञप्रिया → यज्ञ-प्रिया

यज्ञ = sacrifice, offering, rite (from यज् "to sacrifice, to worship")
प्रिया = dear to, fond of, delighting in (from प्री "to please")
"She who delights in sacrifice."

Vigraha: यज्ञः प्रियः यस्याः सा।

Bhāskararāya adds only that यज्ञ, on the authority of the Śruti, means Viṣṇu — on which reading the nama says instead that Viṣṇu is dear to Her.

प्रिया returns from 115 भद्रप्रिया, where what She delighted in was the auspicious; the bahuvrīhi is built the same way.

882. यज्ञकर्त्री → यज्ञ-कर्त्री

यज्ञ = sacrifice
कर्त्री = the doer, she who performs (कृ "to do" with the agent-suffix तृ and feminine ङीप्; masculine कर्तृ)
"She who performs the sacrifice."

Vigraha: यज्ञं करोतीति यज्ञकर्त्री।

कर्त्री is formed exactly as सवित्री at 826 and दात्री at 832 — तृ with ङीप्, the feminine agent-noun. This stretch of the text names Her by her acts considerably more often than by her attributes.

index.html carries 881's gloss on this nama and duplicates 881's body onto it, so the commentary proper to यज्ञकर्त्री survives here only as a heading. The same block-duplication affected 858–859, four verses back.

883. यजमानस्वरूपिणी → यजमान-स्व-रूपिणी

यजमान = the sacrificer — the patron on whose behalf and for whose benefit a rite is performed (present middle participle of यज्)
स्व = own
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying (रूप + इन्, feminine ङीप्)
"She whose very form is the sacrificer."

Vigraha: यजमानः स्वरूपं यस्याः सा।

यजमान is a precise term, and the middle voice is what makes it precise: यज् in the ātmanepada is sacrifice performed for one's own benefit, so the यजमान is not the officiating priest but the one who commissions the rite and receives its fruit.

Bhāskararāya reads the nama through Śiva's eight forms. The last of the eight is called sometimes the sacrificer, Dīkṣita, and sometimes Ātman; the Liṅga and Vāyu Purāṇas give the seventh terrible form as that of the Brāhmaṇas, the sacrificer, "and his wife is called Dīkṣā, and his son Santāna." Since the eighth form is both Self and sacrificer, the nama takes both senses at once — यजमान the sacrificer and यजमान the Self, and रूप, both are Her forms. The Liṅga Purāṇa: "the five elements, the moon, the sun, and Self, the best of Munis say, are the eight forms of the Lord of Devas; the eighth form of him is Self and also the sacrificer."

स्वरूपिणी comes five namas after 878 स्वात्मारामा — स्व twice in a short span, once for the Self She delights in, once for the form She takes.

Note on the verse. Four namas, one long and three short, working the same thought from opposite ends. 880 is rescue: those sunk in the mire, and Her skill at hauling them out. 881–883 are sacrifice, which is what the rescued go on to do.

The three यज्-namas run straight through the grammar of the rite — 881 the one who loves it, 882 the one who performs it, 883 the one for whose benefit it is performed. Lover, agent, patron, and all three are She, which leaves no part of the sacrifice outside Her and no separate standing for the worshipper's share in it.

The metaphors for saṃsāra now number four, each paired with its proper instrument: a forest and an axe at 114, a disease and its cure at 842, a wheel and the hand that turns it at 843, and here a bog and nothing but skill.

Textual note. 880 carries two faults — a space after पङ्क, and a final anusvāra where the nominative पण्डिता is wanted. 882 has 881's gloss and a duplicate of 881's body, so its own commentary is lost but for a heading; this is the block-duplication failure, not a sandhi artifact.

## धर्माधारा धनाध्यक्षा धनधान्यविवर्धिनी । विप्रप्रिया विप्ररूपा विश्वभ्रमणकारिणी

*dharmādhārā dhanādhyakṣā dhanadhānyavivardhinī । viprapriyā viprarūpā viśvabhramaṇakāriṇī*

Verse 165, namas 884–889.

884. धर्माधारा → धर्म-आधारा

धर्म = dharma — right order, duty, law; literally that which upholds (from धृ "to hold, to support")
आधारा = support, foundation, that which bears up (आ + धृ, the same root)
"She who is the support of Dharma."

Vigraha: धर्मस्य आधारा।

Sandhi: धर्म + आधारा → धर्माधारा (आ by 6.1.101). Both members come from धृ, so the compound stacks one root twice: धर्म is what upholds, आधार is what upholds it — the support of that-which-supports.

Bhāskararāya turns it both ways. Either Dharma is Her support, on Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 22.1, "everything is established in Dharma"; or She is the one by whom Dharma becomes the support of all things. A syllabic reading takes आ as "in all places" and धारा as a flowing stream.

His definition of धर्म is worth keeping, because it is customary rather than absolute: "the mode of life handed down in each country by the tradition of the wise, and not contrary to the Vedas." The Saṃvarta Smṛti in the same terms — "in each country that rule of conduct which is handed down by tradition and is not contrary to the Vedas is distinguished as Dharma."

The nama continues a thread. At 829 प्रतिष्ठा She was what all things stand on; at 877 निरालम्बा She herself stood on nothing; here what She upholds is named, and it is the law.

885. धनाध्यक्षा → धन-अध्यक्षा

धन = wealth, riches
अध्यक्षा = overseer, presiding officer (अधि + अक्ष "eye" — one set over as an eye upon a thing)
"She who presides over wealth."

Vigraha: धनस्य अध्यक्षा।

Sandhi: धन + अध्यक्षा → धनाध्यक्षा (6.1.101). अध्यक्ष names an office rather than a quality.

Bhāskararāya's gloss compresses a whole theology into two clauses: धनाध्यक्ष is Kubera, "because there is no difference between the worshipper (Kubera) and the worshipped (Devī)." The treasurer of the gods holds his office as Her, not under Her — the same principle that had just made Her every party to the sacrifice at 881–883.

886. धनधान्यविवर्धिनी → धन-धान्य-विवर्धिनी

धन = wealth, money
धान्य = grain, corn — what is stored (related to धा "to place")
विवर्धिनी = she who causes to increase, who makes grow (वि + वृध् "to grow," in the causative)
"She who increases wealth and grain."

Vigraha: धनं धान्यं च विवर्धयतीति।

index.html carries no commentary for this nama.

धन and धान्य are the two forms in which an agrarian household actually holds its wealth — coin and stored grain — and the pairing is a stock one. Read with 885 the two namas divide the matter cleanly: presiding over wealth, then increasing it. Office, then act.

887. विप्रप्रिया → विप्र-प्रिया

विप्र = a Brāhmaṇa, specifically one learned in the Vedas; literally the inwardly stirred, the inspired (connected with विप् "to quiver, to be stirred")
प्रिया = dear to, fond of (from प्री "to please")
"She to whom the Vipras are dear."

Vigraha: विप्राः प्रियाः यस्याः सा।

The dev field reads विप्रप्रिय, the final आ lost; the nama is विप्रप्रिया, feminine as the verse requires.

Bhāskararāya distinguishes the terms carefully, quoting the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: "a Brāhmaṇa should be known by his birth; he is called Dvija on account of his purificatory ceremonies; he becomes a Vipra by knowledge; one who possesses all these is called Śrotriya." So विप्र names the one made by learning rather than by birth, and that is what the nama singles out for Her affection.

And then the reason he gives for the affection cancels the distinction: "whether he is ignorant or learned, the Brāhmaṇa is my body." He sets the careful gradation beside a line that overrides it and leaves both standing.

प्रिया for the third time — 115 भद्रप्रिया, 881 यज्ञप्रिया, and here: the auspicious, the sacrifice, the learned.

888. विप्ररूपा → विप्र-रूपा

विप्र = a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas
रूपा = form; in a second reading taken instead in the sense of nourishing
"She whose form the Vipras are."

Vigraha: विप्राः रूपं यस्याः सा।

index.html carries 887's gloss on this nama and duplicates 887's body onto it — the third block-duplication in this run, after 858–859 and 881–882. Here, unlike at 882, the commentary proper to विप्ररूपा does survive, buried inside the shared body under the heading "of whom the Vipras are her manifestations."

The Śruti: "all the deities reside in the Brāhmaṇa who knows the Vedas." The Parāśara Smṛti: "the Brāhmaṇas are known in the three worlds as sacred places in motion, for by the flow of their speech sinful people are purified." Tīrthas that walk — which is what allows them to be Her form and not merely Her devotees.

The second reading takes रूप as nourishing: She nourishes the Brāhmaṇas by the repetition of mantras and by homa. The Āpastamba Smṛti is quoted with some edge — "by disgrace their penance is increased, by adulation their penance is destroyed; if the Brāhmaṇa is adored and worshipped he becomes exhausted like a cow after milking. Just as the cow is nourished by tender grass, so the Brāhmaṇa is nourished by repetition of the mantras and by homa."

887 and 888 make the same move as 881–883 did: from what She loves to what She is. The Vipras are dear to Her, and then they are Her form.

889. विश्वभ्रमणकारिणी → विश्व-भ्रमण-कारिणी

विश्व = all, the whole, the universe — Bhāskararāya glosses it as all the brahmāṇḍas; and in a second reading, Viṣṇu
भ्रमण = whirling, revolving; and also wandering, bewilderment (from भ्रम् "to revolve, to be confused")
कारिणी = she who makes, who causes (कृ + णिनि, feminine ङीप्)
"She who causes the universe to revolve."

Vigraha: विश्वस्य भ्रमणं करोतीति।

Bhāskararāya takes भ्रमण not as rotation merely but as the whole cycle — "their creation, preservation and destruction." Śvetāśvatara 6.1: "some wise call it nature, some confused call it time; that by which the wheel of Brahman is revolved is the glory of the Lord." Gītā 18.61: "all beings are fixed on the wheel of the universe, which he causes to revolve by his māyā."

The wheel returns from 843 भवचक्रप्रवर्तिनी. There it was the wheel of worldly existence, here the cosmos; प्रवर्तिनी then, कारिणी now — one act at two scales.

The second reading turns on भ्रम् meaning bewilderment as well as revolving. विश्व is taken as Viṣṇu, on the authority of the first name of the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma, and भ्रमण as the confusion caused to him. The story is from the Kālikā Purāṇa: Viṣṇu, crossing the sky on Garuḍa, passed the Devī Kāmā on the Nīlācala in Kāmarūpa without saluting her; by the force of her anger he fell into the ocean and lay there bewildered, until Lakṣmī, learning of it from Nārada, appeased the Devī by penance and freed him. He then worshipped Her and went to Vaikuṇṭha.

Note on the verse. Six namas in two triads, and each triad climbs from office to identity. The ध-triad runs through a household's goods in their proper order — the law first (884), then who presides over wealth (885), then who increases it (886). The वि-triad begins with the learned being dear to Her (887), makes them Her form (888), and then opens the scale abruptly to the turning of the whole universe (889).

The doctrine holding the verse together is the one Bhāskararāya states flatly at 885: there is no difference between worshipper and worshipped. Kubera holds his office as Her; the Vipras are not merely Her devotees but Her form; and the same move had already made Her the sacrifice's lover, performer and patron at 881–883. Three verses running have now said it.

Textual note. 887's dev reads विप्रप्रिय, the final आ lost. 888 carries 887's gloss and a duplicate of its body, the third such duplication in this run, though here the buried commentary is recoverable. 886 has no body at all.

## विश्वग्रासा विद्रुमाभा वैष्णवी विष्णुरूपिणी । अयोनिर्योनिनिलया कूटस्था कुलरूपिणी

*viśvagrāsā vidrumābhā vaiṣṇavī viṣṇurūpiṇī । ayonir yoninilayā kūṭasthā kularūpiṇī*

Verse 166, namas 890–897.

890. विश्वग्रासा → विश्व-ग्रासा

विश्व = all, the whole — Bhāskararāya glosses it as all things animate and inanimate
ग्रासा = a mouthful, a morsel, food (from ग्रस् "to swallow, to devour")
"She whose food is the universe."

Vigraha: विश्वं ग्रासः यस्याः सा।

ग्रास is specifically a mouthful, the morsel taken at a single swallow, which makes the compound stronger than "devourer of the universe" — the whole of it is one bite.

Bhāskararāya cites Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.25: "the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya are both his food, death is his condiment — who is able to know where he is?" And Vedānta Sūtra 1.2.9: "the eater is the highest Self, since what is moveable and what is immoveable is mentioned as his food." The attṛ or eater passage is the standard proof-text for Brahman as devourer, and the nama puts it in the feminine.

891. विद्रुमाभा → विद्रुम-आभा

विद्रुम = coral — the sea-tree (वि + द्रुम "tree")
आभा = lustre, sheen, splendour (आ + भा "to shine")
"She whose lustre is that of coral."

Vigraha: विद्रुमस्य आभा इव आभा यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: विद्रुम + आभा → विद्रुमाभा (आ by 6.1.101). विद्रुम is itself a compound, वि + द्रुम, coral being taken for a tree of the sea — which is why the word can be pulled apart again.

And Bhāskararāya does pull it apart, though along a different seam: विद् knowledge and द्रुम tree, the tree of knowledge. index.html preserves only that alternative in its body; the primary sense, coral-red, survives in the gloss alone.

892. वैष्णवी → वैष्णवी

वैष्णवी = belonging to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu's Śakti (vṛddhi derivative of विष्णु, feminine ङीप्)
"Vaiṣṇavī — the Śakti of Viṣṇu."

Vigraha: विष्णोः शक्तिः वैष्णवी।

The formation is the ordinary vṛddhi derivative — विष्णु → वैष्णव, feminine वैष्णवी — the same shape as सौभाग्य from सुभग at 117 and कौलिनी from कुल at 94.

Bhāskararāya reports the Devī Purāṇa as giving four senses at once. The passage is damaged in this text and its numbering partly lost, but the four are recoverable: She is Vaiṣṇavī because she bears the conch, the disc and the club; because she is the mother of Viṣṇu; because she destroys Hari's foes; and because she is Viṣṇu himself. They run from emblem to identity, and the last of them becomes the next nama.

893. विष्णुरूपिणी → विष्णु-रूपिणी

विष्णु = Viṣṇu (traditionally from विष् "to pervade")
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying (रूप + इन्, feminine ङीप्)
"She whose form is Viṣṇu."

Vigraha: विष्णुः रूपं यस्याः सा।

This is the fourth of the Devī Purāṇa's senses of वैष्णवी, lifted out and made a nama of its own. The commentary on it is the longest in the verse and its whole burden is that the two are not two.

The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa's Lalitopākhyāna has Devī say, "my male form, bewildering the milkmaids" — the same claim on Kṛṣṇa made at 838 मुकुन्दा, now with its source named. In the same place Viṣṇu tells Vīrabhadra: "the ancient Śakti of the Lord is divided into four forms; that Śakti becomes Bhavānī in her ordinary form, in battle she takes the form of Durgā, in anger that of Kālī, and she is also my male form." Since Bhavānī was nama 112, this makes one nama of the text a quarter of Her.

The Kūrma Purāṇa has Himavān salute "thy form called Nārāyaṇa, O Lalitā, which has a thousand heads, which is of infinite energy, having a thousand arms, the ancient Person, reclining on the waters." Elsewhere in the same Purāṇa, Śiva shows Maṅkaṇaka his universal form and is asked who it is that shines at his side; he answers, "she is my supreme Māyā and Prakṛti of triple qualities, said by the Munis to be the ancient womb of the universe."

The Sanatkumāra Saṃhitā puts the doctrine most economically. Having taught devotion to Viṣṇu to king Prabhākara and devotion to Pārvatī to his wife Padminī, it concludes: "Janārdana is thus in the form of Devī as well as in his own form, for husband and wife being one production, the only one is worshipped as two." Bhāskararāya then stacks the practical corollaries — worship of Durgā or Kātyāyanī gains the world of Viṣṇu (Bṛhat-Parāśara Smṛti); bathing Caṇḍikā's image in sugarcane juice gains His presence (Padma Purāṇa); worshipping Devī on the Māgha full moon gains the fruit of the Aśvamedha and Viṣṇu's world (Vāmana Purāṇa).

894. अयोनिः → अ-योनिः

अ = not (the negative नञ्)
योनिः = womb, source, origin; also abode, place (traditionally connected with यु "to join")
"She who has no origin."

Vigraha: योनिः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Bhāskararāya takes योनि here in the sense of abode rather than womb, citing the Śruti "I prepared a place of abode (योनि) for thee, O Indra." So अयोनि is having no abode, and therefore unlimited — the negation states unboundedness, not orphanhood.

A second reading takes अ as Viṣṇu and योनि as mother: the mother of Viṣṇu. That is the second of the four senses of वैष्णवी two namas back, restated here as a syllabic split.

The dev field reads अयोनि, the visarga lost — and it went into the next word. अयोनिः + योनिनिलया gives अयोनिर्योनिनिलया, the visarga becoming र् before य्, and the word-division has been taken across the joint. This is the same fault as 848–849 उदारकीर्तिः + उद्दामवैभवा; 895 carries the other half of it.

895. योनिनिलया → योनि-निलया

योनि = womb, source; Prakṛti; Māyā; the causes of the universe; the downward triangle of the cakra
निलया = abode, dwelling; in one reading, that which limits
"She who dwells in the Yoni."

Vigraha: योनेः निलया।

The dev field reads यनिनिलया, the ो of योनि lost. Together with 894's missing visarga this is a single mis-division across the sandhi joint.

Bhāskararāya works योनि through four senses. As Prakṛti, on Muṇḍaka 3.1.3 — "doer, lord, person, Brahman, yoni" — which the commentary unpacks as possessing the energy of action, the director, the Self, the full, and Prakṛti; with Vedānta Sūtra 1.4.27, "he is yoni, the material cause, for the scriptures say so." As Māyā, on Śvetāśvatara 4.11, "he who presides over the yoni," where निलय is taken as limit: She limits Māyā. As the causes of the universe, Brahmā and the rest, in whom all these rest.

The fourth sense is technical and draws the longest passage of commentary in this whole run. योनि is the downward-pointing triangle, and She dwells within it as the Bindu. The Śaunaka recension of the Atharvaveda is quoted: "in that golden bud which is three-angled and contains the three, which is to be worshipped, those who know the Self know that as Brahman" — with the preceding verse, "it consists of eight cakras and nine doors, the city of the Devas, unconquerable; in that city there is a golden bud, the heavenly world enveloped in light."

His unpacking of it is a description of the Śrīcakra, enclosure by enclosure. अयोध्या, unconquerable, means unattainable even by the gods — where the earthly Ayodhyā is merely unattainable by men. पुर, the city, is the Śrīcakra itself, and Śaṅkarāraṇya's Viśva gives पुर the senses of cakra, one's own, house, room, cave. The eight cakras are the aṣṭāra, the two daśāras, the manvasra, the eight-petalled and sixteen-petalled lotuses, the bhūmitraya and the bhūgrahatraya. The nine doors are the nine triangles — the Nityāhṛdaya, "by the union of the five Śaktis and the four fires the cakra is produced," those with apexes pointing downward belonging to Śakti and those upward to fire. The golden bud is the triangle, called heaven because it is blissful; and within it is the Bindu, in which the knowers of Brahman perceive Brahman "separated neither from the Self nor from the Bindu."

894 and 895 are a deliberate pair — the same word denied and then located. She has no योनि, and She dwells in the योनि. The device is the one 870–871 used with मुख.

896. कूटस्था → कूट-स्था

कूट = deception, illusion; a mountain peak; an anvil; a machine; the gate of a city; a multitude
स्था = abiding, standing; also governing
"Kūṭasthā — she who abides in the imperceptible."

Vigraha: कूटे तिष्ठतीति कूटस्था।

Bhāskararāya gets a distinct reading out of nearly every sense of कूट, and the range is wide even for him. Taking कूट as deception — the veiling of one's own nature, which is bliss, and which is what makes one fall into saṃsāra, hence ignorance — with स्था as governing: the Śruti's "governing ignorance, immovable, firm." Or कूट as ignorance and स्था as seat: the foundation of ignorance is in Her. Or कूट as mountain peak: She stands motionless as a peak. Or कूट as the anvil, which stays still upon the ground while iron tools are shaped on it: She remains unchanged so. Or कूट as the multitude of universes, which reside in Her. Or कूट as the three kūṭas of the Pañcadaśī, Vāgbhava and the rest, in which She abides. Or कूट as the city-gate, meaning the triangle within the Śrīcakra, where She remains.

The Viśva's list is worth having entire: "kūṭa means a machine, deception, zodiac, anvil, illusion, mountain peak and summit, insignificance, part of a plough, vanity, the gate of a city."

The anvil is the best of them, because it makes the immobility functional rather than merely static: the unmoving thing is precisely what lets everything else be worked.

कूट returns from 85–87 and 89 मूलकूटत्रयकलेबरा, where the three kūṭas of the mantra were mapped onto Her body — the sixth reading above is that same identification. And स्था stands for the fifth time in this run, after 829, 855 and 874.

897. कुलरूपिणी → कुल-रूपिणी

कुल = family, noble lineage; in Śrīvidyā the Kula — the path of the Kaulas, external worship; also race, also conduct
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying
"She whose form is the Kula."

Vigraha: कुलं रूपं यस्याः सा।

index.html carries no body for this nama; its gloss preserves the commentary's opening line — "Kula means the path of the Kaulas, external worship, race or conduct."

कुल was worked at length once already, at 90–96: कुलामृतैकरसिका, कुलसंकेतपालिनी, कुलाङ्गना, कुलान्तस्था, कौलिनी, कुलयोगिनी, and then अकुला, the hinge that named Her as what lies past kula altogether. Those seven approached the word from every side but this one. रूपिणी now simply says She is it.

रूपिणी for the sixth time in this stretch — 833, 840, 850, 883, 893, and here.

Note on the verse. Eight namas in two quartets. The first four all begin वि- and move from the cosmic to the personal: the universe as Her mouthful, the coral of Her body, Viṣṇu's Śakti, Viṣṇu's own form. The second four fall into two pairs, and all of them concern where She is — nowhere, in the triangle, in the imperceptible, in the Kula.

894–895 use one word twice, negated and then located, exactly as 870–871 had done with मुख. The device is becoming recognisable: a term is denied of Her and then affirmed of Her, and both readings are kept standing.

Two long threads close here. The Kṛṣṇa-claim of 838 मुकुन्दा returns at 893 with its source named, and the four-fold division quoted there makes Bhavānī — nama 112 — one quarter of Her. And कुल, carried through seven namas at 90–96 and left at अकुला, is at 897 simply declared to be Her form.

The verse also holds the longest single passage of commentary in this run: the Śrīcakra description under 895, which reads the Atharvaveda's golden bud in the city of nine doors as the cakra's own geometry.

Textual note. 894 has lost its visarga and 895 the ो of योनि — one mis-division across a sandhi joint, the same fault as 848–849, and the second instance of that exact pattern. 891 and 897 have no commentary body. 892's body is badly damaged, its four-fold enumeration surviving only in part. 896 and 897 both have the opening of their commentary stranded in the gloss field rather than the body.

## वीरगोष्ठीप्रिया वीरा नैष्कर्म्या नादरूपिणी । विज्ञानकलना कल्या विदग्धा बैन्दवासना

*vīragoṣṭhīpriyā vīrā naiṣkarmyā nādarūpiṇī । vijñānakalanā kalyā vidagdhā baindavāsanā*

Verse 167, namas 898–905.

898. वीरगोष्ठीप्रिया → वीर-गोष्ठी-प्रिया

वीर = hero; in Kaula usage, the foremost among devotees
गोष्ठी = an assembly, a company, a gathering for discourse (गो "cow" + स्थ "standing" — a cow-pen, hence any place where a company stands together)
प्रिया = dear to, fond of (from प्री "to please")
"She who delights in the assembly of heroes."

Vigraha: वीरगोष्ठी प्रिया यस्याः सा।

index.html carries no body for this nama.

गोष्ठी is literally a cow-stall, and came to mean any gathering, then a gathering for talk. The वीरगोष्ठी is the Kaula assembly, the circle of adepts — and 836 वीरमाता had already given वीर its Kaula sense, the chief among devotees, or on the Viśva's reading the vessel that holds the ritual mead. Read with that, this nama places Her in the ritual circle and not on a battlefield.

प्रिया for the fourth time — 115 भद्रप्रिया, 881 यज्ञप्रिया, 887 विप्रप्रिया, and here.

899. वीरा → वीरा

वीरा = heroic, valorous; and as a noun, per the Nāmamālā, a woman possessing both husband and sons
"The Valorous One."

Vigraha: वीरा शूरा।

Bhāskararāya's only gloss is lexical, and unexpected: the Nāmamālā says "she who has a husband and sons is called Vīrā." The word is therefore not primarily martial here but domestic — the woman established in her household, wife to a living husband and mother of sons. Set after 898, the two namas take वीर in its two registers, the ritual circle and the family.

वीर for the third time in this stretch, after 836 वीरमाता and 898, and here at last as the bare adjective.

900. नैष्कर्म्या → नैष्कर्म्या

नैष्कर्म्या = free from action, actionless (vṛddhi derivative of निष्कर्म — निः "without" + कर्म "action")
"She who is beyond action."

Vigraha: निष्कर्मणः भावः नैष्कर्म्यम्, तद्वती नैष्कर्म्या।

The form is doubly derived: निः + कर्म gives निष्कर्म, and the vṛddhi with its abstract suffix gives नैष्कर्म्य, the state of actionlessness, which is then made feminine. So the nama names not merely one who does not act, but the condition of not-acting itself.

Bhāskararāya's citations are all about the taint of action rather than its absence. Kaivalya Upaniṣad 22: "I am neither sinful nor righteous." Gītā 5.10: "he is free from the taint of action." Yoga Sūtra 1.24: "Īśvara is a person untainted by affliction, action, the result of action, and mental impression." Actionlessness here is freedom from consequence, not idleness — which the text needs, having made Her the performer of sacrifice at 882 and the turner of the universe at 889.

This nama also closes the ninth hundred. index.html preserves the colophon inside its body: "thus ends the Bodhinī Kalā with the ninth hundred in the Saubhāgyabhāskara composed by Bhāsurānanda" — Bhāsurānanda being Bhāskararāya's initiatory name — followed by the heading "Tenth Hundred." The commentary is arranged in kalās of a hundred namas, and the division falls here.

901. नादरूपिणी → नाद-रूपिणी

नाद = sound; the primal resonance that stands above the praṇava (from नद् "to sound")
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying
"She whose form is Nāda."

Vigraha: नादः रूपं यस्याः सा।

Bhāskararāya places नाद precisely: it is above the praṇava. The line he quotes is the finest in the verse — "thy blissful form, O Queen, is manifested as Nāda in the place called Anāhata, experienced by the mind turned inwards; the blessed ones express it by tears in their eyes and by hairs standing erect." The evidence offered for the experience is bodily, which is rare in this commentary.

अनाहत means the unstruck, and both its senses are live: the heart-cakra, and the sound not produced by any striking. That cakra was discussed at 843, where Bhāskararāya argued whether it can properly be called a cakra at all, having petals but no angles.

A second reading has Her form in Nāda rather than as Nāda. The Svacchanda Tantra: above Rodhinī resides Nāda, and above that the supreme Śiva, seated upon its lap. Bhāskararāya cross-refers to nama 296.

"The mind turned inwards" is अन्तर्मुख again — the condition of this experience, as 870 अन्तर्मुखसमाराध्या had made it the condition of the worship.

902. विज्ञानकलना → विज्ञान-कलना

विज्ञान = discriminative knowledge, direct perception (वि + ज्ञा "to know")
कलना = producing, causing, making one's own; in one reading, a blossoming (from कल् "to impel, to produce")
"She who brings about direct knowledge."

Vigraha: विज्ञानस्य कलना।

Bhāskararāya glosses विज्ञान as the direct perception of Brahman and कलना as making that perception one's own — so the nama concerns appropriation rather than knowing merely. The Kūrma Purāṇa gives विज्ञान its scholarly sense instead: "retaining in the mind the fourteen Vidyās with their meanings."

A second division comes from the Bhāgavata-Nārāyaṇa: विज्ञान means the jīvas and कलन their blossoming — She who makes the individual souls open out. On that reading the nama is cosmological rather than epistemic.

ज्ञा for the third time in this run, after 828 आज्ञा and 841 भावज्ञा, here compounded with वि.

903. कल्या → कल्या

कल्या = able, competent, skilful; specifically able to create (from कल्)
"The Capable One."

Vigraha: कल्या समर्था।

Bhāskararāya's gloss is "able to create," which makes this creative competence rather than skill at large. And it stands on the same root कल् as कलना in the nama before, so the two make a pair: She who causes knowledge to unfold, and She who is able to bring forth.

The Viśva's range is given: कल्य means creation, dawn, one free from disease, a skilful man; in the neuter and feminine, auspicious speech, and liquor. Dawn and creation sit together naturally enough — कल्य as the beginning of things.

904. विदग्धा → विदग्धा

विदग्धा = skilled, clever, accomplished; literally burnt through, thoroughly cooked (वि + दह् "to burn")
"The Accomplished One."

Vigraha: विदग्धा निपुणा।

index.html gives only the single word "Artful" for both gloss and body; the commentary proper is not preserved.

The etymology is worth having, because the sense has travelled a long way from the root: वि + दह्, burnt through — hence cooked, hence refined, hence clever. Sanskrit makes cleverness a matter of having been through the fire. Placed after कल्या it continues a sequence of competences: capable, then accomplished.

905. बैन्दवासना → बैन्दव-आसना

बैन्दव = of or belonging to the Bindu (vṛddhi derivative of बिन्दु)
आसना = seat; she whose seat it is (from आस् "to sit")
"She whose seat is the Baindava."

Vigraha: बैन्दवम् आसनं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: बैन्दव + आसना → बैन्दवासना (आ by 6.1.101).

Bhāskararāya gives three identifications of the बैन्दव. It resembles the round mark above the brows; the Svacchanda Tantra places it above the Hākinī circle — "there is a disc called Bindu, and there, after the lotus and Śiva, the energy Manonmanī, which is above Śānti, on his left side." Or बैन्दव is the Sarvānandamaya cakra, the ninth and innermost enclosure of the Śrīcakra. Or बैन्दव is the collection of Bindus, and आसन is what indicates their meaning.

On that third reading the Jñānārṇava is quoted, and it turns into a doctrine of bīja-construction: "ह with Bindu is Brahmā; स with Bindu and Sarga is Hari and myself; the relation between Hari and Hara is that of inseparable association." Having then described Vāmā and the rest, Icchā and the rest, the waking state and the rest, all as forms of Bindus, it concludes — "thus, as Devī is joined to the three Bindus, she is named Tripurā." The name Tripurā is thus derived from three Bindus and not from three cities, which bears directly on 875 त्रिपुरमालिनी.

The last reading is the loveliest, and it works by prefixing a syllable — the device already used at 830, 847 and 868. Prefix अ and read अप् "in the water" with ऐन्दव "the multitude of moons," meaning the jīvas, and आसन "she remains": She remains one and undivided among the individual souls, which are Her reflections as one moon is reflected in many waters. The Brahmabindu Upaniṣad 12 is quoted for it — Brahman "is seen as one and as many, like the moon in the water."

Note on the verse. Eight namas: वीर twice, न- twice, then three competences and a seat.

898–899 take वीर in its two registers, the ritual assembly and the household. 900–901 are the pair that carries the verse: beyond action, and formed of sound — the two ways of standing prior to the world, doing nothing and being pure resonance. 902–904 then grade the capabilities, causing knowledge, able to create, accomplished; and 905 seats Her at the centre of the cakra.

900 marks a structural boundary as well: it closes the ninth hundred of the Saubhāgyabhāskara, and the colophon survives in the data.

The Bindu-reading at 905 reaches backwards. If Tripurā is named from three Bindus rather than three cities, then 875 त्रिपुरमालिनी — where She was identified as goddess of the inner ten-cornered enclosure — belongs to the same geometry rather than to a mythology of fortresses. And the moon-in-many-waters figure answers 878 स्वात्मारामा, where Her self-delight had required dividing into two: here the division into many is only apparent.

Textual note. 898 and 904 have effectively no commentary — 904's body is the single word "Artful." 905 carries 904's heading "(Vidagdhā.)" in its gloss field, its own heading having been pushed down into the body. 900's body, by contrast, preserves something worth having: the section colophon naming Bhāsurānanda and marking the end of the ninth hundred.

## तत्त्वाधिका तत्त्वमयी तत्त्वमर्थस्वरूपिणी । सामगानप्रिया सौम्या सदाशिवकुटुम्बिनी

*tattvādhikā tattvamayī tattvamarthasvarūpiṇī । sāmagānapriyā saumyā sadāśivakuṭumbinī*

Verse 168, namas 906–911.

906. तत्त्वाधिका → तत्त्व-अधिका

तत्त्व = a reality, a category of existence — literally "that-ness" (तत् "that" + the abstract suffix त्व)
अधिका = exceeding, surpassing, standing beyond (अधि + क)
"She who transcends the tattvas."

Vigraha: तत्त्वेभ्यः अधिका।

Sandhi: तत्त्व + अधिका → तत्त्वाधिका (आ by 6.1.101). तत्त्व is built straight from the demonstrative — तत् + त्व, "that-ness" — so the word means whatever is genuinely a "that," a real constituent of the real.

Bhāskararāya supplies the criterion by which the thirty-six are counted, and it is a criterion of duration: "what remains till the pralaya, giving enjoyment to all beings, that is called tattva — hence the body, the pot and the like are not tattvas." A pot is real enough but perishes before the dissolution, so it does not qualify. The nama then puts Her beyond even what lasts that long.

907. तत्त्वमयी → तत्त्व-मयी

तत्त्व = a reality, a category of existence
मयी = made of, consisting of (the suffix मय, feminine ई)
"She who consists of the tattvas."

Vigraha: तत्त्वैः निर्मिता तत्त्वमयी।

906 and 907 stand as a flat contradiction — beyond the tattvas, made of the tattvas — and the commentary here is given over entirely to resolving it, four times.

The first resolution reads तत्त्वाधिका as Śiva and तत्त्वमयी as Śiva himself, then maps the pair onto the two samādhis: She is both the samprajñāta and the asamprajñāta. The Jñānārṇava is quoted — "the samprajñāta samādhi arises by transcending Śiva; the asamprajñāta arises with the Śiva-tattva" — and then gives bodily signs for each. The samprajñāta is twofold, quick and very quick, "indicated by laughing, crying, hair standing erect, trembling and perspiration." The asamprajñāta is slow and very slow, "indicated by the fixity of the eyes and of the body." Both are reached by concentration upon a certain light, and that light "must be perceived through a teacher alone."

The second resolution takes तत्त्व as the three — Ātma-tattva, Vidyā-tattva and Śiva-tattva — of which She is at once the form and what exceeds them. A fourth, the Turīya, is the collection of the three. Ātma-tattva corresponds to Māyā, Vidyā to Sadāśiva, Śiva-tattva to Śiva and Śakti.

The third is the most systematic. The three tattvas are Sat, Cit and Ānanda, and the thirty-six from Śiva down to earth are born from the Brahman who is these three. Śiva and Śakti belong to Ānanda; Sadāśiva, Īśvara and Śuddhavidyā to Cit; all from Māyā to earth to Sat. And each of the three contains the others in trace — Śiva-tattva includes both the rest; Vidyā-tattva includes itself and the third with a trace of the first; Ātma-tattva the third with traces of the other two. Bhāskararāya calls this "the secret of the three tattvas."

The fourth takes the thirty-six as Brahman's limbs. The Kāmika: "those who know the Āgamas say the thirty-six tattvas, earth and the rest, are the semen, marrow and bone of the body of him in his aspect of tattva."

908. तत्त्वमर्थस्वरूपिणी → तत्-त्वम्-अर्थ-स्व-रूपिणी

तत् = "That" — the demonstrative, standing for Śiva or Brahman
त्वम् = "Thou" — the pronoun, standing for the jīva
अर्थ = meaning, sense, referent
स्व = own
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying
"She whose very form is the meaning of 'That' and 'Thou'."

Vigraha: तत् त्वम् इति पदयोः अर्थः स्वरूपं यस्याः सा।

The compound quotes the mahāvākya, तत् त्वम् असि, and names Her as what it refers to. Bhāskararāya's gloss is one sentence: "तत् is Śiva, त्वम् the jīvas as used in the Mahāvākyas; that is, She is both Śiva and the jīvas."

The pun is what makes the nama. तत्त्वम् read as one word is "that-ness," the तत्त्व of the two preceding namas; read as two words it is the That and the Thou of the great sentence. So 906–908 are a single movement: beyond the tattvas, made of the tattvas, and then the identity which the word तत्त्व had been concealing all along.

The moon-in-many-waters figure at 905, three namas back, had already said this — one undivided among the jīvas that are Her reflections. Here it is said in the Vedāntic idiom rather than the Tantric.

909. सामगानप्रिया → साम-गान-प्रिया

साम = the Sāman, the chanted Veda — the melody to which a ṛc is sung
गान = song, singing (from गै "to sing")
प्रिया = dear to, fond of
"She who delights in the singing of the Sāman."

Vigraha: सामगानं प्रियं यस्याः सा।

A second division gives सामग + अन + प्रिय — सामग the singers of the Sāmaveda, अन life, प्रिय dear: "she is fond of them as of her own life." The reading moves the affection from the chant to the chanters and makes it as dear as breath.

गान returns from 857 गानलोलुपा, where She was avid for song at large; here the song is specified as the Sāman, and both namas rest on गै. That makes three musical namas in the run, counting the Geyacakra — the chariot of song — at 69.

प्रिया for the fifth time: 115, 881, 887, 898, and here.

910. सौम्या → सौम्या

सौम्या = relating to Soma; hence gentle, benign, placid; also lunar (vṛddhi derivative of सोम, feminine)
"The Benign One."

Vigraha: सोमसम्बन्धिनी सौम्या।

सौम्य is the vṛddhi derivative of सोम, and सोम carries all its senses at once — the ritual draught, the moon, and by extension whatever is cool and mild. Bhāskararāya uses each in turn. She is सौम्या as being fit to be adored in the Soma sacrifice. Or सोम is the moon, and also camphor, so सौम्या is pleasing as the moon or as camphor is.

The third reading is a syllabic split and it inverts the hierarchy: स "accompanied" and उमा "with Devī," so सोम is Śiva — the one who has Umā with him — and सौम्या then means that Śiva is but a part of Her. The grammar of the derivative does the theological work: if Śiva is सोम, then She, being सौम्या, is that to which he belongs.

911. सदाशिवकुटुम्बिनी → सदाशिव-कुटुम्बिनी

सदाशिव = Sadāśiva, the ever-auspicious — one of Śiva's higher forms, and the fifth of the Śaiva tattvas (सदा "always" + शिव)
कुटुम्बिनी = a housewife, the mistress of a household; she who has a family (कुटुम्ब + इन्, feminine ङीप्)
"The Consort of Sadāśiva."

Vigraha: सदाशिवस्य कुटुम्बिनी।

कुटुम्बिनी is domestic rather than regal — the word is householder's wife, she who keeps a कुटुम्ब. After the abstractions of 906–908 the verse ends in a household, just as 899 वीरा had ended its own pair in one.

Bhāskararāya's note is brief and takes कुटुम्ब as the family rather than the marriage: the household may mean the deities Śyāmalā, Śuddhavidyā, Aśvārūḍhā and the rest. So She is not merely Sadāśiva's wife but mistress of that whole retinue.

Sadāśiva had already been used technically four namas earlier, at 907, where Vidyā-tattva was said to correspond to him. The verse closes on the personal form of a term it had spent as a category.

Note on the verse. Six namas in two triads, and the first triad is the densest doctrine in this run. 906 puts Her beyond the tattvas, 907 makes Her consist of them, and 908 dissolves the contradiction by splitting the word itself. The commentary on 907 offers four separate reconciliations before 908 supplies the pun that makes them one.

The second triad descends deliberately — the Sāman's chant, then mildness, then a household. And each of its three namas has a syllabic alternative that turns it round: सामग-अन makes the chanters as dear as life; स-उमा makes Śiva a part of Her; कुटुम्ब makes the marriage into a retinue.

910's second reading belongs to a pattern these verses have been building steadily. Kubera holds his office as Her at 885, the Vipras are Her form at 888, Viṣṇu is Her form at 893, and now Śiva is Her part. Four verses running, four different gods, one claim.

Worth noting also the bodily signs under 907 — laughing, crying, hair erect, trembling and perspiration for the quicker samādhis, fixity of eye and body for the slower. With the tears and standing hair at 901, the commentary has twice within seven namas offered physical evidence for inner states, and both times insisted the light itself must be had from a teacher.

Textual note. This verse is clean — the second such, after 162.


---

## सव्यापसव्यमार्गस्था सर्वापद्विनिवारिणी । स्वस्था स्वभावमधुरा धीरा धीरसमर्चिता

*savyāpasavyamārgasthā sarvāpadvinivāriṇī । svasthā svabhāvamadhurā dhīrā dhīrasamarcitā*

Verse 169, namas 912–917.

912. सव्यापसव्यमार्गस्था → सव्य-अपसव्य-मार्ग-स्था

सव्य = left — and also right, the word carrying both senses
अपसव्य = the reverse of सव्य (अप "away from" + सव्य)
मार्ग = path, road, way (from मृग् "to seek, to track")
स्था = abiding, standing
"She who abides in the right and the left paths."

Vigraha: सव्ये अपसव्ये मार्गे च तिष्ठतीति।

The dev field reads सव्यापसव्य मार्गस्था with a space before मार्गस्था; it is one compound.

सव्य is ambiguous by lexicon — it means both left and right — and अपसव्य is simply its reverse, so the compound fixes no absolute direction at all. Bhāskararāya works that looseness through four readings, and the commentary on this nama is the longest given to any nama in this run.

The first is astronomical. The three paths are those of the solar disc: Uttara, Madhyamā, Dakṣiṇā. Three nakṣatras make a vīthi and three vīthis a mārga, and the Vāyavīya Purāṇa enumerates them. Uttara — Nāgavīthi (Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, Bharaṇī), Gajavīthi (Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, Mṛgaśiras), Airāvatīvīthi (Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Punarvasu). Madhyamā — Ṛṣabhavīthi (the two Phalgunīs and Maghā), Govīthi (Hasta, Citrā, Svāti), Jāradgavīvīthi (Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, Anurādhā). Dakṣiṇā — Ajavīthi (Mūla and the two Āṣāḍhās), Mṛgavīthi (Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj), Vaiśvānaravīthi (the two Bhādrapadās and Revatī). He then assigns सव्य to the northern path, अपसव्य to the southern, मार्ग to the middle — and immediately offers the contrary assignment, deriving मार्ग from मृग and so attaching it to the north through Mṛgaśiras, with सव्य as the middle path "because it is the left side of the south."

The second is eschatological. सव्य is the devayāna, the path of light, attained only by renunciation; अपसव्य the pitṛyāna, the path of smoke, taken by worldly men; and मार्गस्थ is Dhruva, the pole-star on which the paths of the sun and planets depend. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa (II.8) is quoted at length. South of the Ajavīthi lies the road of the Pitṛs, where the great Ṛṣis and Agnihotrins dwell, re-establishing the interrupted Vedic rites as the worlds are destroyed and renewed, "residing south of the solar orb as long as the moon and stars endure." North of the Nāgavīthi lies the path of the gods, where eighty-eight thousand continent Siddhas "enjoy immortality, for they are holy, exempt from covetousness and concupiscence, love and hatred, taking no part in the procreation of living beings" — immortality meaning here existence to the end of the kalpa. And the space between the seven Ṛṣis and Dhruva is "the splendid celestial path of Viṣṇu," the abode of those in whom virtue and vice alike are annihilated.

The third is ritual, and it is set out concretely. सव्य and अपसव्य are the Dakṣiṇa and Vāma paths of worship. The Vāma method affixes the Goddess's name to the Vedic formulae — "Tripurā Bhairavī" after आपः पुनन्तु in the ācamana, "Bhairava" inserted into इदं विष्णुर्विचक्रमे, the name suffixed to the Gāyatrī, "Mārtāṇḍa Bhairava" in the arghya, "let Brahmā Bhairavī be satisfied" in the tarpaṇa. The Dakṣiṇa path instead performs the pañcayajñas, discharging by rule and piety and gift the debts owed to ṛṣis, devas, pitṛs, men and all other beings. The Vāma follower need not perform them, since whatever he offers goes to the deity of that path and he has no debts to discharge; he attains mokṣa after long enjoyment of the world.

The same passage then sorts the deities. Tripurā Bhairavī and her like are worshipped by the Vāma path only; Mahāmāyā, Śāradā and the daughter of Himavat by the Dakṣiṇa path alone, and worshipping them otherwise brings disease and a fall from all virtuous worlds; Śivadūtī and the rest by either. The verdict is then given without hedging, and Bhāskararāya attributes it to Śiva speaking to Betāla and Bhairava: "the follower of the Vāma path does not observe many ceremonies, but he of the Dakṣiṇā path fulfils all — hence the Dakṣiṇā path is better." What he draws from it for the nama is that Tripurasundarī is not separate from any of these deities, whichever path reaches them.

The fourth is the compactest, on Śiva Sūtra 3.45: सव्य is the Iḍā, अपसव्य the Piṅgalā, मार्ग the Suṣumnā, and स्था means She is reached by restraining the breath.

Four readings, and the three paths are in turn the sun's, the dead's, the worshipper's and the breath's.

913. सर्वापद्विनिवारिणी → सर्व-आपत्-विनिवारिणी

सर्व = all
आपत् = misfortune, calamity — literally what falls upon one (आ + पद् "to fall")
विनिवारिणी = she who wards off, drives away utterly (वि + नि + वृ "to ward off")
"She who wards off every misfortune."

Vigraha: सर्वाः आपदः विनिवारयतीति।

Sandhi: सर्व + आपत् → सर्वापत् (आ by 6.1.101), then आपत् + विनिवारिणी → आपद्विनिवारिणी, the त् voicing to द् before व्. विनिवारिणी stacks two prefixes on वृ, so the warding is thorough rather than partial.

Bhāskararāya's placement of the nama is exact: it follows 912 in order to provide for those who fall from both the paths just described — "as the Śruti says (Chāndogya 6.2.16), those who do not recognise these two paths become worms, birds and the like."

The Kūrma Purāṇa passage he quotes is generous in a way worth noticing. It lists the qualified devotee at length — compassionate, tranquil, self-controlled, free from envy, humble, wise, ascetic, of vows performed, whether sannyāsin or gṛhastha or vānaprastha or brahmacārin — and then adds "and even those who are devoid of these characteristics, if they repeat my name." The whole list is built and then set aside. "I quickly destroy in the same birth even mountains of misfortune by the lamp of wisdom."

The Harivaṃśa has Viṣṇu tell Her: "the bondage of men consists of death, difficulty, the death of sons, loss of wealth — in all these misfortunes thou alone dost protect; there is no doubt." And the saying Bhāskararāya adds is the plainest thing in the verse: "What should be done in misfortune? One should remember the feet of the mother. What does that remembrance do? It makes even Brahmā and the rest his servants."

He also drops a counting marker here: the thirty-first verse divides thirty-seven names.

914. स्वस्था → स्व-स्था

स्व = one's own, oneself; also, lexically, heaven (स्वर्)
स्था = abiding, standing
"She who abides in herself."

Vigraha: स्वस्मिन् तिष्ठतीति स्वस्था।

स्वस्थ in ordinary Sanskrit means healthy, at ease — literally self-abiding — and Bhāskararāya keeps that sense: "as she is devoid of the agitation created by pain and the rest, she is independent." Chāndogya 7.24.1 supplies the primary reading — "Where does that lord abide? He abides in his own majesty."

Taking स्व as heaven gives a second: abiding in Svarga as its ruler. A third divides सु + अस्था, well fixed, without return.

स्था for the sixth time in this run, after 829, 855, 874, 896 and 912 — the last of them in the immediately preceding nama. And स्वस्था answers 877 निरालम्बा with 878 स्वात्मारामा: having no support, She rests on herself, and delights there.

915. स्वभावमधुरा → स्व-भाव-मधुरा

स्व = one's own
भाव = nature, state of being; also residence, disposition, devotion
मधुरा = sweet, honeyed (from मधु "honey")
"She who is sweet by her very nature."

Vigraha: स्वभावेन मधुरा।

The primary sense is that the sweetness needs no vehicle: "without contact with the upādhis, she is to be desired by all." The Viśva gives मधुर for what is sweet and for what all men like; in the feminine, the flower Śatapuṣpā, and also a mountain.

Then six further divisions — this is the most heavily re-split nama in the run.

स्व "her" with भाव "residence" and मधुरा "at Madhurā": the goddess Mīnākṣī in the Hālāsya-kṣetra. Or स्व with भा "light," अवम "the best," and धुर "yoke" — She bears the yoke of the wise, and since the yoke is the chariot's chief part, She is their leader; Bhāskararāya defends अवम as "best" against the obvious objection that it means inferior, citing the pairing of अवम and उत्तम for first and last, and the Śruti's "Agni is the best of gods." Or स्वभ "knowledge of the Self" with वाम "to create" and धुर — She is leader of those who teach self-knowledge. Or सु "well" with अभाव "absence" and मधुर — absence of desire, hatred, partiality and mercilessness, the सु implying that those who possess such qualities are not good ones. Or स्व "in her devotees" with भाव "by remaining" — sweet by dwelling in them. Or स्व "their own" with भाव "by devotion," मधु "best fruit," र "gives" — She gives the best fruit, which is knowledge, on the Śruti "following it he attains madhu."

Bhāskararāya then says outright that the remaining senses of भाव — opinion, incarnation and so on — may be added here as one likes. The nama is left open rather than settled, which is unusual even for him.

916. धीरा → धीरा

धीरा = wise, steady, firm; also possessed of strength (from धी "thought, settled understanding")
"The Wise One."

Vigraha: धीः अस्याः अस्तीति धीरा।

धीर carries wisdom and steadiness together, since धी is the settled understanding and not mere quickness.

Bhāskararāya splits it: धी as "the knowledge of non-duality" and र as "gives" — She who gives it. The Avadhūtagītā's opening verse is cited: "by the grace of the Lord alone men obtain the tendency to non-duality." A third reading takes धी as knowledge and इरा as the deity of the tenth day, which gives knowledge.

The र-as-"gives" device has just been used in 915's last division, मधु-र. Two namas running are read as gift-compounds on the same syllable.

917. धीरसमर्चिता → धीर-सम्-अर्चिता

धीर = the wise, the steady
सम् = fully, completely
अर्चिता = worshipped, honoured (from अर्च् "to worship")
"She who is fully worshipped by the wise."

Vigraha: धीरैः समर्चिता।

अर्चिता returns from 825 बुधार्चिता, where the worshippers were the बुध; here they are the धीर, and सम् is added. The two namas make the same claim with a different word for the wise.

The Śruti: "the wise and poets praise him." Bhāskararāya then illustrates that wisdom with a line whose defiance is the whole point — "Throw me, O mother, into hell or raise me into the rulership of all the worlds: surely I will never forsake thy feet, certainly not."

A second division takes धी as the wisdom called Dhī, रस as bliss, and अर्चिता as worshipped — one worships Her for the sake of obtaining that bliss. The split moves the nama from who worships to why.

Note on the verse. Six namas in three pairs, organised by sound: स-व, then स्व, then धी. 912–913 pair as the paths and the fall from them; 914–915 as self-abiding and self-sweetness; 916–917 as the wise and Her worship by them.

912 is the widest-ranging nama in this run. Its four readings take the "three paths" through four domains in succession — the sun's course through the nakṣatra-vīthis, the two roads of the dead, the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa methods of worship, and the three nāḍīs. One compound made to hold astronomy, eschatology, ritual polemic and yoga, and the ambiguity of सव्य is what lets it.

913 then does something structurally deliberate: having described two paths, the text immediately provides for those who fall from both. And the Kūrma Purāṇa passage quoted there erects a long list of qualifications only to waive it — "and even those who are devoid of these characteristics, if they repeat my name."

915 is worth marking for method rather than content. Six divisions, and then an explicit invitation to add more. Where 906–908 had used four resolutions to converge on a single point, this nama accumulates readings without any attempt to close them.

Textual note. 912's dev carries a space before मार्गस्था. Otherwise the verse is sound.

## चैतन्यार्घ्यसमाराध्या चैतन्यकुसुमप्रिया । सदोदिता सदातुष्टा तरुणादित्यपाटला

*caitanyārghyasamārādhyā caitanyakusumapriyā । sadoditā sadātuṣṭā taruṇādityapāṭalā*

Verse 170, namas 918–922.

918. चैतन्यार्घ्यसमाराध्या → चैतन्य-अर्घ्य-सम्-आराध्या

चैतन्य = consciousness, sentience — the state of being cit (vṛddhi derivative of चेतन)
अर्घ्य = the water and other substances offered in worship; also, lexically, knowledge, and the root of a tree
सम् = fully, completely
आराध्या = to be worshipped, to be propitiated (आ + राध्, with the gerundive यत्)
"She who is worshipped with consciousness as the oblation."

Vigraha: चैतन्यम् अर्घ्यं कृत्वा समाराध्या।

Sandhi: चैतन्य + अर्घ्य → चैतन्यार्घ्य (आ by 6.1.101).

Śiva Sūtra 1.1 supplies the term — "Caitanya is the Self." The point of the nama is that the offering is not a substance at all: this is निराधार worship, worship without material support, whose nature is meditation on the non-duality of consciousness. The Bhāvanā Upaniṣad (10) states it as a rule — "wisdom is arghya." And the Sūta Saṃhitā (1.5.19): "one should worship with devotion the Maheśvarī who becomes oneself by one's own spiritual experience; that worship alone confers salvation."

A second reading takes चैतन्य as a proper name. Caitanyā is a female deity and अर्घ्य a vidyā or mantra, so the compound names the Bhuvaneśvarī mantra and समाराध्या is she who is worshipped by means of it. Bhāskararāya notes the convention in passing: mantras belonging to female deities are called vidyās, those of male deities mantras. The Sūta Saṃhitā (4.42.52) — "by repeating the Caitanya mantra ten thousand times he is released from the multitude of great sins as well as from other sins" — where the commentator identifies that mantra as Bhuvaneśvarī's.

A third takes चैतन्य as the essence of wisdom, on the Viśva's "cetana means wisdom," with the Rudrayāmala: "of wisdom and mead, wisdom is the better." Given the ritual mead that stood behind वीर at 836 and 898, that is a pointed line to quote.

समाराध्या returns from 870 अन्तर्मुखसमाराध्या. There the qualification lay in the worshipper's inward-turned face; here it lies in the substance of the offering. Both namas replace an outward rite with an inward act.

919. चैतन्यकुसुमप्रिया → चैतन्य-कुसुम-प्रिया

चैतन्य = consciousness; in Tāntrika usage, the fifth essence
कुसुम = flower, blossom
प्रिया = dear to, fond of
"She who delights in the flower of consciousness."

Vigraha: चैतन्यकुसुमं प्रियं यस्याः सा।

Two quite different readings. The first is ritually specific: चैतन्य, "according to the Tāntrikas, means the fifth essence," the कुण्डगोलोद्भव, so called because it arises from human beings. Bhāskararāya refers the reader to the Tripurā Upaniṣad rather than expanding on it.

The second reading is the one that governs. चैतन्य is consciousness, and consciousness is itself called कुसुम because it produces the highest result; the poets compare it to a flower, and Saundaryalaharī 3 has "Devī is the flow of honey in the flower of Caitanya."

The flower then stands for a set of eight, which Bhāskararāya lists: non-injury first, then restraint of the senses, pity, compassion, wisdom, penance, truth, and meditation eighth. In index.html the first of these has been separated from its list — the words "Non-injury is" appear stranded at the head of nama 920's body, where they make no sense; they belong here.

प्रिया for the sixth time in this run — 115, 881, 887, 898, 909, and here.

920. सदोदिता → सदा-उदिता

सदा = always, ever
उदिता = risen, arisen (उत् + इ "to go" — gone up, hence manifest, exalted)
"She who is ever risen."

Vigraha: सदा उदिता।

Sandhi: सदा + उदिता → सदोदिता (आ + उ → ओ by guṇa, Pāṇini 6.1.87 आद्गुणः).

उदिता returns from 101 मणिपूरान्तरुदिता, where She rose within the maṇipūra. Here the rising has no setting to answer it.

A second division reads सत् "among good men," अ "for ever," and उदिता "appears" — She appears perpetually among the good.

921. सदातुष्टा → सदा-तुष्टा

सदा = always, ever
तुष्टा = pleased, satisfied, content (past participle of तुष् "to be pleased")
"She who is ever content."

Vigraha: सदा तुष्टा।

Bhāskararāya's alternative is a single clause: ever contented with the good — सत् taken as good men, which gives Her satisfaction an object instead of leaving it a disposition.

The sense answers 869 क्षिप्रप्रसादिनी, where She was quickly pleased. The two namas differ in whether the pleasure is a response or a state.

920 and 921 are built identically, सदा with a participle, and together they make a doubled claim about permanence. Since उदिता is a rising and तुष्टा a resting, the pair holds motion and stillness both as constant.

922. तरुणादित्यपाटला → तरुण-आदित्य-पाटला

तरुण = young, tender, newly risen
आदित्य = the sun, son of Aditi
पाटला = pale red, rose-coloured — the colour named after the trumpet-flower
"She who is rosy as the newly risen sun."

Vigraha: तरुणादित्यः इव पाटला।

Sandhi: तरुण + आदित्य → तरुणादित्य (आ by 6.1.101). पाटल is itself a flower's name used for its colour, so the simile is doubled — the tint of the young sun, called after a blossom. It falls three namas after the flower of 919.

The commentary here is not about this colour but about the problem of Her having many. She is Śyāmā, dark, and Gaurī, fair, and now पाटला — so Bhāskararāya must reconcile them, and he does it by making colour a function of the meditation rather than of Her: "she assumes different colours according to the form under which she is contemplated, hence there is no contradiction."

The Smṛti he cites gives the whole scheme, and it is a scheme of purposes. White and peaceful in appearance when conferring salvation. Red in the aspects that control men, women or kings. The colour of saffron for controlling wealth. Black in the act of slaying. Tawny when creating enmity. Rosy in the śṛṅgāra. "Devī, the supreme light, is to be meditated upon as differently coloured according to her different activities." The rose of this nama is therefore the colour of the erotic aspect specifically. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.3.6 is quoted for the principle of such comparison — the Self likened to silver, to white cloth, to white wool, "or like the colour of the indragopa stone."

Her red has been named before, at 891 विद्रुमाभा, the coral — thirty-one namas back, and not the same red. Coral is Her substance; the young sun's rose is a colour taken on for a purpose.

Note on the verse. Five namas: two pairs and a close. 918–919 both open on चैतन्य and both replace a material offering with a mental one — consciousness as the arghya, consciousness as the flower. 920–921 both open on सदा and both assert permanence, one of rising and one of rest. 922 stands alone and turns to colour.

The doctrine of the first pair is the sharpest thing in the verse. निराधार worship, worship without support, in which the substances of the rite are dispositions: the eight flowers Bhāskararāya lists are non-injury, restraint, pity, compassion, wisdom, penance, truth, meditation — not one of them a thing. And the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad's "wisdom is arghya" makes the substitution a rule rather than a figure. Set beside 912's long and careful defence of the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa procedures only ten namas earlier, this is the same commentary arguing that the whole procedure may be internal.

922 then supplies a principle that governs much of the Sahasranāma without often being stated: the descriptions are of what is to be meditated upon, not of how She looks. Once colour is a function of purpose, the text's contradictory epithets stop being contradictions — which is a considerable amount of work for one nama on a shade of pink.

Textual note. No sandhi or spelling faults here. But 919's heading has leaked into its gloss field, and the first of its eight flowers has been carried down into 920's body, where "Non-injury is" sits without a subject. 922's heading is likewise split between gloss and body.
