## श्रीमाता श्रीमहाराज्ञी श्रीमत्सिंहासनेश्वरी । चिदग्निकुण्डसंभूता देवकार्यसमुद्यता

*śrīmātā śrīmahārājñī śrīmatsiṃhāsaneśvarī । cidagnikuṇḍasaṃbhūtā devakāryasamudyatā*

Verse 1, namas 1–5.

> **The first five namas are the text's frame, and the closing note at 1000 says so.** Bhāskararāya there states that "the first three names indicate Her as creator, preserver and destroyer; the next two as possessing two further functions, annihilation and re-manifestation, which belong to no other deity; and from the sixth name to the last, the same deity possessing these five functions is described in various ways." He says the same thing here in the other direction, at 3: "having thus by the above three names indicated Brahman in his three aspects of creator, preserver and destroyer, the author proceeds to state from names 4 to 999 the birth of the Mother." So the thousand names have a five-nama head and a nine-hundred-and-ninety-five-nama body, and both ends of the commentary agree on where the seam is.
>
> The three functions are moreover assigned from **one Upaniṣadic sentence divided across three namas**. Taittirīya 3.1.1 runs *yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante, yena jātāni jīvanti, yat prayanty abhisaṃviśanti* — that from which these beings are born, that by which when born they live, that into which they enter at death — and Bhāskararāya cites its first clause at 1, its second at 2, its third at 3. That is the same device the text uses at 669–670, where Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.24's "giver of food and giver of wealth" becomes two namas, and at 992–993, where Gītā 10.11's compassion and lamp become two. Here it is three, and it is the opening move.

1. श्रीमाता → श्री-माता

श्री = splendour, auspiciousness, prosperity; also Lakṣmī, also Sarasvatī; also the Vedas; also poison
माता = mother (from मा "to measure," or from मान् — the mother as the one who forms); also, per the divisions, मा "to measure," "to fix," and the classifier of the Vedas
"The holy Mother."

Vigraha: श्रीमती माता। or श्रियः माता।

The entry opens on the practical ground for calling Her mother, and it is an argument about insufficiency: "the mother is usually called upon in times of sorrow, but our natural mothers are not able to remove the three kinds of pains." Then the verse of the great men, which is the finest thing in the nama — "since I have had many thousands of births I have had many mothers, many also have been my fathers; I know not how many I am yet to have in the future, and their number is beyond calculation. O treasure-house of compassion, save me, who am overpowered with fear and have no other refuge, from the vast and disastrous ocean of saṃsāra." The conclusion: "the greatest world-mother is the only one capable of removing the endless misery. We should praise her as the mother so that she may be induced to show mercy."

Then Bhāskararāya divides the two words six ways, and the range is remarkable for a first nama.

श्री as Lakṣmī or Sarasvatī, with माता mother — so mother of those two. The Viśva's senses of श्री are then given entire: "Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, nurse or earth, group or family, prosperity, success, beauty, means of subsistence, the decoration of ornaments, wisdom, and the first day of the fortnight." And the conclusion drawn is a demotion of the obvious reading: "hence Śrīmātā does not mean here the wife of Rudra, the equal of Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī, but the creator of the three, the spouse of Paramaśiva, the Great Queen."

Or मा is "to measure" — she who measures Śrī, "that which limits being necessarily superior to the thing limited." So she is the limitless Śrī, which is salvation. That inference from limiter to superior is one Bhāskararāya uses again at 943 विमानस्था and 944 वज्रिणी, where one reading of each makes Her the limitator of Brahman.

Or श्री is the Vedas, "which is the ambrosia to great men," and मा is "little by little" — she who taught Brahmā the three Vedas by degrees, on Śvetāśvatara 6.18, "he who made Brahmā in the beginning and taught the Vedas to him." Or she is the first manifestation in the form of Vyāsa, मा being the classifier of the Vedas.

Or — and this is the odd one — श्री is poison and मा "to fix," referring to the poison fixed in Śiva's throat. Bhāskararāya notes what that costs: "in these two last cases the name Śrīmātā is masculine, Śiva and Śakti being one and the same." So the very first nama admits a reading on which it is not feminine. The Paribhāṣā at 1000 counts four masculine namas in the thousand — Guṇanidhi, Ātman, Rogaparvata, Mahālāvaṇya — and this is not among them, because the masculine reading here is an alternative and not the received one.

Or श्री is simply the honorific, as in Śrīcakra, Śrīśaila, Śrīvidyā, Śrīphala, and माता is the progenitor of all, on Taittirīya 3.1.1, "that from which these beings are born." Bhāskararāya's argument for the honorific is from usage and it is neat: "as we do not find the word Śrī prefixed to the names Īśvara, Īśāna and the rest, meaning Paraśiva, so also the word Mātā means Tripurasundarī" — the honorific attaches to Her names and not to His.

And last, a mantra. The six letters ह, स, र, क, ल, द of the Bālā mantra, combined with three vowels at the end, give the mantra forming the three kūṭas, and that is called Mātā — with the commentators on Laghustuti 18 cited in support.

Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa's reading is added: श्री the universe with माता creator; or श्री aiśvarya with माता knower or witness.

2. श्रीमहाराज्ञी → श्रीमत्-महा-राज्ञी

श्रीमत् = possessing śrī, resplendent (श्री + मतुप्)
महा = great
राज्ञी = queen (feminine of राजन्, from राज् "to shine, to rule")
"The great Queen."

Vigraha: श्रीमती महाराज्ञी।

The gloss is four words — "the controller of the created universe" — and the citation is the second clause of Taittirīya 3.1.1: "that by which, when created, they live." So 1 is the origin and 2 is the sustaining.

The rest of the entry is about what the name conceals. "The three letters of Śrīvidyā are hidden here; one of them is called Ṣoḍaśīkalā," the sixteenth and last part — "that kalā should be imparted to a faithful student devoted to his Guru." Bhāskararāya notes that most modern students have not had it from a teacher, and that Lolla revealed it in his commentary on Saundaryalaharī 32, making it "the first among the mantras of Caturlakṣmī."

The other two letters are Prakāśa and Vimarśa, and the Saṅketapaddhati identifies them: "अ is the first of all letters, Prakāśa, and the supreme Śiva; ह is the last and stands for Kālī, and it is said to be Vimarśa." Yoginīhṛdaya 2.21 states it more obscurely — "to Her the Viyat and Kalā, that is अ and ह, are the other forms, which are in the second bindu and at the end of visarga respectively" — and Bhāskararāya refers the reader to his own Varivasyārahasya for the full treatment.

That pair governs the whole opening. 5's closing remark makes namas 1–5 the Prakāśa form and 6 onwards the Vimarśa form, and विमर्शरूपिणी is nama 548, where Bhāskararāya defines Vimarśa as "the inherent vibration of Parabrahman who is in the Prakāśa aspect."

And a mantra again: "the part of the word Rājñī contains the mantra called Māyārājñī." So both of the first two namas are said to hold mantras inside them.

3. श्रीमत्सिंहासनेश्वरी → श्रीमत्-सिंह-आसन-ईश्वरी

श्रीमत् = resplendent, possessing śrī
सिंह = a lion; and per the commentary, pain — derived from हिंस् by metathesis
आसन = a seat, a throne (from आस् "to sit"); and per one reading, expelling
ईश्वरी = mistress, sovereign lady
"The Sovereign upon the resplendent lion-throne."

Vigraha: श्रीमत् सिंहासनम्, तस्य ईश्वरी।

Sandhi at two joints: सिंह + आसन → सिंहासन (आ by 6.1.101), and आसन + ईश्वरी → आसनेश्वरी (अ + ई → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87).

The plain sense first: "the throne occupied by kings is called siṃhāsana, the best seat," and Sastry's note adds that "thrones are generally supported by golden figures of lions placed at the corners." Or सिंह is the lion that is Her vehicle, and the Devī Purāṇa's chapter on the meaning of Her names gives the biography: "the Devī, in her girlhood, seated on a lion, slew Mahiṣa; hence she is known as the slayer of Mahiṣa and as Siṃhāsaneśvarī."

Then the etymology, which is the entry's best passage and worth having whole. "Siṃha, pain. The grammarians say: the word siṃha came out of the root हिंस्, pain, and शिव from the root वस्, desire; these two words are formed by reversing their respective letters, like the word पश्यक, seer, to कश्यप." So सिंह is हिंस् read backwards and शिव is वस् read backwards, on the model of a known metathesis pair. On that reading आसन is "expelling" and ईश्वरी "powerful," giving *she who expels pain* — or, taken cosmologically, the destroyer of the universe, which is the third clause of Taittirīya 3.1.1: "that into which they enter at their death."

So the three namas hold the three functions and the three clauses together, and each is got by a different route: 1 by the honorific plus माता as progenitor, 2 by राज्ञी as controller, 3 by a metathesis.

A further reading counts thrones. "There are eight mantras called Siṃhāsana, from Caitanyabhairavī to Sampatpradābhairavī. Six of these taken together form three pairs, which with the remaining two make up five, situated in the four quarters and in the centre." And the Jñānārṇava supplies the story of how the five arose. Śiva, asked how Tripurā ascended the five thrones, answers: "Brahmā, when he began to create, was devoid of intellect; he worshipped Tripurasundarī and became the creator. Having with great tapas worshipped Brahmā, Indra became king of the Devas and protector of the eastern quarter. Then Tripurā became pleased and established herself in the eastern part of the throne" — and so on for the rest.

Brahmā unable to create until he worships Her is the same claim 648 लीलाक्लृप्तब्रह्माण्डमण्डला makes in Bhāskararāya's own verse, where "even Śiva is powerless to create, preserve or destroy Brahmā, Viṣṇu and other gods, but, O mother, the regulation of the universe is but sport to you."

Sastry's footnote to this nama records that Bhāskararāya wrote the Setubandha, his commentary on the Yoginīhṛdaya, *after* the Saubhāgyabhāskara, and gives its four bindus: Turīya or Kāmakalā, the unity of Śiva and Devī; Kāmabindu or Madhyabindu, अ, Śiva himself; Visarga, ह, Devī; and Hārdakalā. Kāmakalā is nama 712, the single-vowel nama.

ईश्वरी opens the text's long series of ईश्-namas, of which there are some fourteen.

4. चिदग्निकुण्डसंभूता → चित्-अग्नि-कुण्ड-संभूता

चित् = consciousness (from चित् "to perceive")
अग्नि = fire
कुण्ड = a pit, a bowl; a sacrificial fire-altar
संभूता = arisen, born, come fully into being (सम् + भू "to be")
"She who arose from the altar of the fire of consciousness."

Vigraha: चिदग्निकुण्डात् संभूता।

Sandhi: चित् + अग्नि → चिदग्नि, the त् voicing before the vowel.

The identification is given first — "cit is pure Brahman, and he is the altar of fire, for he dispels the darkness of ignorance" — and then justified by the figure's currency: "in the fire of consciousness that burns within uninterruptedly, without fuel, dispelling the darkness of illusion." The commentary on the Śakti Sūtra's *citvahni* says "consciousness is fire because by its nature it consumes the universe," and Gītā 4.37 supplies the same simile: "O Arjuna, so does the fire of wisdom reduce all actions to ashes."

Then the philosophical difficulty, and Bhāskararāya takes it head on. संभूता says she was born, and what is eternal is not born. His answer denies the birth while keeping the word: "by the quality called consciousness she abides in that fire, but is not born from it, because consciousness and the thing possessed of that is one and the same." Saṅkṣepaśārīrakācārya is quoted for it — "the pure energy of consciousness of the Highest Lord is said to be consciousness itself."

And then the birth as narrative, twice. The Reṇukā Purāṇa: in Ikṣvāku's family a prince named Reṇu performed penance, and "meanwhile, out of the sacrificial fire, slowly arose a woman divinely beautiful, adorned with divine ornaments and bright as the moon, and stepped out quickly. She is the only one, the supporter of the universe; there is none beside her."

The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa's is the fuller and stranger account, and it is the origin-story the whole text presupposes. Indra, persecuted by Bhaṇḍāsura, "constructed a very beautiful sacrificial altar many yojanas in area, and the Devas offered the flesh of their body as oblations. When the Devas were about to offer up the whole of their bodies there appeared a great blaze of light, bright as millions of suns and cool as millions of moons put together; in the midst of this light was seen an indescribable wheel-form" — the Śrīcakra — "and from its centre arose the great Devī, shining like the morning sun. On beholding the great Devī, the soul of all, Indra and the Devas were filled with ecstasy and they bowed down to her again and again."

So Her emergence is from a self-immolating sacrifice, and what she emerges from the centre of is the diagram. That places the Śrīcakra before Her in the narrative order, which is worth holding beside 996 श्रीचक्रराजनिलया, where "the Śrīcakra is the body of Śiva and Devī" and they reside in it as the jīva in a body.

The Bhaṇḍāsura of this passage is the demon of namas 65–82, so the war-narrative is the reason for the birth.

And the entry closes by handing the difficulty forward: "to the doubter of the birth of the eternal Devī, the reply is given by the following name."

5. देवकार्यसमुद्यता → देव-कार्य-सम्-उद्यता

देव = a god (from दिव् "to shine")
कार्य = a task, that which is to be done (कृ with the gerundive ण्यत्)
सम् = fully
उद्यता = risen up, girded, set upon, undertaken (उत् + यम् "to raise")
"She who rose up to accomplish the task of the gods."

Vigraha: देवकार्याय समुद्यता।

This is the promised reply, and it is a rule about when eternal beings are born. The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "though eternal, she is said to be born whenever she manifests herself for the accomplishment of the object of the Devas." So birth is not origination but manifestation-on-occasion, and 4's संभूता is licensed.

The Kūrma Purāṇa then gives Her own account of one such birth, to Himavat, and its motives are mixed in an interesting way: "called upon by the Devas, and remembering the greatness of the task, disregarding my father Dakṣa who insulted Maheśvara my husband, and for the sake of establishing righteousness, and by reason of your devotion, I was born from the body of Menā, having chosen you as my father." Four reasons — the Devas' petition, contempt for Dakṣa, dharma, and Himavat's devotion — and the choice of father is Hers.

That is the Satī–Pārvatī sequence, and the text works it elsewhere: 598 दाक्षायणी makes Her Dakṣa's daughter and 600 दक्षयज्ञविनाशिनी the destroyer of his sacrifice, two namas apart; 635 गौरी has her "burned by the fire of Yoga and again born of Himālaya"; 634 शैलेन्द्रतनया and 956 धरसुता give the mountain-parentage, and 932 महेशी says instead that she was "born from Mahādeva."

कार्य returns at 862 कार्यकारणनिर्मुक्ता, where Bhāskararāya identifies कार्य as the tattva-series beginning with Mahat and frees Her from it. And उद्यत is the word of 65 भण्डासुरवधोद्युक्त- and 72, where the Śaktis are girded for slaughter — so what She is girded for here has its object named sixty namas on.

The entry closes with the second structural remark of the verse: "thus having described the real (Prakāśa) form of Devī, he now describes her secondary (Vimarśa) form."

Note on the verse. Five namas, and they are the text's architecture rather than its description.

Three functions in three namas, each carrying one clause of Taittirīya 3.1.1, and each reaching its function by a different route — the honorific and माता as progenitor at 1, राज्ञी as controller at 2, and at 3 a metathesis that makes सिंह into हिंस्, pain, so that आसनेश्वरी becomes the expeller of it. Then 4 and 5 add the two functions Bhāskararāya says belong to no other deity: emergence from the fire, and manifestation on occasion.

The seam is marked twice from opposite ends. Here at 3 he says names 4 to 999 describe the Mother's birth; at 1000 he says the first three give the three functions, the next two the other two, and "from the sixth name to the last, the same deity possessing these five functions is described in various ways." So the commentary's account of the text's shape is stated at both its head and its foot, and the two statements agree.

Three mantras are also said to be concealed in these namas — the three kūṭas in Mātā at 1, the Ṣoḍaśīkalā and the Māyārājñī in 2, the Siṃhāsana set in 3 — which sets the pattern that 8–11 will carry much further.

And 4's Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa passage is the text's own origin-story: the gods offering their flesh, the blaze, the Śrīcakra appearing within it, and Devī rising from the diagram's centre.

Textual note. 5's body opens by repeating its gloss verbatim before the commentary begins. 3's body has two of Sastry's footnotes pulled inline — the note on the Setubandha's four bindus, and Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa's reading — with their footnote markers surviving as bare numerals.

---

## उद्यद्भानुसहस्राभा चतुर्बाहुसमन्विता । रागस्वरूपपाशाढ्या क्रोधाकाराङ्कुशोज्ज्वला

*udyadbhānusahasrābhā caturbāhusamanvitā । rāgasvarūpapāśāḍhyā krodhākārāṅkuśojjvalā*

Verse 2, namas 6–9.

6. उद्यद्भानुसहस्राभा → उद्यत्-भानु-सहस्र-आभा

उद्यत् = rising (present participle of उत् + इ "to go up")
भानु = the sun; light (from भा "to shine")
सहस्र = a thousand
आभा = lustre, sheen, radiance (आ + भा)
"She whose radiance is that of a thousand rising suns."

Vigraha: उद्यद्भानुसहस्रस्य आभा इव आभा यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: उद्यत् + भानु → उद्यद्भानु, the त् voicing before भ्; and सहस्र + आभा → सहस्राभा (आ by 6.1.101). The verse text reads सहस्नाभा with स्न for स्र — a fault in the verse and not in the nama, whose dev field is correct.

"This indicates that she is very red," and the redness is technical. The Svacchandatantra: "Lalitā the universal form is said to be Her own self, that is Prakāśa; the red colour is her Vimarśa. To worship Her is to meditate on Her as such." The Vāmakeśvara Tantra: "the Devī Tripurā herself is her real form, and her red complexion is the manifested one."

So the nama is where 5's transition takes effect: the colour is the Vimarśa aspect, and everything from here to 48 is the manifested form.

Then the threefold scheme that governs the next five namas, and it is the most useful thing in the verse. "There are three forms of Devī which equally partake of both the Prakāśa and Vimarśa aspects — the physical (sthūla), the subtle (sūkṣma), and the supreme (parā). The physical form has hands, feet and the rest; the subtle consists of mantra; and the supreme is the vāsanā." Bhāskararāya adds a warning about the last word: वासना, "though it means ideal or mental, according to Mantra Śāstra is a technical word meaning real or own."

The subtle form is then said to be itself threefold, with a cross-reference to the commentary on nama 11 — where the syllabic decoding of the weapon-namas is given.

This is Her first red of many, and none of the later ones is the same red: coral at 891, the young sun's rose at 922, bandhūka at 964, pomegranate at 560. And 922 supplies the principle that reconciles them all — colour is a function of the meditation's purpose, white for salvation, red for control, black for slaying, "rosy in the śṛṅgāra." A thousand rising suns here is the aspect the whole text takes as primary.

7. चतुर्बाहुसमन्विता → चतुर्-बाहु-सम्-अन्विता

चतुर् = four
बाहु = an arm
सम् = fully
अन्विता = endowed with, accompanied by (अनु + इ "to follow")
"She who is endowed with four arms."

Vigraha: चतुर्भिः बाहुभिः समन्विता।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

The nama exists to be filled by the four that follow: noose, goad, bow, arrows, one to each hand, and Bhāskararāya assigns them by position — lower left, lower right, upper left, upper right. So 7 is a heading rather than a description, and 8–11 are its items. The commentary uses that arrangement often; the clearest later instance is 521, where a yoginī's dhyāna-śloka stands at the head of a set and the six namas following are its clauses one by one.

समन्विता is the word of 65 भण्डासुरवधोद्युक्तशक्तिसेनासमन्विता, where what accompanied Her was the army, and 525 हंसवतीमुख्यशक्तिसमन्विता, where it was two śaktis.

8. रागस्वरूपपाशाढ्या → राग-स्वरूप-पाश-आढ्या

राग = desire, passion; also colour (from रञ्ज् "to be dyed")
स्वरूप = own form, essential nature
पाश = a noose, a snare
आढ्या = rich in, endowed with, holding
"She who holds the noose whose very nature is desire."

Vigraha: रागस्वरूपेण पाशेन आढ्या।

Sandhi: पाश + आढ्या → पाशाढ्या (आ by 6.1.101).

Bhāskararāya marks the group first: "after mentioning her arms he describes her weapons, which are of three kinds, by this and the three next names." Then the gloss: "desire, or a peculiar mental modification or wish. Desire is the supreme, the third, vāsanā form, the noose being the gross form. This weapon she has in her lower left hand."

So the three kinds of weapon are the three forms of 6 applied to one object: the noose is gross, its mantra is subtle, and desire itself is the supreme. Each of 8–11 is therefore a single weapon named at all three levels at once, which is why the commentary can decode the same four namas into bīja-syllables at 11 without changing the subject.

राग also means colour, from रञ्ज् "to dye" — the same double sense that 937 विरागिणी turns on, where the privative makes Her uncoloured as much as unattached. Given that 6 has just made redness Her manifested aspect, the pun is live in this verse.

आढ्या is the word of 631 दिव्यगन्धाढ्या and 969 सुवेषाढ्या, where the governing construction made the claim one of abundance.

9. क्रोधाकाराङ्कुशोज्ज्वला → क्रोध-आकार-अङ्कुश-उज्ज्वला

क्रोध = wrath, anger (from क्रुध् "to be angry")
आकार = form, shape; and per the commentary, worldly knowledge
अङ्कुश = an elephant-goad, a hook
उज्ज्वला = blazing, shining out (उत् + ज्वल् "to blaze")
"She who blazes with the goad that is wrath and worldly knowledge."

Vigraha: क्रोधाकारेण अङ्कुशेन उज्ज्वला।

Sandhi at three joints: क्रोध + आकार → क्रोधाकार and आकार + अङ्कुश → आकाराङ्कुश (आ by 6.1.101 both), then अङ्कुश + उज्ज्वला → अङ्कुशोज्ज्वला (अ + उ → ओ by guṇa, 6.1.87). The computed pada reads क्रोधा | कारा | अङ्कुश | उज्ज्वला, which is wrong at both of the first two joints — it gives क्रोध a long आ it does not have and leaves आकार without its own initial. The members are क्रोध and आकार.

"Wrath is the mental modification known as hatred. Ākāra, worldly knowledge." And then Bhāskararāya rejects a rival reading on scriptural grounds: "some say krodha means knowledge, but it is opposed to the Śruti which says *wrath is the elephant-goad*." So the goad is hatred-and-knowledge both, held in the lower right hand.

The authorities for the whole set are then gathered, and they do not quite agree. The Pūrvacatuṣṣaṭī: "the noose and the elephant-goad of Her are spoken of as desire and anger." The Tantrarāja's Vāsanā chapter: "mind is the bow of sugarcane, desire the noose, anger the goad, and the five subtle elements the five arrows of flowers." And the Yoginīhṛdaya 1.53, which assigns them differently and more consequentially: "the noose is Icchāśakti, the goad Jñāna, and the bow and arrows Kriyāśakti."

That last is the triad of nama 658 इच्छाशक्तिज्ञानशक्तिक्रियाशक्तिस्वरूपिणी, where the Saṅketapaddhati makes desire Her head, wisdom Her trunk and action Her feet, and where each energy is said to cause the next. So the four weapons of 8–11 are the three śaktis distributed over four hands — and the reason the goad carries both wrath and knowledge is that Jñāna is what it stands for.

Sastry's manuscript also preserves a passage of the Yogavāsiṣṭha here, which states the two-form doctrine plainly: "O sinless one, know that I have two forms, ordinary and supreme. The ordinary is possessed with hands and the rest, which the ignorant men worship. My supreme form, which has no beginning nor end, the only one, without affliction, is named by the words Brahman, Ātman, Paramātman." And then the subdivision — "the ordinary is divided into two, as physical and subtle" — with a fourth and denser form given elsewhere as "the water of the Gaṅgā."

Note on the verse. Four namas, and three of them are structural.

6 completes the turn announced at 5: the redness is the Vimarśa aspect, and with it the manifested description begins. It also lays out the three forms — sthūla, sūkṣma, parā — that make sense of the weapons.

7 is a heading with nothing in it, and 8–11 are what fills it.

8 and 9 then start the weapon-series, and each weapon is named at all three levels at once: the noose is gross, desire is supreme, and the mantra between them is what 11 decodes. Which authority assigns which energy to which weapon is unsettled — the Pūrvacatuṣṣaṭī and Tantrarāja pair them with desire and anger, the Yoginīhṛdaya with Icchā, Jñāna and Kriyā — and the second is the one that ties this verse to 658.

Textual note. The verse text reads सहस्नाभा for सहस्राभा at 6, where the nama's own dev field is correct — the reverse of the usual pattern, in which the dev is corrupt and the gloss preserves the reading. 7 has no commentary body. 9's computed pada is wrong at two joints, reading क्रोधा and कारा for क्रोध and आकार.

---

## मनोरूपेक्षुकोदण्डा पञ्चतन्मात्रसायका । निजारुणप्रभापूरमज्जद्ब्रह्माण्डमण्डला

*manorūpekṣukodaṇḍā pañcatanmātrasāyakā । nijāruṇaprabhāpūramajjadbrahmāṇḍamaṇḍalā*

Verse 3, namas 10–12.

10. मनोरूपेक्षुकोदण्डा → मनस्-रूप-इक्षु-कोदण्डा

मनस् = mind (from मन् "to think")
रूप = form
इक्षु = sugarcane
कोदण्डा = a bow; and per the commentary's syllabic reading, the anusvāra
"She whose sugarcane bow is mind itself."

Vigraha: मनोरूपः इक्षुकोदण्डः यस्याः सा।

Sandhi at both joints: मनस् + रूप → मनोरूप, the अस् becoming ओ before a voiced consonant, as at 941 मनोमयी; then रूप + इक्षु → रूपेक्षु (अ + इ → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87).

The whole gloss is nine words: "mind characterised with both saṃkalpa and vikalpa. This is in her left upper hand." The pair is the standard one — determination and doubt, the mind's two motions — so the bow is mind taken as what alternately fixes and wavers, which is apt for a thing that bends.

The sugarcane bow is the text's most persistent single object. It stands at 571 महाप्रलयसाक्षिणी among Her weapons at the dissolution, "bearing the noose, the elephant hook, the bow of sugarcane and the arrow of flowers... witnessing the dance of the divine Parabhairava"; and it stands at nama 1000, in the verse that explains Her name — "thou art rightly called Lalitā, for thy bow is made of sugarcane, thy arrows are flowers, and everything connected with thee is lovely." So the same bow is in her hand at the text's opening, at the end of the world, and in the derivation of the name it closes on.

मनस् returns at 930 मनस्विनी, where "the mind depends upon her," and 941 मनोमयी, where she consists of it.

11. पञ्चतन्मात्रसायका → पञ्च-तन्मात्र-सायका

पञ्च = five
तन्मात्र = a subtle element — literally "only that" (तत् + मात्र), the bare quality of which a gross element is the vehicle
सायका = an arrow (साय, from सि "to bind"?; the word is a standard synonym of शर)
"She whose arrows are the five subtle elements."

Vigraha: पञ्च तन्मात्राणि सायकाः यस्याः सन्ति सा।

The computed pada takes पञ्चतन्मात्र as one member; it is two.

"The five subtle elements, sound, touch and the rest, are the arrows; these are in her upper right hand." The Vāmakeśvara Tantra: "sound, touch and other subtle elements are her arrows, and mind her bow." And the Kādimata gives the three-level scheme of 6 applied to the arrows specifically: "the arrows are of three kinds — gross, subtle and supreme; the gross are flowers, the subtle are the mantras, and the supreme are the vāsanās. The gross arrows are the five flowers: the lotus, the rakta-kairava, the kalhāra, the indīvara, and the mango-flower."

Then the five are named by their effects, and four texts give four lists that do not match.

The Kālikā Purāṇa: "causing joy, pleasing, causing confusion, causing to fade, and causing death — the five arrows which produce confusion even in ascetics." The Jñānārṇava: "confusing, putting to flight, attracting, controlling, and causing madness." The Tantrarāja: "exciting, maddening, confusing, stimulating, and causing to fade." Only *confusing* appears in all three, and the Kālikā's fifth is death where the others' is madness or fading. The number is fixed and the content is not — which is exactly the pattern at 946 पञ्चयज्ञप्रिया, where six competing sets of five sacrifices are listed and none preferred.

And then the syllabic decoding, which is the substance of the entry and which is why 6 promised a cross-reference here. "These names, 8 to 11, contain the weapon-mantras."

रागस्व is divided र + अग + स्व. अग means स्थाणु, that is Śiva, whose letter is ह — "the lexicon says ह means Śiva, ether, and Sthāṇu." स्व is इ with the bindu. "Thus the subtle form of the noose is the mantra formed by combining र, ह and इ with the bindu; of course र follows ह as usual."

क्रोधाकार is क्रो + ध + आ, "the word कार joining at the end of each of the three," with अङ्कुश meaning the anusvāra. मनोरूप: मनस् means ठ — "the lexicon says ठ means the ruler of the right nose, and mind" — and कोदण्ड is again the anusvāra, on the Kośa's "kodaṇḍa means anusvāra."

The tally is then given: "the names 9, 10 and 11 contain द, र, क, ल, य, स and व, and अ, इ, उ with the bindu. When combined according to the rules, these give the bīja of the mantras of the weapons."

And then the refusal: "the division of the bījas for the weapons can only be learned from the Guru." Sastry's footnote confirms the consequence — "here the commentator has not given the mantra, the result of the division."

That is the earliest of the text's guru-referrals and there are at least six: the weapon-bījas here, the light of the two samādhis at 907, the five M's at 948, the mudrā's use in correcting mantra-errors at 982, the Nityā cosmology at 775, and the nature of Kāmakalā at 713 — where the referral is itself the content of the nama, and Yoginīhṛdaya 1.3 is quoted for why: "into this world this secret was handed down from ear to ear."

12. निजारुणप्रभापूरमज्जद्ब्रह्माण्डमण्डला → निज-अरुण-प्रभा-पूर-मज्जत्-ब्रह्माण्ड-मण्डला

निज = one's own
अरुण = red, rosy, the colour of dawn
प्रभा = radiance, effulgence (प्र + भा "to shine")
पूर = a flood, a filling, a stream (from पूर् "to fill")
मज्जत् = sinking, being immersed (present participle of मज्ज् "to sink")
ब्रह्माण्ड = a cosmic egg, a universe
मण्डला = a circle, a whole round
"She in the flood of whose own rosy radiance the round of universes lies submerged."

Vigraha: निजारुणप्रभापूरे मज्जत् ब्रह्माण्डमण्डलं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: निज + अरुण → निजारुण (आ by 6.1.101), and मज्जत् + ब्रह्माण्ड → मज्जद्ब्रह्माण्ड, the त् voicing before ब्.

The whole commentary is a rubric: "rosy effulgence, as prescribed for the morning contemplation in the nyāsas, viz. Saubhāgya and the rest," with a reference to Yoginīhṛdaya 3.48–74. So this is not a description but a time of day — the red is the dawn meditation's colour, and 6's thousand rising suns is the same hour.

The image is of drowning, and मज्जत् is a strong choice: the universes are not lit by the radiance but sunk in it. मज्ज् is the root of निर्मग्न at 880 संसारपङ्कनिर्मग्नसमुद्धरणपण्डिता, where those sunk in the mire of existence are hauled out by Her skill, and of मज्जा the marrow at 524 — the constituent named as what lies deepest.

ब्रह्माण्डमण्डल is the compound of 648 लीलाक्लृप्तब्रह्माण्डमण्डला, where She fashioned the same round of universes in play, and 620 अनेककोटिब्रह्माण्डजननी counts them by crores. Here they are submerged in her light.

Note on the verse. Three namas, closing the weapon-set and then opening out.

10 and 11 finish the four hands, and 11 carries the verse. Its two halves do different work: the five arrows are named by four texts in four incompatible ways, and then the four weapon-namas are taken apart into syllables to yield the bījas — at which point the commentary stops and refers the reader to a teacher. It is the first of the text's several such refusals and the only one where a footnote records what was withheld.

The three-level scheme of nama 6 is what makes the decoding possible. If the gross arrow is a flower, the subtle is a mantra and the supreme is a vāsanā, then one nama can be read as a description of a weapon and as a string of bīja-letters without ambiguity, because both are the same object at different levels.

12 then leaves the hands and floods the cosmos, and even that turns out to be a rubric: the rosy colour is prescribed for the morning contemplation.

Textual note. 11's computed pada takes पञ्चतन्मात्र as a single member where the compound has two. 12's is sound.

## चम्पकाशोकपुन्नागसौगन्धिकलसत्कचा । कुरुविन्दमणिश्रेणीकनत्कोटीरमण्डिता

*campakāśokapunnāgasaugandhikalasatkacā । kuruvindamaṇiśreṇīkanatkoṭīramaṇḍitā*

Verse 4, namas 13–14.

13. चम्पकाशोकपुन्नागसौगन्धिकलसत्कचा → चम्पक-अशोक-पुन्नाग-सौगन्धिक-लसत्-कचा

चम्पक = the campaka, a fragrant yellow flower
अशोक = the aśoka tree and its blossom — literally the sorrowless (अ + शोक)
पुन्नाग = the punnāga tree
सौगन्धिक = the sugandha flower; literally the sweet-scented (vṛddhi derivative of सुगन्ध)
लसत् = shining, glistening (present participle of लस् "to shine, to play")
कचा = hair (कच)
"She whose hair glistens with campaka, aśoka, punnāga and sugandhika."

Vigraha: चम्पकाशोकपुन्नागसौगन्धिकैः लसत् कचं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: चम्पक + अशोक → चम्पकाशोक (आ by 6.1.101).

Bhāskararāya marks the beginning of the aṅga-description here, and he gives the reason for starting at the top: "the physical form of Devī as born from the altar of fire is described from head to foot, the head being taken up first as it also represents the first kūṭa named Vāgbhava of the Pañcadaśī mantra."

That single clause joins two schemes the text otherwise treats separately. The head-to-foot sequence runs from here to 48 — hair, crown, forehead, mark, brows, eyes, nose, nose-jewel, ears, earrings, cheeks, lips, teeth, betel, and on down through neck, arms, breasts, waist, thighs, knees, calves, ankles and feet. And namas 85–87 map the three kūṭas onto the same body: 85 श्रीमद्वाग्भवकूटैकस्वरूपमुखपङ्कजा makes the lotus-face one with the Vāgbhava kūṭa, 86 makes throat-to-waist the Kāmarāja, and 87 makes below the waist the Śakti. So the description of the limbs is at the same time a description of the mantra, and Bhāskararāya says so at the moment the limbs begin.

The rest of the entry is a verse addressed to a bee, and it is the only place in these ten verses where the commentary turns aside into poetry: "thou knowest, O honey-bee, the smell of the flowers. Give me the truth. Can I compare the odours of the hair of Devī with anything?" The gloss preceding it inverts the compound's obvious sense — "her hair gives scent to the flowers" — so the four blossoms are not what perfumes the hair but what the hair perfumes.

लस् is the root of लास्य at 738 लास्यप्रिया, where She delights in dancing, and of अलसा at 575 माध्वीपानालसा, where the privative gave the stillness after wine.

14. कुरुविन्दमणिश्रेणीकनत्कोटीरमण्डिता → कुरुविन्द-मणि-श्रेणी-कनत्-कोटीर-मण्डिता

कुरुविन्द = the kuruvinda ruby; a variety of padmarāga
मणि = a gem, a jewel
श्रेणी = a row, a line, a series
कनत् = glittering, shining (present participle of कन् "to be bright")
कोटीर = a crown, a diadem
मण्डिता = adorned, decorated (from मण्ड्)
"She whose glittering crown is adorned with rows of kuruvinda gems."

Vigraha: कुरुविन्दमणिश्रेणीभिः कनत् कोटीरं, तेन मण्डिता।

The gems are placed and then given a use. "Kuruvinda gems are called padmarāga," and the Garuḍa Purāṇa's chapter on jewels "describes different kinds of rubies which can be obtained from different mines and rivers. The rubies obtained from Kuruvinda are to be preferred to those from Sphaṭika; they confer love, prosperity, and devotion to Hari."

And then the conclusion, which converts a jeweller's note into a meditative instruction: "the drift is, if one meditates on Her as wearing such gems, his devotion will be increased." So the choice of stone in the nama is not descriptive but efficacious — the gem's own virtue passes to whoever visualises it on Her. That is the same logic as 922 तरुणादित्यपाटला, where colour is a function of the meditation's purpose rather than of Her appearance.

कनत् is the participle of 864 कनत्कनकताटङ्का, where the glitter was on the earrings and the metal was gold — and where the dev field reads फनत् for कनत्, so the word survives correctly here and not there.

The body also carries the verse-division marker (4), and two of Sastry's footnotes have been pulled inline: the note recording that Bhāskararāya withheld the weapon-mantra at 11, and Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa's remark that "like the idea of a serpent in a rope, the whole universe is false."

Note on the verse. Two namas, hair and crown, opening the body-description.

13 is the important one, and only for its first clause. By saying that the head is taken first "as it also represents the first kūṭa named Vāgbhava," Bhāskararāya makes the thirty-six namas from here to 48 a double description — of a body and of the Pañcadaśī — and gives the mantra-body identity of 85–87 its foundation seventy namas before it is stated.

14 then shows the method that governs the ornament-namas throughout. The gem is named because meditating on it increases devotion, not because She is wearing it.

Textual note. 14's body holds the verse marker and two intruded footnotes, one of them belonging to nama 11.

---

## अष्टमीचन्द्रविभ्राजदलिकस्थलशोभिता । मुखचन्द्रकलङ्काभमृगनाभिविशेषका

*aṣṭamīcandravibhrājadalikasthalaśobhitā । mukhacandrakalaṅkābhamṛganābhiviśeṣakā*

Verse 5, namas 15–16.

15. अष्टमीचन्द्रविभ्राजदलिकस्थलशोभिता → अष्टमी-चन्द्र-विभ्राजत्-अलिक-स्थल-शोभिता

अष्टमी = the eighth day of a lunar fortnight
चन्द्र = the moon
विभ्राजत् = shining forth, radiant (present participle of वि + भ्राज् "to shine")
अलिक = the forehead
स्थल = a place, a surface, an expanse
शोभिता = made beautiful, adorned (from शुभ् "to shine")
"She who is adorned with a forehead radiant as the moon of the eighth day."

Vigraha: अष्टमीचन्द्रः इव विभ्राजत् अलिकस्थलं, तेन शोभिता।

Sandhi: विभ्राजत् + अलिक → विभ्राजदलिक, the त् voicing before the vowel.

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

The simile is exact rather than general, and that is its point: the eighth-day moon is the half moon, so the figure is of a brow's curve and not merely of brightness. The text uses the half moon again at 594 इन्द्रधनुःप्रभा, where the Nityāhṛdaya sets an ardhacandra above the bindu in the forehead at a quarter of its measure — the same spot, once as a feature and once as a nyāsa station.

शोभिता is the participle of शुभ्, the root of 682 शुभकरी and 972 आशोभना, and of 529 सर्ववर्णोपशोभिता, where what adorned Her was every colour and every letter.

16. मुखचन्द्रकलङ्काभमृगनाभिविशेषका → मुख-चन्द्र-कलङ्क-आभ-मृग-नाभि-विशेषका

मुख = the face
चन्द्र = the moon
कलङ्क = a stain, a spot, a blemish
आभ = resembling, having the appearance of (आ + भा)
मृग = a deer
नाभि = the navel — मृगनाभि, musk, named for the deer's pod
विशेषका = a mark on the forehead, a caste-mark (विशेष "distinction" with the diminutive)
"She whose musk forehead-mark is like the spot on the moon of her face."

Vigraha: मुखचन्द्रस्य कलङ्काभं मृगनाभिविशेषकं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: कलङ्क + आभ → कलङ्काभ (आ by 6.1.101). The computed pada takes मृगनाभि as one member and it is two, though the compound is a fixed term for musk.

index.html carries only the verse-division marker (5).

The figure completes 15's rather than repeating it. The forehead was the eighth-day moon; the face is the full moon; and the musk mark is the lunar blemish — so one nama is needed to establish the moon and a second to put the spot on it. And the compound is doubly figurative, since मृगनाभि is itself a metaphor: musk named as the deer's navel.

चन्द्र stands twice in this verse and again at 592 चन्द्रनिभा, where Bhāskararāya made the moon in the brahmarandhra the third kūṭa of the mantra. Its digits are Hers at 612 कलानाथा, and the nectar in the moon at the sahasrāra's pericarp is the stream of 879 सुधासृतिः.

Note on the verse. Two namas and no commentary at all, which is the first such verse in the text.

They work as a single figure divided: the brow is the half moon of the eighth day, the face is the moon entire, and the musk mark is its spot. What the pair shows is that the aṅga-description is not a list of independent epithets — it builds one image across adjacent namas and needs both to complete it.

Textual note. 15 has no body. 16's body is the verse marker alone. 16's computed pada merges मृग and नाभि.

## वदनस्मरमाङ्गल्यगृहतोरणचिल्लिका । वक्त्रलक्ष्मीपरीवाहचलन्मीनाभलोचना

*vadanasmaramāṅgalyagṛhatoraṇacillikā । vaktralakṣmīparīvāhacalanmīnābhalocanā*

Verse 6, namas 17–18.

17. वदनस्मरमाङ्गल्यगृहतोरणचिल्लिका → वदन-स्मर-माङ्गल्य-गृह-तोरण-चिल्लिका

वदन = the face, the mouth (from वद् "to speak")
स्मर = Smara, Kāma — literally the recollector (from स्मृ "to remember")
माङ्गल्य = auspicious, nuptial (vṛddhi derivative of मङ्गल)
गृह = a house, a palace
तोरण = an arched gateway, a festal arch
चिल्लिका = an eyebrow
"She whose eyebrows are the festal arches of the nuptial palace that is her face, the house of Kāma."

Vigraha: वदनम् एव स्मरस्य माङ्गल्यगृहम्, तस्य तोरणे चिल्लिके यस्याः सा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

The compound is the most elaborate conceit in the aṅga-series. A तोरण is the arch raised over a doorway at a wedding, so the brows are not merely arch-shaped: they are the marriage-decoration of a house, and the house is her face, and the householder is Kāma. Every member of the compound is doing work, which is unusual even here.

स्मर is Kāma named from स्मृ, to remember — the god who works by recollection. The text has him burnt to ash and revived by Her at 84 हरनेत्राग्निसंदग्धकामसंजीवनौषधिः, and at 586 कामसेविता the Aruṇa Upaniṣad's bodiless Kāma, who "though without fingers worshipped" and "though without tongue tasted it," is made the Ṛṣi who saw the jewel of Śrīvidyā. So the god whose gateway her brows are is elsewhere the seer of her mantra.

माङ्गल्य is built on मङ्गल, which the Viṣṇu Purāṇa at 967 सुमङ्गली makes a name of Brahman defined by its effect — "that, by remembering which, drives away misfortune from men."

18. वक्त्रलक्ष्मीपरीवाहचलन्मीनाभलोचना → वक्त्र-लक्ष्मी-परीवाह-चलत्-मीन-आभ-लोचना

वक्त्र = the face, the mouth (from वच् "to speak")
लक्ष्मी = beauty, splendour, fortune
परीवाह = an overflow, a channel carrying off flood-water (परि + वह् "to bear")
चलत् = moving, darting (present participle of चल् "to move")
मीन = a fish
आभ = resembling
लोचना = an eye (from लोच् "to see")
"She whose eyes are like fish darting in the overflow of her face's beauty."

Vigraha: वक्त्रलक्ष्म्याः परीवाहे चलन्मीनाभे लोचने यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: चलत् + मीन → चलन्मीन, the त् assimilating in nasality before म् (Pāṇini 8.4.45, यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा) — the same rule that gives श्रीमन्नगर- at 56 and प्रतिपन्मुख्य- at 610. The computed pada records चलन्, the sandhi-form, where the stem is चलत्; it also takes वक्त्रलक्ष्मी as one member where the compound has two.

index.html carries only the verse-division marker (6).

परीवाह is the precise word and the figure depends on it: not a pool but the channel by which a full tank overflows. So the face's beauty is imagined as more than the face can hold, running off, and the eyes are the fish that come with the water. The comparison of eyes to fish is conventional; the overflow-channel is not.

The fish returns at 915 स्वभावमधुरा, where one division makes स्व with भाव as residence and मधुरा as "at Madhurā," identifying Her with Mīnākṣī — the fish-eyed goddess of the Hālāsya-kṣetra. So the simile here is the etymology of a name the text gives Her later. And Her eyes are worked three more times: wide at 936 विशालाक्षी, where Bhāskararāya makes them a pīṭha; fawn-like at 561 मृगाक्षी; long and faintly moving at 601 दरान्दोलितदीर्घाक्षी.

Note on the verse. Two namas, brows and eyes, and both are extended conceits with no commentary attached.

They are the high point of the aṅga-description's artifice. 17 builds a nuptial house out of a face and makes the brows its wedding-arches; 18 makes the face's beauty a flood too great for its channel and the eyes the fish in the overflow. Neither is a simple comparison, and neither is glossed — Bhāskararāya passes both in silence, as he does most of the purely ornamental namas.

Textual note. 17 has no body. 18's body is the verse marker alone, and its computed pada gives चलन् for the stem चलत् and merges वक्त्र with लक्ष्मी.

---

## नवचम्पकपुष्पाभनासादण्डविराजिता । ताराकान्तितिरस्कारिनासाभरणभासुरा

*navacampakapuṣpābhanāsādaṇḍavirājitā । tārākāntitiraskārināsābharaṇabhāsurā*

Verse 7, namas 19–20.

19. नवचम्पकपुष्पाभनासादण्डविराजिता → नव-चम्पक-पुष्प-आभ-नासा-दण्ड-विराजिता

नव = new, fresh, newly opened
चम्पक = the campaka flower
पुष्प = a flower, a blossom
आभ = resembling
नासा = the nose
दण्ड = a staff, a stalk, a stem
विराजिता = made resplendent, shining (वि + राज् "to shine")
"She who is resplendent with a nose-stem like a newly opened campaka bud."

Vigraha: नवचम्पकपुष्पाभेन नासादण्डेन विराजिता।

Sandhi: पुष्प + आभ → पुष्पाभ (आ by 6.1.101). The verse text reads पुप्पाभ with प्प for ष्प, where the nama's own dev field is correct — the second such fault in these ten verses, after सहस्नाभा at 6.

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

दण्ड for the nose's ridge is standard but worth noting for what it shares: the same word is the rod of chastisement in दण्डनाथा at 70, Vārāhī the commander-in-chief, and the science of government in 608 दण्डनीतिस्था — the only nama placing Her in a secular discipline.

चम्पक had been one of the four flowers in Her hair at 13, six namas back. The text is using the same blossom twice within one verse-group, once for scent and once for shape, and नव specifies the second: an unopened campaka bud is a narrow tapering thing, which is the comparison wanted.

20. ताराकान्तितिरस्कारिनासाभरणभासुरा → तारा-कान्ति-तिरस्कारिन्-नासा-आभरण-भासुरा

तारा = a star; and per the commentary, the goddesses Maṅgalā and Śuklā, or the goddess Tārakā
कान्ति = loveliness, brilliance (from कम् "to desire")
तिरस्कारिन् = surpassing, putting to shame, eclipsing (तिरस् + कृ "to set aside")
नासा = the nose
आभरण = an ornament
भासुरा = shining, resplendent (from भास् "to shine")
"She who is resplendent with a nose-ornament that eclipses the brilliance of the stars."

Vigraha: ताराकान्तेः तिरस्कारिणा नासाभरणेन भासुरा।

Sandhi: नासा + आभरण → नासाभरण (आ by 6.1.101).

The whole commentary is two lines of identification: "Tārā may also mean two goddesses, Maṅgalā and Śuklā; or one of the goddesses, Tārakā. The jewels are māṇikya and mauktika."

So the star is either a star, or two named deities, or one — and the ornament's stones are specified as ruby and pearl, which the nama does not say. That is characteristic of the ornament-namas: 14 named the kuruvinda ruby for its effect on the meditator, and here the stones are supplied where the nama gives only "ornament."

तिरस्कारिन् is one of a small set of eclipsing-words the aṅga-series uses. The cheeks at 23 outdo a ruby mirror by परिभावि, the lips at 24 shame coral and bimba by न्यक्कारि, and the feet at 45 outdo lotuses by पराकृत — four namas, four different words for the same figure of outdoing. It is the description's most repeated move.

Note on the verse. Two namas, the nose and its jewel, and between them they show the two registers the aṅga-series alternates: a shape-simile with no commentary, and an ornament whose materials the commentary has to supply.

Textual note. The verse text reads पुप्पाभ for पुष्पाभ at 19, the nama's dev field being correct. 19 has no commentary body.

---

## कदम्बमञ्जरीक्ऌप्तकर्णपूरमनोहरा । ताटङ्कयुगलीभूततपनोडुपमण्डला

*kadambamañjarīkḷptakarṇapūramanoharā । tāṭaṅkayugalībhūtatapanoḍupamaṇḍalā*

Verse 8, namas 21–22.

21. कदम्बमञ्जरीक्ऌप्तकर्णपूरमनोहरा → कदम्ब-मञ्जरी-क्ऌप्त-कर्ण-पूर-मनोहरा

कदम्ब = the kadamba tree and its globular blossom
मञ्जरी = a cluster, a spray of blossom
क्ऌप्त = arranged, formed, made (from क्ऌप् "to be arranged")
कर्ण = the ear
पूर = filling — कर्णपूर, an ear-ornament, literally the ear's filling (from पूर् "to fill")
मनोहरा = captivating, heart-stealing (मनस् + हर, "mind-taking")
"She who captivates with ear-ornaments made of kadamba clusters."

Vigraha: कदम्बमञ्जरीभिः क्ऌप्तेन कर्णपूरेण मनोहरा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

The orthography is worth a note. Both the nama's dev field and the verse text read क्ऌप्त with the vocalic ऌ — क् followed by the independent vowel-sign for ḷ — where the computed pada reads क्लृप्त, spelling the same sound as क् + ल + ृ. The root is क्ऌप्, whose vowel is genuinely vocalic ḷ, so the dev field's spelling is the correct one and the pada's is the common misencoding. This is the reverse of the usual situation in these fields, and it is the only place in the text where the rare ऌ appears.

The same participle stands at 648 लीलाक्ऌप्तब्रह्माण्डमण्डला, where what was arranged in play was the round of universes. Ear-clusters here, cosmogony there, one word.

कदम्ब is the tree of Her grove at 60 कदम्बवनवासिनी, so the flower in her ear is from the wood she lives in. And मनोहरा is the only compound in the aṅga-series that names an effect on the beholder rather than a resemblance.

22. ताटङ्कयुगलीभूततपनोडुपमण्डला → ताटङ्क-युगली-भूत-तपन-उडुप-मण्डला

ताटङ्क = a large ear-ornament, an ear-pendant
युगली = a pair, a couple (युगल with the feminine)
भूत = become (past participle of भू "to be")
तपन = the sun — the burner (from तप् "to burn")
उडुप = the moon — literally the star-lord or the raft (उडु "star" + प)
मण्डला = a disc, an orb, a circle
"She whose pair of ear-pendants are the orbs of the sun and the moon."

Vigraha: ताटङ्कयुगलीभूते तपनोडुपमण्डले यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: तपन + उडुप → तपनोडुप (अ + उ → ओ by guṇa, 6.1.87).

The commentary is one citation and it is a strong one: "the sun and the moon are the breasts, eyes, and earrings of Devī; so says the Śruti." Three organs for two luminaries, which is more than this nama claims — the same pair serves as eyes at 762 त्र्यम्बका, where the Devī Purāṇa names Her three eyes as "the moon, the sun and the fire," and as breasts elsewhere.

This is the nama I referred back to at 864 कनत्कनकताटङ्का, where the same ornament is described as glittering gold. Set beside this one the later nama is a deliberate reduction in scale: the identical object, once as cosmology and once as jewellery, and Bhāskararāya passes 864 without comment.

तपन and उडुप are both descriptive rather than proper names — the burner and the star-lord — so the compound gives the luminaries by function. That fits the nyāsa at 592 and 596, where a moon in the head is the third kūṭa of the mantra and a sun in the heart is the second.

Note on the verse. Two namas, both of the ears, and they divide as flower and luminary.

22 is where the aṅga-description briefly stops being a description. Up to here the comparisons have been to flowers, gems and fish; this one makes two of Her ornaments the sun and the moon, and the Śruti quoted extends the identification to her eyes and breasts as well. The body being described is not consistently human-scaled, and 12 has already sunk the universes in her radiance.

Textual note. Both dev and verse text read क्ऌप्त with vocalic ऌ — correct, and unique in the text — where the computed pada substitutes the mis-spelling क्लृप्त. 21 has no commentary body.

---

## पद्मरागशिलादर्शपरिभाविकपोलभूः । नवविद्रुमबिम्बश्रीन्यक्कारिरदनच्छदा

*padmarāgaśilādarśaparibhāvikapolabhūḥ । navavidrumabimbaśrīnyakkāriradanacchadā*

Verse 9, namas 23–24.

23. पद्मरागशिलादर्शपरिभाविकपोलभूः → पद्म-राग-शिला-आदर्श-परिभाविन्-कपोल-भूः

पद्म = a lotus
राग = colour — पद्मराग, the ruby, "lotus-coloured"
शिला = a stone, a slab
आदर्श = a mirror (आ + दृश् "to see")
परिभाविन् = surpassing, overcoming (परि + भू "to be, to prevail over")
कपोल = a cheek
भूः = ground, surface, expanse (from भू "to be")
"She whose cheeks surpass a mirror of ruby."

Vigraha: पद्मरागशिलादर्शं परिभावि कपोलभूः यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: शिला + आदर्श → शिलादर्श (आ + आ → आ by 6.1.101). The computed pada reads शिला | दर्श, which mistakes the second member: the आ of आदर्श was swallowed in the sandhi, and दर्श is not the word. आदर्श, a mirror, is what the figure needs — a polished ruby slab used as a looking-glass, which the cheek outshines.

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

पद्मराग is the same stone as the kuruvinda of nama 14 — Bhāskararāya says there that "kuruvinda gems are called padmarāga" — so the ruby is on her crown at 14 and being outdone by her cheek at 23.

भूः for a surface is the same word as in 606 गुहजन्मभूः, where जन्मभू is Skanda's birth-ground, and in 718 मही, the earth. Here it is the plane of a cheek.

24. नवविद्रुमबिम्बश्रीन्यक्कारिरदनच्छदा → नव-विद्रुम-बिम्ब-श्री-न्यक्कारिन्-रदन-छदा

नव = new, fresh
विद्रुम = coral — the sea-tree (वि + द्रुम "tree")
बिम्ब = the bimba fruit, a bright scarlet gourd
श्री = beauty, splendour
न्यक्कारिन् = putting down, humbling, putting to shame (न्यक् + कृ)
रदन = a tooth (from रद् "to gnaw")
छदा = a covering — रदनच्छद, the lip, "tooth-cover"
"She whose lips put to shame the beauty of fresh coral and the bimba fruit."

Vigraha: नवविद्रुमबिम्बश्रियं न्यक्कारि रदनच्छदं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: रदन + छदा → रदनच्छदा. A short vowel before छ takes the तुक् augment (Pāṇini 6.1.73, छे च), and that त् becomes च् before छ — so the च् is an inserted sound and belongs to neither member. The computed pada records च्छदा as the member, which absorbs the augment into the word; the member is छद.

The verse text reads नवबिद्रुम with ब for व, where the nama's dev field is correct — the third such fault in these ten verses, after 6 and 19.

index.html carries only the verse-division marker (9).

रदनच्छद is a good word for a lip: the tooth's covering, so the lip is named by what it hides, and the next nama uncovers it to describe the teeth.

विद्रुम returns at 891 विद्रुमाभा, where Her lustre is coral's — and there Bhāskararāya divides the compound along a different seam, विद् knowledge with द्रुम tree, making it the tree of knowledge, with the result that index.html preserves only that alternative and the plain sense of coral-red survives in the gloss alone. So the same stone is Her colour at 891 and something she outshines here.

Note on the verse. Two namas, cheeks and lips, and both work the eclipsing figure — परिभावि at 23, न्यक्कारि at 24 — which with 20's तिरस्कारि makes three different words for outdoing in five namas.

What the two have in common is that each is compared to a red thing and beats it. The ruby is on her own crown at 14 and coral is her own lustre at 891, so the description is outdoing materials it elsewhere claims for her.

Textual note. Three faults here, one of them consequential. The verse text reads नवबिद्रुम for नवविद्रुम at 24, the dev being correct. 23's computed pada reads दर्श for आदर्श, losing the mirror that the simile turns on. And 24's pada takes the तुक्-augment च् as part of छद. 23 has no body and 24's is the verse marker alone.

## शुद्धविद्याङ्कुराकारद्विजपङ्क्तिद्वयोज्ज्वला । कर्पूरवीटिकामोदसमाकर्षद्दिगन्तरा

*śuddhavidyāṅkurākāradvijapaṅktidvayojjvalā । karpūravīṭikāmodasamākarṣaddigantarā*

Verse 10, namas 25–26.

25. शुद्धविद्याङ्कुराकारद्विजपङ्क्तिद्वयोज्ज्वला → शुद्ध-विद्या-अङ्कुर-आकार-द्विज-पङ्क्ति-द्वय-उज्ज्वला

शुद्ध = pure, cleansed (past participle of शुध् "to purify")
विद्या = knowledge; a mantra of a female deity — शुद्धविद्या, here the Ṣoḍaśī
अङ्कुर = a sprout, a bud, a shoot
आकार = form, shape
द्विज = twice-born — a Brāhmaṇa; and also a tooth, which grows twice
पङ्क्ति = a row, a line
द्वय = a pair, two
उज्ज्वला = blazing, brilliant (उत् + ज्वल्)
"She who shines with two rows of teeth shaped like the buds of the pure Vidyā."

Vigraha: शुद्धविद्याङ्कुराकारे द्विजपङ्क्तिद्वये उज्ज्वला।

Sandhi at three joints: विद्या + अङ्कुर → विद्याङ्कुर and अङ्कुर + आकार → अङ्कुराकार (आ by 6.1.101 both), then द्वय + उज्ज्वला → द्वयोज्ज्वला (अ + उ → ओ by guṇa, 6.1.87).

This is the longest commentary in the ten verses and the aṅga-series' one genuinely doctrinal nama.

शुद्धविद्या is identified first, and the identification is argued: "in the Sabhāpati-śuddhavidyā-pariṇaya the identity of the idea *I* and *this* is set forth. In the Dattātreya Saṃhitā and other works also Śrīvidyā is explained from the standpoint of that identity. Hence Śrīvidyā is meant by Śuddhavidyā." शुद्ध is then "that which is the negation of the stain of ignorance," and विद्या specifically the Ṣoḍaśīvidyā, the sixteen-syllabled.

Then the four stages of speech, which is the entry's substance and the clearest statement of them in the text. The Ṣoḍaśī "sprang from the Mūlādhāra of the great Mother, and proceeding through the stages of Parā, Paśyantī and the rest, emerged from her mouth in the Vaikharī form; and it was transmitted from teacher to pupil." And each stage is given a phase of a sprouting seed:

Parā is "mere sound, Śabdabrahman — the potentiality of growth in the seed."
Paśyantī is "the seed beginning to sprout."
Madhyamā is "when the first two small leaves appear, but are not yet separated."
Vaikharī is "when these two small leaves are separated but joined at the root."

And the last is the one the nama needs: "this is what is here called the bud, and in that state there is a resemblance to the teeth." Two leaves parted at the tip and joined below is the shape of an upper and lower row meeting — so the simile is precise, and it required the whole four-stage scheme to be set out before it could be stated.

Then the arithmetic: "as they are thirty-two in number, so are the sixteen twofold buds of the sixteen-syllabled mantra." Thirty-two teeth, sixteen syllables doubled. The count also governs 587 श्रीषोडशाक्षरीविद्या, where Bhāskararāya has to reconcile sixteen with the Gauḍapāda Sūtra's twenty-eight.

द्विज then yields two further readings, and both keep the count. As Brāhmaṇa: "the Vedas chiefly belong to the Brāhmaṇas — the Śruti says, *Vidyā approached a Brāhmaṇa*; taught by him it spread abroad. Hence the Brāhmaṇas are the buds of Vidyā. Moreover, as the Brāhmaṇas came forth from the mouth of Devī, they may be compared to her teeth." That is the identification 888 विप्ररूपा makes outright, where "whether he is ignorant or learned, the Brāhmaṇa is my body" and the Parāśara Smṛti calls Brāhmaṇas "sacred places in motion."

And as initiation: "there are thirty-two initiations laid down in the Tantras — Śuddhavidyā, Bālā, Dvādaśārdhamātaṅginī and the rest, up to Anuttara; these are called the two rows of the twice-born, for initiation is a birth." Bhāskararāya then meets an objection about the numbering — the saying that "initiation is the third birth" does not conflict, "because there the birth from the mother's womb is counted as the first," with the thread-ceremony as the second. Sastry's note adds the pun the whole reading rests on: "twice-born refers also to teeth, as they grow twice."

The conclusion is severe and it is the point of the nama: "Devī can only be attained by those great men whose souls are purified by the thirty-two dīkṣās, from Śuddhavidyā to Anuttara, handed down according to tradition, and not by others." So a nama about teeth ends in a requirement of thirty-two initiations — which stands against 681 सुखाराध्या, where She is worshipped "without bodily pain by fasting and without restrictions on the mode of meditation," and 682, where She does good "even to him who but imperfectly worships her." The text's disagreement with itself about how hard access is starts here.

26. कर्पूरवीटिकामोदसमाकर्षद्दिगन्तरा → कर्पूर-वीटिका-आमोद-सम्-आकर्षत्-दिक्-अन्तरा

कर्पूर = camphor
वीटिका = a roll of betel, the prepared quid (वीटी)
आमोद = fragrance, perfume; also delight (आ + मुद् "to rejoice")
सम् = fully
आकर्षत् = drawing, attracting (present participle of आ + कृष् "to draw")
दिक् = a direction, a quarter of space
अन्तर = interior, the space within — दिगन्तर, the regions between the quarters
"She whose camphor-scented betel draws all the quarters of space to itself."

Vigraha: कर्पूरवीटिकाया आमोदेन समाकर्षत् दिगन्तरं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: वीटिका + आमोद → वीटिकामोद (आ by 6.1.101), and आकर्षत् + दिगन्तरा → आकर्षद्दिगन्तरा, the त् voicing before द्. The computed pada takes दिगन्तरा as one member; it is दिक् + अन्तर.

index.html carries only the verse-division marker (10).

आमोद is the word Bhāskararāya reaches for at 940 परमोदा, where he glosses आमोद as "sweet smell" and hence fame — fragrance being the standard figure for renown. Here it is literal, and the conceit is of a scent so strong it draws space itself.

The betel returns at 559 ताम्बूलपूरितमुखी, where her mouth is filled with it — and there the nama stands immediately before 560 दाडिमीकुसुमप्रभा, the pomegranate-flower radiance, because betel reddens the mouth. So the same substance is described twice: here for its scent and there for its stain.

समाकर्षत् is from कृष्, to drag — the root of आकर्षिणी in the attracting-mudrās, and the fifth of the five arrows in the Jñānārṇava's list at 11 is "attracting."

Note on the verse. Two namas, teeth and betel, and they are as unlike each other as any adjacent pair in the description.

25 is the aṅga-series' one heavily doctrinal nama, and everything in it turns on a shape. To say that the teeth resemble the bud of Śuddhavidyā, Bhāskararāya has to set out the four stages of speech — Parā the potency in the seed, Paśyantī the sprouting, Madhyamā the two leaves still joined, Vaikharī the two leaves parted at the tip and joined at the root — because only the last has the shape of two rows meeting. Then the count carries three readings at once: thirty-two teeth, sixteen syllables doubled, thirty-two Brāhmaṇa-buds, thirty-two initiations. And the entry closes by making those initiations a condition of attaining Her.

26 then returns to ornament, and the verse ends on a scent that pulls space in.

Textual note. 26's computed pada takes दिगन्तरा as a single member where it is दिक् + अन्तर. 26's body is the verse marker alone.

---

Textual note for verses 1–10.

**A new class of fault, and it runs the other way.** Three namas in these ten verses have a correct `dev` field and a corrupt verse text: 6 सहस्राभा appears in the verse as सहस्नाभा, 19 पुष्पाभ as पुप्पाभ, and 24 नवविद्रुम as नवबिद्रुम. Everywhere else in this text the damage is in the nama's own `dev` and the gloss or commentary preserves the reading — 864 फनत् for कनत्, 872 यी for त्रयी, 964 बन्धक for बन्धूक, 778 विराड्पा for विराड्रूपा. Here the namas are sound and the verse line is not, so the verse texts and the nama fields are independently corrupt and neither can be trusted as a check on the other.

**An orthographic point in the other direction.** At 21 both the `dev` field and the verse text read क्ऌप्त with the vocalic ऌ, which is correct for the root क्ऌप्, while the computed pada substitutes क्लृप्त — the common misencoding of that vowel as ल + ृ. It is the only appearance of ऌ in the text, and here the fields the text usually gets wrong are right and the computed field is wrong.

**Computed pada faults, five of them, and two damage the sense.** 9 reads क्रोधा | कारा for क्रोध | आकार, mis-dividing at both joints; 23 reads शिला | दर्श for शिला | आदर्श, losing the mirror the simile depends on. The other three are merges or sandhi-forms: 11 पञ्चतन्मात्र as one member; 18 चलन् for the stem चलत् and वक्त्रलक्ष्मी as one member; 24 च्छदा absorbing the तुक्-augment into छद; 16 मृगनाभि and 26 दिगन्तरा each merged.

**Empty and marker-only bodies, eleven of the twenty-six.** No commentary at all at 7, 15, 17, 19, 21, 23. Verse-division markers only at 16, 18, 24, 26, and effectively so at 20. The concentration is entirely in the aṅga-description: from 15 to 24 only nama 20 has any gloss beyond a marker. Bhāskararāya comments where the nama carries doctrine — 13's kūṭa-identification, 14's gem, 22's luminaries, 25's four stages of speech — and passes the ornamental namas in silence.

**Footnote intrusions.** 3's body carries two of Sastry's footnotes inline, one on the Setubandha's four bindus and one giving Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa's reading. 14's body carries two more, one of which — "here the commentator has not given the mantra, the result of the division" — belongs to nama 11 and records what Bhāskararāya withheld there. 5's body opens by repeating its own gloss verbatim before the commentary starts.

**No sandhi mis-divisions and no stray avagrahas.** Ten verses and twenty-six namas without a single instance of the text's commonest fault — the word-boundary taken one letter late across a visarga — and none of the avagraha-carrying namas of the 50, 828, 926, 972, 985, 988 class. The first avagraha in the text falls at 50 ऽनवद्याङ्गी, in the verse immediately after this run.

## निजसल्लापमाधुर्यविनिर्भर्त्सितकच्छपी । मन्दस्मितप्रभापूरमज्जत्कामेशमानसा

*nijasallāpamādhuryavinirbhartsitakacchapī । mandasmitaprabhāpūramajjatkāmeśamānasā*

Verse 11, namas 27–28.

> **The body-description that began at 13 runs to 48 and completes in this batch.** Bhāskararāya said at 13 that the head was taken first "as it also represents the first kūṭa named Vāgbhava of the Pañcadaśī," and namas 85–87 later map the three kūṭas onto the same body — face to Vāgbhava, throat-to-waist to Kāmarāja, below the waist to Śakti. Those boundaries fall inside this run. The neck is 30 कन्धरा, so the Kāmarāja section opens there; the waist is 37 कटीतटी and the belt 38, so the Śakti section opens at 39 with the thighs. The description and the mantra divide at the same two places.

27. निजसल्लापमाधुर्यविनिर्भर्त्सितकच्छपी → निज-सल्लाप-माधुर्य-विनिर्भर्त्सित-कच्छपी

निज = one's own
सल्लाप = conversation, talk (सम् + लप् "to speak")
माधुर्य = sweetness (vṛddhi abstract of मधुर)
विनिर्भर्त्सित = utterly put to shame, reviled, outdone (वि + निः + भर्त्स् "to revile")
कच्छपी = the Kacchapī — Sarasvatī's lute, named from the tortoise (कच्छप)
"She by the sweetness of whose own speech the Kacchapī is put to shame."

Vigraha: निजसल्लापमाधुर्येण विनिर्भर्त्सिता कच्छपी यस्याः सा।

The verse text reads विनिर्भत्सिंत, having lost the र् of भर्त्स् and gained a stray anusvāra, where the nama's own dev field is correct — the fourth such fault in the opening verses, after 6, 19 and 24.

Bhāskararāya begins by naming the four lutes, from the Amaraśeṣa, and two of them are namas of this text: "the vīṇā of Viśvāvasu is named Bṛhatī, that of Tumburu Kalāvatī, that of Nārada Mahatī, and of Sarasvatī Kacchapī." बृहती is nama 673, where the note attached to it is that the word is a metre of thirty-six syllables; and महती is nama 774, where Bhāskararāya's third gloss is precisely "Mahatī means also the Vīṇā of Nārada." So the instrument named here in passing becomes a nama seven hundred later, and its owner's name is given only here.

Then the argument for the comparison, which is graded and unusually careful for an ornamental nama. Instrumental music pleases by *indistinctness*: "the desire for hearing the vīṇā in the world is due to the beautiful melody coming out indistinctly from ṣaḍja and the rest of the gamut, though there is no clear hearing of the letters." Sarasvatī's Kacchapī is a step up, because it half-articulates — it "speaks like the parrot's speech, a little distinct, along with melody." And Her speech is above both, having full articulation and greater sweetness besides: "it is indisputable that with distinct utterance the sweeter melody of her words excels all the musical instruments."

Saundaryalaharī 66 is then quoted, and it stages the defeat: "when Sarasvatī with her vīṇā sings the various triumphs of Paśupati, O thou of beautiful speech, she has immediately to close her instrument with her finger tips, directly you start your vocal music, shaking your head, and with sweet melody which has the power of influencing the vīṇā-sound." The triumphs are glossed as the destruction of Tripura and of Dakṣa.

The text's other music-namas are 857 गानलोलुपा, avid for song, 909 सामगानप्रिया, delighting in the Sāman, 613 काव्यालापविनोदिनी, delighting in the discourse of poetry — which uses आलाप, this nama's सल्लाप without the सम् — and 636 गन्धर्वसेविता, attended by the celestial musicians. Sarasvatī herself is a girl of two at 704 and one of the two chowrie-bearers at 614.

28. मन्दस्मितप्रभापूरमज्जत्कामेशमानसा → मन्द-स्मित-प्रभा-पूर-मज्जत्-कामेश-मानसा

मन्द = slow, gentle, faint
स्मित = a smile (from स्मि "to smile")
प्रभा = radiance (प्र + भा)
पूर = a flood, a filling (from पूर् "to fill")
मज्जत् = sinking, drowning (present participle of मज्ज् "to sink")
कामेश = Kāmeśa, Kāmeśvara — and per the commentary, the Bindu of the Kāmakalā
मानसा = the mind (vṛddhi derivative of मनस्)
"She in the flood of whose faint smile's radiance the mind of Kāmeśa lies drowned."

Vigraha: मन्दस्मितप्रभापूरे मज्जत् कामेशमानसं यस्याः सा।

The compound is 12 निजारुणप्रभापूरमज्जद्ब्रह्माण्डमण्डला with two members exchanged — प्रभापूरमज्जत् in both, and the drowned thing is the round of universes there and Kāmeśa's mind here. Sixteen namas apart, one figure at two scales.

काम is then given its technical sense, and it takes the nama out of the erotic register altogether: "Kāma means Bindu, which forms part of the body of the Kāmakalā, and which is the sun termed fire, and moon." The Kāmakalāvilāsa is quoted: "Bindu is the form of Ahaṃkāra; the sun is the form of the pair, Kāma and Kāla, of equal essence. Kāma is that which is desired, so also the Kāla. The two Bindus are manifested as fire and moon." ईश is then simply "lord, that is Rājarājeśvara" — nama 684.

Kāmakalā is the Turīya bindu of Sastry's note at 3 and the whole content of nama 712, the single-vowel nama ई, where Bhāskararāya calls it "the Turīya known as Kāmakalā" and refers the reader to a guru for the rest.

And then the logical point, which is the best thing in the nama: "according to the doctrine of Mīmāṃsā the mind is omnipresent; when it is said that mind is *drowned*, it shows that Devī's glory is unlimited." The inference runs from the premise to the size of what could submerge it — if mind has no boundary, then whatever drowns it has none either. That is the same form of argument Bhāskararāya uses at nama 1, where śrī is measured by मा and "that which limits is necessarily superior to the thing limited," and at 877 निरालम्बा, where what supports all can have no support "or we obtain regression to infinity."

The body also carries the verse-division marker (11).

Note on the verse. Two namas, speech and smile, and both are about an effect on someone else — an instrument silenced, a mind submerged.

27 is the only nama in the aṅga-series that argues its comparison instead of stating it, and the argument is about articulation: instruments please by indistinct melody, Sarasvatī's lute half-articulates like a parrot, and her speech does both fully. It also preserves the only list of the four divine lutes in the text, two of whose names — Bṛhatī and Mahatī — are namas 673 and 774.

28 then reads काम not as the god but as the Bindu of the Kāmakalā, so the smile that drowns "Kāmeśa's mind" is drowning a technical term.

Textual note. The verse text reads विनिर्भत्सिंत for विनिर्भर्त्सित at 27, the dev being correct.
