125. शर्मदायिनी → शर्म-दायिनी

शर्म = happiness, joy; also shelter, refuge (शर्मन्)
दायिनी = she who gives
"The Bestower of happiness."

Vigraha: शर्म ददातीति शर्मदायिनी।

The Devī Bhāgavata's gloss is circular and Bhāskararāya reproduces it without comment: "she bestows happiness on devotees, hence she is called the bestower of happiness."

शर्मन् carries shelter as well as joy — it is what covers, hence what comforts — so what is given is a refuge rather than a pleasure. The nama is 953 शर्मदा with the fuller suffix, and the two stand 828 apart with the same first member.

Note on the verse. Eight namas in two quartets, भक्ति then श.

118–120 are the text's account of devotion and they run from definition to consequence. 118 defines it — primary as longing, secondary as service — and then lists eight, nine and ten kinds without choosing. 119 argues that devotion makes the unmanifest perceptible, and then offers a second reading on which भक्ति means *characteristic*, because words like satya and jñāna "cannot describe the unqualified Brahman directly." 120 then says She is subdued by it, which sits against 723 स्वतन्त्रा's independence with nothing said to join them.

The श-quartet is mostly identification, and its two Purāṇic entries pair: 122's Śāmbhavī mudrā, eyes neither shut nor open, and 124's Śarva the earth-form with a wife and son, which is 112's water-form done again.

122 also brings the girl-age series to six, and with Durgā at 190 the ages run 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 across seven namas of the thousand.

Textual note. 122's gloss and body split mid-sentence; 124's are duplicates.

---

## शांकरी श्रीकरी साध्वी शरच्चन्द्रनिभानना । शातोदरी शान्तिमती निराधारा निरञ्जना

*śāṃkarī śrīkarī sādhvī śaraccandranibhānanā । śātodarī śāntimatī nirādhārā nirañjanā*

Verse 43, namas 126–133.

126. शांकरी → शम्-करी

शम् = well-being, happiness, tranquillity (from शम् "to be quiet")
करी = she who makes (from कृ "to do")
"She who makes happiness."

Vigraha: शं करोतीति शांकरी।

"Śam, happiness, and kara, doer." And the Kālikā Purāṇa is quoted, and what it gives is a cyclical account of Her marriage: "in the beginning of each cycle I always accompany the stainless Śambhu, in the form of a woman, being born of Dakṣa. Then the Devas will praise me — the all-pervading illusion, the Yoga-sleep, the universe itself — by the name of Śaṃkarī and Rudrāṇī."

So the birth from Dakṣa is not one event but a recurrence, once per kalpa. That bears on the Satī–Pārvatī material at 5, 598, 600, 635, 754 and 820, where the two births are treated as a sequence; here the first is periodic.

Yoga-sleep in that passage is Yoganidrā, whom 656 योगानन्दा identifies with Her — "because bliss chiefly pervades in sleep, and that state belongs to Devī," with the Harivaṃśa on her "ever in the presence of Nārāyaṇa, thus causing him to sleep."

शम् is the root of 963 शमात्मिका, where Bhāskararāya defines शम not as a mood but as "tranquillising the activity of the world"; of 551 सर्वव्याधिप्रशमनी and 696 दैत्यशमनी, where the quieting is of disease and of demons; and of शम्भु at 122.

127. श्रीकरी → श्री-करी

श्री = splendour, prosperity, Lakṣmī
करी = she who makes
"She who makes prosperity."

Vigraha: श्रियं करोतीति श्रीकरी।

The whole commentary is a cross-reference to another thousand names: "according to the Viṣṇusahasranāma, Śrīkara is Viṣṇu and his wife is Śrīkarī."

So the nama is formed by taking a nama of Viṣṇu's thousand and putting it in the feminine — which is what 838 मुकुन्दा does with Mukunda, and there Bhāskararāya justified it from the Tantrarāja rather than treating it as a loan: Lalitā "once appeared in a male body as Kṛṣṇa." Here he simply notes the correspondence.

Bhāskararāya marks the division: "11th — 46 names are divided."

128. साध्वी → साध्वी

साध्वी = a virtuous woman, a chaste wife (feminine of साधु, from साध् "to succeed, to be accomplished")
"The Chaste."

Vigraha: साध्वी पतिव्रता।

**The Paribhāṣā at nama 1000 prescribes that साध्वी be split into two namas, साधु + ई** — and this is not that nama. The split falls at 711–712, where 712 is the single vowel ई, "belonging to the Turīya known as Kāmakalā." So the word साध्वी occurs twice in the thousand, once undivided here and once divided there, and only the Paribhāṣā's rule keeps the two apart.

The chastity is defined by extent in time: "because in the three times — past, present and future — she is attached to none but to her own husband; hence she has unequalled virtue." That is the पतिव्रता of 709 सदाशिवपतिव्रता, where the vow to one husband "in all the three times" was chosen precisely because the relation does not vary while its describable qualities do.

Then Saundaryalaharī 96, which argues the point comparatively and rather sharply: "how many poets share the wife of Brahmā? Cannot every one, by means of wealth, become the lord of Śrī? But, O virtuous one, first among faithful women, your breasts are untouched save by Mahādeva, not even by the paste of Kuravaka." Sarasvatī is any poet's, Lakṣmī any rich man's; She alone is one man's. Sastry's note explains the last clause: kuravaka is "a paste made of the leaves of the red amaranth, used to redden the cheeks, breasts, palms and soles" — so even a cosmetic would be a second toucher.

And the Devī Bhāgavata: "thou art praised as sādhvī on account of unequalled fidelity."

129. शरच्चन्द्रनिभानना → शरत्-चन्द्र-निभ-आनना

शरत् = autumn (शरद्)
चन्द्र = the moon
निभ = resembling, like
आनना = faced (आनन "face, mouth," with the feminine)
"She whose face is like the autumn moon."

Vigraha: शरच्चन्द्रनिभम् आननं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi at two joints: शरत् + चन्द्र → शरच्चन्द्र, the त् assimilating to च् before च् (Pāṇini 8.4.40, स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः); and निभ + आनना → निभानना (आ by 6.1.101).

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

The autumn moon is the specific comparison — the sky being clearest after the rains — where 16 मुखचन्द्रकलङ्काभमृगनाभिविशेषका made the face the moon in order to put a spot on it, and 15 made the brow the eighth-day half moon. So this is the third lunar face-nama and the only one that names a season.

निभ is the word of 592 चन्द्रनिभा, where the resemblance to the moon became a nyāsa station — a moon in the brahmarandhra identified with the third kūṭa of the Pañcadaśī. And आनन is the formal word for face that 523 षडानना used for Hākinī's six.

130. शातोदरी → शात-उदरी

शात = thin, slender, sharpened (from शो "to whet"); and per the second reading, शत, a hundred
उदरी = bellied, having a belly (उदर with the feminine ई); and per that reading, a cave
"She who is slender of waist."

Vigraha: शातम् उदरं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: शात + उदरी → शातोदरी (अ + उ → ओ by guṇa, 6.1.87).

The alternative is a pun that changes the referent entirely: "śatodara, having hundreds of caves, that is, Himavat, whose daughter she is." So a slender waist becomes a mountain full of caverns, and the nama's subject becomes her father.

That is the same device 847 तलोदरी uses on the same word — there Bhāskararāya prefixes अ to get अतलोदरी and makes Atala-loka her waist in the Virāṭ form, so "the slender waist and the lowest of the nether worlds become the same thing seen at two scales." Two उदरी-namas, both converted from anatomy to cosmology, and by the same trick of a modified first member.

Her waist is also 35 लक्ष्यरोमलताधारतासमुन्नेयमध्यमा, where it must be inferred because it cannot be seen, and 36, where it is buckling under a weight.

131. शान्तिमती → शान्ति-मती

शान्ति = peace, tranquillity (from शम् "to be quiet"); also the fourth of the five Śaiva kalās
मती = possessing (मतुप्, feminine ङीप्)
"She who possesses peace."

Vigraha: शान्तिः अस्याः अस्तीति शान्तिमती।

The gloss is seven words and it makes the peace relational: "as she does not appear rough to the devotees." So शान्ति is her aspect towards them rather than a state of her own — which is worth setting against 827 प्रचण्डा, where the fierceness is grounded in Taittirīya's "for fear of Him the wind blows," and 121, where she removes fear.

शान्ति is the fourth of the five kalās — निवृत्ति, प्रतिष्ठा, विद्या, शान्ति, शान्त्यतीता — of which प्रतिष्ठा is nama 829, विद्या is 549, शान्त्यतीता is 853, and the lower four are Her śaktis at 929. This nama makes the fourth a possession.

132. निराधारा → निर्-आधारा

निर् = without, free from (निः)
आधार = support, a prop, that on which a thing rests (आ + धृ "to hold"); and as a technical term, the support used in worship
"She who is without support."

Vigraha: आधारः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Sandhi: निः + आधारा → निराधारा, the visarga becoming र् before the vowel.

The primary reading is the argument from regress, stated in one clause: "as she is the true support of the universe, she herself has no dependence." That is 877 निरालम्बा's gloss exactly — "because there is no support for that which supports all; otherwise we obtain regression to infinity" — and the two namas are 745 apart with the same claim on different stems, आधार here and आलम्ब there.

But the second reading makes निराधार a technical term for a kind of worship, and the passage is the fullest account of worship's divisions in the text. The Sūta Saṃhitā 1.5.3 is quoted at length: "there are two kinds of worshipping the supreme Śakti" — external and internal; the external again Vedic and Tāntric. "The internal worship is also of two kinds, one with support, sādhāra, and the other without support, nirādhāra, and the latter is higher. The sādhāra worship is by means of mental images; the nirādhāra worship is by pure intellect. In the sādhāra worship Devī should be joyfully worshipped in a figure made up of the sacred syllables, according to the instructions of the Guru. The worship described as nirādhāra is the absorption of the understanding, manolaya, in that kind of meditation."

And the conclusion identifies the medium with the goal: "in reality, pure intellect means nothing else but the supreme Śakti. Hence for the destruction of saṃsāra one should worship the supreme Śakti, the very self, the witness, free from the glamour of the manifold universe. By one's own direct experience of Maheśvarī as the Self, She should be worshipped with much reverence; this is the worship which leads to salvation."

That is the doctrine 918 चैतन्यार्घ्यसमाराध्या states in one compound — consciousness itself as the oblation, with the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad's "wisdom is arghya" — and 919's eight flowers, of which not one is a thing. Here the scheme those namas presuppose is set out in full: external / internal, and internal with support / without.

आधार is the word of 659 सर्वाधारा and 884 धर्माधारा, where what She supports is everything and the law; and 35's आधारता, where what was supported was a line of hair.

133. निरञ्जना → निर्-अञ्जना

निर् = without, free from
अञ्जन = ointment, collyrium; hence a stain, a blemish; and per the commentary, blackness, attachment to ignorance (from अञ्ज् "to smear")
"The Stainless."

Vigraha: अञ्जनं यस्याः नास्ति सा।

**Bhāskararāya announces his programme in this nama's body, and it governs the next fifty.** "Next, by certain names, the text sets forth: first, the determination of the nature of the pure intellect which is the object of Nirādhāra worship, by assertion, by negation, by positive definition, and by elimination of attributes; then the means of obtaining it; and the real nature of the results thereby produced."

So the नि-run is not a heap of privatives. It is the negative determination of what 132's supportless worship worships, followed by the means and then the fruits — and 156 will announce the second half of it.

Then the scheme the next three namas use. **Three kinds of bound soul, each with its own impurity:**

"There are three kinds of ignorant souls, paśus. The Vijñānakevala, he who sees the self in the non-self and has therefore that impurity alone. The Pralayākala, he who has the impurity of Karma, which is imperceivable and which gives him new bodies. And the Sakala, he who has the impurity of Māyā, which creates the idea of duality. In these three, the second has also the impurity of the first, and the third that of the second." He refers to his own Setubandha for the details.

That is the Śaiva doctrine of the three malas — āṇava, kārma, māyīya — nested so that the lowest carries all three. And **133, 134 and 135 deny them in order**: "she is called stainless because she is free from the impurity of the Sakala" here; 134 निर्लेपा free of the Pralayākala's; 135 निर्मला free of the Vijñānakevala's. Three namas, three impurities, ascending.

The three paśus are also the three meditations of 113. The Setubandha, quoted at 134, maps them: "Sakala is he who worships Devī from Mūlādhāra to Ājñā; Pralayākala, who worships from Ājñā to Unmanī; and Niṣkala or Vijñānakevala worships Devī in the supreme abode, Mahābindu." Those are the three stations Yoginīhṛdaya 1.27 gave at 113 as Sakala, Sakalaniṣkala and Niṣkala. So the same three-fold division is a taxonomy of meditations at 113 and of meditators at 133–135, and Bhāskararāya supplies the bridge himself.

The nama's own gloss then explains why अञ्जन means what it does: "añjana, black, that is, attached to ignorance, because ignorance has the quality of veiling owing to its quality of darkness." The Yogavāsiṣṭha on attachment: "existence and non-existence of desired objects produce joy and sorrow, O Rāma; impure inclination is termed attachment." Śvetāśvatara 6.19, "blameless and stainless." And a last division: नि much, रञ्जन redness or joy.

Note on the verse. Eight namas, and the second half is the text's philosophical turn.

126–131 are identification and description — Śaṃkarī and Śrīkarī by their roots, the chaste wife, the autumn moon, the slender waist, the peaceful aspect. Two of them convert into something larger: 130's श्रोत waist becomes Himavat's hundred caves, and 126's marriage becomes a per-kalpa recurrence.

Then 132 and 133 change the register entirely. 132 gives the full division of worship — external Vedic, external Tāntric, internal with support, internal without — and identifies the last with worship "by pure intellect," which "means nothing else but the supreme Śakti." 133 then announces the programme for the next fifty namas and supplies the three-fold scheme of bound souls that the next two namas will use.

128 also puts साध्वी into the thousand for the first of two times, the second being the 711–712 pair that the Paribhāṣā at 1000 has to legislate a division for.

Textual note. 129 has no commentary body. 133's body carries a footnote on the ambiguity of the Sūta Saṃhitā's terms — "the words in the text are ādhāra and saṃvit, so they may mean mūlādhāra and anāhata cakras as the places of worship" — pulled inline before the commentary proper begins.

---

## निर्लेपा निर्मला नित्या निराकारा निराकुला । निर्गुणा निष्कला शान्ता निष्कामा निरुपप्लवा

*nirlepā nirmalā nityā nirākārā nirākulā । nirguṇā niṣkalā śāntā niṣkāmā nirupaplavā*

Verse 44, namas 134–143.

> **This verse and the next two carry the text's only doxography.** Beginning at 136, eight consecutive or near-consecutive namas are read as refutations of named rival schools — Buddhist momentariness, Vijñānavāda, Śūnyavāda, Nyāya, the part-holders, the Jainas, the eternal-will doctrine, and the Cārvākas — with two further namas accommodating Sāṃkhya and Mīmāṃsā rather than refuting them. Nothing comparable occurs anywhere else in the thousand.

134. निर्लेपा → निर्-लेपा

निर् = without
लेप = a smearing, a stain; and per the commentary, the impurity arising from action, karma (from लिप् "to smear")
"She who is without stain."

Vigraha: लेपः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Second of the three malas: "she is called so because she is free from the impurity of the Pralayākala. Lepa, the impurity arising from action."

Gītā 4.14 is cited — "actions never pollute me" — and then the lotus-leaf simile twice over. The Sūta Saṃhitā 4.25.25: "the best amongst the knowers of Brahman is never stained by any action, as the lotus leaf is not stained by water." Gītā 5.10: "he is not polluted by sin, as a lotus leaf is not polluted by water." And a second reading transfers the freedom to the devotee: "by the knowledge of Devī the devotee becomes free from impurity."

This nama's body also carries the Setubandha passage that maps the three paśus onto the three cakra-stations, and Bhāskararāya's cross-reference to nama 354 for more detail. Sastry notes that "the MS. copy has no reference to the Setubandha," so the citation is an addition to the printed text.

The lotus-leaf figure returns at 167 पापनाशिनी, where the Padma Purāṇa applies it to Durgā's devotee, "not affected by water" though committing heinous crimes.

135. निर्मला → निर्-मला

निर् = without
मल = dirt, impurity, a stain; and per the commentary, आणवमल, the primal impurity, or avidyā
"She who is without impurity."

Vigraha: मलः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Third of the three: "she is said to be so because she is free from the impurity of the Vijñānakevala. Mala, āṇavamala, or any spot. Or avidyā is called spot, which causes continual impurity, darkness and confusion."

So 133–135 have denied the three malas in ascending order — māyīya, kārma, āṇava — the same order in which they are nested, and the Vijñānakevala who has only the first is the least bound.

निर्मला is the word of 973 शुद्धमानसा's neighbourhood and of 765 शुद्धा, "free from the stains of avidyā"; and 992's अव्याज and 987's अनघा are two more of the text's privatives of blemish.

136. नित्या → नित्या

नित्या = eternal, perpetual, constant; also the fifteen Nityā deities of the lunar days; also a mantra of that name
"The Eternal."

Vigraha: नित्या शाश्वती।

The argument is stated as a consequence of the last three namas: "though impurities are not permanent, their ruler is not so, because she is irresistible in the three times."

**And then the first refutation: "this means the rejection of the theory of those who say all is ideal and momentary, Kṣaṇikavijñānavāda."** That is the Buddhist doctrine of momentariness, and the authority against it is Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.5.14: "O, this Self is indestructible."

Two further senses: "the deities of fortnights, or of time, or the mantra called by this name." The fifteen Nityās are the lunar days of 610 प्रतिपन्मुख्यराकान्ततिथिमण्डलपूजिता, the sixteen of the Meru Prastāra at 775, the respirations of 784 प्राणरूपिणी, and the Śaktis whose valour She is eager to watch at 73.

नित्य is also the first member of 144 नित्यमुक्ता, 148 नित्यशुद्धा and 149 नित्यबुद्धा in the next verse, and of 566 नित्यतृप्ता.

137. निराकारा → निर्-आकारा

निर् = without
आकार = form, shape — and per the commentary, "the form to which the qualities are attributed" (आ + कृ "to make")
"She who is without form."

Vigraha: आकारः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

**The second refutation, and it names two schools**: "this rejects the theory of those who hold that everything has form, and it belongs to the Vijñānavāda School, idealism, and is called Mādhyamika."

आकार is then defined narrowly: "the form to which the qualities are attributed" — so what is denied is not shape but the substrate of predication, which is the उपाधि of 708 सर्वोपाधिविनिर्मुक्ता and 154 निरुपाधिः.

The Viṣṇu Bhāgavata is quoted, and it is a chain of eleven negations ending in a positive: "that Brahman is neither Devas, nor Daityas, nor human, nor animal, nor woman, nor eunuch, nor man, nor insect, nor quality, nor action, nor existence, nor non-existence. May victory attend Him, the infinite who remains after all negation."

That last clause is the whole method of this verse stated in a phrase — what remains after all negation — and it is the substratum-argument of 680 भावाभावविवर्जिता, where Vyāsa answers the objection that one cannot be devoid of non-existence: "the substratum is different from these two, and is not destroyed, because it is ever real."

आकार stands positively at 619 पावनाकृतिः, 830 प्रकटाकृतिः, 933 मङ्गलाकृतिः and 766; denied here, and denied again in another word at 813–814's मूर्ता/अमूर्ता pair.

138. निराकुला → निर्-आकुला

निर् = without; and per the second reading, far from
आकुल = agitated, confused, crowded (आ + कुल्); and per the third reading, अकुल, void
"She who is without agitation."

Vigraha: आकुला न भवति इति निराकुला।

Three readings, and the third is a refutation.

"Though in contact with avidyā, she is not agitated" — which is the point 177 निराबाधा makes with the mother-of-pearl. Or "she is far from those whose minds are agitated."

**Then: "or akula, void; this destroys the theory of the Gambhīra School, which holds that all is void, nihilism."** That is Śūnyavāda, and it is the third school named in three namas.

The privative here is worth a note against the text's other use of the same letters. 96 अकुला makes Her *Akula* — beyond kula, one with Śiva, seated in the sahasrāra — and it is the hinge of the seven kula-namas at 90–96. Here अकुल is read as void and rejected. So one string does opposite work eighty namas apart, and the text does not remark on it.

139. निर्गुणा → निर्-गुणा

निर् = without
गुण = a quality, an attribute; and literally a strand of cord
"She who is without qualities."

Vigraha: गुणाः यस्याः न सन्ति सा।

**The fourth refutation, named in five words: "the opinion of the Tarka School is rejected here."** That is Nyāya, whose categories include quality as a real ontological kind.

Śvetāśvatara 6.11 is the authority — "the witness, the thinker, pure, and without qualities" — and then the reason: "as the qualities are connected with the body, matter, they are absent from what belongs to spirit, cit."

The Matsya and Padma Purāṇas then give Nārada's explanation to Himavat, and it distinguishes two words the argument needs: "as I have said, Devī is devoid of attributes; listen well to the explanation of the meaning of this saying. Attributes, lakṣaṇa, are the marks of Devas, and qualities, guṇa, depend upon body. This Devī is without qualities and cannot be distinguished by attributes."

That is the same Nārada passage 44 नखदीधितिसंछन्ननमज्जनतमोगुणा draws on, where he reads Pārvatī's bodily marks to Menā and turns "devoid of good bodily marks" into a distinction — "because she is unconditioned." So one Purāṇic conversation supplies both the ornamental nama and the philosophical one.

The guṇas as strands are the three the text takes four incompatible positions on — beyond them at 961 गुणातीता, made of them at 984 त्रिगुणा, their equilibrium at 763 त्रिगुणात्मिका, the whole condition negated at 789 निस्त्रैगुण्या. This nama is a fifth position and the earliest.

140. निष्कला → निष्-कला

निष् = without (निः, retroflexed before क्)
कला = a part, a portion; and per the second reading, contemplation on the partless
"She who is without parts."

Vigraha: कला यस्याः न सन्ति सा।

**The fifth refutation: "this rejects the theory of those who say that Brahman has parts."** And here Bhāskararāya has to handle scripture on the other side, which he does by the standard move.

Vedānta Sūtra 2.3.43 is quoted for the opposing view — "the soul is a part of the Lord, on account of the declarations of difference" — and Gītā 15.7, "in the world my part is Jīva." His answer: "these two, Śruti and Smṛti, are not opposed to one another, because the parts are merely attributed."

That Gītā verse is the authority for 728 चित्कला, where a nama of Hers names the jīva — "my part alone in the world are the eternal Jīvas" — and for 729's "other beings live by a part of this bliss." So the doctrine of parts this nama rejects is the doctrine two later namas are built on, and the reconciliation offered here is that the parts are attributed and not real.

Then a second reading, from the Vijñānabhairava: "meditation on Brahman is without parts, since he is without dependence and with no fixed resting-place. It is not meditation upon form as attributing face, hands and the rest." So निष्कल names a technique — and it is the third of the three states at 113, where Yoginīhṛdaya 1.27 placed Niṣkala meditation in the Mahābindu.

141. शान्ता → शान्ता

शान्ता = tranquil, at peace, calmed (past participle of शम् "to be quiet"); and per the divisions, शा + अन्त, and आ-शान्त
"The Tranquil."

Vigraha: शान्ता निवृत्तसर्वव्यापारा।

Śvetāśvatara 6.19 is quoted for the pair with the previous nama: "without parts, without motion, tranquil."

Then two syllabic readings, and the second is the sixth refutation.

The first: "the syllable शा is anta, at the end of the Amṛtabīja mantra — that is, Devī is the Amṛtabīja mantra itself." So the nama names a formula by its final letter.

**The second: "or Aśānta — āśā, quarters; anta, reaching to; that is, all-pervading. By this teaching, Digambara's theory that the Self is limited is refuted."** That is the Jaina doctrine of the soul's finite extension, and the Digambaras are named.

The refutation works by reading शान्ता as आशान्ता, reaching to the quarters — so a nama of stillness is turned into a claim about extent, which is what the Jaina position denies. It is the boldest of the eight, because the nama has to be re-divided before it can refute anything.

Jaina material returns at 149 नित्यबुद्धा eight namas on, and there it is accommodated rather than refuted; and 925 कौलिनीकेवला cites the term kevala "because we often see it thus used in the Jaina Tantras."

142. निष्कामा → निष्-कामा

निष् = without
काम = desire, wish
"She who is without desire."

Vigraha: कामः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

**The seventh refutation, and its target is a doctrine rather than a school: "this refutes the theory of those who hold, according to the Upaniṣads, that the Lord's will is eternal, and thought also."**

The Devī Bhāgavata supplies the ground: "when her wishes are all fulfilled, nothing remains for her desire." And then the two Śrutis Bhāskararāya needs for the reconciliation: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.3.6, "the Ātman is defined by *not this, not this*"; and 5.1.1, "that is filled, this is filled." The conclusion: "the other Śrutis which treat of guṇa relate to upādhis."

That last is the same rule 708 सर्वोपाधिविनिर्मुक्ता states for reading scripture — "all the Vedāntas mean directly or indirectly one and the same supreme Brahman, which is non-duality; the other scriptures which advocate duality are to be taken as explaining the ordinary vision," with the eclipse-tables' finger-widths as the analogy.

काम as the creative desire is what 796 कामरूपिणी makes Her form, on Taittirīya 2.6.1's "he desired, let me become many." So the desire denied here is what 796 affirms, 654 namas on.

143. निरुपप्लवा → निर्-उपप्लवा

निर् = without
उपप्लव = calamity, affliction, overwhelming; also an eclipse (उप + प्लु "to float, to overflow")
"She who is without calamity."

Vigraha: उपप्लवः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Sandhi: निः + उपप्लवा → निरुपप्लवा.

The plain sense is indestructibility. But Bhāskararāya divides the word to get a physiological reading, and it is the more interesting: "nir, much; upa, near, that is, in the body; plava, flowing of the nectar — that is, by whom the abundant flowing of nectar in the body occurs," with a cross-reference to nama 111.

Nama 111 बिसतन्तुतनीयसी is where the kuṇḍalinī-sequence closes and where "the fire liquefies the lunar orb and so causes the nectar to flow." So the same प्लु that means calamity means the amṛta-flood, and the nama is read as the nectar-shower of 106 सुधासाराभिवर्षिणी and the stream of 879 सुधासृतिः.

The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1 is quoted for it, and the instruction is quantitative: "wet the whole body in the streams of ambrosia, and further wet the seventy-two thousand channels." And a last line: "know me always as born from the universe — that is, the individual soul is a part and parcel of the universal one."

Note on the verse. Ten namas, the longest so far in the text, and seven of them are refutations or their scaffolding.

133–135 have just denied the three malas in order. 136 then makes Her eternal and refutes Buddhist momentariness; 137 formless, refuting Vijñānavāda and the Mādhyamikas; 138 unagitated, refuting Śūnyavāda; 139 qualityless, refuting Nyāya; 140 partless, refuting the part-holders; 141 tranquil, refuting the Digambaras; 142 desireless, refuting the eternal-will doctrine. Six named schools and one named doctrine in seven consecutive namas.

The method is uniform: each privative is read as denying a thesis, and where scripture supports the thesis it is reclassified as speaking of upādhis. 137's Viṣṇu Bhāgavata line — "the infinite who remains after all negation" — states the whole procedure.

And two of the seven turn against the text's own claims elsewhere. 140 rejects the doctrine of parts that 728–729 are built on, resolving it by calling the parts attributed; 142 denies the desire that 796 makes Her form.

143 then closes the verse by re-dividing a word for calamity into the flooding of nectar, and sends the reader back to 111.

---

## नित्यमुक्ता निर्विकारा निष्प्रपञ्चा निराश्रया । नित्यशुद्धा नित्यबुद्धा निरवद्या निरन्तरा

*nityamuktā nirvikārā niṣprapañcā nirāśrayā । nityaśuddhā nityabuddhā niravadyā nirantarā*

Verse 45, namas 144–151.

144. नित्यमुक्ता → नित्य-मुक्ता

नित्य = eternal, perpetual
मुक्ता = released, liberated (past participle of मुच् "to loose")
"The Ever-free."

Vigraha: नित्यं मुक्ता।

Two readings and both are brief: "or, whose devotees are ever free; or, as she is eternally free — that is, Salvation personified." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (44).

मुक्ति is what She gives at 736 मुक्तिदा, houses at 839 मुक्तिनिलया and is at 737 मुक्तिरूपिणी, where the definition proceeds by refuting the six Vaiśeṣika categories one by one. "Salvation personified" here is 737 in two words.

145. निर्विकारा → निर्-विकारा

निर् = without
विकार = change, modification, a product (वि + कृ "to make")
"She who is without modification."

Vigraha: विकारः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The technical identification is Sāṃkhya's: "vikāras, the twenty-three categories of the Sāṃkhyas, beginning with Mahat." And the Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī on Kārikā 3 is quoted whole, which is the school's own map of what is productive and what is produced: "the Mūlaprakṛti, the root of all, is no production; the seven principles, Mahat and the rest, are productions and productive; sixteen are productions but unproductive; the soul is neither a production nor productive."

So this nama does not refute Sāṃkhya but adopts its enumeration and puts Her outside it — which is 862 कार्यकारणनिर्मुक्ता's move, where कार्य is "the tattva-series beginning with Mahat" and कारण is Mūlaprakṛti, and She is free of both. The two namas are 717 apart and use the same two terms.

The thirty-six tattvas of 906–907 and 801 are the Śaiva count; the twenty-three vikāras here are the Sāṃkhya one, and the text uses both.

146. निष्प्रपञ्चा → निष्-प्रपञ्चा

निष् = without
प्रपञ्च = expansion, manifoldness, the phenomenal world (प्र + पञ्च् "to spread out")
"She who is without manifoldness."

Vigraha: प्रपञ्चः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The Viśva is cited for the word — "prapañca means accumulation, extension, expansion" — and Māṇḍūkya 7 for the state in which it is absent: "they think the fourth state is the negation of illusion, peace, bliss and non-duality."

The fourth is turīya, which 963 शमात्मिका names by शम — "tranquillity of the activity of the world, peace, non-dual, the fourth" — on the same Māṇḍūkya verse. So this nama and 963 quote one passage for one state, 817 apart.

147. निराश्रया → निर्-आश्रया

निर् = without
आश्रय = a support, a resting-place, a substratum; here specifically the body (आ + श्रि "to lean on")
"She who is without a resting-place."

Vigraha: आश्रयः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

**The eighth refutation, and the last of the run: "this refutes the theory of the Cārvākas, who hold that the Brahman is inseparable from the body."** The materialists are the only school named in the run whose position is about embodiment rather than about substance or momentariness.

Then the regress-argument again, and this time as an epigram: "as she is that on which all depends, she herself depends on nothing. It is said: *where is the foundation of Her on whom the universe is founded?*"

That is the third statement of one argument in fifteen namas — 132 निराधारा, 877 निरालम्बा, and here — and each uses a different stem: आधार, आलम्ब, आश्रय.

आश्रित is the word of 688 राजपीठनिवेशितनिजाश्रिता, where those who lean on Her are seated on Indra's throne. Here the leaning has no object.

148. नित्यशुद्धा → नित्य-शुद्धा

नित्य = eternal
शुद्धा = pure, cleansed (past participle of शुध् "to purify")
"The Ever-pure."

Vigraha: नित्यं शुद्धा।

"Because in the three times she is without blemish." The Śruti: "she is free from contact, great, and purity itself." And a Smṛti whose antithesis is neat: "the body is very impure, and the dweller in it is very pure."

शुद्धा stands alone at 765 and as the first member of 973 शुद्धमानसा; and Śuddhavidyā, built on it, is the Ṣoḍaśī at 25 शुद्धविद्याङ्कुराकारद्विजपङ्क्तिद्वयोज्ज्वला, one of the three Vidyās at 840, and one of the three corresponding to Cit at 907.

149. नित्यबुद्धा → नित्य-बुद्धा

नित्य = eternal
बुद्धा = awakened, enlightened, wise (past participle of बुध् "to wake, to know")
"The Ever-wise."

Vigraha: नित्यं बुद्धा।

The primary reading is an identity: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.30 — "for knowledge is inseparable from the knower" — and "as she is in the form of cit itself, she is ever wise." That is 981 ज्ञातृज्ञेयस्वरूपिणी's claim, where She is both knower and known, and 651 विज्ञात्री's, where the citation is Bṛhadāraṇyaka's "O, how is the knower to be known?"

**And then the run's one accommodation of the Jainas, which is unexpected after 141 refuted them.** "Or Śuddha and Buddha may apply to the two individuals — Tīrthaṅkaras — of the Jainas, who have become immortal, nityās, by the grace of Devī. Because we see that one of the worships of Devī is by following the six systems of philosophies, in which the Jaina scriptures are included. The meaning is that Devī is the Tārā, a deity of the Jainas, who is worshipped by these two."

So 148 and 149 are read as naming two Jaina Tīrthaṅkaras made immortal by Her, and the ground is that worship by any of the six systems reaches Her. That is the same argument 770 प्रियव्रता uses for vows made to other gods — "he who makes a vow to any god or to any goddess, all is for the delight of Śiva and Devī... there is no difference here, because the whole world is Śiva and Śakti" — and 678 भाषारूपा for praise in Mleccha languages.

Eight namas after refuting the Digambara doctrine of the soul's limit, the text makes two of their Tīrthaṅkaras Her devotees. The refutation is of a thesis and the accommodation is of the worshippers, and

150. निरवद्या → निर्-अवद्या

निर् = without
अवद्य = blameworthy, censurable; and per the second reading, the name of a hell (अ + वद्, "not to be spoken of")
"The Blameless."

Vigraha: अवद्यं यस्याः नास्ति सा।

अवद्य is literally what should not be said — अ with वद् — so blame is named by unspeakability. The gloss makes it "the modifications of Avidyā," with Śvetāśvatara 6.19, "blameless and spotless."

Then the second reading makes it a place: "avadya is the name of a hell; by her grace the devotees escape that hell." The Kūrma Purāṇa: "hence if anyone remembers Devī day and night, he never goes to the hell called Avadya, as he is cleansed from all sins." And the Liṅga Purāṇa gives the scale: "there are twenty-eight crores of hells from Ghora to Māyā; in these cursed hells the sinners are scorched, who here failed to take refuge in the Lord of Devī."

Twenty-eight is the number 749 मृत्युदारुकुठारिका encodes by Vararuci's rule — दारु as 28, "the twenty-eight kinds of pains described before." So the same figure counts the pains and the crores of hells, in two places that do not cite each other.

अनवद्य is nama 50 अनवद्याङ्गी, whose limbs are faultless, and where the text's first avagraha falls.

151. निरन्तरा → निर्-अन्तरा

निर् = without
अन्तर = an interval, a difference, an opening; and per the Amara, thirteen other things
"She who is without interval."

Vigraha: अन्तरं यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The Amara 468 is quoted whole and the list is one of the widest in the text: "antara means opening, period, clothing, disappearance, difference, behalf, a hole, self, absence, outside, opportunity, middle, and individual soul."

Then Taittirīya 2.7.1 — "he who makes but the smallest distinction in separateness, fear arises in him" — and the refutation it supports: "by this is refuted the theory of those who hold that Brahman is subject to three kinds of distinction, that is, sajātīya and the rest: difference within the same species, difference between different species, and individual differences."

So the logicians' threefold भेद is denied, which makes this a ninth refutation if it is counted; and 178 निर्भेदा twenty-seven namas on will deny भेद again in the technical vocabulary of अनुयोगित्व and प्रतियोगित्व.

The Taittirīya verse also stands behind 665 एकाकिनी's neighbourhood, where fear and solitude are joined; here the fear comes from distinction rather than from being alone. Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (45).

Note on the verse. Eight namas, and the tone changes at its middle.

144–147 continue the negative determination and end with the last of the eight refutations, the Cārvākas at 147 — and that nama also gives the regress-argument its third stem in fifteen namas.

145 is the entry to keep for method. It does not refute Sāṃkhya; it quotes the Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī's own map of the productive and the produced and places Her outside it. So the run's procedure is not uniformly polemical: Buddhists, Mādhyamikas, Śūnyavādins, Naiyāyikas, Digambaras and Cārvākas are refuted, while Sāṃkhya is used and — at 155 four namas on — Mīmāṃsā and Sāṃkhya are both claimed.

And 148–149 make the sharpest turn. Eight namas after 141 refuted the Digambara doctrine of the limited soul, these two are read as naming two Jaina Tīrthaṅkaras "who have become immortal by the grace of Devī," on the ground that "one of the worships of Devī is by following the six systems of philosophies, in which the Jaina scriptures are included." The thesis is refuted and the worshippers are taken in.

---

## निष्कारणा निष्कलङ्का निरुपाधिर्निरीश्वरा । नीरागा रागमथना निर्मदा मदनाशिनी

*niṣkāraṇā niṣkalaṅkā nirupādhir nirīśvarā । nīrāgā rāgamathanā nirmadā madanāśinī*

Verse 46, namas 152–159.

152. निष्कारणा → निष्-कारणा

निष् = without
कारण = a cause; and per the second reading, कारण the ritual liquid
"She who is without cause."

Vigraha: कारणं यस्याः नास्ति सा।

"Since she is the cause of everything she is without cause" — the regress-argument once more, now on the fourth stem. Śvetāśvatara 6.9: "he is the cause, he is the lord of the rulers of causes; none created him, none is his superior."

Then a reading that shifts the register completely: "or nis, much; kāraṇa, the first liquid — that is, in her is fullness of the first liquid and she is ever joyful by that means." कारण is a Kaula technical term for the ritual draught, and the verse quoted places it: "residing in the big lotus garden in the Sahasrāra and sharing the joy caused by Kāraṇa, the ambrosia."

So the same word gives the first cause and the ritual liquor, and the second reading puts her in the sahasrāra drinking. The mead behind वीर at 836 and 898, the माध्वी of 575, and the amṛta of 143's reading are all the same substance under different names.

153. निष्कलङ्का → निष्-कलङ्का

निष् = without
कलङ्क = a stain, a blemish, a spot — especially the moon's spot
"The Spotless."

Vigraha: कलङ्कः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The body breaks off mid-quotation: Īśa 8, "pure, untouched by —" and the field ends; the missing word is sin, which has been carried up into 152's body, where the stray word "sin." stands after the Kāraṇa passage.

कलङ्क is the moon's blemish, which 16 मुखचन्द्रकलङ्काभमृगनाभिविशेषका made the model for the musk mark on Her brow. So the spot is put on Her face at 16 and denied of Her here.

154. निरुपाधिः → निर्-उपाधिः

निर् = without
उपाधिः = a conditioning attribute, a limitation, a superimposed quality (उप + आ + धा "to place upon")
"She who is without limiting attributes."

Vigraha: उपाधिः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Both the dev field and the verse text read निरुपाधि, the visarga lost — and the next nama has gained the र् it became. See the textual note below.

उपाधि is defined etymologically and then by the standard simile: "upa, near; adhi, gives. The red flower transfers its colour to the crystal near it — this is the upādhi. Similarly, ignorance is the upādhi which causes the appearance of plurality in consciousness."

That crystal is the same figure the Devī Purāṇa uses at 666 भूमरूपा — "as the crystal is coloured by the transmission of different colours, so by the qualities Devī is described as Bhūmā" — where the multiplicity is put in what passes through rather than in the crystal. Here the transmission is ignorance.

Then a division of the term: "or there are two upādhis, one whole, the other fragmentary, and she is free from both."

उपाधि carries the whole argument of 708 सर्वोपाधिविनिर्मुक्ता, the fifth move of the eleven-nama dialogue at 703–713, where the mother-of-pearl replaces the crystal — "the relation between the qualities and the thing which is qualified is illusory, like the relation of the silver in the mother-of-pearl" — and where the examples dissolved are the ones the previous namas had used to establish duality.

155. निरीश्वरा → निर्-ईश्वरा

निर् = without
ईश्वर = a lord, a ruler, a superior
"She who has no superior."

Vigraha: ईश्वरः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The dev field reads र्निरीश्वरा, carrying the र् that belongs to 154's visarga (निरुपाधिः + निरीश्वरा → निरुपाधिर्निरीश्वरा). The verse text has it too, with a space in the wrong place: निरुपाधि र्निरीश्वरा.

The plain reading is the regress-argument for the fifth time: "because she is the ruler of all, she herself has no superior."

Then a remark that has to be handled carefully, because it is the run's second accommodation: "or there are two systems, Mīmāṃsā and Sāṃkhya — the former is monism and the latter atheism — and she belongs to both."

So a nama which read one way denies that anything is above Her is read another way as making Her at home in a system that has no Īśvara at all. Sāṃkhya is nirīśvara in the technical sense, and the nama's letters say so. That is the same accommodation 145 made by adopting the twenty-three vikāras, and the same logic as 149's Jaina Tīrthaṅkaras and 770's vows to other gods.

ईश् has fourteen turns in this text. This is the only one where the root is negated.

156. नीरागा → निः-रागा

निः = without
राग = passion, desire, attachment; also colour (from रञ्ज् "to be dyed, to be coloured")
"She who is without passion."

Vigraha: रागः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Sandhi: निः + रागा → नीरागा, the visarga dropping and the इ lengthening before र् (Pāṇini 6.3.111 ढ्रलोपे पूर्वस्य दीर्घोऽणः).

**Bhāskararāya announces the second half of his programme here**: "the text now proceeds to reject the theory that the differences in the mind belong to the Self, and to teach that renunciation is the means of overcoming the six impediments — that is, desire, wrath, covetousness, bewilderment, pride and envy."

And the namas from here to 175 do exactly that, in pairs: a privative and then a destroyer. नीरागा / रागमथना for passion; निर्मदा / मदनाशिनी for pride; निर्मोहा / मोहनाशिनी for bewilderment; निष्पापा / पापनाशिनी for sin; निष्क्रोधा / क्रोधशमनी for anger; निर्लोभा / लोभनाशिनी for greed; निःसंशया / संशयघ्नी for doubt; निर्भवा / भवनाशिनी for existence itself. Eight pairs, and two odd namas — निश्चिन्ता and निरहंकारा — with 164–165 निर्ममा / ममताहन्त्री making a ninth pair on self-interest.

So the structure is: She lacks it, and she destroys it in the devotee. The first member is about Her and the second about them, which is what 167's Padma Purāṇa citation makes explicit.

The gloss on राग: "desire, because she has obtained all her desires." Or, on Śāṇḍilya 1.6 — "devotion is longing, as it is opposed to hatred and as it is expressed by the word rasa" — राग is devotion itself, and "she is free from it, as she herself is supreme and she has no object to long for." So the very thing 118–120 made Her delight is denied of Her here, on the ground that she has nothing to be devoted to.

And a syllabic reading: "Nīra, water, and aga, mountain — both of them being her forms."

राग also means colour, from रञ्ज् to dye, and 937 विरागिणी turns on exactly that: the privative makes Her uncoloured as much as unattached, which agrees with 922's doctrine that no colour is properly Hers.

157. रागमथना → राग-मथना

राग = passion, desire
मथना = she who churns, agitates, destroys (from मन्थ् "to churn")
"The Destroyer of passion."

Vigraha: रागं मथ्नातीति रागमथना।

"By not endowing her devotees with passion" — so the destruction is a withholding.

And राग is then given the Yoga Sūtra's technical range: "desire, aversion, and ardent attachment to life, as described in Yoga Sūtra 2.3." Those are three of the five klеśas — rāga, dveṣa and abhiniveśa — so the nama covers more than its first member says.

मथ् is to churn, and मथन is the word for the churning of the ocean, which 562 मोहिनी's Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa makes Her second appearance: "causing enchantment of all, transcending mind and speech, was during the churning for nectar, seeing which even the omniscient Śiva was enchanted."

158. निर्मदा → निर्-मदा

निर् = without
मद = pride, intoxication, rut (from मद् "to be exhilarated")
"She who is without pride."

Vigraha: मदः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

मद is the root of मत्ता at 576, where the plain reading is drunkenness and Bhāskararāya's alternative makes it "the state of egoism, the Parāhantā of Parā Śiva" — supreme I-ness. So the pride denied here is, on that reading, what 576 affirms; and 856 गर्विता locates it precisely as "supreme egoism concerning the creation of the universe."

The text therefore has Her proud at 856, intoxicated at 576, and without pride here, and the reconciliation is only available in 856's specification: the pride is a creator's I-ness and not vanity.

159. मदनाशिनी → मद-नाशिनी

मद = pride; and per the second reading, मदन, excessive anxiety
नाशिनी = she who destroys (from नश् "to perish," causative)
"The Destroyer of pride."

Vigraha: मदं नाशयतीति मदनाशिनी।

The alternative re-divides across the boundary: "or madana, excessive anxiety, and aśana, consuming" — so मदनाशिनी becomes मदन + अशन, the consuming of anxiety, and the destroyer becomes an eater. अश् is the root of 753 महाशना, "the great Devourer."

Note on the verse. Eight namas, and 156 is the hinge of the whole नि-run.

152–155 finish the negative determination, and each of the four repeats the regress-argument on a fresh stem — कारण here after आधार at 132, आलम्ब at 877, आश्रय at 147. 154 then supplies the crystal-and-red-flower simile for उपाधि, which is the figure the eleven-nama dialogue at 703–713 rests on in its mother-of-pearl form.

155 carries the run's second accommodation, and it is the boldest: the nama can be read as saying She belongs to Mīmāṃsā and to Sāṃkhya, "the former monism and the latter atheism." A nama beginning निर्-ईश्वर claiming the atheistic system is a good joke and Bhāskararāya makes it without comment.

Then 156 announces the second programme and the namas turn from what She lacks to what she removes. From here to 175 the pattern is privative-then-destroyer, eight or nine times over, and the six impediments are named in advance.

Textual note. 154's dev and verse text have lost the visarga of निरुपाधिः, and 155's have gained the resulting र् — the text's commonest fault, and here it appears in both arrays at once, with the verse text additionally putting a space before the stray र्. 152's body carries the word "sin." belonging to 153's Īśa citation, which breaks off mid-phrase. 158 has no commentary body.

---

## निश्चिन्ता निरहंकारा निर्मोहा मोहनाशिनी । निर्ममा ममताहन्त्री निष्पापा पापनाशिनी

*niścintā nirahaṃkārā nirmohā mohanāśinī । nirmamā mamatāhantrī niṣpāpā pāpanāśinī*

Verse 47, namas 160–167.

160. निश्चिन्ता → निः-चिन्ता

निः = without
चिन्ता = thought, anxiety, care; and per the Viśva, delusion (from चिन्त् "to think")
"She who is without anxiety."

Vigraha: चिन्ता यस्याः नास्ति सा।

चिन्ता is narrowed: "recollection generally; here it means recollection of painful topics."

And then a proverb built on a near-homophone, which is the best thing in the verse: "anxiety should be known as resembling a funeral pile, the only difference being the additional sound in *cintā* — but as the pile, *citā*, burns the corpse, so anxiety burns the living."

So चिन्ता and चिता differ by one nasal, and the difference is that one burns the dead and the other the living. The Viśva's other sense is added: चिन्ता means delusion, so she is without delusion — which the next but one nama says outright.

चिन्ता is the first member of चिन्तामणि at 57, the wish-fulfilling gem whose palace she inhabits; and चिन्ताक at 32, where Bhāskararāya reads it as a meditator and gets three classes of worshipper out of an ornament.

161. निरहंकारा → निर्-अहंकारा

निर् = without
अहंकार = egoism, the I-making faculty (अहम् "I" + कार "making")
"She who is without egoism."

Vigraha: अहंकारः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

index.html's body is scrambled — the words of two sentences interleaved — but what survives is the threefold division: "ahaṃkāra is of three kinds: Vaikārika, Taijasa and Bhūtādi," corresponding respectively to sattva, rajas and tamas.

That is the Sāṃkhya-Purāṇic classification of the ego-principle by guṇa, so the nama denies all three at once. And the term is the one the text affirms of Her repeatedly under other names: पूर्णाहन्ता at 854, गर्विता at 856, मत्ता at 576, and — decisively — 711, where the eleven-nama dialogue closes by making Parāhantā Her *inherent* quality, "as we see burning to be the inherent quality of fire only."

So 161 denies the ahaṃkāra and 711 makes the Parāhantā inalienable, and the distinction the text needs is between the three guṇa-inflected egoisms named here and the supreme I-ness named there. The threefold division is what makes it available.

162. निर्मोहा → निर्-मोहा

निर् = without
मोह = bewilderment, confusion, infatuation (from मुह् "to be confused")
"She who is without bewilderment."

Vigraha: मोहः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The gloss is a definition: "moha is confusion of thought, distraction of the mind."

मुह् is the text's most reversible root. मुग्धा at 868 makes Her the bewildered one, the Viśva giving "beautiful and ignorant" from the same stem; मोहिनी at 562 the enchantress; शंभुमोहिनी at 954 the bewilderer of Śiva; सर्वमोहिनी at 703 the bewilderer of everyone, where the bewildering is the answer to how She can bear contradictory attributes. Here the root is denied of Her. Five namas, one root, and the positions do not add up unless — as 704 सरस्वती argues — the bewilderment is specific to non-dual knowledge and does not touch ordinary cognition.

163. मोहनाशिनी → मोह-नाशिनी

मोह = bewilderment
नाशिनी = she who destroys
"The Destroyer of bewilderment."

Vigraha: मोहं नाशयतीति।

"By imparting the idea of unity to her devotees," with Īśa 7: "to him who perceives unity, what bewilderment and what sorrow can there be?"

So the destruction is by substitution — unity replaces confusion — and the Upaniṣad supplies the mechanism rather than the mere claim.

164. निर्ममा → निर्-ममा

निर् = without
मम = mine (genitive of अहम्) — hence self-interest, the sense of *mine*
"She who is without the sense of mine."

Vigraha: ममेति भावः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The argument is one clause and it is a good one: "self-interest necessarily implies separateness, and as she is without separateness, she is said to be without self-interest."

So ममता is denied of Her as a consequence of 151 निरन्तरा and 178 निर्भेदा rather than as a separate fact. The word मम is the genitive of the pronoun, so the vice is named by a case-form — which is exactly the construction 908 तत्त्वमर्थस्वरूपिणी uses on तत् and त्वम्, two pronouns made into a nama.

165. ममताहन्त्री → ममता-हन्त्री

ममता = the sense of mine, selfishness (मम with the abstract suffix ता)
हन्त्री = she who slays (हन् "to strike" with the agent-suffix तृ and feminine ङीप्)
"The Destroyer of selfishness."

Vigraha: ममतां हन्तीति।

index.html's body merely repeats the gloss, and the nama's own heading has been carried down into 167's body, which opens "(Mamatāhantrī.)"

हन्त्री is the तृ agent-noun of 557 कालहन्त्री, where what was slain was Time; 599 दैत्यहन्त्री, the demons; 811 पाशहन्त्री, the noose; and 191 दुःखहन्त्री twenty-six namas on, pain. Five objects for one root, and here it is a pronoun's abstract.

166. निष्पापा → निष्-पापा

निष् = without
पाप = sin, evil
"The Sinless."

Vigraha: पापं यस्याः नास्ति सा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

पाप is the forest at 743 पापारण्यदवानला, where She is the wildfire consuming it; and 987 अनघा denies sin of Her on the other stem, where Bhāskararāya widens अघ to "sin, pain, misery."

167. पापनाशिनी → पाप-नाशिनी

पाप = sin
नाशिनी = she who destroys
"The Destroyer of sin."

Vigraha: पापं नाशयतीति।

This is the longest entry in the verse, and every citation is about sin destroyed on terms that look too easy — which is the text's standing position and it is nowhere better documented.

"By the repetition of her mantra she destroys the sins of devotees," with Chāndogya 5.24.3: "like the point of a reed in the fire, so all his sins are burned up."

Then the Vasiṣṭha Smṛti, and the claim is startling: "the Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to learning and penance and who continually repeats mantras — even if he is always committing sinful actions, he is not afflicted thereby. Sin never resides in those who repeat mantras, or offer oblations, or meditate, or make pilgrimages, or who perform Śirovrata, the rite of carrying fire on the head."

The Padma Purāṇa's Puṣkarakhaṇḍa adds the mountain and the lotus-leaf: "the mass of sins, though as great as Mount Meru, is instantly destroyed by approaching Kātyāyanī. He who is devoted to Durgā is not stained even by committing heinous crimes, in the same manner as the lotus leaf which is not affected by water."

And the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa removes the last qualification, that of caste and station: "the sinful actions of those who are devoid of varṇa and āśrama, and the wretched, by mere meditation on Devī become virtuous."

That is the same leniency as 736 मुक्तिदा, where liberation comes to those who recite "even unconsciously" and worship "whether regularly or irregularly"; 913, where the Kūrma Purāṇa builds a list of qualifications and then waives it; 681–682, where worship needs no fasting and She does good to the imperfect worshipper; and 815 अनित्यतृप्ता, where a leaf or a little water suffices. Kātyāyanī, named here, is nama 556; the lotus-leaf figure is 134's.

Note on the verse. Eight namas, four pairs, and the programme of 156 running.

Two of them are pairs on the announced impediments — मोह at 162–163 and, by extension, पाप at 166–167 — and two are the odd namas, चिन्ता and अहंकार, with ममता making its own pair at 164–165.

160's proverb is the verse's best line: चिन्ता differs from चिता by one nasal, and the pile burns the corpse while anxiety burns the living.

161 is the one with consequences. Its threefold division of ahaṃkāra — Vaikārika, Taijasa, Bhūtādi, by sattva, rajas and tamas — is what makes it possible to deny egoism here and yet make Parāhantā Her inherent quality at 711. The distinction is available in the text but never drawn.

And 167 is the fullest statement of the text's leniency about sin. Four citations, and each removes a condition: mantra-repetition covers continual sinning; devotion to Durgā covers heinous crime; and mere meditation makes the actions of those "devoid of varṇa and āśrama" virtuous.

Textual note. 161's body is scrambled, two sentences interleaved. 165's heading has been carried into 167's body. 167's body also opens with a footnote belonging to the previous entry — "Śirovrata, according to the Sūta Saṃhitā, is the Śaiva initiation" — which stands in 170's field. 166 has no commentary body.

---

## निष्क्रोधा क्रोधशमनी निर्लोभा लोभनाशिनी । निःसंशया संशयघ्नी निर्भवा भवनाशिनी

*niṣkrodhā krodhaśamanī nirlobhā lobhanāśinī । niḥsaṃśayā saṃśayaghnī nirbhavā bhavanāśinī*

Verse 48, namas 168–175.

168. निष्क्रोधा → निष्-क्रोधा

निष् = without
क्रोध = wrath, anger (from क्रुध् "to be angry")
"She who is without anger."

Vigraha: क्रोधः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The reason is that anger needs an object she does not have: "because she has no object of hatred," with Gītā 9.29 — "there is none hateful to me nor dear." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (47).

That Gītā verse is the same one 790 परापरा quotes for its foe-and-friend reading of परा and अपरा. And क्रोध is what 9 क्रोधाकाराङ्कुशोज्ज्वला makes Her goad — "wrath is the mental modification known as hatred," held in the lower right hand, and identified by the Yoginīhṛdaya with the Jñānaśakti. So the anger denied here is a weapon in her hand at 9, and 827 प्रचण्डा grounds her fierceness in Taittirīya's "for fear of Him the wind blows."

169. क्रोधशमनी → क्रोध-शमनी

क्रोध = anger
शमनी = she who quiets, allays (from शम् "to be quiet," causative)
"The Allayer of anger."

Vigraha: क्रोधं शमयतीति।

"Anger is one of the six enemies" — the cross-reference is to 156, where the six were named — and Āpastamba supplies the reason it must be quieted, which is ritual rather than moral: "he who sacrifices, offers oblation, or worships while angry is deprived of all benefit therefrom, like water in a vessel of unbaked clay."

So anger is disqualifying in the way ritual impurity is, and the simile is exact: the vessel does not hold.

शमनी rather than नाशिनी here, which is the pattern's one variation in this verse — and शम् is the root of 126 शांकरी, 963 शमात्मिका and 551 सर्वव्याधिप्रशमनी.

170. निर्लोभा → निर्-लोभा

निर् = without
लोभ = greed, covetousness (from लुभ् "to covet")
"She who is without greed."

Vigraha: लोभः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The gloss is four words and it makes the absence of greed a positive: "because she is exceedingly liberal."

index.html's body also opens with a footnote belonging to 167: "Śirovrata, according to the Sūta Saṃhitā, is the Śaiva initiation."

लुभ् is the root of लोलुपा at 857 गानलोलुपा, a reduplicated intensive — so She is greedy for song there and without greed here, and the root is the same.

171. लोभनाशिनी → लोभ-नाशिनी

लोभ = greed
नाशिनी = she who destroys
"The Destroyer of greed."

Vigraha: लोभं नाशयतीति।

One proverb: "greed destroys all good qualities."

And then the Tantrarāja on the characteristics of the guru, which is placed here because it introduces the next pair: "he is the guru who is without doubt, the remover of doubt, and expects nothing." Bhāskararāya notes that "after this, the characteristics of these latter two qualities are explained" — meaning 172–173.

So the guru-definition supplies the transition: freedom from greed is his third mark, and freedom from doubt and the removal of doubt are the first two, which the next two namas take up. The pattern of the नि-run is being made to describe a teacher.

The guru-namas of the text are 713 गुरुमण्डलरूपिणी, where the circle of teachers is Her form and the secret "was handed down from ear to ear"; 603 गुरुमूर्तिः; 591 शिरःस्थिता, where she resides in the brahmarandhra "assuming the form of the Guru"; and 722 गुरुप्रिया.

172. निःसंशया → निः-संशया

निः = without
संशय = doubt, uncertainty (सम् + शी "to lie" — a lying-together of alternatives)
"She who is without doubt."

Vigraha: संशयः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The whole body is two words repeating the gloss.

संशय is सम् + शी, alternatives lying together — so doubt is named by the suspension itself, and 171's guru is defined as one in whom they have separated.

173. संशयघ्नी → संशय-घ्नी

संशय = doubt
घ्नी = she who slays, destroys (from हन् "to strike"; feminine of घ्न)
"The Destroyer of doubt."

Vigraha: संशयं हन्तीति।

Both the dev field and the verse text read संशयनी, the घ् lost — and the gloss preserves the correct reading in transliteration, "(Saṃśayaghnī)." That is the same fault as 842 भवरोगघ्नी, where the printed text reads भवरोगनी and the gloss again supplies the घ्.

Muṇḍaka 2.2.8 is cited — "all doubts are cut away" — and the Smṛti echoes it. Bhāskararāya marks the division: "12th verse divides 49 names."

घ्नी is the same हन् as हन्त्री at 165, 191, 557, 599 and 811, in its compound-final form.

174. निर्भवा → निर्-भवा

निर् = without
भव = origin, becoming, birth; also worldly existence
"She who is without origin."

Vigraha: भवः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Gītā 13.12: "the Supreme Brahman is without origin."

भव is the word this batch opened on at 112 भवानी, where it was Śiva, saṃsāra and Manmatha at once; and at 114 भवारण्यकुठारिका it is the forest She fells. Here the first sense is denied of Her and the next nama denies the second.

175. भवनाशिनी → भव-नाशिनी

भव = worldly existence, saṃsāra; and per the Bṛhajjābāla, a river's name
नाशिनी = she who destroys
"The Destroyer of worldly existence."

Vigraha: भवं नाशयतीति।

The Śaktirahasya is quoted, and it is entirely procedural: "on the ninth day of the lunar month, according to the rule, as to him who anoints Caṇḍikā with ghee — hear the result of that action. He is raised out of the ocean of saṃsāra and shines in the Durgā-loka, together with the preceding ten and also succeeding ten generations."

So one anointing on one day saves twenty-one generations, which belongs with the leniency-citations at 167 and 736. The Kūrma and Devī Bhāgavata are said to agree.

And a last note, from the Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad 26: "Bhavanāśinī is the name of a river."

That closes the eight-pair sequence 156 announced, and it closes it on the largest object. The pairs have moved from passion, pride, bewilderment, self-interest, sin, anger, greed and doubt to existence itself — so the sixth impediment becomes the whole of saṃsāra, and भवनाशिनी is 842 भवरोगघ्नी and 843 भवचक्रप्रवर्तिनी in the plainest possible words.

Note on the verse. Eight namas, four pairs, and the sequence 156 opened closes here.

The progression across 156–175 is worth setting out because it is deliberate: passion, pride, anxiety, egoism, bewilderment, self-interest, sin, anger, greed, doubt, existence. The six impediments Bhāskararāya named at 156 are all there, and the list has been extended past them to sin, doubt and finally saṃsāra — so the sequence ends on something larger than it set out to treat.

171 is the structural entry. Its Tantrarāja quotation defines the guru by three marks — "without doubt, the remover of doubt, and expects nothing" — and Bhāskararāya says the next two namas explain the first two of them. So the privative-destroyer pattern is briefly made into a description of a teacher.

And 175 closes on twenty-one generations saved by anointing an image with ghee on one lunar day.

Textual note. 173's dev and verse text both read संशयनी for संशयघ्नी, the घ् lost — the same fault as 842, and in both cases the gloss preserves the reading. 170's body opens with a footnote belonging to 167. 172's body repeats its gloss.

## निर्विकल्पा निराबाधा निर्भेदा भेदनाशिनी । निर्नाशा मृत्युमथनी निष्क्रिया निष्परिग्रहा

*nirvikalpā nirābādhā nirbhedā bhedanāśinī । nirnāśā mṛtyumathanī niṣkriyā niṣparigrahā*

Verse 49, namas 176–183.

176. निर्विकल्पा → निर्-विकल्पा

निर् = without
विकल्प = a false notion, fancy, a construct of words without a corresponding object; also an alternative, a doubt (वि + कल्प् "to arrange")
"She who is without false constructs."

Vigraha: विकल्पः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The definition is Patañjali's and Bhāskararāya gives it verbatim, Yoga Sūtra 1.9: "vikalpa, fancy, is a notion conveyed by mere words, but of which there is no object corresponding to reality."

Then two more authorities for the same idea, and both are from logic rather than yoga. Śrīharṣa's Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya: "the word gives knowledge of an object which cannot possibly exist." And Gautama's Sūtra 4.50, "that is not real which is created in the mind."

That definition is the one 661 सदसद्रूपधारिणी uses for असत् in its second reading — "the remaining modifications, called vikalpa, fanciful," on the same Yoga Sūtra and the same Gautama sūtra. So the two namas are 485 apart and rest on one pair of citations.

Then the technical sense: "Nirvikalpa — in the last mental modification, that is the last stage of meditation, there are no specific distinctions." निर्विकल्प समाधि is the standard term, and the nama names it. Bhāskararāya adds: "she is in the form of unconditioned eternal knowledge."

And a further division: "vi, opposed; kalpa, theory. There is no theory opposed to her existence, because everything is inseparable from her." With Vedānta Sūtra 3.2.14 — "for Brahman is merely devoid of form, on account of this being the main purport of Scripture" — and the conclusion: "by this it is established that the special characteristic of Brahman is that it has no such distinction as that of subject and object."

That is what 981 ज्ञातृज्ञेयस्वरूपिणी asserts by making Her both poles, and 908 तत्त्वमर्थस्वरूपिणी by making Her the That and the Thou. Here it is stated as the defining characteristic.

Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (48).

177. निराबाधा → निर्-आबाधा

निर् = without
आबाधा = molestation, disturbance, liability to error (आ + बाध् "to press, to vex")
"She who is undisturbed."

Vigraha: आबाधा यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The gloss is a single simile and it is the mother-of-pearl again: "when it is seen that the appearance of silver in the shell is deceptive, the illusion vanishes; there is no such liability to error in her nature."

So what is denied is not being troubled but being mistakable. The same figure carries 735 मिथ्याजगदधिष्ठाना — "she is the basis of the illusory universe as the mother-of-pearl is the basis of the silver illusorily perceived" — and 708 सर्वोपाधिविनिर्मुक्ता, where the relation of quality to qualified is "illusory, like the relation of the silver in the mother-of-pearl." Three namas, one figure, and here it is used to say the figure does not apply to Her.

178. निर्भेदा → निर्-भेदा

निर् = without
भेद = difference, distinction, splitting (from भिद् "to cleave")
"She who is without difference."

Vigraha: भेदः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The reason is stated in the logicians' vocabulary, which is unusual for a privative: "as she is neither connected with anuyogitva, *for*, nor with pratiyogitva, *against*, to the mutual non-existence, she is said to be without difference."

अन्योन्याभाव, mutual non-existence, is the Nyāya analysis of difference: A differs from B just in case A is the locus (anuyogin) of the absence whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is B. Denying Her both relations denies that she can stand on either side of a difference — which is a more precise claim than 151 निरन्तरा's rejection of the three kinds of bheda.

The Kūrma Purāṇa: "thou art the Supreme Śakti, infinite, supreme ruler, devoid of all differences and the destroyer of all difference." And elsewhere in the same Purāṇa, a line that anticipates 999 exactly: "some ignorant persons say there is a difference between Śakti and the possessor of it, but those Yogins who meditate on reality recognise non-separateness."

That is the Saura Saṃhitā's argument at 999 शिवशक्त्यैक्यरूपिणी — "the Śakti which is separate from Brahman is not different from Brahman itself; it is only called Śakti by the ignorant" — so two Purāṇas make the same claim in nearly the same words, 821 namas apart.

179. भेदनाशिनी → भेद-नाशिनी

भेद = difference; and per the gloss, dual knowledge
नाशिनी = she who destroys
"The Destroyer of difference."

Vigraha: भेदं नाशयतीति।

"Bheda, the dual knowledge; she causes its destruction by the knowledge of reality."

So भेद is here epistemic rather than ontological — not difference but the cognition of it — which is what 703 सर्वमोहिनी makes her responsible for producing: "she bewilders all the ordinary people who believe in the reality of the apparent duality." She creates the dual knowledge there and destroys it here.

180. निर्नाशा → निर्-नाशा

निर् = without
नाश = destruction, end, perishing (from नश् "to perish")
"She who is without end."

Vigraha: नाशः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

"Nāśa, end," with Taittirīya 3 — "Brahman is being, knowledge, and infinity" — which is the same *satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ* verse that 791 सत्यज्ञानानन्दरूपा is built from. There the three words are her form; here the third alone is the point.

The nama is also a formal curiosity: नाश is the word that has been the second member of five namas in this run — मदनाशिनी, मोहनाशिनी, पापनाशिनी, लोभनाशिनी, भेदनाशिनी, भवनाशिनी — and here it is what she lacks. So the destroyer is undestroyable, stated with the same stem.

181. मृत्युमथनी → मृत्यु-मथनी

मृत्यु = death (from मृ "to die")
मथनी = she who churns, crushes, destroys (from मन्थ् "to churn")
"The Crusher of death."

Vigraha: मृत्युं मथ्नातीति।

Both the dev field and the verse text read मृत्युमधनी, ध् for थ् — a letter fault in both arrays.

The gloss narrows the object: "the death of devotees." And the Tripurā Upaniṣad 82 gives the sequence: "why it is said — because from mortality he obtains immortality, attains the imperishable state, attains the eternal existence, and he himself becomes Rudra."

मथ् is the root of 157 रागमथना in the same run, where what is churned is passion; and मृत्यु is what She wards off at 552 सर्वमृत्युनिवारिणी, specifically "untimely death"; the axe to whose timber she is at 749; and the second member of 851's triad.

182. निष्क्रिया → निष्-क्रिया

निष् = without
क्रिया = action, a rite (from कृ "to do")
"She who is without action."

Vigraha: क्रिया यस्याः नास्ति सा।

"Because she is without action, whether ordained or prohibited" — so what is denied is the whole field of vidhi and niṣedha, which is 834 विशृङ्खला's claim: "injunction and prohibition apply only to the ignorant," with the saying about golden and iron fetters.

Chāndogya 8.12.1 is cited: "only one who has no body is unaffected by likes or dislikes."

Then a second reading which turns the privative into an account of effortless causation: "one who has become the actor and the cause without the two means of action, material and instrumental." And the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's simile is well chosen: "just as the fragrant object is enough by its very presence to distract the mind, so does the Supreme Lord without help create the Universe."

Creation by mere presence is what 648 लीलाक्लृप्तब्रह्माण्डमण्डला says with लीला — "without effort," where even Śiva is powerless while the universe is Her sport — and 900 नैष्कर्म्या says with the vṛddhi abstract, where the citations are all about freedom from the taint of action rather than its absence.

क्रिया is also the third of the three śaktis at 658, made Her feet by the Saṅketapaddhati; so the action denied here is one third of Her form there.

183. निष्परिग्रहा → निष्-परिग्रहा

निष् = without
परिग्रह = taking, acceptance, possession; a retinue; a wife; and per the Medinī, a root (परि + ग्रह् "to grasp")
"She who accepts nothing."

Vigraha: परिग्रहः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The whole commentary is lexical and it is a list of what she is not: "according to the Medinī, parigraha means attendants, wife, appropriation, root. She is none of these."

That is a striking denial in a text which makes Her Sadāśiva's कुटुम्बिनी at 911 with a household of Śyāmalā, Śuddhavidyā and Aśvārūḍhā; which gives her attendants at 518, 525, 614 and 741; and which calls her मूलविग्रह, the root-form of all śaktis, at 840. Four of the Medinī's four senses are affirmed of Her elsewhere and denied of Her here.

परि + ग्रह् is also the same ग्रह् as विग्रह, the body, which the text uses six times — so what is grasped-around is refused where what is grasped-together is affirmed.

Note on the verse. Eight namas, and the negative determination reaches its most technical point.

176 defines विकल्प with three citations from three traditions — Yoga, Śrīharṣa's Advaita polemic, and Gautama — and then names the nirvikalpa samādhi. 178 denies difference in the Nyāya vocabulary of अनुयोगित्व and प्रतियोगित्व, which is more precise than 151's rejection of the three bhedas and is the only place in the text where that analysis is used.

177's mother-of-pearl is the figure 735 and 708 both rest on, turned here to say that She is not liable to the error it describes.

And 183 closes the verse by denying four things the text affirms elsewhere — attendants, a wife's status, appropriation, and being a root — on the authority of a lexicon.

Textual note. 181's dev and verse text both read मृत्युमधनी for मृत्युमथनी.

---

## निस्तुला नीलचिकुरा निरपाया निरत्यया । दुर्लभा दुर्गमा दुर्गा दुःखहन्त्री सुखप्रदा

*nistulā nīlacikurā nirapāyā niratyayā । durlabhā durgamā durgā duḥkhahantrī sukhapradā*

Verse 50, namas 184–192.

184. निस्तुला → निः-तुला

निः = without
तुला = a balance, a scale; hence comparison, likeness
"The Incomparable."

Vigraha: तुला यस्याः नास्ति सा।

The whole surviving commentary is a broken citation: "the Tripurā Upaniṣad 82 says, *comparison*" — and the sentence the quotation belonged to is lost. The reading is recoverable from 187's body, where the phrase "without cause or comparison" stands displaced.

तुला is a weighing-balance, so incomparability is named by the absence of a scale — and the nama belongs with 29 अनाकलितसादृश्यचुबुकश्रीविराजिता, where no likeness for her chin could be reckoned, and with the seven eclipsing-words of the aṅga-description. There the comparison was defeated; here there is no instrument for making one.

185. नीलचिकुरा → नील-चिकुरा

नील = dark blue, black
चिकुरा = hair (चिकुर)
"The Dark-haired."

Vigraha: नीलाः चिकुराः यस्याः सा।

No commentary survives for this nama; index.html carries 184's gloss and body on it. The reading is preserved in 187's gloss, which holds the stranded heading "Blue haired. (Nīlacikura.)"

Her hair is 13 चम्पकाशोकपुन्नागसौगन्धिकलसत्कचा, glistening with four flowers and perfuming them rather than perfumed by them; 942 व्योमकेशी, where the ether is her hair in the Virāṭ form; and 547 बर्बरालका, curling — whose dev field is the most corrupt in the text. Here the colour is given, and नील is the only place the text calls anything of hers dark: her colours elsewhere are red five times over, white at 522, and fair or yellow at 635.

186. निरपाया → निर्-अपाया

निर् = without
अपाय = departure, destruction, loss (अप + इ "to go away")
"The Imperishable."

Vigraha: अपायः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

No commentary survives; index.html carries 184's again. The reading stands in 187's body: "Imperishable. (Nirapāya.)"

अपाय is a going-away, so imperishability is named as not-departing — where 180 निर्नाशा four namas back used नाश, a destroying. Two privatives of the same idea in one verse-group, one passive and one active.

187. निरत्यया → निर्-अत्यया

निर् = without
अत्यय = transgression, passing away; also punishment, obstruction, fault, emaciation (अति + इ "to go beyond")
"She who is without transgression."

Vigraha: अत्ययः यस्याः नास्ति सा।

index.html's fields here carry the material of 185, 186 and 187 all together — the gloss holds 185's heading, the body holds 186's and then 187's — so this nama is where the four-nama displacement chain that began at 184 finally deposits what it has been carrying.

The one thing proper to it is the lexical range: "atyaya means transgression, punishment, obstruction, fault, and emaciation." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (49).

अति + इ is the same formation as अतीत in the triad at 960–962 and 991 षडध्वातीतरूपिणी — a going-beyond, which is affirmed of Her there and denied of her here. The difference is that अतीत is her transcending and अत्यय is her being transgressed.

188. दुर्लभा → दुर्-लभा

दुर् = hard, difficult (दुस्)
लभा = to be obtained (from लभ् "to get")
"She who is hard to obtain."

Vigraha: दुःखेन लभ्या।

Two words: "even to yogins."

That is the plainest of the text's difficulty-namas, and they are unevenly matched against its leniency-namas. 871 बहिर्मुखसुदुर्लभा stacks सु on दुर् for the outward-faced, citing Saundaryalaharī 95; 771 दुराराध्या makes Her impossible to worship for the fickle-minded; 990 अभ्यासातिशयज्ञाता makes her known only by unremitting practice; 683's alternative reads the path as *not* easily attained, with the Triśatī's "the fifteen-syllabled Mantra is to be attained by him alone whose present birth is his last, or by Śaṃkara himself." Against those stand 681, 682, 736, 815, 167 and 175. The text asserts both and reconciles them only at 771, by distinguishing the method from the worshipper.

189. दुर्गमा → दुर्-गमा

दुर् = hard, difficult
गमा = to be gone to, approachable (from गम् "to go")
"She who is hard to approach."

Vigraha: दुःखेन गम्या।

Three readings in one line: "or Adurgamā, accessible; or Durgama is the name of a Daitya whom Devī caused to be slain."

The first is the prefix-अ device, which the text uses at 830, 847, 868, 905, 926, 939 and 113 — a nama made to say its opposite by adding a syllable. Here it turns the inaccessible into the accessible, in a verse that has just said she is hard to obtain even for yogins.

The third supplies the next nama's etymology.

गम् is the root of the four गम्या-namas — 113, 119, 641, 980 — where the means are meditation, devotion, dhyāna and knowledge. Here the going is denied.

190. दुर्गा → दुर्गा

दुर्गा = Durgā; literally hard to go through, impassable (दुर् + गम्); and per the etymologies, the slayer of Durgama, and the deliverer from difficulty
"Durgā."

Vigraha: दुर्गमं दैत्यं हतवती दुर्गा। or दुर्गात् त्रायते इति दुर्गा।

index.html's gloss and body are duplicates.

Two etymologies, and they disagree about whether the name comes from a demon or from a difficulty.

The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa and the Pāñcarātra's Lakṣmītantra: "in that place I am going to kill a great Daitya named Durgama, hence my name shall be Durgā." Bhāskararāya adds the location — "this is the goddess who resides in the place called Sannati, on the bank of the river Bhīmarathī."

The Devī Purāṇa instead derives it from what she delivers from: "the Devas were delivered from mental and physical fear, in Indra and other difficulty and in battle, hence Devī is called Durgā, the deliverer." So दुर्ग is the difficulty rather than the demon's name.

Then a second location: "this Devī, solicited by king Subāhu, who begged a boon of her, established herself under this name at Benares." Benares is also where 936 विशालाक्षी is the presiding deity per the Padma Purāṇa, so two namas place two forms of Her in one city.

**And the girl-age: "according to this, a nine year old girl also is called Durgā."** That completes the series. Sarasvatī two (704), Trimūrti three (628), Subhagā five (761), Caṇḍikā seven (755), Śāmbhavī eight (122), Durgā nine here, Gaurī ten (635) — seven namas of the thousand doubling as ages, and the sequence runs 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 with only four and six missing.

Durgā is also one quarter of Her at 893 विष्णुरूपिणी — "in battle she takes the form of Durgā" — and the deity whose worship gains the world of Viṣṇu at 893's Bṛhat-Parāśara citation, and whose devotee is unstained by heinous crime at 167.

191. दुःखहन्त्री → दुःख-हन्त्री

दुःख = pain, sorrow (traditionally दुः + ख, the bad aperture — running badly, as of an axle-hole)
हन्त्री = she who slays (हन् with the agent-suffix तृ and feminine ङीप्)
"The Destroyer of pain."

Vigraha: दुःखं हन्तीति।

Both the dev field and the verse text read दु खहन्त्री, with a space where the visarga belongs — so the visarga has been dropped and replaced by a word-break, splitting the compound into two non-words.
