दुःख is glossed as "pain caused by saṃsāra," and the definition of salvation is then taken from Nyāya rather than Vedānta: Gautama's Sūtra 1.22, "salvation is the complete release from that pain." With the Śruti, "he lives completely freed from pain."

The etymology of दुःख is worth keeping because it makes the pair with the next nama exact: दुः with ख, the badly-bored axle-hole, against सु with ख, the well-bored one. So 191 and 192 are the two ways a thing can run, and 968 सुखकरी uses the same word.

192. सुखप्रदा → सुख-प्रदा

सुख = happiness, ease (सु + ख, the good aperture)
प्रदा = giving fully (प्र + दा "to give")
"The Bestower of happiness."

Vigraha: सुखं प्रददातीति।

सुख is given three ranges: "happiness in this world, in the next world, and beatitude." So the nama covers the whole scale, which is what 764 स्वर्गापवर्गदा does with two terms — heaven and release — and what 698 सर्वार्थदात्री does with the four objects of human desire.

Taittirīya 2.7 is cited: "only after obtaining the essence, rasa, that is Brahman, does one become blissful." That is the *raso vai saḥ* verse which 800 रसशेवधिः is built on, and where the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa's chain ends by making rasa the vital breath.

Bhāskararāya sends the reader to the last six chapters of the Padma Purāṇa's Puṣkarakhaṇḍa for details, and marks the verse: (50).

प्रदा with प्र is the form of 727 शिवज्ञानप्रदायिनी and 989 वाञ्छितार्थप्रदायिनी. And 191–192 close this batch as a matched pair on one etymology — the axle running badly and running well.

Note on the verse. Nine namas in two groups: four privatives closing the नि-run, then five on दुर् and सु.

184–187 are where the text's block-duplication does its worst in this batch. Four consecutive namas share one gloss and body, and the material proper to 185, 186 and 187 has all been carried down into 187's fields, so the chain deposits three headings in one place.

188–190 then reverse the run's direction. After sixty namas of privatives asserting what She lacks, three namas assert that she is hard to get — "even to yogins" — and 189 immediately offers अदुर्गमा, accessible, by prefixing a syllable. Whether She is easy or hard is the one question the text never settles.

190 completes the girl-age series to seven, and gives Durgā two incompatible etymologies and two locations.

And 191–192 close on the axle-hole: दुःख and सुख are the same word with different prefixes, one badly bored and one well, so the last pair of the batch is a single figure divided.

Textual note. 184–187 form a four-nama displacement chain: 185 and 186 carry 184's gloss and body, and 187's fields hold the headings and glosses of 185, 186 and 187 together. 191's dev and verse text both read दु खहन्त्री, the visarga replaced by a space. 190's gloss and body are duplicates.

---

Textual note for verses 41–50.

**The structural finding is the doxography.** Bhāskararāya announces a programme at 133 — the nature of pure intellect determined "by assertion, by negation, by positive definition, and by elimination of attributes; then the means of obtaining it, and the real nature of the results" — and a second at 156, "to reject the theory that the differences in the mind belong to the Self, and to teach that renunciation is the means of overcoming the six impediments." The नि-run of verses 43–49 executes both.

Within it, eight namas refute named rival positions:

| nama | | refutes |
|---|---|---|
| 136 | नित्या | Kṣaṇikavijñānavāda — Buddhist momentariness |
| 137 | निराकारा | Vijñānavāda and the Mādhyamikas |
| 138 | निराकुला | Śūnyavāda, "the Gambhīra School" |
| 139 | निर्गुणा | the Tarka school — Nyāya |
| 140 | निष्कला | those who hold Brahman has parts |
| 141 | शान्ता | the Digambaras, on the soul's limited extent |
| 142 | निष्कामा | the eternity of the Lord's will and thought |
| 147 | निराश्रया | the Cārvākas |
| 151 | निरन्तरा | the threefold bheda of the logicians |

And two accommodate rather than refute: 145 निर्विकारा adopts the Sāṃkhya count of twenty-three vikāras and places Her outside it; 155 निरीश्वरा says She belongs to both Mīmāṃsā and Sāṃkhya, "the former monism and the latter atheism." 149 नित्यबुद्धा goes further and makes two Jaina Tīrthaṅkaras Her devotees, eight namas after 141 refuted the Digambara thesis — on the ground that "one of the worships of Devī is by following the six systems of philosophies."

**Three malas in three namas.** 133 निरञ्जना sets out the three bound souls — Vijñānakevala with the āṇava impurity, Pralayākala with the kārma, Sakala with the māyīya, each carrying the ones below — and 133, 134, 135 deny them in ascending order. Bhāskararāya's own Setubandha, quoted at 134, maps the three onto the three cakra-stations that Yoginīhṛdaya 1.27 gave at 113 as Sakala, Sakalaniṣkala and Niṣkala. So one three-fold scheme is a taxonomy of meditations at 113 and of meditators at 133–135.

**Nine pairs of privative-and-destroyer**, from 156 to 175: rāga, mada, moha, mamatā, pāpa, krodha, lobha, saṃśaya, bhava. The first member is about Her, the second about the devotee, and the sequence ends on something larger than the six impediments it set out to treat.

**Sandhi mis-division, one instance, and it is in both arrays at once.** 154 निरुपाधिः has lost its visarga and 155 निरीश्वरा has gained the resulting र् — in the dev fields *and* in the verse text, which additionally puts a space before the stray र् (निरुपाधि र्निरीश्वरा). Every earlier instance of this fault — 537–541, 615–617, 628–629, 662–663, 748–749, 848–849, 894–895, 992–993 — was confined to the nama fields.

**Letter faults, three, and all three are in both arrays:** 116 भद्रमूर्ति for भद्रमूर्तिः; 173 संशयनी for संशयघ्नी, the same loss of घ् as at 842 भवरोगघ्नी and again corrected only by the gloss; 181 मृत्युमधनी for मृत्युमथनी. And 191 दु खहन्त्री has its visarga replaced by a space, splitting the compound into two non-words.

**Block-duplication:** 184–187, a four-nama chain in which 185 and 186 carry 184's fields and 187's hold three headings at once. 116's body carries the whole of 117's commentary. 112, 124 and 190 have duplicate gloss and body. 165's heading stands in 167's body; 167's footnote stands in 170's; 153's citation breaks off and its last word stands in 152's.

**A third count of the sacred places.** 112 gives Sthāneśvara as one of "the hundred and eight places of pilgrimage," per the Padma Purāṇa — against 793's sixty-eight and 833's fifty-one, where Bhāskararāya argued the count at length. Three enumerations, no reconciliation.

**The girl-ages are now complete at seven**, 122 Śāmbhavī at eight and 190 Durgā at nine joining Sarasvatī two, Trimūrti three, Subhagā five, Caṇḍikā seven and Gaurī ten. The run is 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10.

**Empty bodies, only five of eighty-one** — 114, 129, 158, 166, and 185–186 by duplication. For a stretch this long that is unusually good preservation, and the substantial commentary is very heavily concentrated: 113, 118, 119, 132, 133, 167 and 176 carry perhaps half the words in the batch between them.


---

## दुष्टदूरा दुराचारशमनी दोषवर्जिता । सर्वज्ञा सान्द्रकरुणा समानाधिकवर्जिता

*duṣṭadūrā durācāraśamanī doṣavarjitā । sarvajñā sāndrakaruṇā samānādhikavarjitā*

Verse 51, namas 193–198.

193. दुष्टदूरा → दुष्ट-दूरा

दुष्ट = corrupt, wicked, spoiled (past participle of दुष् "to be corrupted")
दूरा = far, distant, remote
"She who is far from the wicked."

Vigraha: दुष्टेभ्यः दूरा।

The Devī Bhāgavata names one class of the wicked in particular: "those who argue sophistically never worship Devī, the ruler of the Universe, the benevolent."

So the distance is from a habit of mind rather than from a class of act — which is the same qualification 771 दुराराध्या makes with "impossible to be worshipped by the fickle-minded" and 871 बहिर्मुखसुदुर्लभा with the outward-faced. And it is worth setting against 167 पापनाशिनी twenty-six namas back, where the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa says that "the sinful actions of those who are devoid of varṇa and āśrama, and the wretched, by mere meditation on Devī become virtuous." Crime is forgiven; sophistry is not.

दूर is the word 990 अभ्यासातिशयज्ञाता's difficulty implies without using.

194. दुराचारशमनी → दुर्-आचार-शमनी

दुर् = bad, evil (दुस्)
आचार = conduct, observance, custom (आ + चर् "to move, to behave")
शमनी = she who quiets, allays, puts an end to (from शम् "to be quiet," causative)
"She who puts an end to evil practices."

Vigraha: दुराचारं शमयतीति।

आचार is defined by its opposite: "evil customs are contrary to the Scriptures." And the gloss then forecasts a later nama — "concerning this more will be said below, as *she quickly destroys all the sins of men committed by neglecting the daily rites and observing the prohibited ones*." So दुराचार covers both halves of ritual failure, omission and commission.

आचार is the word of 98 समयाचारतत्परा, where She is devoted to the observances of the Samaya path, and the same आ + चर् gives उपचार at 235 and 950. So the conduct She is devoted to and the conduct she destroys are one word with different prefixes.

शमनी for the second time in twenty-five namas, after 169 क्रोधशमनी; and 551 सर्वव्याधिप्रशमनी and 696 दैत्यशमनी use it for disease and demons.

195. दोषवर्जिता → दोष-वर्जिता

दोष = a fault, a defect, a blemish; and per the commentary, passion and hatred (from दुष्)
वर्जिता = devoid of, excluding (from वृज् "to avoid")
"She who is devoid of faults."

Vigraha: दोषेण वर्जिता।

The gloss is three words: "doṣa — passion, hatred, and the rest."

दोष is from the same दुष् as दुष्ट in 193, so the verse's first and third namas share a root — the wicked are far from Her, and the fault is absent in Her. वर्जिता is the word of 652 वेद्यवर्जिता and 668 द्वैतवर्जिता, and its intensive at 680 भावाभावविवर्जिता where Bhāskararāya answers the objection that one cannot be devoid of non-existence.

196. सर्वज्ञा → सर्व-ज्ञा

सर्व = all
ज्ञा = knowing, she who knows (from ज्ञा "to know")
"The Omniscient."

Vigraha: सर्वं जानातीति सर्वज्ञा।

Muṇḍaka 1.1.9: "one who perceives all and knows all." And the Devī Purāṇa's gloss is a tautology Bhāskararāya reproduces without comment: "as she knows everything she is called Omniscient."

ज्ञा as the bare root-noun stands at 828 आज्ञा's second reading, 841 भावज्ञा, 799 रसज्ञा and 902; and 149 नित्यबुद्धा made knowledge inseparable from the knower on Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.30.

197. सान्द्रकरुणा → सान्द्र-करुणा

सान्द्र = thick, dense, intense; also unctuous, viscid
करुणा = compassion, pity
"She whose compassion is dense."

Vigraha: सान्द्रा करुणा यस्याः सा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

सान्द्र is a word for physical thickness — of curds, of a forest, of darkness — so the compound makes compassion a substance with a consistency rather than a disposition with a degree. That is the same kind of choice घन makes at 574 प्रज्ञानघनरूपिणी, where knowledge is "concentrated" and the simile is a lump of salt whose taste is "neither inside nor outside but everywhere."

करुणा is the word of 992 अव्याजकरुणामूर्तिः, where the compassion needs no pretext, and one of the four vāsanās at 570; दया at 581 and कृपा at 687 are the text's other two words for it.

198. समानाधिकवर्जिता → समान-अधिक-वर्जिता

समान = equal, like, the same
अधिक = superior, exceeding, greater
वर्जिता = devoid of, excluding
"She who has neither equal nor superior."

Vigraha: समानेन अधिकेन च वर्जिता।

Sandhi: समान + अधिक → समानाधिक (आ by 6.1.101).

Śvetāśvatara 6.8: "no one is seen equal or superior to him." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (51).

That verse is quoted again at 541 अनुत्तमा, where Bhāskararāya makes the grammatical point that अनुत्तम "does not mean *not the highest* but *having none higher*, the negation falling on any possible superior rather than on Her." This nama says the same thing with both terms spelled out — and 155 निरीश्वरा and 809 परात्परा make it twice more, so the claim stands four times in the thousand on four constructions.

The Devī Bhāgavata's argument at 541 is the best of the four and it is from usage: "people never say of a man devoid of strength *he is deprived of Rudra* or *of Viṣṇu*, but say *deprived of Śakti*."

Note on the verse. Six namas in two triads, दु- then स-, and they divide neatly by whom they concern.

193–195 are about the wicked: far from them, ending their practices, without their faults. And 193's specification is the interesting one — the Devī Bhāgavata makes sophistical argument the disqualifying habit, in a text which twenty-six namas earlier forgave heinous crime.

196–198 are about Her: omniscient, densely compassionate, without equal. 197's सान्द्र is the choice to notice: compassion given a thickness rather than a degree.

Textual note. 197 has no commentary body.

---

## सर्वशक्तिमयी सर्वमङ्गला सद्गतिप्रदा । सर्वेश्वरी सर्वमयी सर्वमन्त्रस्वरूपिणी

*sarvaśaktimayī sarvamaṅgalā sadgatipradā । sarveśvarī sarvamayī sarvamantrasvarūpiṇī*

Verse 52, namas 199–204.

> **The नि-run ends and the qualified description begins here, and Bhāskararāya says so in one clause at 199: "the text now sets forth her qualified form, saguṇa."** So verses 43–51 denied attributes — the negative determination announced at 133 — and verses 52 onward affirm them. The सर्व-run of this verse and the twenty-seven-nama महा-run that follows are the positive half of the same programme, and the seam falls exactly between 198 and 199.

199. सर्वशक्तिमयी → सर्व-शक्ति-मयी

सर्व = all; and per the second reading, infinite
शक्ति = power, energy; a Śakti
मयी = made of, consisting of (मय with the feminine ई)
"She who consists of all the Śaktis."

Vigraha: सर्वाः शक्तयः मयं यस्याः सा।

The identification is with the named goddesses: "she is not to be separated from any of the Śaktis, such as Bālā, Bagalā and the rest. Or she is the aggregate of all the divine powers."

That is 840 मूलविग्रहरूपिणी's claim — मूलविग्रह glossed as "the Rājarājeśvarī Śakti, root of all the other śaktis, Bālā, Bagalā and the rest" — with the same two examples, 641 namas apart.

Then the Lakṣmītantra of the Pāñcarātra, where Devī speaks to Indra, and the passage explains the gods' weapons: "O Indra, I am Mahālakṣmī; in the Svayambhava Kalpa I was born as the slayer of Mahiṣa for the well-being of all Devas. Those portions of my powers which entered the bodies of the Devas together became my supremely beautiful form. My powers, O Indra, became manifest in the form of the weapons of the Devas."

So the divine armoury is Her powers externalised, and Her own form is those portions gathered back. The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa is said to explain it in detail. And the Liṅga Purāṇa is quoted for the widest sense of सर्व: "the wise recognise whatever energies belong to objects as Gaurī" — which is the doctrine 572 पराशक्तिः states outright, that substance is Śiva and the power in it is She.

मयी is the suffix of 907 तत्त्वमयी, 941 मनोमयी and 705 शास्त्रमयी.

200. सर्वमङ्गला → सर्व-मङ्गला

सर्व = all
मङ्गला = auspicious, fortunate; welfare, good fortune
"She who is all good fortune."

Vigraha: सर्वं मङ्गलं यस्याः सा।

The Devī Purāṇa gives two reasons and the second is domestic: "she gives all the good fortune longed for in the heart, all desired good objects, hence she is called Sarvamaṅgalā. And she removes the pain of the devotees and gives to Hara all the best and choicest things, hence Sarvamaṅgalā."

मङ्गल is what the Viṣṇu Purāṇa at 967 सुमङ्गली makes a name of Brahman defined by its effect — "that, by remembering which, drives away misfortune from men" — and what 933 मङ्गलाकृतिः and 116 भद्रमूर्तिः make Her very form.

**This nama closes the second hundred, and the colophon survives in its body**: "thus ends the third Kāla, called Dhāmrika, with the second hundred, in the Saubhāgyabhāskara, composed by Śrī Bhāsurānanda," followed by "The Third Hundred."

**That is the fifth of the text's colophons, and it confirms the kalā-rule at a fifth and much earlier point.** The four already known all fall in the last four hundreds — 700 (eighth Kalā, Bhogadā, seventh hundred), 800 (ninth, Viśva, eighth), 900 (Bodhinī, ninth), 1000 (eleventh, Dhāriṇī, tenth) — and from those alone the pattern that the kalā-number runs one ahead of the hundred it closes was a generalisation from a short and contiguous run. Here the third Kalā closes the second hundred, seven hundred namas earlier, and the rule holds. So the commentary is arranged in eleven kalās over ten hundreds throughout, and five of the ten division-points survive.

201. सद्गतिप्रदा → सत्-गति-प्रदा

सत् = good; being, existence; and per one reading, Brahman
गति = a going, a path, a state, a goal (from गम् "to go")
प्रदा = giving fully (प्र + दा)
"She who bestows the good path."

Vigraha: सद्गतिं प्रददातीति।

Sandhi: सत् + गति → सद्गति, the त् voicing before ग्.

Three divisions. "Satgati includes all stages from Svarga to Mokṣa" — so the whole ladder, as 192 सुखप्रदा gave "happiness in this world, in the next world, and beatitude" nine namas back. Or "sat, Brahman; gati, knowledge." Or "sat, of the wise; gati, goal."

Then a line of the great men which is the neatest thing in the verse: "thou art the way, thou alone art the way, O Bhavānī." So the giver of the path is the path, which is 683 शोभनासुलभागतिः's compound stated as a vocative.

And the Padma Purāṇa supplies a rubric with a sliding scale: "he who worships Devī at the three times on the fourteenth day goes to the supreme abode where Devī is. Having performed on a large or small scale the rites according to his means, he shines in the world of Rudra." Rites proportioned to means, which is 974 बिन्दुतर्पणसंतुष्टा's principle — the act single, the substance graded by the doer.

गति is the word of 859 काष्ठा, the finishing-post, and 683.

202. सर्वेश्वरी → सर्व-ईश्वरी

सर्व = all
ईश्वरी = mistress, sovereign lady (from ईश् "to rule")
"Sovereign of all."

Vigraha: सर्वस्य ईश्वरी।

Sandhi: सर्व + ईश्वरी → सर्वेश्वरी (अ + ई → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87).

The gloss makes it the reason for the previous nama: "because she is the ruler of all, she leads into the right path."

ईश् has fifteen turns in the text and this is the widest of them, matched only by 569 निखिलेश्वरी — where निखिल is नि with खिल, a remainder, so "all with nothing left over," a stronger word than सर्व. 758 सर्वलोकेशी narrows it to the worlds.

203. सर्वमयी → सर्व-मयी

सर्व = all — and per the commentary, all the tattvas from earth to Śiva
मयी = made of, consisting of
"She who consists of all."

Vigraha: सर्वं मयं यस्याः सा।

The argument for the nama is a dependency: "without non-separation there cannot be unlimited dominion, hence this name." So 202's sovereignty over all requires 203's identity with all — rule presupposes non-difference, which is 178 निर्भेदा's claim put to work.

Then the Kāmika is quoted, and it is the longest passage in this verse: **five methods of meditating on Śiva as a body**, each taking a different enumeration for a different tissue.

"There are two hundred and twenty-four worlds; these should be meditated upon as if they were the hairs on the body of the Lord. This is the Bhuvana method. One who praises by means of the fifty letters should meditate on them as on the skin of the Lord of Devas, the holder of the trident. This is the letter method. One should meditate on the blood of Śiva by means of the seven crores of mantras which arise from the root Vidyās. This is the mantra method. The words of the mantras, which are various according to different arrangements, stand for the flesh and the blood-vessels of the Lord. This is the word method. The thirty-six Tattvas beginning with the earth are the form's sinews, bones and marrow. This process the comprehenders of the Vedas call the Tattva method."

So worlds are hair, letters are skin, mantras are blood, words are flesh and vessels, tattvas are sinew and bone. Five countings of the real mapped onto one body — and the next nama but one does the same thing with the twenty-eight Āgamas.

The text uses this procedure often but never so systematically: 769 यज्ञरूपा maps the sacrifice limb by limb; 847, 936 and 942 assemble the Virāṭ form piece by piece; 85–87 lay the three kūṭas on Her body; 591–597 lay them into the worshipper's.

The fifty letters here are the mātṛkās of 577 and the pīṭhas of 833; the thirty-six tattvas are 906–907's; and the seven crores of mantras return at 204.

204. सर्वमन्त्रस्वरूपिणी → सर्व-मन्त्र-स्व-रूपिणी

सर्व = all
मन्त्र = a mantra — here the seven crores
स्व = own
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying
"She whose very form is all the mantras."

Vigraha: सर्वे मन्त्राः स्वरूपं यस्याः सा।

Bhāskararāya marks the structure: "this and the next two following names together express the previous name." So 204, 205 and 206 — mantra, yantra, tantra — are the unpacking of 203's सर्वमयी, and the three together say what "all" covers.

"Mantras, viz., seven crores of mantras" — the same figure the Kāmika used for Śiva's blood in the previous nama.

The Sundarītāpanīya Upaniṣad: "many mantras are arranged on either side of the Vidyā" — the fifteen-syllabled mantra — so the whole mantra-corpus is disposed around the Pañcadaśī as a centre. Gauḍapāda's Sūtras 3 to 9 are cited as explaining it more clearly, with the commentator concluding "that she is the essence of all Mantras." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (52).

That is 846 मन्त्रसारा's claim, where मन्त्र is derived as मननात् त्रायते, what saves by being thought, so the nama names "the saving power inside the syllable rather than the syllable itself."

Note on the verse. Six namas, and the verse is the text's hinge from negative to positive determination.

199's opening clause does the work: "the text now sets forth her qualified form." Everything from 132 निराधारा to 198 has been privative — sixty-seven namas of it, with the doxography at 136–151 and the nine impediment-pairs at 156–175 — and from here the description is by affirmation. The सर्व- of this verse and the महा- of the next five are the two prefixes that carry it.

200 then closes the second hundred, and its colophon is the fifth to survive. It matters more than the four in the nineties because it is early: the rule that the kalā-number runs one ahead of the hundred it closes was a generalisation from a contiguous run, and this confirms it seven hundred namas back.

203 is the substantial entry. Its Kāmika passage gives five methods of meditating on Śiva as a body — 224 worlds as hair, 50 letters as skin, 7 crore mantras as blood, mantra-words as flesh and vessels, 36 tattvas as sinew and bone — and 204–206 then unpack "all" as mantra, yantra and tantra, which Bhāskararāya says explicitly.

---

## सर्वयन्त्रात्मिका सर्वतन्त्ररूपा मनोन्मनी । माहेश्वरी महादेवी महालक्ष्मीर्मृडप्रिया

*sarvayantrātmikā sarvatantrarūpā manonmanī । māheśvarī mahādevī mahālakṣmīr mṛḍapriyā*

Verse 53, namas 205–211.

205. सर्वयन्त्रात्मिका → सर्व-यन्त्र-आत्मिका

सर्व = all
यन्त्र = an instrument, a device; a mystical diagram (from यम् "to restrain")
आत्मिका = having the nature of, being the very self of
"She whose nature is all the yantras."

Vigraha: सर्वे यन्त्राः आत्मा यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: यन्त्र + आत्मिका → यन्त्रात्मिका (आ by 6.1.101). Both the dev field and the verse text read सर्बयन्त्रात्मिका with ब for व — a letter fault in both arrays.

The whole commentary is three words: "yantras are ghaṭa, argala and the rest." A fuller list stands at 228 महायन्त्रा twenty-three namas on — "Pūjācakra, Padmacakra, Amṛtaghaṭa, Merulinga."

यन्त्र is from यम्, to restrain — the same root as नियन्त्री at 568 and यामिणी at 819 — so a diagram is named as what holds a thing in place. And the text's one narrative yantra is Viśukra's Jayavighna at 78, which Gaṇeśa shatters.

आत्मिका for the fifth time: 611, 763, 853, 963, and here.

206. सर्वतन्त्ररूपा → सर्व-तन्त्र-रूपा

सर्व = all
तन्त्र = a Tantra, a doctrine, a system (from तन् "to stretch, to weave")
रूपा = form
"She whose form is all the Tantras."

Vigraha: सर्वे तन्त्राः रूपं यस्याः सा।

"Tantras are the Vāmakeśvara and others. Or she is to be sought after by means of all the Tantras." And the verse quoted for the second reading is the text's clearest statement of that inclusiveness: "many paths, different according to the scriptures, and all leading to success, merge in thee alone as the rivers do into the ocean."

**Then the Kāmika maps the twenty-eight Śaiva Āgamas onto Her body, limb by limb**, and it is the fullest anatomy of a canon in the text:

Kāmika the lotus feet; Yogaja the ankles; Kāraṇa and Prasṛta the toes; Ajita the knees; Dīpta the thighs; Aṃśumān the back; Suprabheda the navel; Vijaya the stomach; Niśvāsa the heart; Svāyambhuva the bosom; Anala the three eyes; Vīrāgama the throat; Ruru the ears; Makuṭa the crown; Vipula the arms; Candrajñāna the chest; Bimba the lotus face; Prodgīta the tongue; Lalitā the cheeks; Siddha the forehead; Santāna the earrings; Kiraṇa the red-coloured gems; Vātula the garments — "and all other auxiliary and supplementary Tantras, the hair on the body. Thus the body of the Great Queen should be contemplated on under the form of the Tantras."

Sastry's footnote supplies what is missing: "four numbers are left here, as there are twenty-eight Śaiva Āgamas, viz. Sarvokta, Parameśvara, Cintya, Sūkṣma; and for Sahasra, Pragati is substituted." So the printed list gives twenty-three of the twenty-eight and the note names the four omitted.

That is the same procedure the previous nama's Kāmika passage used with worlds, letters, mantras and tattvas, and the two together make 203–206 a single exercise: five enumerations as tissues, and then a canon as limbs. And one of the Āgamas is called Lalitā, which is Her own name at 1000 — it supplies her cheeks.

तन्त्र is worked at 723 स्वतन्त्रा, where three senses are got out of it, and 724 सर्वतन्त्रेशी, where "the Tantras are sixty-four in number" and ईशी means not ruler but promulgator. Twenty-eight Āgamas here and sixty-four Tantras there are different canons, and the text uses both.

207. मनोन्मनी → मनस्-उन्मनी

मनस् = mind (from मन् "to think")
उन्मनी = the mind lifted out of itself, the transmental state (उत् + मनस्)
"Manonmanī — the mind raised beyond mind."

Vigraha: मनसः उन्मनी अवस्था यस्याः सा।

index.html splits this entry mid-sentence, the gloss breaking off after "just below the Brahmarandhra."

The primary reading is a location: "Manonmanī is the eighth place from the centre between the eyebrows, just below the Brahmarandhra; being of that form, she is so called." And Sastry's footnote gives the whole ladder, from Yoginīhṛdaya 1.26: "from the Bhrūmadhya there are eight places — Indu, Rodhinī, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, Unmanī (or Manonmanī) — and each succeeding one is more subtle than those preceding it. The ninth is called Mahābindu."

That ladder is what 113's third scheme and 134's Setubandha both use: meditation "from Indu to Unmanī is Sakalaniṣkala," and "in the supreme abode, Mahābindu, is Niṣkala." So the eight stations above the brow are the middle term of the three-fold scheme, and this nama is the last of the eight.

The Svacchandasaṃgraha then describes what is there, entirely by negation: "there is a Śakti the cause of all causes; above that comes Unmanī. In that centre there is no time or space, no Tattva, no deity — complete freedom, purity, supremacy; what is called Rudravaktra, the mouth of Rudra. This is called the Śakti of Śiva; in it there is neither subject nor object, spotless." The Rudrādhyāya's "salutation to Vāmadeva, supreme excellence" is glossed as naming that Śakti Manonmanī.

The Tripurā Upaniṣad gives the condition: "when the mind, free from attachment to object, fixed on the heart, attains the state of Unmanī, then the supreme abode one reaches."

**And then the Manonmanī mudrā, whose formula is 122 शांभवी's almost word for word**: "by this process the eyes neither close nor open, by which breath is neither inhaled nor exhaled, and the mind is a blank, neither speculating nor doubting — direct that Manonmanī towards me." At 122 the Śāmbhavī mudrā was "the object is within, the sight without closing or opening the eyes is outside." Two namas, eighty-five apart, and the same paradox of eyes neither shut nor open.

The Bṛhannāradīya supplies the definition by collapse: "when the process of meditation, the meditator and the object of meditation are entirely destroyed, then the Unmanī stage arises; consequently he enjoys the ambrosia of wisdom." That triad — meditation, meditator, meditated — is the one Kālidāsa's line at 792 सामरस्यपरायणा requires to be calm before the coequality can be tasted.

And a last reading makes it transitive: "the minds of the devotees are raised to the higher knowledge."

208. माहेश्वरी → माहेश्वरी

माहेश्वरी = belonging to Maheśvara; his consort (vṛddhi derivative of महेश्वर, feminine ङीप्)
"Māheśvarī."

Vigraha: महेश्वरस्य पत्नी माहेश्वरी।

**This opens the महा-run: twenty-seven consecutive namas from here to 234 are built on महा or its derivatives, the longest single-prefix run in the text.** The नि-run it answers was sixty-seven namas of privation; this is twenty-seven of magnitude, and 199's announcement of the qualified form is what licenses it.

index.html splits the entry mid-sentence, the gloss ending "The Śruti" and the body opening "referring to Maheśvara says."

The Śruti quoted is about the praṇava: "it is the Svara, Oṃkāra, which is proclaimed in the beginning of the Vedas and also established at the end, and which is involved in its own nature, indicates him who is supreme Maheśvara." And the point drawn from it is a rank: "here the Śruti declares Maheśvara as transcending the three guṇas."

The Liṅga Purāṇa then distributes the four: "in his dark quality he is called Rudra the destroyer; in his passionate quality the one born from the golden egg, Brahmā; in his pure quality the all-pervading Viṣṇu; devoid of the three qualities he is Maheśvara." So Maheśvara is the nirguṇa fourth above the three guṇa-gods, and the nama makes Her his.

The Vātulaśuddha Āgama adds another reckoning: "Maheśvara as the aggregate of twenty-five Tattvas." That is neither the Śaiva thirty-six of 203 and 906 nor the Sāṃkhya twenty-three-plus-two of 145, but a third count.

Māheśvarī is also one of the three kinds of भावना at 113 and 907 — Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Akṣara — and 918's Sūta Saṃhitā has "one should worship with devotion the Maheśvarī who becomes oneself by one's own spiritual experience."

209. महादेवी → महा-देवी

महा = great; and per the commentary, from a root मह् meaning "to worship"
देवी = a goddess (from दिव् "to shine")
"The Great Goddess."

Vigraha: महती देवी।

The Devī Purāṇa gives two derivations of महा at once, one by size and one by root: "her body is immense and cannot be computed by any measurements; the root मह् means worship — hence she is termed Mahādevī." So महा is both immeasurable and to-be-worshipped, and 580 महनीया takes the second sense alone as a gerundive.

Then the eighth of Śiva's eight forms: "Śiva in his eighth form, that of the moon, is known as Mahādeva; his wife is Rohiṇī, his son is Mercury." The Liṅga and Vāyu Purāṇas are cited.

**That completes three of the eight forms in this text, each with a household.** 112 भवानी gave Bhava the water-form, with Uṣā for wife and Śukra for son; 124 शर्वाणी gave Śarva the earth-form, with Sukeśī and Aṅgāraka; and here Mahādeva the moon-form, with Rohiṇī and Budha. One Purāṇic passage supplying three namas ninety-seven apart, and in each case the nama is the wife's name and the son is a planet — Śukra, Aṅgāraka, Budha, that is Venus, Mars and Mercury.

The eight forms are enumerated at 662 अष्टमूर्तिः, where the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's version is "sun, water, earth, fire, air, ether, the sacrificing Brāhmaṇa, and the moon"; and 883 यजमानस्वरूपिणी turns on the eighth being "sometimes the sacrificer and sometimes Ātman."

And the Padma Purāṇa places her: "Mahādevī is the presiding deity at the Cakratīrtha on the Gaṇḍakī river."

210. महालक्ष्मीः → महा-लक्ष्मीः

महा = great
लक्ष्मीः = Lakṣmī; fortune, prosperity
"Mahālakṣmī."

Vigraha: महती लक्ष्मीः।

Both the dev field and the verse text read महालक्ष्मी, the visarga lost — and the next nama has gained the र् it became, with the verse text additionally putting a space in the wrong place. See the textual note.

Five readings, and the second is an etymology from a demon.

The Padma Purāṇa places her at Karavīra. Or simply महा with Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu's wife. Then the Mailāra Tantra: "Mahala is the name of a Daitya whom she destroyed — hence she is called Mahalasā and Mahālakṣmī, residing on the shore of the western sea at the foot of the Sahya Mountain."

Mahālasā is the wife of Mailāra at 793 कपर्दिनी, "decked with a garland of cowdung cakes," and Mailāra is the Mallāri of 785 — so this is the third appearance of that Mahārāṣṭra form of Śiva and his consort, and here she gets an etymology from a slain demon on the model of 190 दुर्गा.

The Śiva Purāṇa: "the beautiful, azure, all-fascinating supreme Śakti seated on the lap of Śiva is called Mahālakṣmī" — which is 52 शिवकामेश्वराङ्कस्था's posture. The Āyuṣyasūkta identifies Lakṣmī with Pārvatī. And the Mārkaṇḍeya: "Mahālakṣmī is the origin of everything manifested as the three guṇas."

**And Dhaumya's girl-age: "a girl of thirteen years of age is called Mahālakṣmī."** That extends the series to eight — Sarasvatī two (704), Trimūrti three (628), Subhagā five (761), Caṇḍikā seven (755), Śāmbhavī eight (122), Durgā nine (190), Gaurī ten (635), Mahālakṣmī thirteen here. The run is 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13.

211. मृडप्रिया → मृड-प्रिया

मृड = Mṛḍa, Śiva — the gracious (from मृड् "to be gracious"); and per the commentary, happiness, and Śiva in his sattva aspect
प्रिया = dear to; a beloved, a wife
"The Beloved of Mṛḍa."

Vigraha: मृडस्य प्रिया।

The dev field reads र्मृडप्रिया, carrying the र् that belongs to 210's visarga.

"Mṛḍa, happiness; Śiva in his sāttvic quality is called Mṛḍa." And the Mahimnastava: "I bow down to Mṛḍa who predominates in sāttvic nature, for the sake of conferring happiness on men."

So this nama and 208 माहेश्वरी are three namas apart and both place Śiva on the guṇa-scale, but differently: Maheśvara is nirguṇa, above all three, while Mṛḍa is sāttvic, which the Liṅga Purāṇa's own distribution at 208 assigned to Viṣṇu. The text gives two schemes and does not join them.

मृड is one of the words taking the आनुक् augment at Pāṇini 4.1.49, which gives मृडानी at 564 — so the same god's consort is named by a Pāṇinian suffix there and by प्रिया here.

Note on the verse. Seven namas, and the verse divides after three: the last of the सर्व-run, then the first of the महा-run.

206 is the entry to keep. The Kāmika's mapping of the twenty-eight Śaiva Āgamas onto Her body — Kāmika the feet, Bimba the face, Lalitā the cheeks, the supplementary Tantras the body-hair — is the fullest anatomy of a canon in the text, and it stands immediately after 203's five methods of mapping worlds, letters, mantras and tattvas onto Śiva's. Two Kāmika passages in four namas, doing the same thing to two different corpora.

207 is the technical centre. It names the eighth of the eight stations above the brow, gives the whole ladder from Yoginīhṛdaya 1.26, and then supplies a mudrā whose formula is 122 शांभवी's — eyes neither closing nor opening, breath neither in nor out, mind blank.

209 completes three of Śiva's eight forms, each with a wife and a planet for a son. And 210 brings the girl-ages to eight.

Textual note. 205's dev and verse text both read सर्बयन्त्रात्मिका with ब for व. 210 has lost the visarga of महालक्ष्मीः and 211 has gained the resulting र् — in both arrays, with the verse text reading महालक्ष्मी र्मृडप्रिया, the space before the stray र्. That is the second instance in two batches of this fault appearing in the verse text as well as the nama fields, after 154–155. 207's and 208's glosses split mid-sentence.

---

## महारूपा महापूज्या महापातकनाशिनी । महामाया महासत्त्वा महाशक्तिर्महारतिः

*mahārūpā mahāpūjyā mahāpātakanāśinī । mahāmāyā mahāsattvā mahāśaktir mahāratiḥ*

Verse 54, namas 212–218.

212. महारूपा → महा-रूपा

महा = great, supreme
रूपा = form
"She of the great form."

Vigraha: महत् रूपं यस्याः सा।

"Great, supreme form — that is, supreme over the other four forms." And the four are then named from the Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.2: "Puruṣa, O twice-born, is the first form of the supreme Brahman; then the manifested, the five gross elements, and the unmanifested, Pradhāna; and lastly time. The enlightened see the supreme abode of Viṣṇu which transcends these four — Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Vyakta and time. These four forms in their due proportions are the causes of the production of the phenomena of creation, preservation and destruction."

So महा here is a comparative: hers is the fifth form above the four causes. That is the same structure 809 परात्परा uses — "higher than the high" — and the same list 862 कार्यकारणनिर्मुक्ता frees Her from, where कारण is Mūlaprakṛti, that is Pradhāna.

213. महापूज्या → महा-पूज्या

महा = great
पूज्या = to be worshipped, worthy of worship (पूज् with the gerundive यत्)
"The great Object of worship."

Vigraha: महती पूज्या।

The gloss makes it comparative too: "worshipped even by Śiva and others."

And then the Padma and Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇas give a list of sixteen worshippers with sixteen materials, and the pairing is the substance of the entry: Śiva worships by mantra; Brahmā by stone; Viṣṇu by blue stone; Kubera by gold; the Viśvedevas by silver; Vāyu by copper; Vasu by brass; Varuṇa by crystal; Agni by gems; Śakra by pearls; Sūrya by coral; Soma by lapis lazuli; the planets by tin; the Rākṣasas by adamant; the Piśācas and the Mātṛgaṇas by iron. "According to some, Agni, Śukra and Sūrya worship only idols made of gems."

So the material is graded by the worshipper's rank, from a mantra with no material at all down to iron — which is 974 बिन्दुतर्पणसंतुष्टा's principle applied to substances rather than to castes: one rite, and the fitness of the doer determines what he brings. And the highest is not the costliest but the immaterial, which is 918 चैतन्यार्घ्यसमाराध्या's doctrine of nirādhāra worship.

पूज्या stood alone at 803, where the gloss was one clause.

214. महापातकनाशिनी → महा-पातक-नाशिनी

महा = great
पातक = a sin, a crime — literally what causes to fall (from पत् "to fall")
नाशिनी = she who destroys
"The Destroyer of great sins."

Vigraha: महापातकानि नाशयतीति।

पातक is what makes one fall, so a great sin is named by its consequence — and the महापातक are the five capital crimes of the Smṛtis.

The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "the highest expiation of all sin, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, is brought about by the remembrance of the feet of the supreme Śakti." That is the same passage 555 कलिकल्मषनाशिनी and 743 both draw on. And the Brahmottarakhaṇḍa raises the stakes: "briefly, I will tell you in half a verse that the worship of Śiva destroys the crime of even a hundred murders of Brāhmaṇas."

The Arthāratnāvalī then specifies: "great sins, the killing of heroes." And Bhāskararāya points to the practical apparatus — "in the Saubhāgyaratnākara and other works, in the chapter on expiation, the rules for repeating the Pañcadaśī mantra according to the nature of the crime are explained." So the remedy is metered: so many repetitions per offence.

That is the same leniency as 167 पापनाशिनी, where mantra-repetition covers continual sinning and devotion to Durgā covers heinous crime; 743, where standing in water and repeating the Pañcadaśī 1,008 times expiates everything; and 194's promise two verses back.

215. महामाया → महा-माया

महा = great
माया = illusion, the power of appearance; and per one lexicon, pride and compassion
"The great Illusion."

Vigraha: महती माया।

"Because she causes confusion to Brahmā and the rest" — so the illusion's victims are the gods, not men.

The Mārkaṇḍeya: "that divine Devī, Mahāmāyā, forcibly draws away the minds of even the sages and leads them into confusion."

Then the Kālikā Purāṇa's passage, which is the longest and bleakest account of embodiment in the text, and it reads as a biography of a single life: "she who always makes him devoid of knowledge — the being who possessed knowledge of his real nature whilst in the womb — compelled him to take birth by means of the winds of delivery, and leads him by reason of the saṃskāra of previous births to desire of food and the rest; thence into confusion, egotism, doubt; subsequently compelling him again and again to undergo the stages of anger, distress and greediness; and then leads him into sensual desire, and causing anxiety day and night, producing sometimes pleasure and sometimes pain, is called the Mahāmāyā. Hence she is the ruler of the Universe."

The stages listed there — confusion, egotism, doubt, anger, distress, greediness, desire, anxiety — are almost exactly the impediments the नि-run's nine pairs destroyed at 156–175: moha, ahaṃkāra, saṃśaya, krodha, lobha, rāga, cintā. So the same list is what She imposes here and what she removes there, and the two passages are forty namas apart.

And a lexical alternative reverses the nama: "according to one lexicon, māyā means pride and compassion; then Mahāmāyā means full of compassion."

Māyā is Her name at 716 माया, where Bhāskararāya's own definition is privative — "the energy which obscures what is plain" — while the Devī Purāṇa's is productive, "the instrument of marvellous actions." And 703 सर्वमोहिनी's Kūrma Purāṇa has Śiva call Māyā "dear to me, infinite, by which this world is bewildered."

216. महासत्त्वा → महा-सत्त्वा

महा = great
सत्त्वा = being, existence; strength; the first of the three guṇas; and per the Viśva, four further senses
"She of great being."

Vigraha: महत् सत्त्वं यस्याः सा।

The commentary is entirely lexical: "sattva — existence, strength, quality and being." And the Viśva: "sattva means quality of friends and the rest, strength, things, and reality."

सत्त्व is the first of the three guṇas, whose equilibrium She is at 763 त्रिगुणात्मिका; and सत् is the being she bears at 661 सदसद्रूपधारिणी and is devoid of at 680. Here the abstract is simply magnified.

217. महाशक्तिः → महा-शक्तिः

महा = great
शक्तिः = power, energy; and per Yādava, strength, strife, and a weapon
"The great Energy."

Vigraha: महती शक्तिः।

Both the dev field and the verse text read महाशक्ति, the visarga lost — and unlike 210 the following nama has not gained a र्, so the letter is simply dropped, with the verse text putting a space where the sandhi should be.

"Because she is the energy of the whole universe." Yādava is cited for the word's range: "śakti — power, strength, strife, weapon."

And the Viṣṇu Purāṇa supplies a simile that makes the energy graded by distance: "just as the brightness of a fire is spread abroad, so the energy of the supreme Brahman spreads throughout the whole world; just as the brightness is greater or less according to the distance of the fire, so it is with this energy, O Maitreya."

That is a physical model rather than a metaphysical one, and it is unusual. The text's other statements of the same identity — 572 पराशक्तिः, 199 सर्वशक्तिमयी, and the Liṅga Purāṇa's "whatever energy is attributed to any substance, that is Devī" — make the power co-extensive with substance; this one makes it fall off with range.

218. महारतिः → महा-रतिः

महा = great
रतिः = delight, pleasure, love (from रम् "to delight"); also Rati, Kāma's wife
"The great Delight."

Vigraha: महती रतिः।

Two readings, and the second is a marriage: "because sages find more delight in her than in worldly things. Or Mahāratī, the wife of Mahākāma." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (54).

Mahākāma is the काम of 796 कामरूपिणी and 589 कामकोटिका, both of which read the word as Paramaśiva; and 233 महाकामेशमहिषी fifteen namas on makes Her Mahākāmeśvara's queen in as many words. So the same marriage is stated twice in one verse-group, once through Rati's name and once through महिषी.

रम् is the root of आरामा at 878 स्वात्मारामा, where Her self-delight requires dividing into two, and of रम्य at 38.

Note on the verse. Seven namas, all on महा, and three of them read the prefix as a comparative rather than an intensive.

212 makes Her form supreme over the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's four causes; 213 makes Her worshipped "even by Śiva"; 218 makes the sages' delight in Her greater than in the world. So महा is doing the work of परात् in these three, which is 809's construction.

213 is the entry to keep. Sixteen worshippers matched to sixteen materials, from Śiva with a mantra down to the Piśācas with iron — the material graded by rank, and the highest offering immaterial. That is the niradhāra doctrine of 132 and 918 stated as a table of precedence.

And 215's Kālikā Purāṇa passage is worth keeping beside 156–175. The stages Māyā drives a soul through — confusion, egotism, doubt, anger, distress, greed, desire, anxiety — are the same list the नि-run's nine pairs had just destroyed, forty namas earlier.

Textual note. 217's dev and verse text both lack the visarga of महाशक्तिः, with a space in its place; unlike 210–211 nothing has gained the र्.

---

## महाभोगा महैश्वर्या महावीर्या महाबला । महाबुद्धिर्महासिद्धिर्महायोगीश्वरेश्वरी

*mahābhogā mahaiśvaryā mahāvīryā mahābalā । mahābuddhir mahāsiddhir mahāyogīśvareśvarī*

Verse 55, namas 219–225.

219. महाभोगा → महा-भोगा

महा = great
भोगा = enjoyment, possession; also extension, expanse; also a serpent's coil (from भुज् "to enjoy," or भुज् "to bend")
"She of great extension."

Vigraha: महान् भोगः यस्याः सा।

"Extension, that is, of the earth and the rest. Or bhoga, joy, wealth and the rest."

भोग carries both senses because two roots have collapsed into one stem — भुज् to enjoy and भुज् to bend, so a serpent's coil and a king's revenue are the same word. The extension-sense is the one the gloss takes first, which is unexpected in a महा-run about magnitude of quality.

भोग is also the word behind Bhogadā, the eighth Kalā, whose colophon closes the seventh hundred at 700.

220. महैश्वर्या → महा-ऐश्वर्या

महा = great
ऐश्वर्या = lordship, dominion, sovereignty (vṛddhi derivative of ईश्वर)
"She of great dominion."

Vigraha: महत् ऐश्वर्यं यस्याः सा।

The dev field reads महेश्वर्या, which would be महा + ईश्वर्या by guṇa; the standard reading is महैश्वर्या, महा + ऐश्वर्य by vṛddhi (Pāṇini 6.1.88 वृद्धिरेचि). The gloss, "the great ruler," suits either, so this is a variant rather than a plain fault — but the vṛddhi form is what the abstract noun ऐश्वर्य requires.

index.html carries 219's gloss and body on this nama, with the stranded heading "220. The great ruler, (Maheśvaryā)" appearing in both fields. So no commentary proper to it survives.

ऐश्वर्य is the word of 952 शाश्वतैश्वर्या, where the same vṛddhi joint is correctly formed and where Bhāskararāya's alternative division makes the five corpses Her seat.

221. महावीर्या → महा-वीर्या

महा = great
वीर्या = heroism, valour, might; and per the Viśva, semen, glory and strength
"She of great might."

Vigraha: महत् वीर्यं यस्याः सा।

The commentary is one citation: "according to the Viśva, vīrya means semen, might, glory, and strength."

The first of those senses is the one that connects. शुक्ल, semen, is the seventh dhātu at 531 शुक्लसंस्थिता; and 572 पराशक्तिः divides nine bodily substances between Śiva and Devī, with "marrow, semen, breath and vitality" from Śiva. So वीर्य belongs to Him on that reckoning and is Hers here.

वीर्य is what gladdens Her at 76 विशुक्रप्राणहरणवाराहीवीर्यनन्दिता, where the might is Vārāhī's.

222. महाबला → महा-बला

महा = great
बला = strength, power; and per the Viśva, ten other things, among them a crow
"She of great strength."

Vigraha: महत् बलं यस्याः सा।

The Viśva's list is given whole and it is one of the strangest in the text: "bāla — small, taste, colour, soul, corpulence, army, Balarāma, one of the daityas, Mahābali, and a crow."

**And Bhāskararāya takes the last.** "If bāla means a crow, Bhuśuṇḍa and the rest — crows — became great by the grace of Devī." The Yogavāsiṣṭha's address from Bhuśuṇḍa is then quoted: "we are twenty-one crows, brothers, sons of Caṇḍa; by us, together with our sisters, the great Devī was worshipped for a long time; after finishing her contemplation Devī herself, wishing to bless us, favoured us — thus we were liberated."

So महाबला is read as "she by whom the crows were made great," and the crows are twenty-one brothers with sisters, liberated by long worship. It is the only place in the thousand where the beneficiaries of Her grace are birds, and it belongs with the leniency-citations: 213's Piśācas worship her with iron, 167's Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa makes virtuous the actions of "those devoid of varṇa and āśrama," and here crows are liberated.

Bhāskararāya marks the division: "13th verse divides 40 names."

223. महाबुद्धिः → महा-बुद्धिः

महा = great
बुद्धिः = intelligence, understanding (from बुध् "to wake, to know")
"She of great intelligence."

Vigraha: महती बुद्धिः यस्याः सा। or महती बुद्धिः यतः प्राप्यते।

Both dev field and verse text read महाबुद्धि, the visarga lost — the first joint of a three-nama chain; see the textual note.

Two readings, and the first is epistemic: "when the intelligence is directed towards her, nothing remains to be known," with Chāndogya 6.1 — "which, when known, the whole universe is known." Or the compound is read as a source: "from whom one obtains the highest intelligence."

That Chāndogya formula is what 203 सर्वमयी requires and what 149 नित्यबुद्धा asserts through Bṛhadāraṇyaka's "knowledge is inseparable from the knower."

बुद्धि is also the second tattva, Mahat, which 862 कार्यकारणनिर्मुक्ता identifies as कार्य, "the tattva-series beginning with Mahat," and 145 निर्विकारा as the first of Sāṃkhya's seven productive productions. So महाबुद्धि can be read as naming that tattva, and neither reading here does.

224. महासिद्धिः → महा-सिद्धिः

महा = great
सिद्धिः = attainment, accomplishment; a superhuman power (from सिध् "to succeed")
"She of great attainment."

Vigraha: महती सिद्धिः यस्याः सा।

The dev field reads र्महासिद्धि — it has gained the र् of 223's visarga and lost its own.

"This is to be explained in two ways, as in the preceding instance" — so both readings of 223 carry over: she has the siddhis, and she is their source.

"The Siddhis are the well-known superhuman powers, viz. aṇimā and the rest." And then the Skanda Purāṇa's alternative set of eight, which is entirely psychological where the standard eight are physical, and worth having whole:

"The first Siddhi is the manifestation of taste when no object is tasted; the second is the overcoming of the pairs of opposites; the third is the being both superior and inferior, that is, he perceives no difference of degree; the fourth is indifference towards the conditions of pleasure, pain and life; the fifth, called Viśoka, without sorrow, is the illuminator of the body; the sixth is steadfastness in penance and contemplation of the Supreme Self; the seventh is the power of unrestrained motion through space; and the eighth is the power of suspension, uniform equilibrium."

Only the seventh of those is a physical power. The other seven are states of indifference, and the third — perceiving no difference of degree — is 178 निर्भेदा as an attainment rather than an attribute.

225. महायोगीश्वरेश्वरी → महा-योगिन्-ईश्वर-ईश्वरी

महा = great
योगिन् = a yogin, an adept
ईश्वर = a lord, a master — योगीश्वर, a master of yogins
ईश्वरी = mistress, sovereign lady
"Sovereign of the great lords of yogins."

Vigraha: महतां योगीश्वराणाम् ईश्वरी।

Sandhi at two joints: योगिन् + ईश्वर → योगीश्वर (the न् dropping and the vowels contracting, इ + ई → ई by 6.1.101); and ईश्वर + ईश्वरी → ईश्वरेश्वरी (अ + ई → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87). The dev field reads र्महायोगीश्वरेश्वरी, carrying the र् of 224's visarga.

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

The compound stacks ईश्वर on itself — mistress of the masters of the masters of yoga — which is the same doubling 684 राजराजेश्वरी uses with राज and 809 परात्परा with पर. Three namas in the text built by repeating a superlative.

ईश् for the sixteenth turn, and this is the only nama where the root appears twice.

Note on the verse. Seven namas, all on महा, and the two halves differ in what they magnify: 219–222 are extension, dominion, might and strength — quantities; 223–225 are intelligence, attainment and rank.

222 is the verse's find. The Viśva's ten senses of बाल include a crow, and Bhāskararāya takes it, so that the nama becomes "she by whom the crows were made great" — with the Yogavāsiṣṭha's twenty-one crow-brothers, sons of Caṇḍa, liberated by long worship. It is the only place in the thousand where Her grace reaches birds.

224's Skanda Purāṇa set of eight siddhis is also worth keeping, because seven of the eight are states of indifference rather than powers, and only the seventh is physical.

Textual note. 219's gloss and body are duplicates, and 220 carries them too, so no commentary proper to 220 survives; the stranded heading "220. The great ruler" appears in both fields. 220's dev reads महेश्वर्या where the abstract requires महैश्वर्या by vṛddhi.

And 223–225 form **the longest sandhi mis-division chain in the text**: 223 महाबुद्धिः has lost its visarga; 224 महासिद्धिः has gained the resulting र् and lost its own; 225 has gained that one. Three namas, two joints, and the verse text carries it too, with a space before each stray र् — महाबुद्धि र्महासिद्धि र्महायोगीश्वरेश्वरी. Every earlier chain of this kind was two namas long, and only 615–617 was three; that one was confined to the nama fields, and this is in both arrays.

---

## महातन्त्रा महामन्त्रा महायन्त्रा महासना । महायागक्रमाराध्या महाभैरवपूजिता

*mahātantrā mahāmantrā mahāyantrā mahāsanā । mahāyāgakramārādhyā mahābhairavapūjitā*

Verse 56, namas 226–231.

226. महातन्त्रा → महा-तन्त्रा

महा = great
तन्त्रा = a Tantra
"The great Tantra."

Vigraha: महत् तन्त्रं यस्याः सा।

"Great because they confer many results. The Tantras are Kulārṇava, Jñānārṇava and others."

227. महामन्त्रा → महा-मन्त्रा

महा = great
मन्त्रा = a mantra
"The great Mantra."

Vigraha: महान् मन्त्रः यस्याः सा।

"The Mantras are Bālā, Bagalā and others" — the same two examples 199 सर्वशक्तिमयी and 840 मूलविग्रहरूपिणी use for the śaktis, so the goddess and her formula are named by one word.

228. महायन्त्रा → महा-यन्त्रा

महा = great
यन्त्रा = a yantra, a diagram
"The great Yantra."

Vigraha: महत् यन्त्रं यस्याः सा।

The three namas are glossed separately and then together, and the joint reading is where the substance is.

First the list: "the Yantras are Pūjācakra, Padmacakra, Amṛtaghaṭa, Merulinga and the rest" — which fills out the "ghaṭa, argala" of 205.

**Then all three are read as naming one Tantra, one mantra and one yantra**: "Or — Tantra, the Svatantra Tantra; Mantra, Śrīvidyā; and Yantra, Siddhavajra. These are the best belonging to Devī."

And each gets its warrant. The Svatantra "is so called because it is dependent on no other," and the Tantra itself explains why it was asked for: "O great one, all Tantras formerly described by you only create mental confusion, since they depend on one another; therefore, O Lord, relate to me my independent Tantra." The answer: "listen, I will tell you the Kādimata Tantra, which is complete and depends upon no other, to be concealed with all care."

Saundaryalaharī 31 is then quoted for the same point in the other direction: "the Lord of beings stood after promulgating sixty-four Tantras, each of which confer some Siddhi; then again, by your intentness, your Tantra which is independently capable of conferring all objects of desire was brought to this world." So the sixty-four of 724 सर्वतन्त्रेशी are each partial, and this is the one that is not.

For the mantra: "Śrīvidyā is the best of mantras," supported by "a thousand other sayings which can be found in the Kulārṇava and the Śaktirahasya." And for the yantra, the Nityā Tantra with a warning: "he who regards as equal to the other Vidyās the Vidyā of Lalitā, also this mantra with other mantras, and this yantra with other yantras — that man is only bewildered in mind."

That last is worth setting against 149 नित्यबुद्धा's accommodation of the Jaina Tīrthaṅkaras, 770 प्रियव्रता's acceptance of vows to any deity, and 206's "many paths merge in thee alone as the rivers do into the ocean." The text is generous about where worship goes and severe about equating this vidyā with others.

स्वतन्त्र is nama 723, where the same word gets three senses and the third — mutual dependence with Śiva — undercuts the first.

229. महासना → महा-आसना

महा = great
आसना = a seat, a throne (from आस् "to sit")
"She of the great seat."

Vigraha: महत् आसनं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: महा + आसना → महासना (आ by 6.1.101), so the long आ is a joint and not a महा-.

The seat is identified: "the thirty-six tattvas beginning with the earth, which are her seat." And the Devī Bhāgavata: "the divine one remains dwelling in all Tattvas."

That makes the nama 203 सर्वमयी's claim as a posture rather than a constitution — she consists of the tattvas there and sits on them here. And it is the third of the text's seat-namas whose furniture is a hierarchy: 58 पञ्चब्रह्मासनस्थिता makes the five Brahmās the couch, with Sadāśiva for the plank; 947 पञ्चप्रेतमञ्चाधिशायिनी makes them corpses; here it is thirty-six categories.

The thirty-six are 906–907's count, 203's sinews and bones, and 801's body.

230. महायागक्रमाराध्या → महा-याग-क्रम-आराध्या

महा = great
याग = a sacrifice, an offering (from यज्)
क्रम = a sequence, a method, a step (from क्रम् "to step")
आराध्या = to be worshipped (आ + राध्)
"She who is worshipped by the method of the great sacrifice."

Vigraha: महायागक्रमेण आराध्या।

Sandhi: क्रम + आराध्या → क्रमाराध्या (आ by 6.1.101).

The Mahāyāga is identified: "the worship of sixty-four yoginīs from Akṣobhya, who are the part of Brāhmī and the rest; other rites give some results, this gives a quicker result."

So the sixty-four are the eight śaktis of each of the eight mothers, which is exactly the arithmetic 237 महाचतुःषष्टिकोटियोगिनीगणसेविता will spell out seven namas on. The Śāśvata is cited for क्रम: "krama — energy, arrangement, moving and shaking."

And then the second identification, with a restriction: "or Mahāyāga, explained in the Bhāvanopaniṣad 84, is most secret and is to be accomplished by Śivayogins alone. This method is given in detail in the commentary and in the Prayogavidhi compiled by us."

The Bhāvanā Upaniṣad is the same text 918 चैतन्यार्घ्यसमाराध्या quotes for "wisdom is arghya," so the rite reserved for Śivayogins here and the wholly internal worship there come from one source.

आराध्या for the tenth time in the text.

231. महाभैरवपूजिता → महा-भैरव-पूजिता

महा = great
भैरव = Bhairava, the terrible — Paramaśiva; and per the syllabic reading, भ creation, र preservation, व destruction
पूजिता = worshipped (from पूज्)
"She who is worshipped by Mahābhairava."

Vigraha: महाभैरवेण पूजिता।

The identification comes first: "Bhairava is Paramaśiva, the accomplisher of creation, preservation and destruction."

**And then the syllabic derivation, which distributes the three functions over the three letters**: "each letter in the word Bhairava has a meaning — भ, creation, bharaṇa; र, preservation, ramaṇa; and व, destruction, vamana, literally to vomit."

That is the same threefold that namas 1–3 carry one clause each of Taittirīya 3.1.1 for, and that 232 will make Her the witness of. Here it is inside one word.

The Padma Purāṇa then makes Śiva the worshipper: "Śambhu, the origin of the Universe, worships the beneficent Devī who is the Śakti of the Mantras, holding the rosary in his hand, by means of Nyāsa." And the Lalitopākhyāna supplies the reason he might: "the Lord Mahāśambhu, by a great sacrifice, caused Lalitā to become manifest from the altar of the fire of consciousness."

That is nama 4 चिदग्निकुण्डसंभूता's origin-story with a different sacrificer. At 4 the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa has Indra build the altar and the Devas offer their own flesh; here it is Mahāśambhu's sacrifice. Two accounts of the same emergence, and the text gives both without choosing.

Note on the verse. Six namas, all on महा, and the first four are a set.

226–228 name the three instruments and then identify the best of each — the Svatantra or Kādimata Tantra, the Śrīvidyā, the Siddhavajra yantra. The Svatantra's own request for itself is the best passage: all other Tantras "only create mental confusion, since they depend on one another." And Saundaryalaharī 31 makes the sixty-four each partial against this one.

229 then seats Her on the thirty-six tattvas, which is 203's claim as furniture.

230–231 are the two worship-namas, and 231's syllabic reading of भैरव — भ creation, र preservation, व destruction — puts inside one word the threefold that namas 1–3 needed three Upaniṣadic clauses for.

---

## महेश्वरमहाकल्पमहाताण्डवसाक्षिणी । महाकामेशमहिषी महात्रिपुरसुन्दरी

*maheśvaramahākalpamahātāṇḍavasākṣiṇī । mahākāmeśamahiṣī mahātripurasundarī*

Verse 57, namas 232–234.

232. महेश्वरमहाकल्पमहाताण्डवसाक्षिणी → महेश्वर-महा-कल्प-महा-ताण्डव-साक्षिणी

महेश्वर = Maheśvara, Śiva
महाकल्प = the great cycle; here the great dissolution
ताण्डव = the violent dance of Śiva
साक्षिणी = a witness — literally she who is with the eye (स + अक्षि, with इन् and ङीप्)
"She who witnesses Maheśvara's great dance at the great dissolution."

Vigraha: महेश्वरस्य महाकल्पे महाताण्डवस्य साक्षिणी।

At six members this is the longest nama in the batch, and the reason She alone can witness is that nothing else is left: "Mahākalpa, the great dissolution. The great dance is caused by the fact that the Self alone remains, and having become bliss after the universe has been drawn into it; as at that time there is no other beside herself, she is the witness."

That is 571 महाप्रलयसाक्षिणी's argument verbatim — "as Brahmā, Viṣṇu and the rest perish at the time of the dance of Śiva at the great dissolution, she alone is the witness of that dance" — and the two namas are 339 apart with the same claim and the same word.

The Pañcadaśīstava is quoted, and it is the same verse 571 quotes: "your form alone is excellent, having the noose, elephant hook, bow of sugarcane and the arrow of flowers, and witnessing the dance of the axe-bearing Parabhairava started at the time of his drawing the universe into himself." Bhāskararāya cross-refers to namas 8–11 for the four weapons — so the equipment of the text's opening verse is in her hands at the end of the world, as it is again in the derivation of Her name at 1000.

The Devī Bhāgavata adds her part in it: "this Devī, at the dissolution, having drawn the universe into herself, sports, having absorbed the souls of all beings in her own body." So she is not only the witness but the container, which is 637 विश्वगर्भा's claim and 858's, where at the pralaya She holds the souls "in the form of vāsanās."

**And then the Vasiṣṭha's description of the dance, which is the only onomatopoeia in the text.** Bhāskararāya notes it runs to more than a hundred verses and quotes the conclusion: "having a garland on his breast, having the wings of an eagle as his head-ornament, filled with red liquor, holding in his hand the great horn of the buffalo of Yama, dancing to the sounds of his music — such as *Dhimba, Dimba, Sudimba, Paca, Paca, Jhamya, Jhamya, Prajhamya* — may Bhairava with his spouse called Kālarātrī, who delights in dissolution, worshipped, protect you."

Drum-syllables in a Sahasranāma commentary are unique to this passage, and the figure — Bhairava drinking from Death's own buffalo-horn — is the most concrete image of the dissolution the text contains.

233. महाकामेशमहिषी → महा-कामेश-महिषी

महा = great
कामेश = Kāmeśa, Kāmeśvara
महिषी = a queen, a consecrated chief wife; literally a she-buffalo (महिष)
"The Queen of Mahākāmeśvara."

Vigraha: महाकामेशस्य महिषी।

index.html has effectively no commentary — the body holds only the stranded heading.

महिषी is the technical term for the consecrated first queen in a royal rite, not merely a wife — so the nama places Her in a coronation rather than a marriage. And the word is the feminine of महिष, a buffalo, whose bull is the Mahiṣa She slays at 3's Devī Purāṇa citation and at 199's Lakṣmītantra. So the queen's title and the demon's name are one word, and the buffalo-horn of the previous nama is a third use of it in two namas.

Kāmeśvara is Her consort at 52 शिवकामेश्वराङ्कस्था and wholly won at 54 स्वाधीनवल्लभा; रति, his other wife's name, was 218's second reading fifteen namas back.

234. महात्रिपुरसुन्दरी → महा-त्रिपुर-सुन्दरी

महा = great
त्रिपुर = the three cities; and per the commentary, the measurer, the measuring and the measured
सुन्दरी = the beautiful one
"The great Tripurasundarī."

Vigraha: महती त्रिपुरसुन्दरी।

The whole commentary is one clause, and it is **a fifth etymology of Tripurā**: "Tripurā, city of the three — that is, the measurer, the measuring, and the thing measured."

Those three are pramātṛ, pramāṇa and prameya, the logicians' triad of knowledge — so the three cities become the three factors of cognition. And the text's four other accounts do not agree with it or with each other: at 875 त्रिपुरमालिनी she is the sixth enclosure's deity; at 905 बैन्दवासना the Jñānārṇava concludes "as Devī is joined to the three Bindus, she is named Tripurā"; at 976 त्रिपुराम्बिका the three are the states of the jīva, or cities, or Vāmā and the rest; at 997 श्रीमत्त्रिपुरसुन्दरी they are Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra as the three parts of Śiva's body, which makes Tripura masculine. Five accounts across five namas, and 626 त्रिपुरा stands bare with none.

This reading is the one that makes Her the epistemic triad, and it belongs with 981 ज्ञातृज्ञेयस्वरूपिणी, where She is knower and known, and with 207's Bṛhannāradīya line that Unmanī arises when "meditation, meditator and the object of meditation are entirely destroyed."

997 श्रीमत्त्रिपुरसुन्दरी is this nama with श्रीमत् for महा, 763 apart.

Note on the verse. Three namas, and each is long.

232 closes the महा-run's cosmology and it does so with the text's one piece of onomatopoeia — the drum-syllables Dhimba, Dimba, Sudimba — and its most concrete dissolution-image, Bhairava with the horn of Yama's buffalo. It is also 571 महाप्रलयसाक्षिणी twice over: same argument, same Pañcadaśīstava verse, same sugarcane bow.

233 uses महिषी, the consecrated queen's title, whose masculine is the buffalo-demon She kills — and the buffalo has just appeared as a drinking-horn in the previous nama.

And 234 gives Tripurā a fifth etymology, the measurer, the measuring and the measured, which none of the other four resembles.

Textual note. 233's body holds only its own stranded heading.

---

## चतुःषष्ट्युपचाराढ्या चतुःषष्टिकलामयी । महाचतुःषष्टिकोटियोगिनीगणसेविता

*catuḥṣaṣṭyupacārāḍhyā catuḥṣaṣṭikalāmayī । mahācatuḥṣaṣṭikoṭiyoginīgaṇasevitā*

Verse 58, namas 235–237.

235. चतुःषष्ट्युपचाराढ्या → चतुःषष्टि-उपचार-आढ्या

चतुःषष्टि = sixty-four
उपचार = a service, an attendance, a ritual act — literally a moving-towards (उप + चर्)
आढ्या = rich in, endowed with
"She who is rich in the sixty-four services."

Vigraha: चतुःषष्ट्या उपचारैः आढ्या।

Sandhi: चतुःषष्टि + उपचार → चतुःषष्ट्युपचार, the इ becoming य् before a dissimilar vowel (Pāṇini 6.1.77 इको यणचि); and उपचार + आढ्या → उपचाराढ्या (आ by 6.1.101).

"These are enumerated by the holy Paraśurāma in his Kalpasūtras 4.5." And then eight more, from other Tantras, listed in full: "wearing the flowers after dedication; making religious endowments; worshipping the guru; worshipping the devotees; worshipping the Śaiva books; sacrificing in the fire of Śiva; receiving water which has washed the feet of Śiva; and performing the full ceremony called Prāṇāgnihotra. All these seventy-two are explained in our work" — the Varivasyārahasya, in the Pūjā chapter.

So the sixty-four become seventy-two, and Bhāskararāya's own eight include worshipping books and worshipping other devotees. 950 पञ्चसङ्ख्योपचारिणी gives the domestic five instead — scent, flowers, incense, lamp, food — so the text has a five-fold and a sixty-four-fold reckoning of the same word.

उपचार is उप + चर्, service understood as approach — the same root as आचार at 194 and 98.

236. चतुःषष्टिकलामयी → चतुःषष्टि-कला-मयी

चतुःषष्टि = sixty-four
कला = an art, a science; a part
मयी = made of, consisting of
"She who consists of the sixty-four arts."

Vigraha: चतुःषष्टिः कलाः मयं यस्याः सा।

**The sixty-four are enumerated in full, and the list is Bhāskararāya's own compilation** — he names his sources and then signs it: "these are differently enumerated in the Śārṅgadharīya, Śrīdhara's Kathākośa and in the Lakṣmīpīṭhikā, and these are set forth by us."

The list: knowledge of the eighteen scripts; writing and reading them quickly (two); knowledge of different languages; composing verses in them; gambling; the four Vedas and four auxiliary Vedas (eight); the twice-six auxiliary sciences (twelve); Tantra; Purāṇa; Smṛti; poetry; rhetoric; drama; the six magical acts — pacifying, controlling, attracting, causing enmity, ruining, killing; the seven arts of opposing the effects of motion, water, sight, fire, weapons, speech and semen; training elephants, horses, chariots and men (four); divination by bodily marks; gymnastics; cooking; power over snakes; the three classes of instrument, Suṣira, Ānaddha and Ghana; creating illusion; dancing; singing; alchemy; knowledge of gems; thieving; knowledge of the pulse; and disappearance.

"Thus laid down by the poet Bhāskara, the sixty-four sciences, after examining them."

Two things are worth marking. The list is not a list of accomplishments in the polite sense: it contains gambling, thieving, killing by magic, and disappearance alongside the four Vedas and rhetoric. And the three instrument-classes named — suṣira hollow, ānaddha skin-covered, ghana solid — are three of the four 857 गानलोलुपा gives for what गान covers, the fourth being तत, stringed.

कला carries seven senses in this text, and this is the arts-sense, which 794 कलामाला and 611 कलात्मिका also allow. And an alternative: "or kalā, works — the sixty-four of them are enumerated in the Vāmakeśvara Tantra."

237. महाचतुःषष्टिकोटियोगिनीगणसेविता → महा-चतुःषष्टि-कोटि-योगिनी-गण-सेविता

महा = great — and per the commentary, "nine times multiplied"
चतुःषष्टि = sixty-four
कोटि = a crore, ten million
योगिनी = a yoginī
गण = a host, a band
सेविता = attended, served (from सेव्)
"She who is attended by the great sixty-four crores of hosts of yoginīs."

Vigraha: महाभिः चतुःषष्टिकोटिभिः योगिनीगणैः सेविता।

The arithmetic is given twice, and it works.

First the derivation of sixty-four: "the Brāhmī and other seven divinities each has eight Śaktis, Akṣobhya and the rest, who are the parts of them; hence there are sixty-four. Each has a crore of bands." That is the Mahāyāga's set at 230, seven namas back — "the worship of sixty-four yoginīs from Akṣobhya, who are the part of Brāhmī and the rest."

Then the Tantrarāja for the placement: "in Lalitā's nine cakras, O beloved one, there are many Śaktis, numbering to sixty-four crores."

**And then महा is read as a multiplier**: "the Great means nine times multiplied. Amongst the nine cakras, from Trailokyamohana, in each cakra separately there are sixty-four crores of yoginīs dwelling. The total number comes to 5 abja, 7 arbuda and 6 crores of Śaktis."

That total is exact: sixty-four crores in each of nine enclosures is 576 crores, which is five abja, seven arbuda and six crores on the reckoning of abja as a hundred crores and arbuda as ten. So महा here is not an intensive at all but the figure nine, and the nama's number is the product.

This is the second place the text puts arithmetic inside a nama. 529 सर्ववर्णोपशोभिता derives the thousand petals from fifty letters counted forwards and backwards times ten, with उप itself read as ten by Vararuci's rule; 749 मृत्युदारुकुठारिका reads दारु as twenty-eight by the same rule; and 732 नामपारायणप्रीता gets 20,737 names out of the alphabet. Four namas whose commentary is a calculation.

Trailokyamohana is the first of the nine enclosures, which 245 चक्रराजनिकेतना names again eight namas on; and the nine Tripurā-deities of those enclosures are 787, 875, 976 and 978. Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (58).

Note on the verse. Three namas, all on सixty-four, and the number does different work in each: sixty-four ritual services which become seventy-two; sixty-four arts which Bhāskararāya himself compiled; and sixty-four crores of yoginīs which महा multiplies by nine.

236 is the entry to keep for its own sake. A list of sixty-four accomplishments that runs from the four Vedas to thieving, killing by magic and disappearance, compiled by the commentator from three named sources and signed "thus laid down by the poet Bhāskara."

And 237 is the fourth nama in the text whose commentary is a piece of arithmetic, and the only one where महा turns out to mean nine.

---

## मनुविद्या चन्द्रविद्या चन्द्रमण्डलमध्यगा । चारुरूपा चारुहासा चारुचन्द्रकलाधरा

*manuvidyā candravidyā candramaṇḍalamadhyagā । cārurūpā cāruhāsā cārucandrakalādharā*

Verse 59, namas 238–243. The verse table has no row for this verse; see the closing note.

238. मनुविद्या → मनु-विद्या

मनु = Manu, first of the twelve holders of the vidyā
विद्या = knowledge; a mantra of a female deity
"The Vidyā of Manu."

Vigraha: मनोः विद्या।

**This nama and the next name the first two of the twelve recensions of the Pañcadaśī, and the list is given here in full** — the second of two places in the text where it appears: "the Śrīvidyā is of twelve kinds, differentiated according to the twelve devotees: Manu, Candra, Kubera, Lopāmudrā, Manmatha, Agastya, Agni, Sūrya, Indra, Skanda, Śiva and Krodhabhaṭṭāraka. These are the devotees of Devī." The descriptions of each mantra "are given in the Jñānārṇava."

**And the list does not match the one at 812 परमन्त्रविभेदिनी.** There the twelve are "Manu, Candra, Kubera, Lopāmudrā, Manmatha, Agastya, Agni, Sūrya, **Nandi**, Skanda, Śiva and Krodhabhaṭṭāraka." Eleven names agree; the ninth is Nandi at 812 and **Indra** here.

Nandi is the better-supported reading, because 733 नन्दिविद्या is a nama of this text — "the Vidyā worshipped by Nandi," and its whole commentary is those five words, which the twelve-fold scheme is what explains. There is no *Indravidyā* among the thousand names. So the ninth holder is Nandi and this passage has substituted Indra, or Sastry's text has.

**Four of the twelve are namas.** Manu here, Candra at 239, Nandi at 733, and Lopāmudrā at 647 लोपामुद्रार्चिता — where Bhāskararāya's second reading makes Lopāmudrā the mantra itself and prescribes performing all ceremonies "by the third division." Manmatha in the list is the bodiless Kāma whom the Aruṇa Upaniṣad makes the Ṛṣi of the vidyā at 586; Agastya is Lopāmudrā's husband; and Krodhabhaṭṭāraka is Durvāsa, whose Lalitāstavaratna is quoted at 686 and 785.

Sastry's note also records that "the MS. has a different enumeration of the sixty-four Kalās" than the printed list at 236.

239. चन्द्रविद्या → चन्द्र-विद्या

चन्द्र = Candra, the moon; second of the twelve
विद्या = a mantra
"The Vidyā of Candra."

Vigraha: चन्द्रस्य विद्या।

The whole body is the word repeated.

The two namas are the only place in the thousand where two of the twelve stand adjacent, and their order follows the list exactly — Manu first, Candra second. So the verse begins by reciting the head of the scheme its previous appearance at 812 gave whole.

240. चन्द्रमण्डलमध्यगा → चन्द्र-मण्डल-मध्य-गा

चन्द्र = the moon
मण्डल = a disc, an orb
मध्य = the middle
गा = going, abiding (from गम् "to go")
"She who abides in the centre of the moon's disc."

Vigraha: चन्द्रमण्डलस्य मध्ये गच्छतीति।

Three readings, ascending in secrecy.

The physiological: "because Kuṇḍalinī breaks through the moon in the pericarp of the thousand-petalled lotus." That moon is where 879 सुधासृतिः locates the nectar and 528's dhyāna places Yākinī, and the breaking-through is the sequence 99–106 traces.

The liturgical: "in the evening prayer, the ceremony to obtain long life, Devī should be contemplated in the moon's disc."

Then the Śiva Purāṇa's division of the two luminaries between them: "I am residing in the head of fire, you are residing in the head of the moon; thus the world, consisting of fire and moon, is upheld by us." That splits the pair which 22 ताटङ्कयुगलीभूततपनोडुपमण्डला makes both of Her earrings and 762 त्र्यम्बका two of Her three eyes.

**And a last line: "the secret meaning is, the moon's disc is the Śrīcakra itself."** So the nama's centre is the Bindu, which makes it 245 चक्रराजनिकेतना five namas on and 996 श्रीचक्रराजनिलया.

241. चारुरूपा → चारु-रूपा

चारु = beautiful, pleasing, agreeable
रूपा = form
"She of beautiful form."

Vigraha: चारु रूपं यस्याः सा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

चारु opens three consecutive namas, and this is the plainest of the three. The word is also one of the senses ललिता carries at 1000, where the Śabdārṇava gives it simply as "beautiful."

242. चारुहासा → चारु-हासा

चारु = beautiful
हासा = a smile, laughter (from हस् "to laugh")
"She of the beautiful smile."

Vigraha: चारुः हासः यस्याः सा।

One quoted half-line and then a refusal: "*the moon is thy sweet smile.* This saying means there is a certain stage of consciousness, prabodha, which gives the highest bliss, and which should be known from a Guru alone; thus a commentator explains this name."

**That is the seventh of the text's guru-referrals**, after the weapon-bījas at 11, the light of the two samādhis at 907, the five M's at 948, the mudrā's use in correcting mantra-errors at 982, the Nityā cosmology at 775, and Kāmakalā at 713 — where the referral is itself the nama's content and Yoginīhṛdaya 1.3 is quoted for why: "into this world this secret was handed down from ear to ear."

Her smile is faint at 924 दरस्मेरमुखाम्बुजा, where दर read as fear makes it the one face still smiling at the dissolution; and it lights the whole face at 602 दरहासोज्ज्वलन्मुखी; and it drowns Kāmeśa's mind at 28.

243. चारुचन्द्रकलाधरा → चारु-चन्द्र-कला-धरा

चारु = beautiful; and per the commentary, neither waxing nor waning
चन्द्र = the moon
कला = a digit, a crescent; and per the commentary, the eternal Kalā called Sadākhyā
धरा = bearing, wearing (from धृ "to hold")
"She who wears the beautiful crescent moon."

Vigraha: चारुं चन्द्रकलां धरतीति।

The dev field carries two empty daṇḍas after the nama.

The first reading takes चारु privatively and makes the crescent permanent: "cāru, neither waxing nor waning; candrakalā is the everlasting Kalā, Sadākhyā, in the form of consciousness." So the moon's digit is fixed, which is what a crescent worn as an ornament is — it does not change — and Sadākhyā is a named kalā rather than a phase.

The second makes Candrakalā a person, from the Devī Bhāgavata Book III: "Candrakalā is the daughter of a king. To her in a dream Devī appeared and told her to marry a prince by name Sudarśana, who was worshipping Devī" — the Kāmarājabīja. "According to that story the meaning is: cāru, rightly; dharā, supports."

So the nama becomes "she who rightly supported Candrakalā," and the ornament becomes a princess. That is the same move 865 लीलाविग्रहधारिणी makes with लीला — the play becomes Līlā, queen of Padmarāja in the Yogavāsiṣṭha — and 966 लीलाविनोदिनी, where the story is told.

कला carries its moon-sense here, as at 612 कलानाथा, where कलानाथ is an ordinary word for the moon.

Note on the verse. Six namas, and the verse divides three and three.

238–239 recite the head of the twelve-fold scheme of vidyās, and 238's list of the twelve differs from 812's at one place — Indra here for Nandi there, and Nandi is right, because 733 नन्दिविद्या is a nama and no *Indravidyā* is.
