240 then makes the moon's disc the Śrīcakra "in the secret meaning," so the three lunar namas of this verse and the Bindu of 245 are one place.

And 242 is the text's seventh guru-referral, for a stage of consciousness the commentator will not name.

---

## चराचरजगन्नाथा चक्रराजनिकेतना । पार्वती पद्मनयना पद्मरागसमप्रभा

*carācarajagannāthā cakrarājaniketanā । pārvatī padmanayanā padmarāgasamaprabhā*

Verse 60, namas 244–248.

244. चराचरजगन्नाथा → चर-अचर-जगत्-नाथा

चर = moving, animate (from चर् "to move")
अचर = unmoving, inanimate
जगत् = the world — literally "the moving"
नाथा = mistress, protectress (from नाथ् "to be master")
"Mistress of the animate and inanimate worlds."

Vigraha: चराचरस्य जगतः नाथा।

Sandhi at both joints: चर + अचर → चराचर (आ by 6.1.101), and जगत् + नाथा → जगन्नाथा, the त् assimilating in nasality before न् (Pāṇini 8.4.45) — the same rule that gives श्रीमन्नगर- at 56.

The whole surviving body is one word, "worlds," with the verse marker (59) before it.

The compound has a joke in it that the text does not remark on: जगत् is itself "the moving," from गम्, so चराचरजगत् is the moving-and-unmoving moving-thing. 935 जगद्धात्री sets the same word against धात्री, the bearer, so that "one compound holds restlessness and support together."

नाथा is the word of 612 कलानाथा and, as दण्डनाथा, of 70; and the animate-inanimate pair is 890 विश्वग्रासा's food, "all things animate and inanimate," and 753's.

245. चक्रराजनिकेतना → चक्र-राज-निकेतना

चक्र = a wheel, a disc — here the Śrīcakra
राज = king, chief — चक्रराज, the king of cakras
निकेतना = a dwelling, an abode (नि + कित्, or नि + केत)
"She whose dwelling is the royal Cakra."

Vigraha: चक्रराजः निकेतनं यस्याः सा।

"The nine cakras beginning with Trailokyamohana are the only dwelling place of Devī."

चक्रराज is the word of 68 चक्रराजरथारूढसर्वायुधपरिष्कृता, where the Cakrarāja is Her war-chariot in the Bhaṇḍāsura campaign, and 996 श्रीचक्रराजनिलया, where the abode is read as identity — "the Śrīcakra is the body of Śiva and Devī," so "just as the jīva resides in the body, so they reside in the Śrīcakra." A vehicle at 68, a dwelling here, a body at 996.

निकेतन is a fifth word for Her abode, after निलया seven times, स्था many, आसन at 229 and निष्ठा at 573.

246. पार्वती → पार्वती

पार्वती = daughter of the mountain (vṛddhi patronymic of पर्वत, "mountain," feminine ङीप्)
"Pārvatī."

Vigraha: पर्वतस्य दुहिता पार्वती।

index.html's gloss and body are duplicates and hold six words: "the daughter of Mount Himavat."

The commonest of all Her names gets the shortest entry in the batch — six words, where 190 दुर्गा got two etymologies and two cities, and 633 उमा got five divisions. And the text names her father four ways elsewhere: शैलेन्द्रतनया at 634 by title, धरसुता at 956 by the root धृ, "the bearer," 130 शातोदरी's alternative by his hundred caves, and 210's Āyuṣyasūkta by identifying her with Lakṣmī.

पर्वत is also the mountain of disease at 748 रोगपर्वतदम्भोलिः.

247. पद्मनयना → पद्म-नयना

पद्म = a lotus
नयना = an eye (from नी "to lead" — that which leads)
"The Lotus-eyed."

Vigraha: पद्मे इव नयने यस्याः सा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

नयन is the eye named from नी, to lead, so it is the organ that guides — a different figure from अक्षि, लोचन and ईक्षण, the text's three other words for it. And नी is the root of नायिका at 56, the leader of the city.

The lotus-eye is 805 पुष्करेक्षणा, where the compound inverts entirely and becomes "she beholds him with compassion," Viṣṇu asleep on the banyan leaf being Puṣkara; and 558 कमलाक्षनिषेविता, where the lotus-eyed is Viṣṇu and He is the worshipper. Her eyes are otherwise fish at 18, wide at 936, fawn-like at 561, and long and faintly moving at 601.

248. पद्मरागसमप्रभा → पद्म-राग-सम-प्रभा

पद्म = a lotus
राग = colour; also passion — पद्मराग, the ruby, "lotus-coloured"
सम = equal to, like
प्रभा = radiance, lustre (प्र + भा)
"She whose radiance is like the ruby's."

Vigraha: पद्मरागस्य प्रभया समा प्रभा यस्याः सा।

Two readings, and the second dissolves the compound: "or padma, lotus; rāga, red; and prabhā, colour."

Then Kalyāṇacaraṇa's line, which redirects the nama: "protect, O Kuṇḍalinī, whose colour is like the paste of saffron." And the conclusion: "hence this name refers to Amṛta Kuṇḍalinī also."

So the ruby-red becomes the kuṇḍalinī's saffron, and the nama joins the sequence at 107–111 — where 107 तटिल्लतासमरुचिः makes her radiance a lightning-creeper and 111 बिसतन्तुतनीयसी finer than a lotus fibre, both on Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.13.2, which gives "saffron-coloured" among its epithets. This nama's second reading is that verse's colour.

पद्मराग is the stone of 14, where the Garuḍa Purāṇa recommends the kuruvinda variety because it "confers love, prosperity, and devotion to Hari," and of 23, where a ruby mirror is outdone by Her cheek. So Her sixth red, and the count is now coral at 891, the young sun's rose at 922, bandhūka at 964, pomegranate at 560, the china rose at 766, safflower at 37, cochineal at 41, a thousand rising suns at 6, and ruby here — with 49 सर्वारुणा gathering them and 937 विरागिणी denying that any is hers.

Note on the verse. Five namas, and the batch closes on names and colours rather than on doctrine.

245 gives the Śrīcakra as Her only dwelling and names its first enclosure, which 240's "secret meaning" has just identified with the moon's disc — so the two namas five apart put her in one place by two routes.

246 is worth marking for its brevity. Pārvatī, the most familiar of all her names, gets six words, where the text spends paragraphs on Umā, Durgā and Tripurā.

And 248 closes by turning a gem-colour into the kuṇḍalinī's saffron, which sends the reader back to 107–111.

Textual note. 244's body holds one word. 246's gloss and body are duplicates. 247 has no body.

---

Textual note for verses 51–60.

**The structural finding is the hinge at 199.** Bhāskararāya opens that nama with "the text now sets forth her qualified form, saguṇa" — so the sixty-seven privatives from 132 to 198, with the doxography at 136–151 and the nine impediment-pairs at 156–175, are the negative determination he announced at 133, and everything from 199 is the positive. The सर्व-run of verse 52 and the **twenty-seven-nama महा-run from 208 to 234** — the longest single-prefix run in the text — are that positive half.

**A fifth colophon, and it is the one that makes the kalā-rule secure.** Nama 200 सर्वमङ्गला carries: "thus ends the third Kāla, called Dhāmrika, with the second hundred." The four already known — 700 Bhogadā/seventh, 800 Viśva/eighth, 900 Bodhinī/ninth, 1000 Dhāriṇī/tenth — all fall in a contiguous stretch at the end, so the pattern that the kalā-number runs one ahead of the hundred it closes was a local generalisation. This confirms it seven hundred namas earlier: third kalā, second hundred. Five of the ten division-points survive.

**The twelve vidyās are listed twice and the lists disagree.** 812 परमन्त्रविभेदिनी gives the ninth holder as **Nandi**; 238 मनुविद्या gives **Indra**. Nandi is right, because 733 नन्दिविद्या is a nama of the thousand and there is no *Indravidyā*. Four of the twelve are namas: Manu at 238, Candra at 239, Nandi at 733, Lopāmudrā at 647.

**A fifth etymology of Tripurā**, at 234: "the measurer, the measuring, and the thing measured" — the epistemic triad. It agrees with none of the four at 875, 905, 976 and 997, and 626 त्रिपुरा stands bare with none of the five.

**Two Kāmika anatomies in four namas.** 203 सर्वमयी gives five methods of meditating on Śiva as a body — 224 worlds as hair, 50 letters as skin, 7 crore mantras as blood, mantra-words as flesh and vessels, 36 tattvas as sinew and bone. 206 सर्वतन्त्ररूपा then maps the twenty-eight Śaiva Āgamas onto Her body limb by limb, Kāmika the feet through Vātula the garments, with the supplementary Tantras for body-hair; Sastry's footnote names the four omitted from the printed list.

**Sandhi mis-division: the longest chain in the text, and the second batch running in which the fault appears in the verse text as well as the nama fields.** 223 महाबुद्धिः loses its visarga, 224 महासिद्धिः gains the र् and loses its own, 225 gains that one — three namas, two joints, and the verse reads महाबुद्धि र्महासिद्धि र्महायोगीश्वरेश्वरी with a space before each stray र्. Only 615–617 was three namas long before, and that was confined to the nama array. The same batch also has 210–211 (महालक्ष्मी र्मृडप्रिया, in both arrays) and 217, which loses its visarga with nothing gaining the र्.

**Letter fault:** 205 सर्बयन्त्रात्मिका for सर्वयन्त्रात्मिका, ब for व, in both arrays. **Variant:** 220's dev reads महेश्वर्या where the abstract ऐश्वर्य requires महैश्वर्या by vṛddhi.

**Duplicate and displaced fields:** 219–220 share one gloss and body, with 220's own heading stranded in both, so no commentary proper to 220 survives. 246's gloss and body are duplicates. 207's and 208's glosses split mid-sentence. 233's body holds only its own heading. 243's dev carries two empty daṇḍas.

**And the verse table has no row for verse 59.** Verses 59 and 60 are merged into a single row labelled 60, whose text carries `।। ५९ ।।` where the boundary falls. Read correctly, verse 59 is namas 238–243 and verse 60 is 244–248. That is the second instance of a merged verse-row, after verses 138 and 139 — and in both cases the row takes the *later* number and buries the earlier one inside the text.

**The girl-ages reach eight** with 210 Mahālakṣmī at thirteen, so the series runs 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13 across eight namas.

**Three of Śiva's eight forms now have households**, each named by his wife and each with a planet for a son: Bhava the water-form with Uṣā and Śukra at 112, Śarva the earth-form with Sukeśī and Aṅgāraka at 124, Mahādeva the moon-form with Rohiṇī and Budha at 209 — Venus, Mars and Mercury.

**Empty or near-empty bodies, seven of fifty-six:** 197, 220 (by duplication), 225, 233, 241, 244, 247. For a stretch this long that is good preservation, and the substantial commentary is concentrated at 199, 203, 206, 207, 208, 210, 213, 215, 222, 228, 232, 236 and 237.

## पञ्चप्रेतासनासीना पञ्चब्रह्मस्वरूपिणी । चिन्मयी परमानन्दा विज्ञानघनरूपिणी

*pañcapretāsanāsīnā pañcabrahmasvarūpiṇī । cinmayī paramānandā vijñānaghanarūpiṇī*

Verse 61, namas 249–253.

249. पञ्चप्रेतासनासीना → पञ्च-प्रेत-आसन-आसीना

पञ्च = five
प्रेत = a corpse, one departed — literally gone forth (प्र + इ "to go")
आसन = a seat, a couch (from आस् "to sit")
आसीना = seated (आ + सद् "to sit")
"She who is seated on the couch of five corpses."

Vigraha: पञ्चप्रेतासने आसीना।

Sandhi at both joints: प्रेत + आसन → प्रेतासन and आसन + आसीना → आसनासीना (आ by 6.1.101 both).

**And here the doctrine behind the image is given, which 947 पञ्चप्रेतमञ्चाधिशायिनी states without explaining.** The gloss first: "the five — Brahmā and the rest — when deprived of their respective Śaktis such as Vāmā, are incapable of action; hence, deprived of their power, they become corpses."

Then the Jñānārṇava's dialogue, and Devī asks the question herself: "O great Īśāna, tell me of the five corpses and their cause. How are they imperishable and eternal, and yet lifeless?" The Lord answers: "you have fitly questioned me, O Beneficent one. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara and Sadāśiva — these are the five corpses; they are always motionless. The activity of Brahmā manifested as creation should be known as Vāmā Śakti; devoid of it, Brahmā is certainly a corpse. Śiva in himself has no activity. Wherefore activity belongs to Śakti. Pure Sadāśiva becomes a motionless corpse, O Dear one, without Śakti; O Devī, he is incapable of doing anything."

So प्रेत is not a term of abuse but a technical consequence: a god without his śakti has no activity, and what has no activity is a corpse. The image at 947 — where the four are legs, Sadāśiva the mattress and Maheśāna the pillow, on the Bhairavayāmala and Saundaryalaharī 91 — is that argument made furniture. And 648 लीलाक्ल‍ृप्तब्रह्माण्डमण्डला puts it comparatively in Bhāskararāya's own verse: "even Śiva is powerless to create, preserve or destroy Brahmā, Viṣṇu and other gods, but, O mother, the regulation of the universe is but sport to you."

The five are also the couch at 58 पञ्चब्रह्मासनस्थिता, where they are alive and Sadāśiva is the plank; the chain of command at 995 on Saundaryalaharī 24; and here they are dead. Three postures for one set, and the reason is supplied only here.

250. पञ्चब्रह्मस्वरूपिणी → पञ्च-ब्रह्म-स्व-रूपिणी

पञ्च = five
ब्रह्म = a Brahman — one of the five
स्व = own
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying
"She whose very form is the five Brahmans."

Vigraha: पञ्च ब्रह्माणि स्वरूपं यस्याः सा।

The nama answers the last: the five are corpses at 249 and Her form here, so what is inert as itself is active as Her.

Three enumerations of the five, and they do not agree.

The Tripurasiddhānta gives the cosmological set: "the unconditioned Brahman, by the play of the Māyā in itself, becomes Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara and Sadāśiva. Thus by name only, Brahman is in five forms." Those are 249's corpses.

Or the Śaiva five faces: "Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva and Sadyojāta." Those are the five from which the twenty-eight Āgamas issue at 287, thirty-seven namas on.

Or the Liṅga Purāṇa's psychological set, which is a different kind of list altogether: "Jīva, Prakṛti, Buddhi, Ahaṃkāra and Manas; the senses — ear, skin, eyes, tongue, nose; and the subtle elements are the forms of the five Brahman," with the note that the five tanmātras are the causes creating the five gross elements.

Then the Sūta Saṃhitā 4.14.2 on why one becomes five: "the one Śiva, characterised by existence, knowledge and the rest, without change, pure, becomes five by his own Śakti" — that is, "by the Śaktis of creation, preservation and the rest, he becomes Sadyojāta and the rest."

The Garuḍa Purāṇa supplies a Vaiṣṇava five: "Viṣṇu, although one, becomes five — Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha and Nārāyaṇa." And Śaṅkarācārya's verse distributes Her: "when you sport as a man you become the five persons; your casual talk becomes the three Vedas; O mother, a glance of your eyes becomes the sun, and your sweet smile the moon."

That last is the same distribution 240 चन्द्रमण्डलमध्यगा quotes from the Śiva Purāṇa — "I am residing in the head of fire, you are residing in the head of the moon" — and 22 makes both luminaries Her earrings.

251. चिन्मयी → चित्-मयी

चित् = consciousness (from चित् "to perceive")
मयी = made of, consisting of
"She who consists of consciousness."

Vigraha: चित् मयं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: चित् + मयी → चिन्मयी, the त् assimilating in nasality before म् (Pāṇini 8.4.45).

index.html carries 250's gloss and body on this nama, so no commentary of its own survives.

चित् is the middle term of सच्चिदानन्द, which 700 सच्चिदानन्दरूपिणी gives whole and 646 gives without it; and चैतन्य at 918–919 makes it the oblation and the flower. Here it is the substance.

252. परमानन्दा → परम-आनन्दा

परम = highest, supreme
आनन्दा = bliss (आ + नन्द् "to rejoice")
"The supreme Bliss."

Vigraha: परमः आनन्दः यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: परम + आनन्दा → परमानन्दा (आ by 6.1.101). index.html carries 251's gloss here.

Chāndogya 7.23: "what is infinite, that is happiness." The same verse gives भूमा its plenitude at 666 भूमरूपा and duality its impermanence at 667 निर्द्वैता, so one passage supports three namas.

With 251 and 253 this makes the triad cit–ānanda–vijñāna, which is 700's sat–cit–ānanda with knowledge for being.

253. विज्ञानघनरूपिणी → विज्ञान-घन-रूपिणी

विज्ञान = discriminative knowledge; consciousness; and per the second reading, the jīva (वि + ज्ञा)
घन = dense, compact, a mass
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying
"She whose form is concentrated consciousness."

Vigraha: विज्ञानघनं रूपं यस्याः सा।

Two readings, and they differ in whether the mass is of consciousness or of souls.

The first: "vijñāna here means Caitanya; ghana, one essence — that is, one essence of consciousness," and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.12 is cited, where the word विज्ञानघन is explained. That is 574 प्रज्ञानघनरूपिणी's construction exactly, where the same घन is glossed "not contaminated by avidyā" and the simile is a lump of salt whose taste is "neither inside nor outside but everywhere."

The second is the aggregate: "vijñāna, jīva, because in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.4.2 *remaining in vijñāna* is explained as jīva. Ghana, mass — that is, the aggregate of jīvas. Hiraṇyagarbha is the synthesis of the aggregate of the Jīvas," with Praśna 5.5's जीवघन cited for the usage.

So on one reading the nama is a mass of consciousness and on the other a mass of souls, and the second makes Her Hiraṇyagarbha — which 259 तैजसात्मिका and 285 आब्रह्मकीटजननी both identify her with, six and thirty-two namas on. Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (61).

Note on the verse. Five namas, and the first two carry the doctrine.

249 supplies the reasoning that 947 leaves out. The five gods are corpses because activity belongs to Śakti and not to them, and the Jñānārṇava has Devī ask the question and Śiva answer it — "Śiva in himself has no activity." So the couch of corpses is not an insult but a syllogism, and 250 completes it by making the same five Her form.

250 then gives three incompatible sets of five Brahmans — the cosmological, the five Śaiva faces, and the Liṅga Purāṇa's psychological list — plus a Vaiṣṇava five for good measure, and does not choose.

251–253 close on cit, ānanda and vijñāna, and 253's second reading makes the last a mass of souls rather than of consciousness.

Textual note. 251 carries 250's gloss and body; 252 carries 251's gloss. So the displacement runs two namas and 251's own commentary is lost.

## ध्यानध्यातृध्येयरूपा धर्माधर्मविवर्जिता । विश्वरूपा जागरिणी स्वपन्ती तैजसात्मिका

*dhyānadhyātṛdhyeyarūpā dharmādharmavivarjitā । viśvarūpā jāgariṇī svapantī taijasātmikā*

Verse 62, namas 254–259.

254. ध्यानध्यातृध्येयरूपा → ध्यान-ध्यातृ-ध्येय-रूपा

ध्यान = meditation (from ध्यै "to meditate")
ध्यातृ = the meditator (ध्यै + the agent-suffix तृ)
ध्येय = the object of meditation (ध्यै + the gerundive यत्)
रूपा = form
"She whose form is meditation, meditator and the meditated."

Vigraha: ध्यानं ध्याता ध्येयं च रूपं यस्याः सा।

The dev field breaks the compound with a space before रूपा.

The three members are one root taken three ways — the act, the agent-noun, the gerundive — so the compound is built to exhaust the structure of meditation as 981 ज्ञातृज्ञेयस्वरूपिणी exhausts that of knowing, and Bhāskararāya makes the parallel: "she is the triad of knowledge, of the knower and of the object of knowledge."

Yoga Sūtra 3.2 is cited for ध्यान — "contemplation is unison there of the understanding" — and a lexical note: "the root ध्यै, to think, is also called measurement." That last matters, because 234 महात्रिपुरसुन्दरी derives Tripurā from "the measurer, the measuring, and the thing measured," which is this triad in the vocabulary of pramāṇa. So the two namas are twenty apart and name one structure twice.

The collapse of the triad is what 207 मनोन्मनी's Bṛhannāradīya makes the condition of Unmanī — "when the process of meditation, the meditator and the object of meditation are entirely destroyed" — and what 792's Kālidāsa requires before the coequality can be tasted. Here it is affirmed instead of dissolved, which is the text's usual move with a relation: 908 तत्त्वमर्थस्वरूपिणी does it with तत् and त्वम्, 661 with सत् and असत्.

255. धर्माधर्मविवर्जिता → धर्म-अधर्म-विवर्जिता

धर्म = right order, duty, merit; also an attribute; also, per one reading, bondage; also the letter of Śakti
अधर्म = unrighteousness, demerit; also the qualified thing; also liberation; also the letter of Śiva
विवर्जिता = wholly devoid of, excluding (वि + वृज्)
"She who is devoid of both merit and demerit."

Vigraha: धर्मेण अधर्मेण च विवर्जिता।

Sandhi: धर्म + अधर्म → धर्माधर्म (आ by 6.1.101).

The definitions come first and there are four of them, which makes this the fullest treatment of धर्म in the text after 884 धर्माधारा.

The Matsya Purāṇa's etymology: "dharma comes from the root धृ, to bear, and म, in greatness; so as it bears, and as it is a great one, it is called Dharma." Then a functional definition: "that which leads to a desirable result, and taught by teachers as Dharma; and Adharma is the opposite of this." The Saṃvarta Smṛti's customary one, which 884 also quotes: "that conduct which prevails in each country in accordance with tradition and not contrary to the Scriptures is called Dharma." Yājñavalkya's, which ranks the means: "among sacrifice, good conduct, self-control, non-injury, gift and sacred study, the supreme dharma is that in which one perceives the Self by Yoga." And Jaimini 1.1.2's technical one: "Dharma is a purpose as characterised by the scriptural injunctions."

**Then the reason She is free of both, and it is startling**: "Devī is free from these two because the Scriptures are meant only for the ignorant, and the Devas are not subject to them according to the rules applicable to the animal creation" — the Tiryagadhikaraṇa-nyāya.

So injunction and prohibition do not bind Her by the same principle that exempts animals, which is 834 विशृङ्खला's claim — "injunction and prohibition apply only to the ignorant," with the saying about golden and iron fetters — and 182 निष्क्रिया's and 304 हेयोपादेयवर्जिता's fifty namas on. Four namas make the point and only this one supplies the analogy.

Three further divisions. धर्म as bondage and अधर्म as liberation, on a verse of the Nityā Tantra, with the Tripurā Upaniṣad for the consequence: "no end, no origin, no bondage, no aspirant, no desire of liberation, no liberation — that is the truth." Or धर्म as the thing possessing a quality and अधर्म as the quality itself, so "she neither possesses the quality nor is she the quality itself" — which is 178 निर्भेदा's denial of both sides of a relation, and 154's उपाधि.

And a syllabic reading: "dharma indicates the letter of Śakti, and adharma that of Śiva; vivarjita, great increase. The meaning is that Devī is the tendril of the Pañcadaśī. The two letters are explained in the Nityāhṛdaya and should be learned from the teacher."

That is the eighth guru-referral in the text, and it is the first hint of what the next verses do at length: the namas are encoding the mantra letter by letter.

256. विश्वरूपा → विश्व-रूपा

विश्व = all, the universe; and technically, the jīva in the waking state, manifested through the gross elements
रूपा = form
"She whose form is the universe."

Vigraha: विश्वं रूपं यस्याः सा।

**This is the longest single commentary in the Sahasranāma, and it is a systematic treatise rather than a gloss.** Bhāskararāya announces its scope first: "by nineteen names indicating the difference between Jīva and Īśvara, the text proceeds to praise Devī under both forms." So 256 to 274 are one continuous exposition, and this nama carries its theory.

**The order of creation** comes first, in one sentence: "the first manifestation is darkness, Tamas; the next is that of Mahat; then that of the threefold egotism; next the five subtle elements beginning with sound. Among these are the five energies of knowledge and the five energies of action; the former five individually generate the five senses and collectively the Antaḥkaraṇa; the latter five generate individually the five organs of action and collectively the Prāṇas. The sound and the other four subtle forces generate the five gross elements."

**Then the three vehicles and their two levels.** "The Caitanya manifested through the gross, subtle and causal vehicles is respectively termed Viśva, Taijasa and Prājña; these manifested ones respectively are termed Vaiśvānara, Hiraṇyagarbha and Sūtrātman." So Viśva/Taijasa/Prājña are the individual and Vaiśvānara/Hiraṇyagarbha/Sūtrātman the collective, and Paramātman is a third level: "the Supreme Being manifested in the Antaḥkaraṇa in its causal form is Hiraṇyagarbha; in Prāṇa in its causal form is Sūtrātman; when manifested through these two vehicles without differentiation it is Antaryāmin. These three alone are termed respectively Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra."

**And then the controversy this whole run exists to settle.** "We have here explained the three divisions — the individual jīva, the collective jīva, and Paramātman — according to the opinion of those who follow the Upaniṣads. In this theory they accept only three states, waking, dreaming and sleeping, and three functions, creation, preservation and destruction. In the Tāntric theory the followers of it accept in addition two more states, the ecstatic, Turīya, and the state beyond ecstasy; and two functions, Tirodhāna and Anugraha. Those beings endowed with these two states and their functions, jīva and Īśvara respectively, should also be added. Thus there are five divisions."

So the five states of 256–263 and the five functions of 264–274 are the Tāntric count against the Vedāntin's three, and Bhāskararāya's reconciliation is immediate and unpolemical: "here there is no contradictory theory as between those who hold that there are three or five causes, because this system proceeds from the distinction between the gross and subtle aspects."

**Why the Upaniṣadists do not count the fourth and fifth** is then argued, and the argument is careful. "Since in the sleeping state the Prājña becomes Brahman, he is no longer Jīva; but the Jīva is then not the Supreme One, because it is associated with a trace of avidyā. Hence, because the vehicle of the Jīva in the sleeping state is Kāraṇa, the vehicle of the jīva in the fourth is declared to be Mahākāraṇa. Beyond that, as Śiva Sūtra 3.26 says, *one above it becomes equal to Śiva* — that is, semi-equal to Śiva. Beyond that, as Muṇḍaka 3.1.3 says, *the spotless one attains the highest equality*, where the meaning of highest equality is unity. From this explanation it follows that, owing to the absence in those two states of the full perfection of jīva or of Śiva, they are not separately enumerated by the followers of the Upaniṣads."

And the same reasoning is extended to a fourth case: "similarly the same reason is given for not taking into account the state of swoon," on Vedānta Sūtra 3.2.13 — "in him who is unconscious there is a half union, on account of this remaining."

Two identifications close the theoretical part. "The five vehicles of Jīva may be recognised as the five sheaths" — the kośas of 690 कोशनाथा and 821. And "the Tirodhāna and Anugraha functions of Īśvara and Sadāśiva are otherwise called the producers of bondage and release," with a Śaiva scripture for the pair: "Īśvara the visible one, and Sadāśiva is momentary."

**Then the nama's own gloss**, which is brief: "Viśva, the jīvas in the waking state manifested through the gross elements; and Vaiśvānara is he who is the aggregate of the Jīvas — these two are her forms." Or, taking it from the previous nama: "by 255 is meant that she is inseparable from the Universe; hence this name expresses that Devī is in the form of the Universe," with the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's simile — "just as the plantain tree cannot be seen independently of bark and leaves, likewise the universe, O Lord, is seen depending on you only" — and the Devī Bhāgavata's "I myself am the universe, and there is no other permanency."

A syllabic reading is offered and it is the harshest in the text: "vi, separate; svarūpa, a dog's form — the evolution of human being of Brahman directly is the lowest kind of form, comparable to that of a dog; so inferior service is called svavṛtti, dog's service; the lower human existence is called svarūpa, a dog's form of the devotees; vi, released by means of Devī's grace."

**And then the passage that makes this nama worth the whole batch: the fifteen kalās, the fifteen tithis, and why the Pañcadaśī divides five-six-four.**

The identification first, from the Vāsanāsubhagodaya: "there are fifteen parts from the Darśa to the Pūrṇimā; the sixteenth part is to be known as existence-knowledge-bliss. In the moon's disc there is one Kalā, called Sadā, devoid of growth or decay; the other fifteen are waxing and waning. Though Devī is not separate from any of them, the Kalā called cit — the sixteenth — is termed Tripurasundarī; the others are termed respectively from Kāmeśvarī to Citrā, according to the days of the fortnights."

Then the mantra is folded in: "in the Pañcadaśī Mantra also, which is inseparable from these, there is one syllable which is to be known from the teacher, which is of the form of cit and, by reason of its being contained in the Pañcadaśī, is known as Śrīvidyā. The fifteen syllables known to all the devotees are of the form of Nityās. Thus the moon's disc, Devī, and the fifteen-syllabled Mantra are one."

**And then the arithmetic.** The fifteen fall into three groups of five — Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, Pūrṇā — corresponding to the Vāgbhava group of the mantra. The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.1 is quoted for the names of the fifteen nights of the bright fortnight — "Darśā, Draṣṭā, Darśatā, Viśvarūpā, Sudarśanā; Pyāyamānā, Āpyāyamānā, Pyāyā, Sūnṛtā, Irā; Apūryamāṇā, Pūryamāṇā, Pūrayantī, Pūrṇā, Pūrṇamāsī" — and for the fifteen days: "Saṃjñāna, Vijñāna, Prajñāna, Jānad, Abhijānad; Saṅkalpamāna, Prakalpamāna, Upakalpamāna, Upaklipta, Klipta; Śreya, Vasīya, Āyat, Sambhūta, Bhūta." The Brāhmaṇa itself confirms the assignment at 3.10.10: "these two sections are the names of the days and nights of bright fortnights."

**And here is the point.** "Though the three divisions are here proportioned equally, yet when the tenth day is merged into the eleventh, the latter is treated as part of the tenth — as it is said, *the pure twelfth day is to be observed intact*. Consequently the twelfth day takes the eleventh. So in the mantra, the second division is composed of six letters, whereas the last one has four letters."

So the Pañcadaśī's asymmetrical five-six-four division is explained by the calendrical *vedha* — the overlap by which the tenth tithi absorbs the eleventh, pushing the count. Sastry's note explains the practice: "when the tenth day merges into the eleventh even for a few minutes, that day becomes void; therefore the strict observers of vows on that eleventh day leave out that day and discontinue further ceremony till the twelfth." And Bhāskararāya adds that where no such vedha applies — "in the other mantras of Sūrya and others — the three divisions are equally proportioned," with Lolla's commentary on the Subhagodaya cited for the same conclusion.

**Then the honey-doctrine**, which is the entry's last movement and makes ritual efficacy conditional on the kuṇḍalinī.

The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.13.10: "one who knows the deities who produce honey and saturate the body with it — in him is produced honey from the Baindava. His sacrifices and good works become effective. To him who is ignorant they produce no honey, and his sacrifices and good works become ineffective." And 3.10.10 supplies which is which: "those nights of the bright and dark fortnights are the producers of honey, madhukṛt; their days cause it to flow, madhuvarṣiṇī."

Bhāskararāya's unpacking is explicit about the mechanism: "when the place of Ḍākinī and the other deities is saturated by the waking up of Kuṇḍalinī, by causing the honey to flow in the Sahasrāra, whatever works he does become effective — external actions such as sacrifice become fruitful. In the absence of that flow, the time in which the actions are performed is productive of death of these actions."

The Candrajñāna Tantra states it as a rule with both halves: "of those who are able to produce the flow of honey in the Baindava, and whose bodies are cool by the nectar, the sacrifices and good works become fruitful in course of time. Of those who are devoid of the inner flow, and whose minds continue scorched, death at once terminates all their actions."

So the Vedic rite is efficacious only for one in whom the amṛta is flowing — which is 143 निरुपप्लवा's second reading, where the privative is divided to mean "by whom the abundant flowing of nectar in the body occurs," and 106 सुधासाराभिवर्षिणी and 879 सुधासृतिः.

The last line is the loveliest in the batch. Kālakarṣiṇī, "the destroyer of time," is named; Vaidehī is glossed as the wife of Videha, Kāmeśa; and Saragha means a honey-bee — "Devī is also called a bee because she produces honey." The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.10.10: **"she is bee, fire is the honey."**

The Ḍākinī-deities are the seven cakra-yoginīs of 509–534; the Baindava is 905 बैन्दवासना's and 974's innermost enclosure.

257. जागरिणी → जागरिणी

जागरिणी = wakeful, waking (from जागृ "to be awake")
"The Waking."

Vigraha: जागरः अस्याः अस्तीति जागरिणी।

The Īśvarapratyabhijñā is quoted for the definition: "waking state, dear to all, is the source of an external action through the activity of the senses." And the identification: "the Jīva is called Jāgarin — that is, he who takes upon himself the gross body called Viśva."

So 256 and 257 are the same level twice, once as the vehicle and once as the state, and the four namas following complete the ladder.

258. स्वपन्ती → स्वपन्ती

स्वपन्ती = sleeping, dreaming (present participle of स्वप् "to sleep," feminine)
"The Dreaming."

Vigraha: स्वपिति इति स्वपन्ती।

The Pratyabhijñā again, and the definition is precise about what dream does: "the state of Svapna is objectifying of those visions which are perceived in the mind, due to the perception of ideas latent in the mind." So dream makes objects of what is already mental — which is 176 निर्विकल्पा's विकल्प, "a notion conveyed by mere words but of which there is no object corresponding to reality," given a state to live in.

"Jīva in the state of Svapna is termed Taijasa; its individuality is merged in the subtle body."

259. तैजसात्मिका → तैजस-आत्मिका

तैजस = belonging to light, luminous — the subtle-body level (vṛddhi derivative of तेजस्)
आत्मिका = having the nature of, being the very self of
"She whose nature is Taijasa."

Vigraha: तैजसः आत्मा यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: तैजस + आत्मिका → तैजसात्मिका (आ by 6.1.101).

"Taijasa, called Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the collective form of the Jīvas described above." So this nama gives the collective where 258 gave the individual, and the pair is repeated at 260–261 for sleep.

Hiraṇyagarbha is 253's second reading, "the synthesis of the aggregate of the Jīvas," and 285 आब्रह्मकीटजननी's Brahmā, "a jīva called Hiraṇyagarbha who is the gross form of humanity taken collectively." And 638 स्वर्णगर्भा makes Her Hiraṇyagarbhā outright on the Vāyu Purāṇa.

आत्मिका for the sixth time in the text.

Note on the verse. Six namas, and one of them is the longest entry in the Sahasranāma.

254–255 pair as two triads denied and affirmed: the meditation-triad is Her form, and merit and demerit are not — the second on the ground that scripture binds only the ignorant, "and the Devas are not subject to them according to the rules applicable to the animal creation."

Then 256 carries a treatise. It gives the order of creation, the three vehicles at two levels, the Vedāntin's three states against the Tāntrika's five, the reason the Upaniṣadists omit the fourth and fifth, the identification of the five vehicles with the five kośas, and then the four Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa lists of fifteen day-and-night deities — and out of the calendrical *vedha* by which the tenth tithi absorbs the eleventh it derives the Pañcadaśī's five-six-four division. That is a real explanation of a real asymmetry, and I have not seen the text offer another.

Its closing movement makes Vedic ritual conditional on the kuṇḍalinī: sacrifices are fruitful only for one in whom the honey flows in the Sahasrāra, and for the rest "death at once terminates all their actions." And the Brāhmaṇa's last word is that She is the bee and fire the honey.

257–259 then begin the five states, individual and collective by turns.

Textual note. 254's dev breaks its compound with a space before रूपा.

---

## सुप्ता प्राज्ञात्मिका तुर्या सर्वावस्थाविवर्जिता । सृष्टिकर्त्री ब्रह्मरूपा गोप्त्री गोविन्दरूपिणी

*suptā prājñātmikā turyā sarvāvasthāvivarjitā । sṛṣṭikartrī brahmarūpā goptrī govindarūpiṇī*

Verse 63, namas 260–267.

260. सुप्ता → सुप्ता

सुप्ता = asleep (past participle of स्वप् "to sleep")
"The Sleeping."

Vigraha: सुप्ता निद्रिता।

Śiva Sūtra 1.10 supplies the definition and it is privative: "the state of sleep is incapacity of discrimination, viz. illusion."

Then the argument from recollection, which is the standard one: "one says *I slept happily, I know nothing* — thus one says from recollection. By this saying, three modifications of Avidyā are indicated: ignorance, egoism, and happiness. Sound sleep is that state in which these three exist; such a person is termed Prājña, whose individuality is merged in the causal body."

So deep sleep is not the absence of experience but the presence of three things — not-knowing, still being an I, and being content — which is why it can be reported afterwards. And the happiness in it is what 252 परमानन्दा names at the top of the scale.

261. प्राज्ञात्मिका → प्राज्ञ-आत्मिका

प्राज्ञ = wise, intelligent — technically the causal-body level (प्र + ज्ञा)
आत्मिका = having the nature of
"She whose nature is Prājña."

Vigraha: प्राज्ञः आत्मा यस्याः सा।

"Prājña, Īśvara, who is the collective form of the jīvas above described." So the pair 260–261 is individual and collective as 258–259 was, and the collective at this level is Īśvara — which is why 271 ईश्वरी eleven namas on can be a nama of the functions rather than of rank.

The word is प्र + ज्ञा, so the deepest sleep is named by the fullest knowing, which is the paradox 260's definition depends on: incapacity of discrimination is called *prājña* because nothing is discriminated from Brahman there.

262. तुर्या → तुर्या

तुर्या = the fourth (तुरीय, from चतुर् "four"); the fourth state, ecstasy
"The Fourth."

Vigraha: तुर्या चतुर्थी अवस्था।

**The fourth state is where the Tāntric count exceeds the Vedāntin's, and this is its entry.**

The definition first: "Turya state is the state in which the experience called Śuddhavidyā is acquired, and the result of discrimination of these lower three states and enjoyers thereof." So the fourth is not a further state alongside the three but the standpoint from which the three are seen as three.

The Spanda Śāstra: "he who perceives the object of attainment in the three abodes and the subject thereof, though he participates in it, yet remains unpolluted." Varadarāja: "Turīya is the supreme abode; the participation in that state produces astonishment. Though there are different states, waking and others, this only is realistic for the Yogin."

And Śiva Sūtra 1.7 with the image the whole doctrine turns on: "though there are different states — waking, dreaming and sleeping — real enjoyment exists only in the fourth one. Ecstasy in the fourth state should be allowed, like oil, to permeate the other three."

Oil soaking through cloth is exactly right for a state that is not a fourth item but a saturation of the other three.

"The Jīva is called he who is merged in the great causal body, Mahākāraṇa" — which 256 established: the causal vehicle belongs to sleep, so the fourth needs a Mahākāraṇa above it.

Then the means, from Śiva Sūtra 1.15 with its commentary, and it explicitly sets aside the physical techniques: "*he should project his mind by means of his own thought* — abandoning Prāṇāyāma and other uncertain gross means, by his own knowledge, by the internal experience of astonishment, that is by the aid of Turīya, extinguishing the notion of body, in consequence of merging himself into the fourth state, thus should he enter."

Three further senses close the entry. Turīyā as a deity, per the Śaktirahasya, on Māṇḍūkya 7 — "they consider the fourth calmness, non-dual," the verse 146 निष्प्रपञ्चा and 963 शमात्मिका also rest on. Saundaryalaharī 97: "thou art Turīyā, unlimited mystery, difficult of attainment." And the Tripurā Siddhānta's guru-etymology: "as she is a pleasure to Turīyānandanātha, Devī is known by the name Turīyā."

That last is the same kind of derivation 294 भुवनेश्वरी gets — named for having blessed Bhuvanānandanātha — so two namas thirty apart are derived from the initiatory names of teachers.

Bhāskararāya marks the division: "14th verse divides 40 names."

263. सर्वावस्थाविवर्जिता → सर्व-अवस्था-विवर्जिता

सर्व = all
अवस्था = a state, a condition (अव + स्था "to stand")
विवर्जिता = wholly devoid of, transcending
"She who transcends all the states."

Vigraha: सर्वाभिः अवस्थाभिः विवर्जिता।

Sandhi: सर्व + अवस्था → सर्वावस्था (आ by 6.1.101).

**This is the fifth state, and its whole interest is that it has no name.** "There is a fifth state of Jīvas, but as it has no special name and as it is beyond the Turīya state, it is simply called *beyond Turīyā*; this name indicates the fifth state."

The logic of the privative is then given: "all the states, that is those described above. Because when a man transcends the fourth state, he necessarily transcends the other three. Vivarjitā, transcending — वि, entirely, that is, one does not return to the other states." And it too has both aspects, individual and collective.

Its condition is stability in the fourth: "this fifth state arises from firmness in the fourth one. For it is said: *the supreme state which is beyond the Turīya is only to be attained through a firm hold on the Turīya*." Varadarāja: "the aspirant, by much familiarity with the fourth state, attains the state which transcends the fourth one, and becomes equal to Śiva."

**And then the three Śiva Sūtras describing the man who has attained it, which are the best thing in this verse**: Śiva Sūtra 3.27–29 — "his physical life is a religious observance; his conversation is Japa; his giving is knowledge of Self."

Each is then unpacked. The life: "his physical life is religious and not worldly, because it is the means of worshipping Śiva by searching into his own soul." And Bhaṭṭotpala's prayer is quoted for it — "let me have this body invigorated by the nectar of pure Śakti manifested in me, for the sake of worshipping thee" — the same verse 817 सत्यव्रता uses where the Śiva Sūtra's "cure of the body is a vow" makes bodily health a religious obligation.

The conversation: "his random conversation is Japa, because his mind has grasped the truth," on Yoga Sūtra 1.47–48 — "in the purity of the non-deliberative condition his soul becomes pleased; in that condition knowledge becomes truth-supporting" — with the Śruti "whatever one thinks in his mind, that alone he speaks," so "all his words are in the form of mantras because his thoughts are pure." And the Yogavāsiṣṭha draws the practical consequence: "the wise should always be approached, whether they instruct or not, because their ordinary conversation becomes instruction."

The giving: Kṛṣṇadāsa — "the direct experience of Ātman, described above as consciousness itself, is the knowledge which is his gift, and which with promptness he freely gives."

Saundaryalaharī 27 is cited as saying the same: "the random talk is Japa, his bodily actions are the mudrās." And the Vārtika closes it: "thus one performing the vow herein described, and repeating mantras, and maintaining his physical existence, and equal to Śiva, always being in his own Ātman, devoted to the adoration of Śiva — he alone is called the great Yogin, devoted to the practice of mighty Mantras; he imparts real knowledge to his disciples."

So the fifth state is described entirely by what its holder's ordinary acts have become: living is observance, talking is recitation, giving is teaching. It is the only place the text describes an attainment by its effect on the trivial.

264. सृष्टिकर्त्री → सृष्टि-कर्त्री

सृष्टि = creation, emission (from सृज् "to let loose, to create")
कर्त्री = the doer, she who performs (कृ + तृ, feminine ङीप्)
"The Creator."

Vigraha: सृष्टिं करोतीति सृष्टिकर्त्री।

**Bhāskararāya announces the second half of the nineteen-nama exposition here**: "thus, after the description of the five divisions of Jīvas who are controlled by Avidyā, he proceeds, according to different functions, to describe the five divisions of Īśvara who controls Māyā."

So 256–263 were the five states of the bound soul and 264–274 are the five functions of the ruler, and the two sets are the same fivefold seen from below and from above. Saundaryalaharī 24 is cited — "Brahmā creates the world" — the verse 995 सर्वानुल्लङ्घ्यशासना quotes whole for the chain of command ending at Sadāśiva's assent to Her eyebrows.

And each function is assigned a guṇa: "creation is the function of Īśvara when the Rajas quality predominates."

कर्त्री is the तृ agent-noun of 882 यज्ञकर्त्री, and सृज् is the root of सर्ग.

265. ब्रह्मरूपा → ब्रह्म-रूपा

ब्रह्म = Brahmā, the Creator
रूपा = form
"She in the form of Brahmā."

Vigraha: ब्रह्मा रूपं यस्याः सा।

"The Brahmā, the four-faced one." And the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O Brahman, Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva are the chief Śaktis of Brahman."

So the three gods are Brahman's śaktis, which is 249's argument from the other side — they are corpses without śakti because they *are* śaktis, and a śakti deprived of itself is nothing.

The pattern from here is function-then-god, in pairs: creation and Brahmā, preservation and Govinda, destruction and Rudra, then Tirodhāna with Īśvarī and Anugraha with Sadāśivā. Five pairs, and the last two are the ones the Vedāntin does not count.

266. गोप्त्री → गोप्त्री

गोप्त्री = protectress, preserver (गुप् "to protect" + तृ, feminine ङीप्)
"The Protectress."

Vigraha: गोपायतीति गोप्त्री।

"Sustaining the universe. This is the function of Īśvara when the Sattva quality predominates."

गुप् is the root behind गोप, a cowherd — literally a protector — which 994 आबालगोपविदिता's second reading takes as Sadāśiva.

267. गोविन्दरूपिणी → गोविन्द-रूपिणी

गोविन्द = Govinda, Viṣṇu — and per four competing etymologies, the finder of cows, of the earth, of speech; also Bṛhaspati
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying
"She in the form of Govinda."

Vigraha: गोविन्दः रूपं यस्याः सा।

The Harivaṃśa first, and Nārada's statement makes Viṣṇu a portion of Prakṛti alongside Umā: "the first portion of Prakṛti, the famous Devī called Umā; the second one, the manifested Viṣṇu, the all-pervading protector of the universe, is known as woman."

Then four etymologies of गोविन्द, and each takes गो differently — which the word invites, since it means cow, earth, speech and ray at once, as 605 गोमाता's commentary leaves open.

The Viṣṇu Bhāgavata: "I am the lord of the Devas; thou hast attained to the lordship over the cows — hence in the world men praise thee by the name Govinda." The Mahābhārata's Mokṣadharma: "as I recovered the earth which was taken away and rendered inaccessible, I am praised by devas and by words under the name of Govinda." The Harivaṃśa: "the *gau* stands for sound, which you alone know — hence you are called Govinda by the ascetics." And the Viśvaprakāśa's lexical range: "Govinda means Vāsudeva, cowherd, and Bṛhaspati."

So cows, earth, and speech in three citations, and the fourth makes him the Devas' teacher.

Note on the verse. Eight namas, and the verse spans the seam between the two halves of 256's exposition.

260–263 finish the five states. 262 is where the Tāntric count exceeds the Vedāntin's, and its best image is Śiva Sūtra 1.7's — ecstasy in the fourth state permeating the other three like oil — because it makes the fourth a saturation rather than an item.

263 is the fifth state and has no name of its own, only "beyond the fourth." What it does have is the three Śiva Sūtras on its holder: living is observance, conversation is japa, giving is knowledge of Self. That is the text's only description of an attainment by what it does to ordinary acts.

264 then announces the turn to the five functions, and 264–267 give the first two pairs — creation with Brahmā under rajas, preservation with Govinda under sattva.

---

## संहारिणी रुद्ररूपा तिरोधानकरी ईश्वरी । सदाशिवाऽनुग्रहदा पञ्चकृत्यपरायणा

*saṃhāriṇī rudrarūpā tirodhānakarī īśvarī । sadāśivā'nugrahadā pañcakṛtyaparāyaṇā*

Verse 64, namas 268–274. The verse table has no row for this verse; see the closing note.

268. संहारिणी → सम्-हारिणी

सम् = together, fully
हारिणी = she who takes away, carries off (from हृ "to seize")
"The Destroyer."

Vigraha: संहरतीति संहारिणी।

"Saṃhāra, reducing the universe into atoms. This is the function of Īśvara when the Tamas quality predominates."

The definition is exact and it is what makes the next two functions necessary: saṃhāra reduces the universe to atoms but does not abolish them, so a further function is needed to absorb the atoms, and a fifth to bring them back. The Vedāntin's three-fold scheme stops here.

269. रुद्ररूपा → रुद्र-रूपा

रुद्र = Rudra — and per five competing etymologies, the weeper, the driver-away of sorrow, the senses
रूपा = form
"She in the form of Rudra."

Vigraha: रुद्रः रूपं यस्याः सा।

Five derivations, and they divide on whether Rudra weeps or stops weeping.

The weeping ones first. "Or Rudra, who weeps, रोदति, because the rain which comes at the dissolution of the universe originates from his solar eye in the form of tears," with the Taittirīya Saṃhitā: "he wept; because he wept, he is called the weeper." The Mahābhārata gives it as biography: "to please his parent, the son of Brahmā, the eternal lord of the universe, springing from his forehead, wept loudly and terribly."

The others make him the remover of weeping. The Śivarahasya: "the Lord of Paśus is called Rudra because he drives away sorrow." And the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā spells the syllables: "रु means pain, or the cause of pain; he who drives this out, द्र — Śiva, the supreme cause — is called Rudra."

And a fifth from Chāndogya 3.16.3, which distributes the name: "the Prāṇas, the senses, are the rudras; these cause all this body to cry out."

So the god of destruction is named either from crying or from stopping the cry, and the rain at the dissolution is his tears. That rain belongs with 232's dance, where Bhairava holds the horn of Yama's buffalo, and with 268's reduction to atoms.

पशु here is the bound soul of 133's three paśus, and Rudra their lord.

270. तिरोधानकरी → तिरोधान-करी

तिरोधान = concealment, disappearance (तिरः + धा "to place out of sight")
करी = she who makes
"She who causes disappearance."

Vigraha: तिरोधानं करोतीति।

**This is the fourth function, the first of the two the Vedāntin does not count**, and its definition completes what 268 left over: "Tirodhāna, complete destruction — that is, the absorption even of the atoms into Prakṛti, like the extinction of a light. This is the function of Īśvara when the pure concentrated Sattva quality predominates."

The simile is the right one: a flame does not go anywhere. And the guṇa-assignment is worth noting, because sattva has already been used for preservation at 266 — so the fourth function is sattva "pure and concentrated," a higher grade of the same quality rather than a fourth quality.

Then a personification: "or she is in the form of a Śakti called Tiraskariṇī," with the Tripurasiddhānta — "because you rightly cause the disappearance of all who are not devotees, O fair-faced one, you are called Tiraskariṇī."

तिरोधान is what 273 अनुग्रहदा pairs with as bondage against release, and 256's Śaiva citation makes the pair "the producers of bondage and release."

271. ईश्वरी → ईश्वरी

ईश्वरी = mistress, sovereign lady (from ईश् "to rule")
"The Ruler."

Vigraha: ईश्वरी अधिपतिः।

index.html carries 270's gloss and body on this nama; its own commentary stands at the end of that shared block.

The nama is a technical term here rather than a title, and Bhāskararāya says so: "Īśvara is here used in a special sense, just as Māyā is used in a different sense." The special sense is the agent of the fourth function — Īśvara is the fourth of the five Brahmans, so this nama names him and not lordship in general. Every other ईश्-nama in the text is about rank; this one is about position in a series.

"The Supreme individuality, Parāhantā, is the quality of Īśvara." And the Virūpākṣapañcāśikā's Viśvaśarīra chapter is quoted for its analysis: "lordship, activity, independence, consciousness itself — these are said by wise men to be the successive aspects of the Supreme individuality."

Parāhantā is what 711 makes Her inherent quality, "as we see burning to be the inherent quality of fire only," and what 854, 856 and 576 name three ways. Here it is assigned to a specific one of the five.

The Virūpākṣapañcāśikā is the same text that divides the six paths between Vimarśa and Prakāśa at 991 and assigns Śiva's five śaktis to the five elements at 999.

272. सदाशिवा → सदाशिवा

सदाशिवा = the ever-auspicious — Sadāśiva in the feminine (सदा "always" + शिव)
"Sadāśivā."

Vigraha: सदा शिवा सदाशिवा।

The whole commentary is one clause and it continues the guṇa-scale: "when the superlative Sattva quality predominates she is so called."

So preservation is sattva at 266, tirodhāna is "pure concentrated" sattva at 270, and anugraha is "superlative" sattva here — three grades of one quality for the three functions above rajas and tamas. That is a real scheme and the text nowhere else states it.

Sadāśiva is the fifth of the five Brahmans, the mattress at 947, Her husband at 911 and 709, and the one the Sūta Saṃhitā at 948 ranks above Śiva "because Sadāśiva is with the Mother."

273. अनुग्रहदा → अनुग्रह-दा

अनुग्रह = favour, grace; and technically, the re-manifestation of the universe (अनु + ग्रह् "to grasp")
दा = giving
"The Bestower of grace."

Vigraha: अनुग्रहं ददातीति।

The dev field reads ऽनुग्रहदा. The avagraha marks the अ elided in सदाशिवा + अनुग्रहदा → सदाशिवाऽनुग्रहदा (आ + अ → आ, 6.1.101) — the twelfth instance of that class in the text, and the single mark again correctly signals a short vowel.

**The fifth function, and its definition is a resurrection**: "Anugraha — when, after complete annihilation, the universe again assumes the form of the primordial atoms, the process is called Anugraha. This is the function of Sadāśiva."

So the five run: creation, preservation, destruction to atoms, absorption of the atoms, and re-emergence as atoms. And the closing note at 1000 calls the last two "annihilation and re-manifestation, which belong to no other deity" — which is exactly right, since the Vedāntin's scheme has no room for them.

Then the soteriological reading: "or Tirodhāna and Anugraha mean respectively bondage and release. In this meaning Īśvara and Sadāśiva, who are respectively the external and the internal manifestations, are the causes of bondage and release."

अनुग्रह is also the name of the eighth creation in the Vāyu Purāṇa's list at 296, which is fourfold — inversion, incapacity, perfectness and elation — so the word does cosmological work in two quite different schemes.

274. पञ्चकृत्यपरायणा → पञ्च-कृत्य-परायणा

पञ्च = five
कृत्य = a thing to be done, a function (कृ with the gerundive क्यप्)
परायणा = devoted to, intent upon; also the final resort (परा + अयन)
"She who is devoted to the five functions."

Vigraha: पञ्चकृत्येषु परायणा।

The dev field carries stray daṇḍas.

The Viśva is cited for परायण — "fond of, devoted to, and dependent" — the same gloss 792 सामरस्यपरायणा received.

Then the five functions attested from four sources, and the counts differ. The Mṛgendra Saṃhitā gives four: "that Brahman is one cause of the origin, preservation, destruction and annihilation of the universe." The other Āgamas give five: "the five functions of him are the creation, preservation, destruction, annihilation, and causing the reappearance of the universe, which manifests incessantly."

The Devī Bhāgavata Book 4 makes the gods dependent on Her for the first three: "she creates the universe, she protects, she destroys what she protects at the end of the cycle; she it is who in her three forms bewilders the universe. Brahmā united with her creates the universe, Viṣṇu united with her protects, Rudra united with her destroys. She binds the whole universe and holds it bewildered by the noose of illusion, O king, by the firm noose of *I* and *Mine*. Yogins released from worldly attachments, desiring liberation and seeking after emancipation, worship the beneficent Devī alone."

The noose of *I* and *Mine* there is 161 निरहंकारा and 164 निर्ममा as instruments of binding rather than as qualities denied.

And the Śakti Sūtra gives the five a set of psychological names, which is the entry's oddest touch: "illumination (creation), affection (preservation), dissatisfaction (destruction), planting the seed (causing reappearance), and lamentation (annihilation)." Bhāskararāya refers the reader to the Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, and marks the verse: (64).

Note on the verse. Seven namas closing the nineteen-nama exposition announced at 256.

The five functions and their guṇas are the verse's substance, and the guṇa-assignment is a graded scale the text states nowhere else: rajas for creation, sattva for preservation, tamas for destruction, "pure concentrated" sattva for tirodhāna, and "superlative" sattva for anugraha. So the two functions the Vedāntin omits are assigned higher grades of the quality preservation already uses.

270's definition of tirodhāna is what makes the fourth and fifth necessary at all: destruction reduces the universe to atoms, so something must absorb the atoms and something must bring them back. And its simile — the extinction of a light — is exactly the right one, because a flame that goes out has not gone anywhere.

271 uses ईश्वरी as a technical term for the fourth of the five rather than as a title of rank, which is unique among the text's sixteen ईश्-namas.

Textual note. 271 carries 270's gloss and body, its own commentary standing at the end of the shared block. 273's dev carries the avagraha of the preceding sandhi — twelfth instance of that class. 274's dev carries stray daṇḍas.

## भानुमण्डलमध्यस्था भैरवी भगमालिनी । पद्मासना भगवती पद्मनाभसहोदरी

*bhānumaṇḍalamadhyasthā bhairavī bhagamālinī । padmāsanā bhagavatī padmanābhasahodarī*

Verse 65, namas 275–280.

> **Namas 278–280 spell out the Vāgbhava kūṭa of the Pañcadaśī letter by letter, and 281–284 spell out the other two.** Bhāskararāya gives the key at 280: "this contains the Vāgbhava division of the Kādividyā. Padmāsana indicates the syllable क; Bhaga, ए; and vatī, Kāmakalā, that is ई; Padmanābha, स; and hoda, ह and म — and make ह्रीं. This is the secret meaning." So seven consecutive namas are a cipher for the fifteen-syllabled mantra, and 255 had already announced the method — "dharma indicates the letter of Śakti, and adharma that of Śiva… Devī is the tendril of the Pañcadaśī."
>
> This is the third place the text encodes a mantra in its namas. At 1–3 Bhāskararāya finds the three kūṭas, the Ṣoḍaśīkalā and the Siṃhāsana set concealed in Śrīmātā, Śrīmahārājñī and Śrīmatsiṃhāsaneśvarī; at 8–11 he decodes the four weapon-namas into bīja-syllables and then refuses to give the result, referring the reader to a guru. Here he gives it.

275. भानुमण्डलमध्यस्था → भानु-मण्डल-मध्य-स्था

भानु = the sun (from भा "to shine")
मण्डल = a disc, an orb
मध्य = the middle
स्था = abiding, seated
"She who abides in the midst of the sun's disc."

Vigraha: भानुमण्डलस्य मध्ये स्थिता।

"In the Sandhyā time Devī should be meditated upon in that" — so the nama is a rubric, as 12 निजारुणप्रभापूरमज्जद्ब्रह्माण्डमण्डला was for the morning and 240 चन्द्रमण्डलमध्यगा for the evening. Three namas of the thousand prescribe a time of day.

The scriptural warrant is the golden person: Vedānta Sūtra 1.1.20 explains Chāndogya 1.6.6's "the golden man seen within the sun" as the supreme Lord. And the Kūrma Purāṇa's hymn by Himavat: "I bow down to the form which is in the sun's disc, who is all the Vedas, the one object of knowledge, who fills the different worlds with his brilliance, the cause of the three worlds, known as the supreme Lord."

Then a technical identification, which relocates the disc into the body: "Bhānumaṇḍala is the Anāhata lotus." So the sun is in the heart, which is exactly what 596 रविप्रख्या's nyāsa puts there — "in the heart there is a solar disc, that is the second division of the Mantra" — and 240 puts the moon in the sahasrāra and calls its disc the Śrīcakra.

The golden person in the sun is also 848's fourth division of उदार.

276. भैरवी → भैरवी

भैरवी = the consort of Bhairava (vṛddhi derivative, feminine ङीप्); and per one reading, women collectively
"Bhairavī."

Vigraha: भैरवस्य पत्नी भैरवी।

index.html splits the entry mid-sentence, the gloss ending "Bhairava, all women taken collectively (Bhīru, women)."

Four readings. The consort of Bhairava, that is Paramaśiva — whose syllables 231 महाभैरवपूजिता spells as creation, preservation and destruction.

Or भैरव taken as women collectively, which yields the Liṅga Purāṇa's rule: "meaning is Śiva, words are Devī; day is Śiva and Night is Devī" — and then, after naming Arundhatī, Anasūyā and Śacī each as manifestations of Her, the general conclusion: **"all things indicated by the words in the feminine gender are manifestations of Devī."**

That is a grammatical theology, and it is the widest such claim in the text — wider than 770 प्रियव्रता's acceptance of vows to any deity or 678 भाषारूपा's of praise in any language, because it makes the criterion of Her manifestation a gender-ending. And it bears on the four masculine and two neuter namas the Paribhāṣā counts at 1000: on this rule those six are the anomalies precisely because feminine gender is the mark.

Or a mantra: "in the Tripurācakreśvarī Mantra, in the middle division, when [a syllable] is eliminated, it is known as Bhairavīmantra."

**And Dhaumya's girl-age: "a girl of twelve years old is called Bhairavī."** That brings the series to nine — Sarasvatī two (704), Trimūrti three (628), Subhagā five (761), Caṇḍikā seven (755), Śāmbhavī eight (122), Durgā nine (190), Gaurī ten (635), Bhairavī twelve here, Mahālakṣmī thirteen (210). The run is 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13 — only four, six and eleven missing.

277. भगमालिनी → भग-मालिनी

भग = fortune, dignity, the six attributes; also the female emblem; also the word *bhaga* itself
मालिनी = garlanded, wearing a garland (माला + इन्, feminine ङीप्)
"She who wears the garland of Bhaga."

Vigraha: भगानां मालिनी।

index.html splits the entry mid-sentence again.

Four readings. "Bhaga means six attributes" — the six listed at 279 two namas on — "and Mālinī, possessor."

Or the anatomical sense, with the Liṅga and Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇas for the general rule: "those who have the male emblem are the manifestations of Śiva, and those having the female emblem are the manifestations of Devī." That is 276's grammatical rule restated bodily.

Or "Bhagamālinī is one of the fifteen Nityā deities" — the fifteen of 256's tithi-scheme and 136 नित्या's second reading.

**And then a reading that makes माला a garland of the word itself**: "in this mantra the word Bhaga occurs more frequently, according to the school of Dakṣiṇāmūrti than to those of Tantrarāja and Jñānārṇava. The names of the surrounding deities of that mantra also are preceded mostly by the word Bhaga; hence she has the garland of Bhaga-words."

So the garland is of occurrences of a word in a liturgy — which is a real observation about a text rather than about Her, and the kind of philological note Bhāskararāya makes rarely.

भग is given seven senses at 117, twelve at 761 and the Kośa's twelve at 279; and it is the sun's disc at 715 भगाराध्या.

278. पद्मासना → पद्म-आसना

पद्म = a lotus; and per the readings, Lakṣmī; the demon Padma; the bindu
आसना = a seat; and per the readings, distributing, and killing
"She who is seated on the lotus."

Vigraha: पद्मम् आसनं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: पद्म + आसना → पद्मासना (आ by 6.1.101).

**In the mantra-cipher this nama supplies the syllable क.**

Four readings besides. "The wife of Brahmā" — since the lotus-seat is his. Or the lotus taken allegorically, part by part: "padma, lotus, of it the leaves are Prakṛtis, the filaments are the categories, the stalk is knowledge; such is her seat." That is 805 पुष्करेक्षणा's lotus-cosmology on a different scheme, where the pericarp is earth and the upper petals the Mleccha country.

Or पद्म as Lakṣmī with सन, distributing — and the verse quoted for it is the most domestic in the text, and gives both halves: "O beneficent mother, in whom thou art pleased, that man receives prosperity containing the enjoyment of supreme bliss; his house becomes beautiful and contains much gold, and sitting on his couch he fondles his wife. And when thou art angry, that man becomes supremely miserable, his house appears without beauty, and in it there is much lamentation, and his couch becomes deserted." Sastry notes the wordplay: "according to the peculiar construction of the words *prosperity* and *adversity*, a double meaning is conveyed."

Or पद्म as the demon Padma with सन to kill — "the slayer of the Daitya Padmāsura," which is the same kind of etymology 190 दुर्गा and 210 महालक्ष्मी get.

Or "padma, the bindu," on the Rabhasa: "padma means lotus, numbers called Vyūha, Nidhi and bindu."

279. भगवती → भग-वती

भग = supremacy, righteousness, fame, prosperity, wisdom, discrimination — the six; and per the Kośa, twelve
वती = possessing (मतुप्, feminine ङीप्)
"She who possesses Bhaga."

Vigraha: भगः अस्याः अस्तीति भगवती।

**In the cipher this nama supplies ए and ई** — "Bhaga, ए; and vatī, Kāmakalā, that is ई."

Kāmakalā is nama 712, the single-vowel nama ई, "belonging to the Turīya," where Bhāskararāya refers the reader to a guru for the rest. So the letter that stands as a nama in its own right at 712 is here concealed inside a word.

The six are then given: "the Purāṇas say — the full supremacy, righteousness, fame, prosperity, wisdom, discrimination: these six are called Bhaga." And the Kośa's twelve, which do not include all six: "bhaga means supremacy, magnanimity, wisdom, dispassion, womb, fame, power, effort, desire, righteousness, prosperity, and worldly concerns."

Then two etymologies of the whole word. The Devī Bhāgavata's, which is a list of what she knows: "as she knows the origin and dissolution, the going and coming of beings, knowledge and ignorance, she is called Bhagavatī." And the Śaktirahasya's from the root: "the root भज्, derived from the word worship — she who is worshipped by all Devas, and she blesses them, hence she is called Bhagavatī."

280. पद्मनाभसहोदरी → पद्मनाभ-सहोदरी

पद्मनाभ = the lotus-navelled — Viṣṇu
सहोदरी = a sister — literally one from the same womb (सह + उदर)
"The Sister of Viṣṇu."

Vigraha: पद्मनाभस्य सहोदरी।

**And here the cipher is given, and this nama supplies स, ह and म**: "Padmanābha, स; and hoda, ह and म — and make ह्रीं."

So 278–280 give क, ए, ई, ल, ह्रीं — the Vāgbhava kūṭa of the Kādi-vidyā. The ल is not separately assigned in the printed text, which is consistent with the whole passage being deliberately incomplete: Bhāskararāya gives enough to show the method and stops.

Before the cipher he gives the theology of the sisterhood, and it is the threefold Śaiva scheme: "the one Brahman assumed two forms, attributes and the possessor of them; again attributes become two, male and female; the male is Viṣṇu, who is the material cause of the whole universe; the female became the spouse of Paramaśiva. The secret of the Śaiva theory is that these three in combination become the one indivisible Brahman."

That is nama 712's doctrine verbatim — "the Brahman becomes twofold by becoming both the quality and the thing qualified; again the quality is divided into two, masculine and feminine; the feminine became the wife of Paramaśiva, the masculine became Viṣṇu as the material cause of the Universe; these three together, according to Śaiva doctrine, form the partless Brahman." The same passage, 432 namas apart, and both cite Appayya Dīkṣita's Ratnatrayaparīkṣā, which 113 also cited for the three bhāvanās.

Then two Purāṇic supports for the sisterhood. The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa's Puruṣottamakṣetra Māhātmya: "Subhadrā, who was born from the womb of Menakā in a former birth, in this birth was born along with Kṛṣṇa of Devakī" — with "let there be victory to Viṣṇu, the husband of Subhadrā," and Bhāskararāya's note that "there Subhadrā is Lakṣmī, and there is no contradiction; or, in reality there is no difference."

And a scene at Kāñcī: "Brahmā, the grandsire of all the worlds, in order to see Devī, once performed a severe penance in the sacred Kāñcī. Tripurā, standing on a lotus, having a lotus in her hand, with her victorious brother, appeared to the ascetic."

Note on the verse. Six namas, and the last three are a mantra in cipher.

275 is a rubric for the Sandhyā and then relocates the sun's disc into the anāhata, which 596's nyāsa had already done.

276 carries the widest claim in the text about what counts as Her manifestation: the Liṅga Purāṇa's "all things indicated by the words in the feminine gender are manifestations of Devī." A grammatical criterion, and 277's second reading restates it anatomically.

Then 278–280 encode क, ए, ई and ह्रीं, and Bhāskararāya says so outright — "this is the secret meaning." He had refused to give the equivalent result at 11, referring the reader to a guru; here he prints it. And 280's theology of the threefold Brahman is nama 712's doctrine word for word.

276 also brings the girl-ages to nine.

Textual note. 276's and 277's glosses split mid-sentence.
