## उन्मेषनिमिषोत्पन्नविपन्नभुवनावलिः । सहस्रशीर्षवदना सहस्राक्षी सहस्रपात्

*unmeṣanimiṣotpannavipannabhuvanāvaliḥ । sahasraśīrṣavadanā sahasrākṣī sahasrapāt*

Verse 66, namas 281–284.

281. उन्मेषनिमिषोत्पन्नविपन्नभुवनावलिः → उन्मेष-निमिष-उत्पन्न-विपन्न-भुवन-आवलिः

उन्मेष = an opening of the eyes (उत् + मिष् "to open the eyes")
निमिष = a closing of the eyes, a wink (नि + मिष्)
उत्पन्न = arisen, come into being (उत् + पद्)
विपन्न = perished, gone to ruin (वि + पद्)
भुवन = a world
आवलिः = a row, a series, a line
"She with whose opening and closing of the eyes the series of worlds arises and perishes."

Vigraha: उन्मेषनिमिषाभ्याम् उत्पन्नविपन्ना भुवनावलिः यस्याः सा।

Sandhi at two joints: निमिष + उत्पन्न → निमिषोत्पन्न (अ + उ → ओ by guṇa, 6.1.87), and भुवन + आवलिः → भुवनावलिः (आ by 6.1.101).

**In the cipher this nama supplies "the two Bhuvaneśvarī bījas"** — that is, ह्रीं twice, on the note at 284.

Bhāskararāya's first move is to deny the literal sense: "since the eyes of Devī never close, the expression *opening and shutting* refers to the influence of the destiny of beings, or to her mere wish." So the winking is not physiological, and what the compound names is volition.

The Ājñāvatāra: "by her mere wish the whole universe appears and disappears. The creation of the supreme is simply the expression of His wish." That is Taittirīya 2.6.1's "he desired, let me become many," which 796 कामरूपिणी makes Her form.

Kālidāsa's verse then puts the triad of 254 inside the act: "the universe consisting of the seer, the seen and the seeing, with its parts, existed in you before you thought of creation. At the manifestation of the universe at your will, your eyes open; at the destruction of the universe, your eyes shut."

And Gorakṣanātha's Mahārthamañjarī collapses the interval: "the moment occupied by the Highest Teacher in the creation is the same as that occupied in the destruction of the universe."

निमिष is also the word 256's Śaiva citation uses for Sadāśiva — "Īśvara the visible one, and Sadāśiva is momentary, nimeṣāntaḥ" — so the wink names both the fifth of the five and the duration of creation.

282. सहस्रशीर्षवदना → सहस्र-शीर्ष-वदना

सहस्र = a thousand; and per the gloss, unlimited
शीर्ष = a head
वदना = faced, having faces (वदन "face, mouth," from वद् "to speak")
"She of a thousand heads and faces."

Vigraha: सहस्रं शीर्षाणि वदनानि च यस्याः सा।

The Puruṣasūkta: "Puruṣa is thousand-headed, thousand-eyed and thousand-footed" — and the gloss on the number: "thousand means unlimited." Gītā 13.13 is cited as saying the same, which is the verse 532 सर्वतोमुखी rests on: "everywhere eyes, heads and mouths."

So 282–284 are the Puruṣasūkta's three epithets taken as three namas, and the Sahasranāma applies to Her the hymn's account of the cosmic Person. That is the Virāṭ form 778 विराड्रूपा names and 847, 936 and 942 assemble piecemeal.

And 780 विश्वतोमुखी is where Bhāskararāya reconciles this with the scriptures that deny Her hands and feet: "when a form is created by devotees through meditation, then alone does she become manifest" as having them; "the other passages speak in the real sense."

283. सहस्राक्षी → सहस्र-अक्षी

सहस्र = a thousand
अक्षी = eyed (अक्षि with the feminine)
"The thousand-eyed."

Vigraha: सहस्रम् अक्षीणि यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: सहस्र + अक्षी → सहस्राक्षी (आ by 6.1.101). index.html has no commentary for this nama.

**In the cipher this nama supplies ल.**

सहस्राक्ष is Indra's standing epithet, so the nama takes for Her a title of the god who at 297 stands between the fourteenth and fifteenth walls of the Śrīcakra to worship her. And अक्षि is the fifth of the text's words for eye, after लोचन at 18, नयन at 247, ईक्षण at 805 and its own uses at 561, 601, 936 and 571's साक्षिणी.

284. सहस्रपात् → सहस्र-पात्

सहस्र = a thousand
पात् = footed (पाद्, the compound-final stem)
"The thousand-footed."

Vigraha: सहस्रं पादाः यस्याः सन्ति सा।

**This is the second of only two namas in the thousand that end in a plain consonant**, after 795 कामधुक्. Here the final is त्, the stem being पाद् reduced in pausa — so the recitation stops on a dental stop.

The Devī Bhāgavata Book 3: "Devī, having thousands of eyes, thousands of hands, thousands of heads and feet, vividly shines forth."

**And then the cipher's second half is given**: "or, in this — 281 to 284 — are contained the second and last divisions of the mantra. Bhuvanāvali (281) indicates the two Bhuvaneśvarī bījas; Sahasrākṣī (283) ल; and sahasra (284) ह and स."

So 281–284 supply the Kāmarāja and Śakti kūṭas as 278–280 supplied the Vāgbhava, and the whole Pañcadaśī is distributed over seven namas. Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (66).

Note on the verse. Four namas, and they do two things at once.

Read plainly they are the Puruṣasūkta applied to Her — thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, thousand-footed — with 281 supplying the volition that makes the worlds come and go. Read in cipher they are the mantra's second and third kūṭas, completing what 278–280 began.

281 is the substantial entry, and its first move is a denial: Her eyes never close, so the winking must mean will. Kālidāsa's verse then puts the seer-seen-seeing triad of nama 254 inside that act of will, and Gorakṣanātha makes creation and destruction occupy the same moment.

And 284 is the thousand's second and last consonant-final nama.

Textual note. 283 has no commentary body.

---

## आब्रह्मकीटजननी वर्णाश्रमविधायिनी । निजाज्ञारूपनिगमा पुण्यापुण्यफलप्रदा

*ābrahmakīṭajananī varṇāśramavidhāyinī । nijājñārūpanigamā puṇyāpuṇyaphalapradā*

Verse 67, namas 285–288.

285. आब्रह्मकीटजननी → आ-ब्रह्म-कीट-जननी

आ = as far as, including — the prefix of inclusive extent
ब्रह्म = Brahmā; and per the gloss, Hiraṇyagarbha
कीट = a worm, an insect
जननी = mother, she who gives birth (from जन्, causative जनय्)
"Mother of all, from Brahmā down to the worm."

Vigraha: आ ब्रह्मणः कीटपर्यन्तं जननी।

आ marks inclusive extent — "as far as, and including" — which is 994 आबालगोपविदिता's construction, where the range runs down to children and cowherds and Bhāskararāya reverses its direction to take in Sadāśiva.

Both ends are then specified with some precision. "Brahmā, a Jīva called Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the gross form of humanity taken collectively" — so the top of the range is 253's and 259's aggregate rather than the four-faced god. And the bottom is identified from medicine: "Kīṭa is the small insect eater of the spider's thread; in the Vaidya Śāstras kīṭa is called Stamba, meaning two kinds of parasitical worms, viz. Kākeru and Kāmakeru."

That is the only place in the text where a technical medical authority is cited, and it is cited to fix the lower bound of what She mothers.

जननी stood alone at 823, where Bhāskararāya noted it might be compounded with ब्रह्म and read as "mother of Brahmā"; and 620 अनेककोटिब्रह्माण्डजननी counts what she mothers by crores of universes. Here the range is vertical rather than numerical.

286. वर्णाश्रमविधायिनी → वर्ण-आश्रम-विधायिनी

वर्ण = a caste, a class; also a letter, a colour
आश्रम = a stage of life, an order
विधायिनी = she who ordains, establishes (वि + धा "to place")
"She who establishes the castes and the orders of life."

Vigraha: वर्णाश्रमान् विधातीति।

Sandhi: वर्ण + आश्रम → वर्णाश्रम (आ by 6.1.101).

**Here the text turns from cosmology to scripture, and Bhāskararāya's opening sentence explains the whole verse**: "thus she becomes the Vedas, which are her own commands, in order to lead the created Jīvas into the right path."

So 285 created them and 286–288 govern them, and the instrument is the Veda taken as Her ordinance.

Then the division of the Veda and the reason the ritual half exists: "the Vedas are divided into two parts, the Karmakāṇḍa and the Brahmakāṇḍa. As, according to the rule, the devas and lower animals have no share in the Karmakāṇḍa, the divine Mother established righteousness through the Karmakāṇḍa, after dividing men into four castes and four orders."

That rule — that gods and animals have no share in ritual — is the same Tiryagadhikaraṇa-nyāya 255 धर्माधर्मविवर्जिता used to exempt Her from merit and demerit. So one principle both frees Her from the Veda and explains why the Veda is addressed to men.

The Kūrma Purāṇa then gives Her own instruction to Himavat, and it grades the means: "hear from me this doctrine which is supreme, secret, known to Īśvara only, practised by Brahmavādins alone, describing the means of attaining by meditation, Karma Yoga, devotion and wisdom — this is to be attained by these means, not by crores of other actions." And on Karma Yoga specifically: "Karma is ordained by the Śrutis and Smṛtis according to castes and orders; always perform this Karma associated with the knowledge of the Self, for the sake of liberation. Devotion arises from righteousness; by devotion the supreme is attained… hence the aspirant for liberation should depend on the Vedas, which are my form, for the sake of Dharma. By my command the divine Brahmā, for the sake of protecting the Vedas, created the Brāhmaṇas at the beginning."

वर्ण also means letter, which is the sense 850 वर्णरूपिणी, 577 and 529 take — so the word that makes Her the alphabet elsewhere makes her the caste-system here.

287. निजाज्ञारूपनिगमा → निज-आज्ञा-रूप-निगमा

निज = one's own
आज्ञा = a command, an ordinance (आ + ज्ञा)
रूप = form
निगमा = scripture, the Veda — literally what has come down (नि + गम्)
"She whose scripture is the form of her own command."

Vigraha: निजा आज्ञा रूपं यस्याः निगमः सा।

Sandhi: निज + आज्ञा → निजाज्ञा (आ by 6.1.101).

आज्ञा is a nama in its own right at 828, where the double avagraha marks the elided आ and Bhāskararāya takes it as "the Lord's will expressed in the Vedas as injunction and prohibition." Here the same word makes the Veda Her command's form.

The definition of आज्ञा is procedural: "Ājñā, command, is ascertained by the knowers of the Vedas through reflection on the words, what set forth the object to be attained, the means, and the practical directions, by giving out the real meaning, meditation and praise; these three belong to the Karmakāṇḍa part of the Vedas." Jaimini 1.1.22 is cited: "the words which refer to past things are to be taken with those which refer to action" — the Mīmāṃsā rule that narrative in the Veda serves injunction.

The Kūrma Purāṇa: "the ancient and supreme energy called Vedas, which are my commandments, are manifested at the beginning of creation in the form of Ṛg, Yajus and Sāman." That is 872 त्रयी's citation.

**And then the canon is drawn, and a school is excluded.** "Or, there are twenty-eight Śaiva Tantras beginning with Kāmika which follow the Vedas. There are some more scriptures beginning with Kāpāla, Bhairava, which are opposed to the Vedas. Of these two, those which follow the Vedas are here meant by Nigama; as they sprang from the mouth of Parameśvara, they are said to be the form of my command; those which sprang from below the navel are opposed to the Vedas."

The Devī Bhāgavata and Skanda Purāṇas then distribute the twenty-eight over Śiva's five faces: "the five Tantras beginning with Kāmika have sprung from the Sadyojāta face; the five beginning with Dīptā from the Vāmadeva face; the five, Vijaya and the rest, from the Aghora face; the five, Vairocana and the rest, from the east face, Tatpuruṣa; and the eight, Prodgīta and others, from the Īśāna face. These have sprung from the upward current, and the others from the current below the navel."

Five plus five plus five plus five plus eight is twenty-eight, and the five faces are 250's second set of five Brahmans. So the canon 206 सर्वतन्त्ररूपा mapped onto Her body limb by limb is here given its origin, and the Kāpālika texts are put outside it — anatomically, as issuing from below the navel.

That is the only exclusion Bhāskararāya makes of a Śaiva school, and it is worth setting against 149 नित्यबुद्धा's accommodation of two Jaina Tīrthaṅkaras and 155 निरीश्वरा's claim on Mīmāṃsā and Sāṃkhya. Rival philosophies are refuted or absorbed; the Kāpālikas are placed below the navel.

288. पुण्यापुण्यफलप्रदा → पुण्य-अपुण्य-फल-प्रदा

पुण्य = merit, good action
अपुण्य = demerit, sin
फल = fruit, result
प्रदा = giving fully (प्र + दा)
"She who gives the fruits of merit and demerit."

Vigraha: पुण्यापुण्ययोः फलं प्रददातीति।

Sandhi: पुण्य + अपुण्य → पुण्यापुण्य (आ by 6.1.101).

The placement is explained as a completion: "when the Veda is established in the form of righteousness through castes and orders, the Mother, in order to confirm that establishment, gives the good and bad results arising from ordained and prohibited actions respectively. The respective results of good and bad actions are heaven and hell."

So 286 laid down the law, 287 identified the law with Her command, and this nama supplies the sanction — without which, the argument runs, the establishment would not hold.

The Kūrma Purāṇa states it as administration: "those who do not perform good actions as established — there are hells created by Brahmā, into which by my command Yama throws them. Those who are devoted to me and perform the duty prescribed by the Vedas are by my command brought by Indra and others into Svarga and other places."

**Then a genuine problem is raised and worked.** Kauṣītaki 3.8 is quoted, and it makes Her the author of the acts as well as the judge: "for He makes him perform good actions whom he wishes to lead upwards, and He alone makes him, whom he wishes to lead downwards, perform bad actions." Vedānta Sūtra 3.2.38 is cited for the conclusion — "for that only is possible" — and then the objection that follows from it is met by Vedānta Sūtra 2.1.34: "partiality and mercilessness cannot be attributed, on account of his regarding merit and demerit."

So She causes the acts *and* is impartial, because what she regards in causing them is the prior merit. And the Saura Saṃhitā's contrary position is quoted and rejected: "righteousness and unrighteousness depend on the doer and produce their respective results without Mahādeva exercising any influence. This is not so" — with the Śivarahasya for the opposite: "when the sacrifice sleeps, you alone remain awake in order to grant the result to the sacrificer." The chapter's conclusion: "Śiva is to be attained by reasoning supported by the scriptures. Hence Śiva directly confers the results of righteousness and unrighteousness." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (67).

The nama also stands against 255 धर्माधर्मविवर्जिता thirty-three namas back, where She is devoid of merit and demerit. Free of them herself, she assigns them — which is 843 भवचक्रप्रवर्तिनी's structure, where She turns the wheel of the existence she also cures.

Note on the verse. Four namas, and they are a single argument about scripture as ordinance.

285 establishes the range of what She has made, from the collective Hiraṇyagarbha down to a named parasitic worm. Then 286 makes the Veda Her command and explains why its ritual half addresses men only — gods and animals have no share in it, by the very rule that exempts Her at 255. 287 identifies the Śaiva canon that "follows the Vedas," distributes its twenty-eight texts over Śiva's five faces, and puts the Kāpālika scriptures outside it as issuing from below the navel. And 288 supplies the sanction, then works the difficulty that follows: She causes the good and bad acts and is nonetheless impartial, because in causing them she regards prior merit.

287's exclusion is the only one of its kind in the text. Rival philosophies get refuted at 136–151 or absorbed at 149 and 155; a rival Śaiva canon gets located anatomically.

---

## श्रुतिसीमन्तसिन्दूरीकृतपादाब्जधूलिका । सकलागमसंदोहशुक्तिसंपुटमौक्तिका

*śrutisīmantasindūrīkṛtapādābjadhūlikā । sakalāgamasaṃdohaśuktisaṃpuṭamauktikā*

Verse 68, namas 289–290.

289. श्रुतिसीमन्तसिन्दूरीकृतपादाब्जधूलिका → श्रुति-सीमन्त-सिन्दूरी-कृत-पाद-अब्ज-धूलिका

श्रुति = the Veda, what is heard (from श्रु "to hear") — here personified as goddesses
सीमन्त = the parting of the hair (सीमा "a boundary" + अन्त)
सिन्दूरीकृत = made into the vermilion mark (सिन्दूर with कृत)
पाद = a foot
अब्ज = a lotus (अप् "water" + ज)
धूलिका = dust (धूलि with the diminutive)
"She the dust of whose lotus feet is the vermilion on the parting of the Vedas' hair."

Vigraha: श्रुतीनां सीमन्ते सिन्दूरीकृता पादाब्जधूलिका यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: पाद + अब्ज → पादाब्ज (आ by 6.1.101).

**Bhāskararāya marks the second turn of the verse-group**: "thus, after describing the Karmakāṇḍa part as devoted to rites, he now sets forth the explanation of the established fact of the Brahmakāṇḍa also, through the Mother's command alone." So 286–288 were the ritual half of the Veda and 289–290 are the doctrinal half, and each nama describes a *method* of describing Her.

**This nama's method is negation.** "The expression *dust* means that the Vedas are unable to explain the real form of Devī by direct assertions, by complete definition — a rule called Śṛṅgagrāhika — and describe Her by the method of negation, like one ashamed and afraid, standing afar, describing inadequately; and that description also creates no clear idea as to *this or that*."

So the dust on the parting of the hair is what the Vedas get of Her: not her feet but what has fallen from them, and the figure is chosen because vermilion on a woman's parting is the sign of a married woman — the Vedas wear Her dust as their marriage-mark.

Śṛṅgagrāhika, "seizing by the horn," is the technical name for definition by direct designation, and it is denied.

Bhāskararāya then quotes his own Śivastava, and the shame in the simile is made explicit: "the all-wise scriptures, O Paramaśiva, much beloved by you, do not adequately describe you, like a woman silent from shame. If they negative all your attributes by often saying *not this, not this*, who else can declare thee to be this or that? Certainly not mere men like myself."

The *neti neti* is Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.3.6, which 142 निष्कामा also cites; and 962 सर्वातीता makes the same point by narrowing "transcending all" to transcending all words, on the Jñānārṇava's "know Parabrahman, which transcends speech."

290. सकलागमसंदोहशुक्तिसंपुटमौक्तिका → सकल-आगम-संदोह-शुक्ति-संपुट-मौक्तिका

सकल = all, entire
आगम = a scripture, a traditional text — what has come (आ + गम्)
संदोह = a collection, an aggregate; literally a milking-together (सम् + दुह्)
शुक्ति = an oyster-shell, a pearl-oyster
संपुट = a hollow, a closed casket; a pair of valves (सम् + पुट्)
मौक्तिका = a pearl (vṛddhi derivative of मुक्ता)
"She who is the pearl in the shell formed by the collected scriptures."

Vigraha: सकलागमसंदोहः शुक्तिसंपुटः, तस्य मौक्तिका यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: सकल + आगम → सकलागम (आ by 6.1.101). The dev field breaks the compound with a space after संदोह.

**This nama's method is positive definition by approximation**, and it is named: "the Scriptures, when they describe Brahman by positive definition, only prove it by characteristics, by the method of approximation — Arundhatī-nyāya."

Sastry's gloss explains the figure: "Arundhatī is a very small star, and by locating the surrounding big stars one at last perceives it." So positive scriptural definition works by pointing at neighbours — which is exactly what a pearl in a closed oyster is: located by the shell, not seen.

And the pearl is then read as an ornament rather than as Her: "the *pearl* expression indicates her attributes of creation and the rest. The Scriptures describe only her nose-pearl and other jewels, and not her real nature." With Taittirīya 2.9: "whence all speech, with the mind, turns away without being able to reach it." Sastry adds Bhāskararāya's gloss on that verse — "all speech means the four kinds of speech, Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā and Vaikharī" — which is the ladder 25 शुद्धविद्याङ्कुराकारद्विजपङ्क्तिद्वयोज्ज्वला sets out with the sprouting-seed simile.

So 289 and 290 are the two methods paired: negation, which gets the dust, and approximation, which gets the jewellery. Neither gets Her.

**And then a conclusion about eligibility which the pair is made to carry**: "by the previous name it is indicated that she is to be worshipped by the first three castes. This name indicates that she is to be worshipped by the fourth caste also." The Rudrayāmala: "the abode indicated by the Vedas is also indicated by other scriptures; hence all Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas and Śūdras are fit to worship."

The argument is that 289's श्रुति covers the twice-born and 290's सकलागम — all scriptures, not only the Veda — extends the entitlement to the fourth. So the two epistemological namas are also a ruling on who may worship, and the Āgamas are what open it. Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (68).

That belongs with the text's leniency-thread: 167 पापनाशिनी's Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa makes virtuous the acts of "those devoid of varṇa and āśrama"; 213 महापूज्या grades sixteen worshippers down to Piśācas with iron; 222 महाबला liberates crows; 291 पुरुषार्थप्रदा two namas on says "no castes conjointly attain prosperity and release without the adoration of Tripurā."

Note on the verse. Two namas, and they are the text's clearest statement of what scripture can and cannot do.

The Vedas describe Her by negation and get the dust from her feet, worn as the vermilion in their parting; all the scriptures together describe her by approximation and get her nose-pearl. Two named methods — Śṛṅgagrāhika denied, Arundhatī-nyāya allowed — and both figures are of ornament rather than person.

And the pair carries a ruling: the first nama entitles the three twice-born castes and the second, because its scope is all scriptures and not only the Veda, entitles the fourth.

Textual note. 290's dev breaks its compound with a space after संदोह.

---

## पुरुषार्थप्रदा पूर्णा भोगिनी भुवनेश्वरी । अम्बिका अनादिनिधना हरिब्रह्मेन्द्रसेविता

*puruṣārthapradā pūrṇā bhoginī bhuvaneśvarī । ambikā anādinidhanā haribrahmendrasevitā*

Verse 69, namas 291–297.

291. पुरुषार्थप्रदा → पुरुष-अर्थ-प्रदा

पुरुष = a man, a person; and per the second reading, Śiva
अर्थ = an object, an aim — the four ends of human life; and per that reading, liberation
प्रदा = giving fully
"She who bestows the objects of human life."

Vigraha: पुरुषार्थान् प्रददातीति।

Sandhi: पुरुष + अर्थ → पुरुषार्थ (आ by 6.1.101).

"Artha, the four objects of human desire" — dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa, which 698 सर्वार्थदात्री also names and 873 त्रिवर्गनिलया gives as three.

The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa is then quoted, and it removes both regularity and caste as conditions: "those who worship the Supreme Śakti, whether properly or improperly, are certainly not in Saṃsāra but are liberated souls. Hence no castes conjointly attain prosperity and release without the adoration of Tripurā."

That is 736 मुक्तिदा's Brahmāṇḍa citation — "those who worship the supreme Śakti, whether regularly or irregularly, are not entangled in saṃsāra" — the same passage 445 namas apart, and here with the caste-clause attached. It follows 290's ruling directly.

Then a second reading which narrows both terms: "Purusha, Śiva, as the Śruti says *Puruṣa is Rudra*; artha, liberation — that is, the worship of the unconditioned Brahman, and the results thereof, depend on Śakti alone."

पुरुष is one of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's four forms at 212, and the Puruṣa of the Puruṣasūkta at 282.

292. पूर्णा → पूर्णा

पूर्णा = full, complete (past participle of पूर् "to fill"); also the fifteenth Nityā, the fourteenth bright night, and a river
"The Full."

Vigraha: पूर्णा परिपूर्णा।

The reason is the absence of the three limitations: "as she is free from the limitations of time, place and circumstance" — which is 701 देशकालापरिच्छिन्ना's set exactly, where Bhāskararāya defines all three and adds limitation "as to things."

And the verse quoted is the pūrṇamadaḥ, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 5.1: "that Brahman is fullness; this is fullness; this fullness proceeds from that fullness; on grasping the fullness of this fullness, the fullness alone remains."

Then the technical senses: "Pūrṇā means the fifth, tenth, fifteenth Nityā deities; the fourteenth bright night; also the name of a river." Pūrṇā is the fifth of the five tithi-groups at 256 — Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, Pūrṇā — so the word names a member of the very scheme that nama sets out.

293. भोगिनी → भोगिनी

भोगिनी = enjoying, an enjoyer (भोग + इन्, feminine ङीप्); also a female serpent — one that has coils
"The Enjoyer."

Vigraha: भोगः अस्याः अस्तीति भोगिनी।

The whole commentary is a lexical note: "Bhoginī is the name of a female serpent, Nāgakanyā."

That is available because भोग comes from two collapsed roots — भुज् to enjoy and भुज् to bend — so an enjoyer and a coiled thing are one word, which 219 महाभोगा's "extension" also exploits. And the serpent-reading connects to 110 कुण्डलिनी, where the jīvaśakti sleeps "like a serpent having three and a half coils," and to 248's Amṛta-Kuṇḍalinī.

294. भुवनेश्वरी → भुवन-ईश्वरी

भुवन = a world; the fourteen worlds; also water
ईश्वरी = mistress, sovereign lady
"Sovereign of the worlds."

Vigraha: भुवनानाम् ईश्वरी।

Sandhi: भुवन + ईश्वरी → भुवनेश्वरी (अ + ई → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87).

"Bhuvana, fourteen worlds, or water." Then the identification with a bīja: "Bhuvaneśvarī is the deity indicated by the syllable ह्रीं, or she is in the form of ह्रीं" — which is the bīja 280 and 281 encode in the cipher, and 301 ह्रींकारी names outright seven namas on.

Then the guru-etymology: the Tripurasiddhānta says "the great ruler, the wife of Śiva, is called Bhuvaneśvarī because she has blessed Bhuvanānandanātha and because she is highly celebrated in all the worlds." Bhāskararāya notes that Bhuvanānandanātha is one of the gurus "included under Mānavaugha" — the human lineage, as against the divine and the siddha.

That is the second nama in thirty derived from a teacher's initiatory name, after 262 तुर्या and Turīyānandanātha.

**And then the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Saṃhitā's Ghaṭārgalayantra chapter, which builds the worlds out of the syllable**: "O ruler of the Devas, in one syllable there are many worlds… in the syllables ह and the rest, from which are composed the words ह्रीं and the rest, in the ह — the bīja of the syllables of ether — Kailāsa and other regions are established"; and after describing the origin of each world, "hence, O great ruler, thou art called Bhuvanādhīśvarī." Then a second derivation from the same text: "again, from the word हु sprang the ether; from the fourth svara the air…" and so through the creation, "hence thou art called Bhuvaneśī."

So the fourteen worlds are generated from the letters of Her own bīja, which is 203's letter-method — fifty letters as Śiva's skin — turned into a cosmogony. "Thus two explanations are given."

295. अम्बिका → अम्बिका

अम्बिका = mother (an affectionate diminutive of अम्बा); also Bhāratī, the earth; also night, and sleep
"The Mother."

Vigraha: अम्बिका माता।

Four readings, and the last two take the word away from motherhood entirely.

"The mother of the Universe. Or Ambikā means Bhāratī, the goddess of speech, and earth." Or the triad: "Ambikā, the aggregate of Śaktis of Icchā, Jñāna and Kriyā, which are the form of Rudrāṇī" — the triad of 658, 630 and 110.

**Or night and sleep**, on the Viśva: "Ambikā means deceit, perfection, sleep, and night." The Skanda's Navarātrapradīpa: "Night is the great Devī, and the day is Śiva" — which is 276's Liṅga Purāṇa rule, "day is Śiva and Night is Devī."

And the Harivaṃśa's account of sleep is the darkest personification in the text: "Māyā, the great deceiver, known in the world as sleep. Her body is night, which creates darkness and destroys the day, the consumer of half the life of beings in the world, being terrible. There is none equal to her; except Viṣṇu, none among the Devas can control her." The Mārkaṇḍeya adds the liturgical form: "I praise the divine sleep of Viṣṇu, of unequalled power, the ruler of the Universe, the supporter of the world, and the cause of preservation and destruction."

That is Yoganidrā, whom 656 योगानन्दा identifies with Her — "because bliss chiefly pervades in sleep, and that state belongs to Devī" — and 126 शांकरी's Kālikā Purāṇa names among the titles the Devas praise her by. Here she is "the consumer of half the life of beings."

अम्बिका stands again at 976 and closes the text at 1000; अम्बा alone at 985.

296. अनादिनिधना → अन्-आदि-निधना

अन् = not (नञ् before a vowel)
आदि = a beginning; and per Vararuci's numeral rule, eighty
निधन = an end, death, destruction (नि + धा "to place down")
"She who has neither beginning nor end."

Vigraha: आदिः निधनं च यस्याः न स्तः सा।

The dev field reads नादिनिधनो — the initial अ lost to the sandhi with अम्बिका (आ + अ → आ) with no avagraha to mark it, and ओ standing where आ belongs. The gloss preserves the sense.

**And then the third use of Vararuci's numeral system in the text**, which is the entry's substance: "or, according to the system of Vararuci, नाडि or आदि means eighty — that is, द = 8 and न or अ = 0 — hence she whose worship delivers a man from the eighty causes of death."

The other two uses are 529 सर्ववर्णोपशोभिता, where उप is read as ten and gives the arithmetic turning fifty letters into a thousand petals, and 749 मृत्युदारुकुठारिका, where दारु is twenty-eight, "the twenty-eight kinds of pains described before, as differentiated by energy, success and elation," with a cross-reference to nama 354.

**And this nama supplies what 749's cross-reference points at.** The eighty divide as "Pāśa and Vadha. The latter is of twenty-eight kinds," on the Viṣṇu Purāṇa — "the egoism and self-conceit are of twenty-eight kinds"; "the former is of fifty-two kinds," on the Liṅga Purāṇa — "there are fifty-two Pāśas arising from the knot of avidyā." Twenty-eight plus fifty-two is eighty.

So the twenty-eight of 749 are the vadhas here, and "energy, success and elation" there are the āsakti, siddhi and tuṣṭi this entry now explains at length from Sāṃkhya.

Sāṃkhya Sūtra 3.38–40 is quoted — "disability is of twenty-eight kinds; requiescence is of nine kinds; perfection is of eight kinds" — and then Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Kārikās 49–51 for the composition: "depravity of the eleven organs, together with injuries of the intellect, are pronounced to be disability. The injuries of intellect are seventeen, by inversion of acquiescence and perfectness."

So eleven plus seventeen is twenty-eight, and Bhāskararāya then explains each set. आसक्ति is "inability of the senses to receive their respective objects, defects caused by blindness, deafness and the rest — they are eleven because there are eleven senses."

तुष्टि, elation, is nine, four internal and five external, and the four internal are given as things a man *says*, which makes them recognisable: "First, *I am liberated by the absorption of mind in the eightfold prakṛti* — this is called Prakṛti elation. The second is *I have succeeded on merely receiving the robes of an ascetic* — Upādāna elation. The third is *what is the use of painful meditation? Success will come with time* — Kāla elation. The last is *success will come by the intervention of God* — Bhāgya elation." And the five external correspond to the five objective senses, arising "when, after observing the disadvantages attached to the gratification of objective senses, he ceases their pursuit."

So the nine elations are nine forms of premature satisfaction, and four of them are quotable excuses. That is an unusually concrete piece of psychology for this commentary.

सिद्धि, perfection, is eight and its terms are then defined: "Ūha, reasoning, means understanding the meanings without being taught; Śabda, hearing, understanding the meaning by simply hearing the words; Adhyayana, study, understanding real meaning from the Guru's teaching. The other three Siddhis are the reverse of the three kinds of misery" — ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika — "by gaining good friends he attains Arthasiddhi; and the last arises from serving ascetics and the learned."

The seventeen buddhi-injuries are the inversions of these seventeen items — nine tuṣṭis plus eight siddhis — "and these seventeen added to the injuries of the eleven senses make up twenty-eight Vadhas."

The Vāyu Purāṇa then places the whole apparatus in a cosmogony, and it uses the word this batch has just defined technically: "the eighth creation, called Anugraha, is fourfold — Viparyaya, inversion; Āsakti, incapacity; Siddhi, perfectness; and Tuṣṭi, elation. The first is by inversion leading into the unstable creation; by incapacity, the animal kingdom; by perfectness, human beings; by elation, the Devas."

So अनुग्रह, which at 273 was the fifth cosmic function, is here the name of the eighth creation, and the four Sāṃkhya categories are the four grades of being it produces.

297. हरिब्रह्मेन्द्रसेविता → हरि-ब्रह्म-इन्द्र-सेविता

हरि = Hari, Viṣṇu
ब्रह्म = Brahmā
इन्द्र = Indra
सेविता = attended, served, worshipped (from सेव्)
"She who is attended by Hari, Brahmā and Indra."

Vigraha: हरिब्रह्मेन्द्रैः सेविता।

Sandhi: ब्रह्म + इन्द्र → ब्रह्मेन्द्र (अ + इ → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87).

**The three are located inside the Śrīcakra by wall-number**: "in the Śrīcakra, in the centre between the seventeenth and the eighteenth walls, is the seat of Viṣṇu; between the sixteenth and the seventeenth, is of Brahmā; between the fourteenth and the fifteenth, is of Indra and other Lokapālas. All these reside in their respective places for the sake of worshipping Devī."

That is the same architectural placement 686 राज्यवल्लभा gives on the Lalitāstavaratna — the protectors of the region "between the thirteenth and fourteenth walls," with lakes of sapphire — and 785 मार्ताण्डभैरवाराध्या, where Mārtāṇḍabhairava stands between the twenty-second and twenty-third. So the text places gods in the diagram by wall-number three times, and the numbers are consistent as a scheme: Indra at 14–15, Brahmā at 16–17, Viṣṇu at 17–18.

The Devī Bhāgavata then lists eighteen worshippers: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, Varuṇa, Yama, Vāyu, Agni, Kubera, Tvaṣṭā, Pūṣā, Aśvins, Bhaga, Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, Marutgaṇas — all these meditate on Devī."

**And then a piece of polemic, and it is the sharpest in the batch.** "By this expression, those who see the Vedas which describe Viṣṇu, Brahmā and the rest alone do not obtain the real knowledge about Viṣṇu, because only those who see the Vedas in connection with Devī are marked out by superior excellence. Hence there is no use of worshipping other deities, as it is opposed to the rule for a beggar to beg from a beggar when a non-beggar, a reasonably rich man, is present."

Bhāskararāya's own Śivastava presses it: "O Paramaśiva, why should I, a beggar, beg from Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra and other beggars, who possess dominion given by you, saying *do thou give to me*? Even an ignorant man who already enjoys the result of the twelve days' sacrifice only desires the result of the Jyotiṣṭoma, a superior sacrifice, and not the result of the twelve days' sacrifice."

So worshipping other gods is not wrong but pointless — they are beggars with dominion on loan. That is a different position from 770 प्रियव्रता, where vows to any deity reach Her because "the whole world is Śiva and Śakti," and from 149's Jaina accommodation. Both stand in the text without reconciliation.

Note on the verse. Seven namas, and 296 carries it.

291 follows 290's ruling on eligibility with the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa's removal of both regularity and caste. 292–295 are then four namas of fullness, enjoyment, rule and motherhood, of which 294's cosmogony from the letters of ह्रीं and 295's identification with Yoganidrā are the substantial parts.

296 is where the text's numeral device pays off. Vararuci's rule makes आदि eighty; the eighty are twenty-eight vadhas plus fifty-two pāśas; and the twenty-eight are then unpacked from Sāṃkhya as eleven sense-defects plus seventeen inversions of the nine elations and eight perfections. That supplies exactly what 749 मृत्युदारुकुठारिका's cross-reference pointed at — "the twenty-eight kinds of pains, as differentiated by energy, success and elation." Two namas 453 apart, one apparatus, and the same numeral system decoding both.

And 297 places three gods inside the Śrīcakra by wall-number, then argues that worshipping them is begging from beggars.

Textual note. 296's dev reads नादिनिधनो: the initial अ of अनादि lost to the sandhi with अम्बिका, unmarked by any avagraha, and ओ where आ belongs. Only the gloss preserves the sense.

---

## नारायणी नादरूपा नामरूपविवर्जिता । ह्रींकारी ह्रीमती हृद्या हेयोपादेयवर्जिता

*nārāyaṇī nādarūpā nāmarūpavivarjitā । hrīṃkārī hrīmatī hṛdyā heyopādeyavarjitā*

Verse 70, namas 298–304.

298. नारायणी → नारायणी

नारायणी = the consort or feminine of Nārāyaṇa; also his sister (vṛddhi derivative, feminine ङीप्)
"Nārāyaṇī."

Vigraha: नारायणस्य पत्नी नारायणी। or नारायणस्य स्वसा।

index.html splits the entry mid-sentence, the gloss ending with Manu 1.10's opening.

Four etymologies of नारायण first, and they differ on what नार is. Manu 1.10: "the water is called Naraḥ because it emanated from Nara; that is his first abode, ayana — hence he is named Nārāyaṇa." The Brahmavaivarta: "because his abode is among men, hence he is called Nārāyaṇa." The Devī Bhāgavata: "because Nara means leading, hence the supreme self is called Nara." And the Mahābhārata: "the wise know that the Tattvas emanated from Nara, Brahman, and form his abode."

Then the identification, which takes Nārāyaṇa as Śiva: "here Nārāyaṇa is Paramaśiva, because concerning the fourth state the Kāśīkhaṇḍa says, *he is the husband of Lakṣmī and also of Pārvatī*. Or this saying may indicate non-separation between Lakṣmī and Devī."

Or the sisterhood, which is 280 पद्मनाभसहोदरी's claim: "the sister of Viṣṇu is called Nārāyaṇī, for there is a saying, *adoration to Śiva, the husband of Nārāyaṇī*."

Or the Kūrma Purāṇa's division, in Śiva's own words: "I, the supreme Lord, have divided myself into two forms; one is Nārāyaṇa, the other is Gaurī, the mother of the universe. So my supreme nature is known neither to the Devas nor to the Ṛṣis, because I am one, I am Devī and Viṣṇu."

And the Devī Purāṇa's water-derivation: "because she has her abode in the water, not in air, or she has her seat in the ocean, hence she is called Nārāyaṇī, the creator of men and women." The Padma Purāṇa places her at Supārśva.

299. नादरूपा → नाद-रूपा

नाद = sound, the primal resonance (from नद् "to sound")
रूपा = form
"She whose form is Nāda."

Vigraha: नादः रूपं यस्याः सा।

**The eight stations above the bindu are given again, and the list differs slightly from 207's.** "There are eight notes above the bindu of the syllable ह्रीं — Ardhacandra, Rodhinī, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpikā, Samanā and Unmanī — which are subtle, more subtle, and most subtle; of these the third is Nāda."

At 207 मनोन्मनी the eight ran "Indu, Rodhinī, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, Unmanī" on Yoginīhṛdaya 1.26, with Mahābindu ninth. Here the first is Ardhacandra rather than Indu — the half-moon rather than the moon — which is the same object under two names, since 594 इन्द्रधनुःप्रभा sets an ardhacandra above the forehead-bindu "at a quarter of that" measure. So the ladder is stable and its lowest rung has two names.

Sastry's footnote adds the arithmetic: "अ-उ-म् in the syllable Om, and ह्रीं in the Hrīṃ, and altogether make eleven in number" — three letters plus the eight stations.

The Mahāsvacchanda Tantra then describes the third rung: "Nāda, which resembles the filament of the lotus, shining like crores of suns, surrounded by innumerable cities, is above Rodhinī… the supreme Devī, seated on the lap of that Nāda, leading upward, should be contemplated."

That is 901 नादरूपिणी's material, where the same station is "manifested as Nāda in the place called Anāhata, experienced by the mind turned inwards," with the bodily evidence — "tears in their eyes and hairs standing erect" — and a cross-reference to nama 296. So the two nāda-namas are 602 apart and both place Her on the lap of the third rung; the Svacchanda is cited at both.

300. नामरूपविवर्जिता → नाम-रूप-विवर्जिता

नाम = a name (नामन्)
रूप = a form
विवर्जिता = wholly devoid of
"She who is devoid of name and form."

Vigraha: नामरूपाभ्यां विवर्जिता।

**The analysis is a fivefold division of the knot**: "there are five forms of the universe which appear inextricably intertwined in the knot of spirit and matter. These are, as analysed by great men, *existence, knowledge, bliss, name and form*. The first three belong to Brahman, and the other two belong to the world. As the latter two, name and form, are illusory, she transcends them."

So सच्चिदानन्द plus नामरूप is the whole of what appears, and the seam between the third and fourth is the seam between Brahman and world. "The meaning is that in reality there is no union between being and non-being."

Chāndogya 8.14.1 is then quoted, and it makes Brahman the separator: "Ether, that is Brahman, separates name and form; between them is Brahman." Bhāskararāya's gloss: "that which remains when these two are eliminated by the ether which is the energy of consciousness, is Brahman."

That is 137 निराकारा's method — the Viṣṇu Bhāgavata's "the infinite who remains after all negation" — with two terms rather than eleven; and नाम is what 962 सर्वातीता makes Her transcend when Bhāskararāya narrows "all" to "all words."

**This nama closes the third hundred, and the colophon survives in its body**: "thus in the Saubhāgyabhāskara composed by Bhāsurānanda ends the fourth Kāla called Marīci, with the third hundred of the names," followed by "The Fourth Hundred."

**That is the sixth of the text's colophons, and it is now the second consecutive one.** With 200's third Kalā closing the second hundred, the sequence 200–300 is contiguous, which is the strongest form the evidence has taken: third kalā/second hundred, fourth kalā/third hundred, and then eighth/seventh, ninth/eighth, tenth/ninth and eleventh/tenth at 700, 800, 900 and 1000. Six of the ten division-points survive, and the rule that the kalā-number runs exactly one ahead of the hundred it closes holds at every one. The four missing are at 100, 400, 500 and 600.

301. ह्रींकारी → ह्रीं-कारी

ह्रीं = the bīja hrīṃ, the Bhuvaneśvarī-bīja
कारी = she who makes, who utters (from कृ)
"She who is the maker of the syllable ह्रीं."

Vigraha: ह्रीम् इति कारी।

The formation is 622 क्लींकारी's — a bīja with कारी — and the two are the text's only namas of that shape.

Two readings. "Or Hrīṃ, shame, and kārī, doer." And then the Svatantra Tantra's decoding of the bīja by a *vyākulākṣara* verse, which distributes the functions over the letters: "the Vyoma, ह, indicates the manifestation; Vahni, र, involution; ई protection; and the dot, controlling the three." So "ह्रीं corresponds to creation, preservation and destruction, with the fourth."

That is 231 महाभैरवपूजिता's method applied to a bīja instead of a name — there भ, र and व were bharaṇa, ramaṇa and vamana — and the fourth here, the anusvāra controlling the three, is the tirodhāna-anugraha level the five-function scheme needs.

"Or Hrīṃkāra, the Bhuvaneśvarī-bīja" — which 294 भुवनेश्वरी identified and 280–281 encoded in the cipher.

302. ह्रीमती → ह्रीः-मती

ह्रीः = modesty, shame (ह्री)
मती = possessing (मतुप्, feminine ङीप्)
"She who possesses ह्रीं." — or, on the other reading, "She who possesses modesty."

Vigraha: ह्रीः अस्याः अस्तीति ह्रीमती।

Both the dev field and the verse text read हीमती, the र् lost. The gloss preserves the reading — "Possessor of Hrīṃ" — and the body's first words, "Hrī, shame," confirm it.

The nama turns on the coincidence of the bīja ह्रीं with the word ह्री, modesty, so it can be read as possessing either. And the Śruti is cited for the company modesty keeps: "shame, mind, satisfaction, desire, nourishment." Bhāskararāya marks the division: "15th verse divides 38 names."

The shame-reading pairs with 289's simile, where the Vedas describe Her "like a woman silent from shame."

303. हृद्या → हृद्या

हृद्या = pleasing to the heart, delightful; also abiding in the heart (from हृद् "heart")
"She who abides in the heart."

Vigraha: हृदि भवा हृद्या। or हृद्या मनोहरा।

Two short readings: "that is, in the heart of ascetics. Or hṛdya, delightful."

The word admits both because the suffix यत् on हृद् gives "of the heart" and hence "agreeable to it." हृदय is 595 हृदयस्था's word, where Bhāskararāya gives it three technical senses — the Parābīja, an Upaniṣad, and the seed of the universe on the banyan-simile — and 609 दहराकाशरूपिणी makes the heart's small ether a named locus.

304. हेयोपादेयवर्जिता → हेय-उपादेय-वर्जिता

हेय = to be abandoned, to be rejected (from हा "to abandon," gerundive)
उपादेय = to be accepted, to be taken up (उप + आ + दा, gerundive)
वर्जिता = devoid of, excluding
"She for whom there is nothing to reject or to accept."

Vigraha: हेयेन उपादेयेन च वर्जिता।

Sandhi: हेय + उपादेय → हेयोपादेय (अ + उ → ओ by guṇa, 6.1.87).

The whole commentary is one clause and it is the fourth statement of one principle: "because the scriptures which describe injunction and prohibition are confined to the ignorant ones." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (70).

The other three are 834 विशृङ्खला, with the golden-and-iron fetters; 182 निष्क्रिया, "without action, whether ordained or prohibited"; and 255 धर्माधर्मविवर्जिता, which supplies the analogy — the rule applicable to animals, who like the gods have no share in ritual. So four namas make the claim and only 255 argues it.

The two gerundives are also a matched pair of a kind the text likes: one from हा, to leave, and one from दा with two prefixes, to take up — so what is denied is the whole of choosing.

Note on the verse. Seven namas, four of them on ह and three on न, and the verse closes the fourth hundred.

299 gives the eight stations above the bindu for the second time, with Ardhacandra where 207 had Indu — the same rung under two names, which 594's quarter-measure explains.

300 is the doctrinal entry and the colophon-bearer. Its fivefold analysis — existence, knowledge, bliss, name, form, with the first three Brahman's and the last two the world's — locates the seam between them exactly, and Chāndogya's ether is what separates. And its colophon makes the kalā-sequence contiguous at 200–300, which is the strongest confirmation the rule has had.

301's decoding of ह्रीं into creation, preservation, destruction and the controlling fourth is the same method 231 applied to the name Bhairava.

Textual note. 298's gloss splits mid-sentence. 302's dev and verse text both read हीमती for ह्रीमती, the र् lost, with the gloss preserving the reading.

---

Textual note for verses 61–70.

**The Pañcadaśī is spelled out across seven namas.** Bhāskararāya gives the key at 280 and completes it at 284: Padmāsanā (278) is क, Bhaga (279) ए, vatī (279) ई the Kāmakalā, Padmanābha (280) स, and *hoda* ह and म making ह्रीं — the Vāgbhava kūṭa; then Bhuvanāvali (281) the two Bhuvaneśvarī bījas, Sahasrākṣī (283) ल, and sahasra (284) ह and स — the second and third kūṭas. He had announced the method at 255 ("Devī is the tendril of the Pañcadaśī") and had refused to give the equivalent result at 11, referring the reader to a guru; here he prints it. This is the third and fullest of the text's mantra-ciphers, after 1–3 and 8–11.

**Nama 256 विश्वरूपा carries the longest commentary in the Sahasranāma**, and it is a treatise: the order of creation; the three vehicles at individual, collective and supreme levels; the Vedāntin's three states and functions against the Tāntrika's five, reconciled rather than disputed; why the Upaniṣadists omit the fourth and fifth; the five vehicles identified with the five kośas; four Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa lists of fifteen day- and night-deities for both fortnights; **the derivation of the Pañcadaśī's five-six-four division from the calendrical vedha by which the tenth tithi absorbs the eleventh**; and the honey-doctrine, on which Vedic ritual is efficacious only for one in whom the amṛta flows in the sahasrāra — "of those who are devoid of the inner flow, death at once terminates all their actions." Its last line is the Brāhmaṇa's: "she is bee, fire is the honey."

**Nineteen namas as one exposition.** 256 announces it — "by nineteen names indicating the difference between Jīva and Īśvara" — and 264 marks its halfway turn: five states of the bound soul at 256–263, five functions of the ruler at 264–274. The functions are assigned graded guṇas: rajas for creation, sattva for preservation, tamas for destruction, "pure concentrated" sattva for tirodhāna, "superlative" sattva for anugraha. And 249's Jñānārṇava dialogue supplies the reason the five gods are corpses — "activity belongs to Śakti" — which 947 states as an image without arguing.

**A sixth colophon, and the first consecutive pair.** 300 नामरूपविवर्जिता closes the third hundred with the fourth Kalā, Marīci. With 200's third Kalā closing the second hundred, the sequence is now contiguous, and the rule holds at all six surviving points: 200, 300, 700, 800, 900, 1000. Missing: 100, 400, 500, 600.

**Vararuci's numeral system for the third time, and it closes a cross-reference.** 296 अनादिनिधना reads आदि as eighty (द=8, न=0); the eighty are twenty-eight vadhas plus fifty-two pāśas; and the twenty-eight are unpacked from Sāṃkhya as eleven sense-defects plus seventeen inversions of nine elations and eight perfections. That is precisely what 749 मृत्युदारुकुठारिका's दारु=28 pointed at — "the twenty-eight kinds of pains, as differentiated by energy, success and elation." The other use is 529's उप=10.

**A rival Śaiva canon excluded anatomically.** 287 निजाज्ञारूपनिगमा accepts the twenty-eight Āgamas that "follow the Vedas," distributes them over Śiva's five faces (5+5+5+5+8), and puts the Kāpālika and Bhairava scriptures outside as sprung "from the current below the navel." It is the only exclusion of its kind; rival philosophies are refuted at 136–151 or absorbed at 149 and 155.

**Two named methods of scriptural description, at 289–290.** Definition by direct designation — Śṛṅgagrāhika — is denied of the Vedas, which describe Her by negation and get only the dust of her feet, worn as vermilion in their parting. Positive definition works by Arundhatī-nyāya, locating a faint star by its bright neighbours, and gets only her nose-pearl. And the pair carries a ruling on eligibility: 289's श्रुति entitles the three twice-born castes, 290's सकलागम the fourth.

**Sandhi and letter faults.** 273's dev carries the avagraha of the elided अ from सदाशिवा — twelfth instance of that class. 296's dev reads नादिनिधनो, the initial अ lost *without* an avagraha and ओ standing for आ — so this batch has one marked elision and one unmarked, as verse 154 did at 814–815. 302's dev and verse text both read हीमती for ह्रीमती. No visarga mis-division anywhere in these ten verses, after chains of two and three in each of the last two batches.

**Displaced and split fields.** 251 carries 250's gloss and body and 252 carries 251's gloss, so 251's own commentary is lost. 271 carries 270's, its own standing at the end of the shared block. Glosses split mid-sentence at 276, 277 and 298. Spaces break compounds at 254 (before रूपा) and 290 (after संदोह). 274's dev carries stray daṇḍas. Only 283 has no body at all.

**And the verse table has no row for verse 64.** Verses 64 and 65 are merged into one row labelled 65, whose text carries `।। ६४ ॥` where the boundary falls. Read correctly, verse 64 is namas 268–274 and verse 65 is 275–280. **That is the third instance of a merged verse-row** — after 138/139 and 59/60 — and in all three the row takes the *later* number and buries the earlier one inside the text.

**The girl-ages reach nine** with 276 Bhairavī at twelve: 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13.

**And 284 सहस्रपात् is the thousand's second and last consonant-final nama**, after 795 कामधुक्.

## राजराजार्चिता राज्ञी रम्या राजीवलोचना । रञ्जनी रमणी रस्या रणत्किङ्किणिमेखला

*rājarājārcitā rājñī ramyā rājīvalocanā । rañjanī ramaṇī rasyā raṇatkiṅkiṇimekhalā*

Verse 71, namas 305–312.

305. राजराजार्चिता → राजराज-अर्चिता

राजराज = king of kings — and per the commentary, Manu and Kubera
अर्चिता = worshipped, honoured (from अर्च् "to worship")
"She who is worshipped by the king of kings."

Vigraha: राजराजेन अर्चिता।

Sandhi: राजराज + अर्चिता → राजराजार्चिता (आ by 6.1.101).

"Rājarāja, Manu and Kubera; or the Vidyā of Kubera and others" — with a cross-reference to nama 238. So the राजराज here are two of the twelve holders of the Pañcadaśī recensions, and the nama joins the twelve-fold scheme that 238 and 812 set out.

Then Durvāsa's Lalitāstavaratna is quoted for the placement, and it is a wall-number again: "when he describes the space between the fourteenth and the fifteenth walls, he says: I meditate upon Kubera, the head of a wealthy family, in the Eastern part of that place of Vāyu, and upon the other Yakṣas who depend upon the feet of Mother, such as Maṇibhadra and others."

That is exactly where 297 हरिब्रह्मेन्द्रसेविता put Indra and the Lokapālas — "between the fourteenth and the fifteenth walls" — so Kubera and the Yakṣas share the enclosure with them, and the fourth wall-placement in the text is consistent with the other three.

Sastry's footnote on the *vyākulākṣara* verse has drifted into this body: "a most secret meaning of certain mantras was given out in a perplexing verse, with a key also in another verse in the same way, in order that it may not be understood by the uninitiated. Such verses are called Vyākulākṣara verses." That belongs to 301 ह्रींकारी, where the Svatantra Tantra's decoding of ह्रीं was given by such a verse.

306. राज्ञी → राज्ञी

राज्ञी = queen (feminine of राजन्, from राज् "to shine, to rule")
"The Queen."

Vigraha: राजराजेश्वरस्य राज्ञी।

The whole commentary is one clause: "because she is the queen of Rājarājeśvara" — that is Śiva, and Rājarājeśvarī is nama 684, so this nama is that one shortened to its second half.

राज्ञी had also stood in the text's second nama, 2 श्रीमहाराज्ञी, where Bhāskararāya said "the part of the word Rājñī contains the mantra called Māyārājñī."

307. रम्या → रम्या

रम्या = delightful, pleasing (from रम् "to delight," gerundive)
"The Delightful."

Vigraha: रमणीया रम्या।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

The gerundive of रम् makes this "to be delighted in" rather than "delighting," which the next nama but one supplies in the active. रम् gives four namas in this verse-pair — रम्या, रमणी, रमा, रमणलम्पटा — and आरामा at 878 and रति at 218 and 315.

308. राजीवलोचना → राजीव-लोचना

राजीव = per the Viśva, a deer, a fish, a lotus, or a dependent of a king
लोचना = an eye (from लोच् "to see")
"She whose eyes are like a deer's."

Vigraha: राजीवस्य इव लोचने यस्याः सा।

The Viśva's four senses are given and the last is taken: "in the latter sense she looks favourably on those who depend on the king's bounty."

So a word for an eye's shape becomes a word about whom the eye looks at, which is 805 पुष्करेक्षणा's inversion — there Puṣkara is Viṣṇu asleep on the banyan leaf and the compound becomes "she beholds him with compassion." The other three senses are the text's other eye-similes: deer at 561 मृगाक्षी, fish at 18, lotus at 247 पद्मनयना.

लोचन for the second time, after 18.

309. रञ्जनी → रञ्जनी

रञ्जनी = delighting, gladdening; also dyeing, colouring (from रञ्ज् "to be dyed, to be delighted")
"The Delighter — and the Dyer."

Vigraha: रञ्जयतीति रञ्जनी।

Two readings and the second is the substantial one: "Her devotees. Or Rañjanī, dyeing. By her presence, the rosy-tinted Devī colours the pure Paramaśiva as the red flower colours the crystal."

That is 154 निरुपाधिः's simile exactly — "the red flower transfers its colour to the crystal near it; this is the upādhi. Similarly, ignorance is the upādhi which causes the appearance of plurality in consciousness" — and 666 भूमरूपा's, where the crystal coloured by transmission was the model for Her being called Bhūmā. Here the flower is Her own redness and the crystal is Śiva.

So the figure the text uses for how illusion works is used here for how She affects Him, and the redness is 6 उद्यद्भानुसहस्राभा's Vimarśa-colour. रञ्ज् is also the root of राग, which 937 विरागिणी denies of Her — uncoloured as much as unattached.

310. रमणी → रमणी

रमणी = gladdening, delighting; a lovely woman (from रम्)
"The Gladdener."

Vigraha: रमयतीति रमणी।

"Of her devotees." And Chāndogya 8.12.3: "laughing, playing and rejoicing."

That verse is the description of the bodiless self sporting after release, and 182 निष्क्रिया cites its neighbour, 8.12.1 — "only one who has no body is unaffected by likes or dislikes."

311. रस्या → रस्या

रस्या = to be tasted, savoury (from रस् "to taste," gerundive)
"She who is to be tasted."

Vigraha: रसनीया रस्या।

Taittirīya 2.6.1: "He is alone the essence" — *raso vai saḥ*, the verse 800 रसशेवधिः is built on and 192 सुखप्रदा cites.

So रस is the essence at 800 and the tasting at 799 रसज्ञा, where रसज्ञा was at once the connoisseur of dramatic modes and the tongue. Here She is the object of that tasting, which completes the set: what tastes, what is tasted, and the store of it.

312. रणत्किङ्किणिमेखला → रणत्-किङ्किणि-मेखला

रणत् = tinkling, jingling (present participle of रण् "to sound")
किङ्किणि = a small bell
मेखला = a girdle, a waist-belt
"She whose girdle is of tinkling bells."

Vigraha: रणत्किङ्किणयः मेखला यस्याः सा।

index.html carries 313's material on this nama and 313 carries it too, so the two share one body; the shared block reads "In the form of Lakṣmī. The Sa. Sam. 4.47.66: *she appears like a dancer in the form of Lakṣmī, speech and the rest*." That belongs to 313 रमा.

रणत् is onomatopoeic, as शिञ्जान was at 46 शिञ्जानमणिमञ्जीरमण्डितश्रीपदाम्बुजा; and this is the second girdle in the text after 38 रत्नकिङ्किणिकारम्यरशनादामभूषिता, which used the same किङ्किणि with रशना for मेखला. So the ornament is described twice, 274 namas apart, with one word changed.

Note on the verse. Eight namas, all on र, and four of them from रम्.

309 is the entry to keep. रञ्जनी read as "dyeing" makes Her redness colour Śiva as the red flower colours the crystal — which is the text's standing figure for how upādhi works at 154 and for Her plurality at 666, here turned to the relation between the two of them.

308 gives four senses of राजीव and takes the fourth, so an eye-simile becomes a statement about whom the eye favours; and 311 completes the रस-set, She being what is tasted where 799 was the taster and 800 the store.

Textual note. 305's body carries Sastry's footnote on *vyākulākṣara* verses, which belongs to 301. 307 has no body. 312 and 313 share one body, which is 313's.

---

## रमा राकेन्दुवदना रतिरूपा रतिप्रिया । रक्षाकरी राक्षसघ्नी रामा रमणलम्पटा

*ramā rākenduvadanā ratirūpā ratipriyā । rakṣākarī rākṣasaghnī rāmā ramaṇalampaṭā*

Verse 72, namas 313–320.

> **Namas 313–315 encode the Kāmakalā mantra, and Bhāskararāya says so at 315**: "Ramā indicates ī, rākenduvadanā the anusvāra. Thus the Kāmakalā Mantra is indicated here." That is the fourth mantra-cipher in the text, after the three kūṭas concealed in namas 1–3, the weapon-bījas at 8–11 (where he refused to give the result), and the whole Pañcadaśī at 278–284.

313. रमा → रमा

रमा = Ramā, Lakṣmī (from रम् "to delight"); and per the cipher, the letter ई
"Ramā."

Vigraha: रमते इति रमा।

**In the cipher this nama supplies ई.**

The commentary, shared with 312, is one citation: "in the form of Lakṣmī. The Sūta Saṃhitā 4.47.66: *she appears like a dancer in the form of Lakṣmī, speech and the rest*."

The dancer-figure recurs at 816 मुनिमानसहंसिका, where the second reading makes सहंसिका "a dancer with bangles on the ankles," and at 734 नटेश्वरी, wife of the Naṭarāja. Lakṣmī is one of the two chowrie-bearers at 614 and crores of Her are handmaids at 590.

ई is also the single-vowel nama at 712, the Kāmakalā, where Bhāskararāya refers the reader to a guru — so the letter that is a nama in its own right there is concealed in a word here, exactly as it was at 279 भगवती.

314. राकेन्दुवदना → राका-इन्दु-वदना

राका = the full moon; the night of the full moon
इन्दु = the moon
वदना = faced (वदन "face, mouth," from वद् "to speak")
"She whose face is the full moon."

Vigraha: राकेन्दुः इव वदनं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: राका + इन्दु → राकेन्दु (आ + इ → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87). index.html has no commentary for this nama.

**In the cipher this nama supplies the anusvāra.**

The lunar face is the text's fourth: the eighth-day half moon on the brow at 15, the full moon with its spot at 16, the autumn moon at 129 शरच्चन्द्रनिभानना, and here the full moon simply. And इन्दु is the name of the first of the eight stations above the brow at 207, which 299 calls Ardhacandra instead.

315. रतिरूपा → रति-रूपा

रति = delight, pleasure; Rati, Kāma's wife (from रम्)
रूपा = form
"She in the form of Rati."

Vigraha: रतिः रूपं यस्याः सा।

"The wife of Kāma." And then the cipher: "or Ramā indicates ī, rākenduvadanā the anusvāra. Thus the Kāmakalā Mantra is indicated here."

So ई with the anusvāra gives ईं, and that is the Kāmakalā bīja. Sastry's note at nama 3 listed the four bindus of the Setubandha with Turīya or Kāmakalā first, and 322 कामकलारूपा seven namas on gives the full doctrine — so the mantra is encoded here and expounded there.

Rati is 218 महारतिः's second reading, "the wife of Mahākāma," and this nama with the next makes the same marriage explicit.

316. रतिप्रिया → रति-प्रिया

रति = Rati; also delight
प्रिया = dear to; a beloved
"Beloved of Rati." — or, "She to whom delight is dear."

Vigraha: रतेः प्रिया। or रतिः प्रिया यस्याः सा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

315 and 316 make a pair that can be read two ways: She is Rati's form and Rati's beloved, or she is the form of delight and delight is dear to her. The text does not choose, and प्रिया is here on its thirteenth turn.

317. रक्षाकरी → रक्षा-करी

रक्षा = protection, guarding (from रक्ष् "to protect"); and per the second reading, holy ashes
करी = she who makes (from कृ)
"She who makes protection."

Vigraha: रक्षां करोतीति रक्षाकरी।

The alternative turns on a homonym: "or Rakṣā, the holy ashes; that is the protector and destroyer."

रक्षा is bhasma, the ash smeared as a protective mark, so the same word is the act of guarding and the substance used for it — and ash is what remains of what has been destroyed, which is why Bhāskararāya says "protector and destroyer" in one breath. The Kāma burnt to ash at 84 and revived by Her is the text's own instance.

318. राक्षसघ्नी → राक्षस-घ्नी

राक्षस = a Rākṣasa, a demon (vṛddhi derivative of रक्षस्)
घ्नी = she who slays (from हन् "to strike"; feminine of घ्न)
"The Slayer of Rākṣasas."

Vigraha: राक्षसान् हन्तीति।

Both the dev field and the verse text read राक्षसन्नी, the घ् lost and the न् doubled in its place. index.html has no commentary, so only the gloss — "slayer of Rākṣasas" — preserves the reading.

That is the third instance of exactly this fault: 842 भवरोगघ्नी prints भवरोगनी, 173 संशयघ्नी prints संशयनी, and here राक्षसघ्नी prints राक्षसन्नी. In all three cases the घ् of घ्नी disappears and in all three the gloss supplies it.

And the juxtaposition with 317 is not accidental: रक्षा protection and राक्षस a demon are the same root रक्ष्, the demon being named as one to be guarded against — so the two namas are the root's two faces.

319. रामा → रामा

रामा = a woman, a beautiful woman; also from रम् "to delight"
"Woman."

Vigraha: रमयतीति रामा। or रामा नारी।

**This nama carries the grammatical theology, and it is the second of two places in the text where the Liṅga Purāṇa states it.**

"Or, Yogins delight in her." Then the Liṅga Purāṇa: "all men are Śaṃkara, all women, Devī. The names which denote masculine gender are said to be of Śiva, and those which denote the feminine are the manifestations of Devī. Thus women and men are the manifestations of Devī and Śiva."

At 276 भैरवी the same Purāṇa gave it in the form "all things indicated by the words in the feminine gender are manifestations of Devī," which is wider — a claim about words rather than about people. Here it is narrowed to men and women and then widened again by two further citations.

The Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "the divine Hari lives in the form of a man among Devas, animals, men and the rest, and in the form of women, O Maitreya, Lakṣmī lives, and there is none higher than these two." The Brahmavaivarta: "whatever in the three worlds appears in female form, all that, O Devī, is thy form; thus is declared in the scriptures."

And then the Bṛhat-Parāśara Smṛti draws a domestic consequence, which is the only place the text does so: "if women are pleased the Gods also are pleased; if they are displeased the Gods are displeased. If women are pleased the family increases; if they are displeased the family is spoilt."

320. रमणलम्पटा → रमण-लम्पटा

रमण = a husband, a lover; also enjoyment, play (from रम्)
लम्पटा = devoted to, addicted to, eager for
"She who is devoted to her husband."

Vigraha: रमणे लम्पटा।

The gloss makes the devotion transitive: "as she is the collective form of women, she makes each woman devoted to her husband." So the nama follows 319 as its consequence — she is all women, and what she is in them is this.

That is 128 साध्वी's chastity and 709 सदाशिवपतिव्रता's vow "in all the three times," distributed. And a second reading takes रमण as enjoyment rather than husband: "Ramaṇa, enjoyment, play; lampaṭa, devoted." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (72).

लम्पट is a strong word — addicted, greedy — the same register as लोलुपा at 857 गानलोलुपा, where She is avid for song.

Note on the verse. Eight namas, all on र, and the verse does two quite different things.

313–315 encode the Kāmakalā bīja ईं, which makes this the fourth mantra-cipher in the text; and 322 seven namas on gives that mantra's doctrine, so the cipher and its exposition are close together for once.

Then 319 carries the Liṅga Purāṇa's gender-theology for the second time, and where 276 made the criterion a grammatical ending this one makes it people, with the Bṛhat-Parāśara's consequence about families attached. 320 completes it by making Her devotion to a husband the thing she is in every woman.

317–318 also pair on रक्ष् — protection and the demon to be protected against.

Textual note. 318's dev and verse text both read राक्षसन्नी for राक्षसघ्नी, the third instance of that loss after 842 and 173, and again only the gloss preserves the word. 314, 316 and 318 have no commentary bodies.

---

## काम्या कामकलारूपा कदम्बकुसुमप्रिया । कल्याणी जगतीकन्दा करुणारससागरा

*kāmyā kāmakalārūpā kadambakusumapriyā । kalyāṇī jagatīkandā karuṇārasasāgarā*

Verse 73, namas 321–326.

321. काम्या → काम्या

काम्या = to be desired, desirable (from कम् "to desire," gerundive); also the deity of the twelfth dark night
"The Desirable."

Vigraha: काम्यते इति काम्या।

"Those who desire liberation desire to obtain Her by knowledge. Or Kāmyā is the deity of the twelfth night of the dark fortnight."

The tithi-deities are the fifteen of 256's scheme, and the text names three of them as namas: Pūrṇā the fifteenth at 292, Kāntā the eleventh at 329 eight namas on, and Kāmyā the twelfth here. So three of the fifteen dark-fortnight deities stand among the thousand.

काम्या is the gerundive of कम्, and 860 कान्ता is the participle of the same root — desired there, to-be-desired here.

322. कामकलारूपा → कामकला-रूपा

कामकला = the Kāmakalā — the four bindus taken as one, or the manifestation of desire
रूपा = form
"She in the form of Kāmakalā."

Vigraha: कामकला रूपं यस्याः सा।

**And here the abbreviation is explained by a rule of Pāṇinian grammar, which the text does nowhere else.**

"There are three bindus and the Hārdakalā; in these, the first bindu is called Kāma and the last Kāla. According to the rule of Pratyāhāra, Kāmakalā includes all four."

A pratyāhāra is the grammarians' device by which a whole series is named by its first member and a marker at its end — अच् for the vowels, हल् for the consonants. So *Kāmakalā* is a pratyāhāra: Kāma the first bindu, Kāla the last member, and everything between included. The four are the set Sastry's footnote gave at nama 3: Turīya or Kāmakalā, Kāmabindu (अ, Śiva), Visarga (ह, Devī), and Hārdakalā.

Then the Kāmakalāvilāsa is cited and partly quoted: "the Paraśakti is in the form of the sprout, expanded out of the union of Śiva and Śakti… the two bindus in the middle represent the sun and the moon."

Then three further readings. "Kāma both Śiva and Devī, and Kāla manifestation," on the Tripurasiddhānta: "O Pārvatī, Kāla is the manifestation of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, hence she is known as Kāmakalā." Or simply "the manifestation of desire."

And the Kālikā Purāṇa's derivation, which makes काम a place and an act: "Devī alone is indicated by the word Kāma. Devī is called Kāma because she came to the secret place in the blue peak of the great mountain along with me for the sake of desire. As she is also fulfilling desire, desiring, desirable, beautiful, restoring the body of Kāma, and destroying the body of Kāma, hence she is called Kāma."

The last two clauses hold both sides of 84 हरनेत्राग्निसंदग्धकामसंजीवनौषधिः, where Kāma is burnt by Hara's eye and She is the herb reviving him — restoring and destroying the same body.

काम has now carried five referents: the god at 84, the bodiless Ṛṣi at 586, Paramaśiva at 589, the Bindu at 28, and the creative desire at 796.

323. कदम्बकुसुमप्रिया → कदम्ब-कुसुम-प्रिया

कदम्ब = the kadamba tree and its globular blossom
कुसुम = a flower
प्रिया = dear to, fond of
"She who delights in the kadamba flower."

Vigraha: कदम्बकुसुमं प्रियं यस्याः सा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

The kadamba is the tree of Her grove at 60 कदम्बवनवासिनी and the flower in her ear at 21 कदम्बमञ्जरीक्ऌप्तकर्णपूरमनोहरा. So the blossom she is fond of here is from the wood she lives in and the ornament she wears.

This is the fourth कुसुमप्रिया-nama, after 773 पाटलीकुसुमप्रिया, 776 मन्दारकुसुमप्रिया and 919 चैतन्यकुसुमप्रिया — where the flower is consciousness itself and Bhāskararāya lists eight of them, not one a thing.

324. कल्याणी → कल्याणी

कल्याणी = auspicious, beneficent, blessed (from कल्य "well, sound")
"The Beneficent."

Vigraha: कल्याणं करोतीति कल्याणी।

"Or, according to the Padma Purāṇa, in the Malaya Mountain she is worshipped as Kalyāṇī. Or, kalya, good words; ana, to utter."

So the second reading makes the auspiciousness verbal — she who utters good words — which is the same syllabic move 328 कलालापा makes four namas on. And the Malaya placement joins the located identifications: Viśālākṣī at Benares, Mīnākṣī at Madhurā, Kātyāyanī at Oḍḍiyāna, Gaurī at Kanyakubja, Sāvitrī at Puṣkara, Virajā at Utkala, Mahākālī at Ujjayinī, Vijayā in Kashmir at 346, Vimalā at Puruṣottama at 347, Tanumadhyā at Kāñcī at 360, Lalitā at Prayāga.

325. जगतीकन्दा → जगती-कन्दा

जगती = the world, the earth (from गम् "to go")
कन्दा = a bulb, a tuber, a root; and per Yādava, filling, and a cloud
"The Root of the world."

Vigraha: जगत्याः कन्दा।

"According to Yādava, kanda means filling, root of plants, cloud."

कन्द is specifically a bulbous root — the swollen underground stem from which a plant grows again — so the figure is of the world as a plant with Her for its tuber. That is a different image from मूल at 840 मूलविग्रहरूपिणी, where मूलविग्रह is the root-form from which all śaktis branch, and from 955 धरा, where the earth is the bearer.

जगती is the feminine of जगत्, so the same "moving" word as 244 चराचरजगन्नाथा and 935 जगद्धात्री.

326. करुणारससागरा → करुणा-रस-सागरा

करुणा = compassion, pity
रस = water, juice; also flavour, essence
सागरा = the ocean
"The Ocean of the waters of compassion."

Vigraha: करुणारसस्य सागरा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

रस here is water rather than taste, which is its other standing sense — so the compound is compassion made a fluid and then given an ocean's volume. That is 197 सान्द्रकरुणा's move at larger scale: there compassion was given a thickness, here a body of water.

करुणा for the third time, after 197 and 992 अव्याजकरुणामूर्तिः where it needs no pretext; and दया at 581, कृपा at 687.

Note on the verse. Six namas, and 322 carries it.

The pratyāhāra reading is the thing to keep. Bhāskararāya explains why one name covers four bindus by invoking the grammarians' abbreviation-device — first member plus terminal marker — which is a technical solution to a technical problem and the only place in the text he reaches for it. And the Kālikā Purāṇa's derivation there ends by making Her both the restorer and the destroyer of Kāma's body, which is 84's story from both ends.

325's कन्द is worth marking as the text's fourth figure for Her relation to the world's origin: root-form at 840, bearer at 955, mother at 934, and here a bulb.

Textual note. 323 and 326 have no commentary bodies.

---

## कलावती कलालापा कान्ता कादम्बरीप्रिया । वरदा वामनयना वारुणीमदाविह्वला

*kalāvatī kalālāpā kāntā kādambarīpriyā । varadā vāmanayanā vāruṇīmadāvihvalā*

Verse 74, namas 327–333.

327. कलावती → कला-वती

कला = an art, a science
वती = possessing (मतुप्, feminine ङीप्)
"She who possesses the arts."

Vigraha: कलाः अस्याः सन्तीति कलावती।

The whole commentary is four words: "the sciences are sixty-four."

That is the list 236 चतुःषष्टिकलामयी gives in full and signs — "thus laid down by the poet Bhāskara, the sixty-four sciences, after examining them" — which runs from the four Vedas to gambling, thieving, killing by magic and disappearance. So this nama is 236 with मयी exchanged for वती, possessing rather than consisting of.

Kalāvatī is also one of the four divine lutes named at 27, Tumburu's — and Bṛhatī and Mahatī from that list are namas 673 and 774. So three of the four lutes are named in the text and this is the third.

328. कलालापा → कला-आलापा

कला = an art, a science; and per the Amara, sweetly sounding
आलापा = speech, conversation (आ + लप् "to speak")
"She whose speech is art."

Vigraha: कला आलापः यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: कला + आलापा → कलालापा (आ by 6.1.101).

Two readings, and the second is one of the oddest syllabic divisions in the text.

The Amara 86 is cited for the first: "kala means sweetly sounding; ālāpa, speech."

Then: "Or, Ka, Brahman; lālā, saliva; ap, attainment. The attainment of the Brahman becomes, through her grace, as natural as the flow of saliva."

So the nama is divided into क + लाला + अप् to yield a claim about how easy realisation is — and the comparison is to salivation, which happens without willing it. That is the text's leniency-doctrine given a physiological figure, alongside 736 मुक्तिदा's liberation to those who recite "even unconsciously" and 815 अनित्यतृप्ता's leaf and water.

आलाप is the word of 613 काव्यालापविनोदिनी, where She delights in the discourse of poetry, and सल्लाप of 27, where Her conversation shames Sarasvatī's lute.

329. कान्ता → कान्ता

कान्ता = beloved, desired, lovely (past participle of कम् "to desire"); also the deity of the eleventh dark night
"The Beloved."

Vigraha: कम्यते इति कान्ता।

Two readings. "Or, Ka, Brahman; anta, final. Brahman unconditioned is her final form. Or she is the deity called Kāntā of the eleventh night of the dark fortnight."

So the syllabic division makes कान्ता the end-point of Brahman, and the tithi-reading makes her the eleventh of the fifteen — with Kāmyā the twelfth at 321 eight namas back and Pūrṇā the fifteenth at 292.

कान्ता stood before at 860, where index.html preserved only the syllabic gloss "end of sin — aka, sin and pain," so the word occurs twice in the thousand and is divided both times.

330. कादम्बरीप्रिया → कादम्बरी-प्रिया

कादम्बरी = mead, a spirituous liquor made from the kadamba fruit
प्रिया = dear to, fond of
"She who delights in mead."

Vigraha: कादम्बरी प्रिया यस्याः सा।

The Tripurā Upaniṣad is quoted, and it is the text's plainest statement of the five substances: "Mead, fish, flesh, cooked cereals offered in the triangle on behalf of the great Devatā — the lucky devotee, recovering his self, attains perfection."

That is the pañcamakāra offered in the Yoni-triangle, which 982 योनिमुद्रा and 895 योनिनिलया name and 986 त्रिकोणगा makes Her destination. And the five M's are what 948 पञ्चमी refuses to expound, referring the reader to a guru — "their meaning, namely gift, purification and so on, must be learned from the Guru." Here the Upaniṣad's list is given without comment, and the next nama's footnote supplies the qualification.

The mead of 575 माध्वीपानालसा, 152 निष्कारणा's कारण, 836 वीरमाता's vessel and 918's Rudrayāmala — "of wisdom and mead, wisdom is the better" — are the same substance. And कादम्बरी is from कदम्ब, the tree of 323 two namas back.

331. वरदा → वर-दा

वर = a boon, a gift
दा = giving (from दा "to give")
"The Giver of boons."

Vigraha: वरं ददातीति वरदा।

**This nama returns to Nārada's reading of Pārvatī's bodily marks at 44, and it takes up the third of the four.**

"To Brahmā, Viṣṇu and other devotees. This is said by Nārada in the Matsya and Padma Purāṇas: *what I told you of this Devī about her ever uplifted hand — for this uplifted hand of Devī ever confers boons. She will become the giver of boons to all Devas, Daityas and ascetics.*"

At 44 the four marks were read as calamitous by Menā and turned round one by one: no husband born for her, because Śiva is uncreated; devoid of good bodily marks, because she is unconditioned; her hand always raised, because "a great giver herself, hers must necessarily be above that of the one who receives"; and her feet shadowed, because the reflected crowns of bowing gods drive the rays of her nails into their hearts. This nama is the third of those, and the Purāṇa is quoted saying so — "what I told you of this Devī about her ever uplifted hand."

Then Bhāskararāya guards against taking the hand literally: "as in the world the hand is the instrument of giving, here the hand of Devī is said to confer boons. In reality, the expression means simply to fulfil the desire of the gods; not having the emblem of granting boons."

And Saundaryalaharī 4 is quoted for why she has no such emblem, which is the sharpest thing in the verse: "with the exception of yourself, all the bands of deities by their hands confer respectively gift and protection. Thou alone doth not do this." Every other deity is depicted making the varada- and abhaya-mudrās; She is not, because her hands hold the noose, goad, bow and arrows of namas 8–11.

The Devī Bhāgavata adds the etymology — "from the root वृ to choose, she is called Varadā, conferrer of boons, that is, giver of the thing chosen" — and the Varāha Purāṇa's Vṛtrāsuravadha chapter a rubric: "this Devī is always to be worshipped by concentration on the ninth day; she will certainly become the giver of boons to all worlds."

वरदा had stood at 639, and Varadā is also the first of the four śaktis attending Her at 518 वरदादिनिषेविता — so a nama of Hers is the name of one of her attendants.

332. वामनयना → वाम-नयना

वाम = fair, lovely; also the left; also, per the Chāndogya reading, the fruit of inaction
नयना = an eye (from नी "to lead"); and per the second reading, a proof, a means of leading to knowledge
"She of the beautiful eyes."

Vigraha: वामे नयने यस्याः सा।

Three readings. "Or, Vāma, fair; and nayana, literally eyes, that is, proofs." Or "vāma, the left path; naya, to lead" — the Vāma-mārga, which 912 सव्यापसव्यमार्गस्था ranks below the Dakṣiṇa and 945 वामकेश्वरी glosses "contemptible, because they do not perform the five sacrifices." Or vāma as "the fruit of inaction," on Chāndogya 4.15.2–3, where the word occurs and is so explained.
