**And here Bhāskararāya's own footnote on the previous nama's mead is preserved, and it is the only moral qualification the text attaches to the five substances**: "Bhāskararāya, commenting on the Upaniṣad, gives injunction to those who are allowed to take mead, fish and the rest, that they should take them first by dedicating them to God, and minimise the habit by gradation." Manu 5.56 and the Viṣṇu Bhāgavata 11.5.11 are cited for the same idea.

So the Tripurā Upaniṣad's list at 330 is licensed and then hedged: dedicate first, and taper off. That is a real position, and it is the only place the text takes one on the pañcamakāra.

नयन is the eye named from नी, to lead, which is exactly what makes the "proof" reading available — a प्रमाण is what leads to knowledge. And the same word stood at 247 पद्मनयना.

333. वारुणीमदाविह्वला → वारुणी-मद-अविह्वला

वारुणी = a spirituous liquor made from dates — named for Varuṇa, who is fond of it; also, per the second reading, belonging to Varuṇa's region; also the Vāruṇī nāḍī
मद = intoxication (from मद्)
अविह्वला = not perturbed, not overcome (अ + विह्वल)
"She who is unshaken by the intoxication of Vāruṇī."

Vigraha: वारुणीमदेन अविह्वला।

Sandhi: मद + अविह्वला → मदाविह्वला (आ by 6.1.101). Both the dev field and the verse text read वारुणीमदविला, having lost the आ of the joint and the ह्व of विह्वला — so the recorded form is not a word, and only the commentary's "avihvala, not perturbed" preserves the reading.

Three readings, and the first has nothing to do with drink.

"Vāruṇīmat, belonging to the regions of Varuṇa, that is Ādiśeṣa, the thousand-hooded snake, because he dwells in that region; avihvala, not perturbed or fatigued — that is, by Her grace Ādiśeṣa is not fatigued in supporting the universe." The Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "in the Varuṇa regions he worships Devī with his own glorious body."

So on this reading the nama is about the world-serpent's stamina, and अविह्वला is predicated of him through Her grace.

The second takes वारुणी as the date-liquor and reads the un-perturbedness as concentration: "the expression means forgetting external objects and simply enjoying Svātmānanda." That is 878 स्वात्मारामा's self-delight, and 575 माध्वीपानालसा's languor after wine.

And the third is physiological: "or Vāruṇīmat, those who conquered the Vāruṇī nāḍī and became firm." The Yoga Śāstra is cited: "Vāruṇīnāḍī is that which is above and below, going everywhere; Pūṣan is the deity of the quarters, and Vāyu is the deity of this vāruṇī nāḍī." Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (74).

Note on the verse. Seven namas, four on क and three on व, and the substance is in the middle.

330–332 make a group the text does not often assemble. 330 gives the Tripurā Upaniṣad's five substances offered in the triangle; 332's body carries Bhāskararāya's own qualification of them — dedicate to God first, and reduce the habit by degrees, with Manu 5.56 for support. That is the only moral note on the pañcamakāra in the thousand, and it sits between the licence and the ranking of the Vāma path.

331 is the entry to keep. It takes up the third of the four bodily marks Nārada read at 44 and cites the same Purāṇic passage, then denies that the raised hand is a varada-mudrā at all — with Saundaryalaharī 4 for the reason: every other deity confers gift and protection by hand, and She alone does not, because her hands are full.

Textual note. 333's dev and verse text both read वारुणीमदविला for वारुणीमदाविह्वला, losing both the sandhi-आ and the ह्व; the commentary preserves the word.

---

## विश्वाधिका वेदवेद्या विन्ध्याचलनिवासिनी । विधात्री वेदजननी विष्णुमाया विलासिनी

*viśvādhikā vedavedyā vindhyācalanivāsinī । vidhātrī vedajananī viṣṇumāyā vilāsinī*

Verse 75, namas 334–340.

334. विश्वाधिका → विश्व-अधिका

विश्व = all, the universe — and per the gloss, the categories from earth to Śiva
अधिका = exceeding, surpassing (अधि + क)
"She who transcends the universe."

Vigraha: विश्वात् अधिका।

Sandhi: विश्व + अधिका → विश्वाधिका (आ by 6.1.101).

"Viśva, the categories from earth to Śiva." So what is transcended is the thirty-six tattvas, which is 906 तत्त्वाधिका's claim in the same construction — अधिका with a different first member — and there Bhāskararāya gave the criterion for counting them: "what remains till the pralaya."

The Śruti: "Rudra, the great seer, transcends the universe."

विश्व for the sixth time, after 889 (turned), 890 (eaten), 934 (mothered), 637 (carried) and 256 (the waking level).

335. वेदवेद्या → वेद-वेद्या

वेद = the Veda (from विद् "to know")
वेद्या = to be known (विद् with the gerundive यत्)
"She who is to be known through the Vedas."

Vigraha: वेदैः वेद्या।

The compound puts विद् at both ends, as 645 सर्ववेदान्तसंवेद्या does. Kaivalya 2.3 — "I alone am to be known from all the Vedas" — and Gītā 15.15 repeats it.

**Then the four Vedas are made the four gates of the Cintāmaṇi palace, which is nama 57.**

"There are four gates to the Cintāmaṇi palace; these are the four Vedas. As the deity cannot be seen unless the gates are entered, hence it is said she is to be known through the Vedas alone."

That is an architectural reading of an epistemological nama, and it uses the topography 55–58 built: Meru's central peak, the city upon it, the cintāmaṇi palace within the city, the pañcabrahma seat within the palace. The palace's gates are now identified.

Then the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa assigns the quarters: "the great quarter, the east, is said to be of the Ṛgs; the endless southern quarter, they say, is that of the Yajus; the west of the Atharva; and the great northern quarter is that of Sāman."

**And then a fourfold scheme of goddesses is mapped onto them**, which is the entry's substance: "Devī should be known through the four goddesses who are the deities of the four Vedas, viz. Śuddhavidyā and others, Saubhāgya and others, Lopāmudrā and others, and Turīyāmbā and others, who are the deities of Ṛg, Yajus, Atharva and Sāman respectively."

Three of those four are namas of the text. Śuddhavidyā is the Ṣoḍaśī of 25 शुद्धविद्याङ्कुराकारद्विजपङ्क्तिद्वयोज्ज्वला and one of the three Vidyās at 840; Lopāmudrā is 647 लोपामुद्रार्चिता, one of the twelve holders at 238 and 812; Turīyā is 262, whose name the Tripurā Siddhānta derives from Turīyānandanātha. And सौभाग्य is the word 117 भक्तसौभाग्यदायिनी identifies with Lalitā herself.

So the four Vedas are four gates, four quarters, and four groups of deities, three of which are named elsewhere in the thousand.

336. विन्ध्याचलनिवासिनी → विन्ध्य-अचल-निवासिनी

विन्ध्य = the Vindhya range
अचल = a mountain — literally the unmoving (अ + चल्)
निवासिनी = dwelling, residing (नि + वस् "to dwell")
"She who dwells on the Vindhya mountain."

Vigraha: विन्ध्याचले निवासिनी।

Sandhi: विन्ध्य + अचल → विन्ध्याचल (आ by 6.1.101).

The Padma Purāṇa's list of sacred places is cited — "Sītā is in the Trikūṭa mountain and Vindhyādhivāsinī in the Vindhya" — and then the Pāñcarātra's Lakṣmītantra gives Her own prophecy of the residence: "in the Vaivasvata Manvantara, two Daityas, Śumbha and Niśumbha, over-elated by their boons, will do injury to the devas. Born in Nandagopa's family, in the womb of Yaśodā, I under the name Nandā, residing in the Vindhya Mountain, shall destroy these two." The Mārkaṇḍeya repeats it.

So the Vindhya residence is tied to the Śumbha-Niśumbha episode and to a birth in Yaśodā's womb — which puts Her in Kṛṣṇa's household, as 838 मुकुन्दा and 893 विष्णुरूपिणी put Kṛṣṇa among her forms.

अचल is the mountain named as the unmoving, so the compound is doubled: the Vindhya-unmoving-thing.

337. विधात्री → वि-धात्री

वि = fully
धात्री = she who bears, sustains; a nurse; also myrobalan (धा "to place, to bear" + तृ, feminine ङीप्)
"The Sustainer."

Vigraha: विदधातीति विधात्री।

Three readings, ending in a lexical surprise.

"Nourisher of the universe." The Devī Purāṇa: "Dhātrī is known as the mother, because she bears." Or "the wife of Brahmā, Vidhātā." And then: "Or, Vi, much; dhātrī, myrobalan, because she is fond of myrobalans."

धात्री is indeed a name for the āmalakī, the myrobalan tree, so the compound admits "very fond of myrobalans" — and Bhāskararāya records it. It is the smallest claim made of Her in the thousand.

धात्री is 935 जगद्धात्री's word, where जगत् the moving is set against धात्री the bearer; and the तृ agent-noun of 826 सवित्री, 832 प्राणदात्री, 882 यज्ञकर्त्री and 264 सृष्टिकर्त्री.

338. वेदजननी → वेद-जननी

वेद = the Veda
जननी = mother, she who gives birth (from जन्, causative जनय्)
"The Mother of the Vedas."

Vigraha: वेदानां जननी।

Muṇḍaka 1.1.5: "the Vedas are the breath of this great Being." The Puruṣasūkta: "Ṛgs and Sāmans came out from Him."

**And then the Devī Purāṇa derives the Vedas from the alphabet and the alphabet from the kuṇḍalinī's triangle**: "because there arose from the Kuṇḍalinī, which is triangular in form, the vowels and consonants, hence she is the mother of the Vedas."

That is the chain the text builds elsewhere in pieces. The triangle is 110 कुण्डलिनी's second derivation, from the śṛṅgāṭaka whose three angles are Icchā, Jñāna and Kriyā; the vowels and consonants are Śakti and Śiva at 577 मातृकावर्णरूपिणी on the Sūta Saṃhitā; and 872 त्रयी derives the Vāgbhava bīja by performing sandhi on the three Vedas' opening letters. So the Vedas come from the letters, the letters from the triangle, and the triangle is Her.

जननी stood at 285 आब्रह्मकीटजननी, 620 and 823.

339. विष्णुमाया → विष्णु-माया

विष्णु = Viṣṇu — and per the gloss, the all-pervading, unlimited by place and time
माया = illusion; also that which limits
"The Māyā of Viṣṇu."

Vigraha: विष्णोः माया।

Two readings, and the first makes Her the limiter: "Viṣṇu, all-pervading, unlimited by place, time and the rest. The Māyā conditions or limits Viṣṇu."

That is the inference-form Bhāskararāya uses at nama 1 — "that which limits is necessarily superior to the thing limited" — and at 943 विमानस्था and 944 वज्रिणी, where one reading of each makes Her the limitator of Brahman. Here the limited party is named.

The second is the ordinary genitive: "the Māyā, illusion, belonging to Viṣṇu," with Gītā 7.14 — "this my divine illusion, consisting of guṇas, is very difficult to transcend" — and the Kālikā Purāṇa: "Viṣṇumāyā is that which differentiates everything into manifested and unmanifested according to the Tamas, Rajas and Sattva qualities."

माया is Her name at 716, where Bhāskararāya's own definition is "the energy which obscures what is plain" against the Devī Purāṇa's "the instrument of marvellous actions"; and 215 महामाया makes the illusion's victims the gods.

340. विलासिनी → विलासिनी

विलासिनी = playful, sportive (वि + लस् "to play, to shine"); and per the third reading, from बिल, a cavity
"The Playful."

Vigraha: विलासः अस्याः अस्तीति विलासिनी।

Three readings, and the third turns on an orthographic licence.

"Vilāsa, that power of projection, Vikṣepaśakti, which she possesses." So the play is technical: vikṣepa is the projecting power of Māyā, paired with āvaraṇa the veiling power. Or "Vilāsa may mean a special power called Pīṭhaśakti."

Then: "Or, Bila — as there is no difference between the syllables व and ब — the Brahmarandhra in the Sahasrāra, as to reside."

That is the same licence 804 पुष्करा invokes for र and ल — "as there is no difference between र and ल, Puṣkalā means complete" — so the text allows two such interchanges, each once.

And the Svacchanda Tantra is quoted for what is in that cavity, with a striking last clause: "there one should know the cavity of Brahman, surrounded by millions of Rudras… this is another Śakti called Brāhmaṇī, seated on the lap of Brahman, obstructing the door of the path of Salvation."

A śakti who blocks the way is unusual in this text, and it belongs with 703 सर्वमोहिनी, where the bewildering of those who believe in duality is Hers. Brāhmaṇī is nama 674.

लस् is the root of 738 लास्यप्रिया and 13's लसत्कचा. Bhāskararāya marks the division: "16th verse divides 38 names."

Note on the verse. Seven namas, all on व, and two of them build structures.

335 is the entry to keep. The four Vedas are made the four gates of the Cintāmaṇi palace — so nama 57's architecture acquires doors — and then the four quarters and four groups of goddesses, three of which are namas elsewhere: Śuddhavidyā, Lopāmudrā, Turīyāmbā.

338 then supplies the chain from Her to scripture: the kuṇḍalinī's triangle produces the vowels and consonants, and the letters produce the Vedas. Read with 577 and 872 that is a complete derivation, and this is the nama that states its first link.

337's myrobalan reading is the smallest thing the text says about Her, and 340's blocking Brāhmaṇī the least expected.

---

## क्षेत्रस्वरूपा क्षेत्रेशी क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञपालिनी । क्षयवृद्धिविनिर्मुक्ता क्षेत्रपालसमर्चिता

*kṣetrasvarūpā kṣetreśī kṣetrakṣetrajñapālinī । kṣayavṛddhivinirmuktā kṣetrapālasamarcitā*

Verse 76, namas 341–345.

341. क्षेत्रस्वरूपा → क्षेत्र-स्व-रूपा

क्षेत्र = a field; hence the body, matter — what is known by the soul (from क्षि "to dwell")
स्व = own
रूपा = form
"She whose very form is the field."

Vigraha: क्षेत्रं स्वरूपं यस्याः सा।

क्षेत्र is literally a field, and its technical sense — matter as the object of the soul's knowing — comes from that: what is worked upon. Sastry's note glosses it "that which is known by the soul, i.e., matter."

"Kṣetra, Kāmarūpa and other abodes, or thirty-six categories from earth to Śiva; these are her body." So the field is either the sacred places or the tattvas, and both are made her body — the pīṭhas being 833 पञ्चाशत्पीठरूपिणी's fifty-one and the tattvas 906–907's thirty-six.

The Liṅga Purāṇa: "Devī, the wife of the destroyer of the three cities, becomes Kṣetra. The divine and eternal lord, the death of death, is the knower of the bodies." So She is the field and He the knower of it, which is the Gītā's pair.

342. क्षेत्रेशी → क्षेत्र-ईशी

क्षेत्र = the field, matter
ईशी = mistress, ruler
"Mistress of the field."

Vigraha: क्षेत्रस्य ईशी।

Sandhi: क्षेत्र + ईशी → क्षेत्रेशी (अ + ई → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87). index.html carries 341's gloss and body on this nama, so no commentary of its own survives; its own heading stands stranded in 343's gloss — "the wife of the ruler of the matter."

That heading gives the reading: She is the consort of the Kṣetreśa, which by 341's Liṅga Purāṇa citation is Śiva the knower of the field. So 341 and 342 make Her the field and the field's mistress in succession — which is the affirm-then-govern pattern of 810–811 and 894–895.

ईशी for the eighth time, and ईश् for its seventeenth turn.

343. क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञपालिनी → क्षेत्र-क्षेत्रज्ञ-पालिनी

क्षेत्र = the field, matter
क्षेत्रज्ञ = the knower of the field — the jīva (क्षेत्र + ज्ञ)
पालिनी = protectress (from पाल् "to protect")
"Protectress of the field and of the field's knower."

Vigraha: क्षेत्रं क्षेत्रज्ञं च पालयतीति।

index.html carries 341's material here too, so three consecutive namas share one body; 343's own commentary follows inside that block.

**And what follows is a survey of five incompatible definitions of क्षेत्र, which is the substance of the verse.**

"Kṣetrajña is the Jīva." The Viṣṇu Smṛti: "this body, O Earth, is called Kṣetra; one who knows this is called Kṣetrajña. O fair one, know me as the Kṣetrajña in all bodies." Gītā 13.1–2 teaches the same.

Then the definitions diverge. The Liṅga Purāṇa: "the wise call the twenty-four categories Kṣetra, and the enjoyer thereof the Kṣetrajña." The Vāyu Purāṇa: "the unmanifested, avyakta, is called Kṣetra" — so the field is Prakṛti rather than the categories. The Brahmā Purāṇa: "Kṣetras are the bodies; the soul united with them is the Yogātman; the enjoyer according to his pleasure is the Kṣetrajña."

And Manu 12.12–15, which multiplies the terms rather than settling them: "he who is the cause of action of the embodied souls, they call him the Kṣetrajña. Him who performs actions, the wise name Bhūtātman, the self consisting of elements. Another internal self that is generated with all bodies is called Jīva, through which he feels all pleasure and pain in the bodies. These two, the great one and the Kṣetrajña, who are closely united with the elements, pervade him who resides in all beings great and small. From his body innumerable bodies arise which constantly impel the multiform creatures to action."

So क्षेत्र is the body, or the twenty-four categories, or the unmanifested; and क्षेत्रज्ञ is the jīva, or the enjoyer, or the cause of action distinct from both Bhūtātman and Jīva. Bhāskararāya lists all of them and adjudicates none — which is his procedure at 946 पञ्चयज्ञप्रिया with the six sets of five sacrifices and at 250 with the five Brahmans.

344. क्षयवृद्धिविनिर्मुक्ता → क्षय-वृद्धि-विनिर्मुक्ता

क्षय = decay, wasting (from क्षि "to waste away")
वृद्धि = growth, increase (from वृध् "to grow")
विनिर्मुक्ता = wholly freed (वि + निः + मुक्ता, from मुच्)
"She who is free from decay and growth."

Vigraha: क्षयवृद्धिभ्यां विनिर्मुक्ता।

"Growth and decay belong to Kṣetra and to changing. Though She controls them, she is free from them" — so the nama follows 341–343 as their consequence: she is the field and its mistress, and what belongs to the field does not touch her.

Gītā 2.23 is cited — "weapons do not cut" — and then the alternative makes the freedom moral rather than physical: "or she is free from these two which are the result of actions." Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.22: "this is the eternal glory of the knower of Brahman. He neither increases by action nor becomes less" — and the gloss, "neither becomes more by good actions nor less by bad ones."

That Bṛhadāraṇyaka verse is 848 उदारकीर्तिः's, where the two lakes of nectar were Ara and Ṇya and Vedānta Sūtra 4.4.22 made the state one of non-return.

The nama is 867 क्षयविनिर्मुक्ता with वृद्धि inserted — and at 867 Bhāskararāya took क्षय in its other sense, a house, to get a doctrine about householders liberated where they stand: "if you desire the supreme abode, do not abandon your own abode." Here only the decay-sense is used.

345. क्षेत्रपालसमर्चिता → क्षेत्रपाल-सम्-अर्चिता

क्षेत्रपाल = Kṣetrapāla, the guardian of a precinct — literally the field's protector
सम् = fully
अर्चिता = worshipped (from अर्च्)
"She who is fully worshipped by Kṣetrapāla."

Vigraha: क्षेत्रपालेन समर्चिता।

The literal sense is given last — "Kṣetra is the precinct of the sacrificial ceremony, and pāla the protector" — and before it a story, which is the best narrative in this batch.

"Kālī was created by Śiva to slay the Daitya Dāruka. Even after killing him the fire of her wrath was not appeased. Seeing the confusion of the world, Śiva, in order to dispel her anger, assumed the form of a crying infant. She suckled the child, who drank up the fire of her anger with the milk. This child, which is that incarnation of Śiva, is called Kṣetrapāla." The Liṅga and other Purāṇas are cited.

So Kṣetrapāla is Śiva as an infant, and what he does is drink Her rage. That is an inversion of the text's usual arrangement: Śiva is elsewhere Her part at 910, her bedding at 947, bewildered by her at 954, and assenting at the motion of her brows at 995 — and here he pacifies her by becoming a baby.

The Dāruka of the story is also the दारु of 749 मृत्युदारुकुठारिका, where the word is read as twenty-eight by Vararuci's rule; the text does not connect them.

अर्चिता for the fifth time, and समर्चिता after 917 धीरसमर्चिता.

Note on the verse. Five namas, all on क्षेत्र except the fourth, and the verse is a single doctrinal unit.

341–343 make Her the field, the field's mistress, and the protector of field and knower both — so the Gītā's pair is distributed over three namas with Her on both sides of it. And 343 then lists five definitions of क्षेत्र from five sources without choosing: the body, the twenty-four categories, the unmanifested, and Manu's three-way division into Kṣetrajña, Bhūtātman and Jīva.

344 draws the consequence — what belongs to the field does not touch its mistress — and 345 closes with Śiva as a crying infant drinking Kālī's rage out of the milk.

Textual note. 341, 342 and 343 share one gloss and body, all three carrying 341's; 342's own heading stands stranded in 343's gloss, and 343's commentary survives inside the shared block. A three-nama duplication, matching 997–999 and 184–186.

---

## विजया विमला वन्द्या वन्दारुजनवत्सला । वाग्वादिनी वामकेशी वह्निमण्डलवासिनी

*vijayā vimalā vandyā vandārujanavatsalā । vāgvādinī vāmakeśī vahnimaṇḍalavāsinī*

Verse 77, namas 346–352.

346. विजया → वि-जया

वि = fully
जया = victory, conquering (from जि "to conquer"); also an auspicious hour; also a building
"The Victorious."

Vigraha: विजयः अस्याः अस्तीति विजया।

Four readings, and the last is a piece of practical astrology.

"Or Vijayā, knowledge itself." Then the placement: "according to the Devī Purāṇa she is the deity of Kashmira, which is one of the sixty-eight sacred places" — the same count 793 कपर्दिनी gave for Chagalaṇḍa and 351 गives again five namas on, against 833's fifty-one pīṭhas and 112's hundred and eight tīrthas.

Then the demon-etymology: "after conquering the very powerful king of the Daityas named Padma, she is known in the three worlds by the epithet Vijayā and Aparājitā." Padma is also the demon of 278 पद्मासना's fourth reading, "the slayer of the Daitya Padmāsura" — so one demon supplies two namas.

Or "Vijaya is the name of a building, mentioned in the Viśvakarmā Śāstra" — one of the eleven 347 lists.

**And then Vijayā as a time**, from the Cintāmaṇi: "in the month Āśvina, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, when the stars appear, that time is known as Vijayā, giving success to all undertakings." And the Ratnakośa: "the time just after twilight when the stars begin to shine is called Vijayā, favourable to all undertakings. The eleventh Muhūrta — eight hours and forty-eight minutes after midday — is named Vijayā. A journey should be begun at that time by all who desire success."

So the nama names an hour with a stated duration, which is the most precise chronology in the text after 594's ardhamātrā of 128 lavas.

347. विमला → वि-मला

वि = without
मला = impurity, dirt — and per the gloss, avidyā
"The Unsullied."

Vigraha: विगतः मलः यस्याः सा।

"Malā, impurity, belongs to Avidyā." Then the placement: "according to the Padma Purāṇa, Vimalā is the deity of the sacred place Puruṣottama" — that is Purī.

And then the list of houses, which 346's fourth reading anticipated: "or Vimalā is a kind of house. The Viśvakarmā Śāstra enumerates the following houses: Dhruva, Dhānya, Jaya, Kāntā, Vipula, Vijayā, Sumukha, Vimalā, Nanda, Nidhana and Manoramā."

Eleven names, of which four are namas of this text — Jaya as part of 346, Kāntā at 329 and 860, Vijayā at 346, Vimalā here — so the architectural manual supplies a small cluster.

मल is the word of 135 निर्मला, where it was the āṇavamala and the third of the three impurities denied at 133–135; and 354 six namas on will give that whole scheme at length.

348. वन्द्या → वन्द्या

वन्द्या = to be praised, to be saluted (वन्द् "to praise" with the gerundive यत्)
"The Adorable."

Vigraha: वन्दनीया वन्द्या।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

वन्द्या is 627 त्रिजगद्वन्द्या without its first member — and 927 स्तोत्रप्रिया cites that nama as the text's own instance of नमस्कार among the six marks of a stotra. So the bare gerundive here is that instance stripped to its root.

349. वन्दारुजनवत्सला → वन्दारु-जन-वत्सला

वन्दारु = worshipping, given to praising (from वन्द्)
जन = people, persons
वत्सला = affectionate, tender — as a cow to its calf (from वत्स "a calf")
"She who is tender towards those who worship."

Vigraha: वन्दारुजनेषु वत्सला।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

वत्सल is built on वत्स, a calf, so the affection named is specifically a cow's for its young — which makes the compound warmer than प्रिया and is why the word is used of parental fondness. It is the only वत्सल-nama in the thousand.

348 and 349 pair on वन्द्: she is to be praised, and she is tender to those who praise.

350. वाग्वादिनी → वाक्-वादिनी

वाक् = speech (from वच् "to speak")
वादिनी = speaking, uttering (from वद् "to speak")
"She who speaks the word."

Vigraha: वाचं वदतीति वाग्वादिनी।

Sandhi: वाक् + वादिनी → वाग्वादिनी, the क् voicing before व्.

The compound puts two roots of speaking together — वच् and वद् — so it is speech uttering itself, which is the point of both citations.

The Tripurā Siddhānta: "as she always abides in the form of speech on the tongue of all her devotees, she is known in the world as Vāgvādinī." And the Laghustava 15: "since thou art the origin of all words, thou art known in the world as Vāgvādinī."

So the nama is not that She speaks but that speech in Her devotees' mouths is her. That is 263 सर्वावस्थाविवर्जिता's Śiva Sūtra — "his conversation is Japa, because his mind has grasped the truth" — and the Śruti there, "whatever one thinks in his mind, that alone he speaks."

वाक् is 640 वागधीश्वरी's, where She is sovereign over speech, and the four stages Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, Vaikharī are 25's and 290's.

351. वामकेशी → वामक-ईशी

वामक = beautiful; and per the readings, men; also the Vāmakeśa Tantra
ईशी = mistress (from ईश्); and per the compound-reading, केशी, haired
"She of the beautiful hair." — or, "Mistress of the Vāmakas."

Vigraha: वामाः केशाः यस्याः सा। or वामकानाम् ईशी।

Three readings, and they divide the compound two ways.

The plain one takes वाम + केशी, beautiful hair. Then: "or Vāmaka, men, and Īśa, lord, that is Śiva; his wife is Vāmakeśī."

Then the placement: "according to the Devī Purāṇa, Vāmakeśa is the deity of Jaḍa, one of the sixty-eight sacred places, and his wife is Vāmakeśī." The sixty-eight again, five namas after 346.

And the textual reading: "or Vāmakeśa is one of the twenty-eight Tantras promulgated by Śiva; as she is treated of in that work, she is Vāmakeśī."

That is the canon of 287 निजाज्ञारूपनिगमा, distributed over Śiva's five faces, and the Vāmakeśvara is the first Tantra named at 206 सर्वतन्त्ररूपा. So the nama can mean "she of whom the Vāmakeśvara treats," which makes it a bibliographical epithet — and 945 वामकेश्वरी says the same with the fuller stem, where वामक is glossed "contemptible, because they do not perform the five sacrifices."

Her hair is 13's four flowers, 185 नीलचिकुरा's dark, 942 व्योमकेशी's ether, and 547 बर्बरालका's curls.

352. वह्निमण्डलवासिनी → वह्नि-मण्डल-वासिनी

वह्नि = fire — literally the carrier, of oblations (from वह् "to carry"); and per the third reading, the number three
मण्डल = a disc, a circle
वासिनी = dwelling (from वस्)
"She who dwells in the circle of fire."

Vigraha: वह्निमण्डले वासिनी।

Three readings, and the third is a numeral.

"Vahnimaṇḍala is that in the Mūlādhāra, or that in the supreme ether." So the fire-circle is at the bottom of the body or above everything.

"Or Vahni means three, hence three maṇḍalas; thus she resides in the three circles of the moon, the sun and the fire."

वह्नि stands for three because the fires are three — the standard numeral convention of the *bhūtasaṃkhyā* system, distinct from Vararuci's letter-numerals. And the three circles are placed at 354's opening, whose body carries the material displaced from here: "the three circles are the moon in the sahasrāra, the sun in the anāhata, and the fire in the mūlādhāra. This may mean also the three parts of the Pañcadaśī mantra."

So the three maṇḍalas are the three stations of the nyāsa at 592–596 — moon in the head, sun in the heart — and also the three kūṭas. Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (77).

Note on the verse. Seven namas, all on व, and the verse is unusually full of placements and lists.

346 gives Vijayā as a deity in Kashmir, a slain demon's conqueror, a building, and an hour with a stated length; 347 gives Vimalā at Purī and in a list of eleven houses; 351 gives Vāmakeśī at Jaḍa and in a canon of twenty-eight Tantras. Three namas, three sacred places, and the sixty-eight-place count invoked twice.

352's वह्नि as the numeral three is the text's use of the *bhūtasaṃkhyā* convention, which is a different device from the Vararuci letter-numerals of 529, 749, 296 and 354.

Textual note. 348 and 349 have no commentary bodies. 352's own material on the three circles has been carried into 354's body.

---

## भक्तिमत्कल्पलतिका पशुपाशविमोचिनी । संहृताशेषपाषण्डा सदाचारप्रवर्तिका

*bhaktimatkalpalatikā paśupāśavimocinī । saṃhṛtāśeṣapāṣaṇḍā sadācārapravartikā*

Verse 78, namas 353–356.

> **Nama 354 carries the second-longest commentary in the Sahasranāma, after 256, and it is where the cross-reference at 134 lands.** Bhāskararāya said there, of the three bound souls and the three impurities: "for more details, the commentator refers the readers to Lalitā Sahasranāma, name 354." This is that place. What it contains is the full Śaiva doctrine of paśu and pāśa — six readings of the compound, three competing enumerations of the afflictions reconciled by Vararuci's numerals, the three malas with their three grades of soul and their subdivisions, a census of the liberated, and a closing argument from Pāṇini that the agent of release must be Śakti and not Śiva.

353. भक्तिमत्कल्पलतिका → भक्तिमत्-कल्प-लतिका

भक्तिमत् = possessing devotion, a devotee (भक्ति + मतुप्)
कल्प = the wish-yielding tree of heaven; and per the second reading, imperfect, incomplete
लतिका = a small creeper (लता with the diminutive); and per the third reading, musk
"She who is the wish-yielding creeper of her devotees."

Vigraha: भक्तिमतां कल्पलतिका।

Three readings, and the second and third both turn on making कल्प mean "imperfect."

"The kalpa creeper yields everything desired. Or kalpa means imperfect — that is, she makes perfect, spreads over, her imperfect devotees. Or Latā, musk; she sheds fragrance on her devotees." The Rabhasa is cited for the last: "latā means heart-pea, musk, jasmine and pani-grass."

And the conclusion: "she gladdens her imperfect — literally half — devotees by the gift of all devotion." The Śaktirahasya supplies the rule: **"he who worships Bhavānī irregularly or with imperfect devotion, in the next birth becomes possessed of regular and perfect devotion."**

That is the leniency-doctrine with a mechanism attached. 736 मुक्तिदा's Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa said that those who worship "whether regularly or irregularly" are not entangled in saṃsāra, and 291 पुरुषार्थप्रदा said "properly or improperly"; here the imperfect worship is said to produce perfect devotion in the next life, which explains how the earlier claims work rather than merely repeating them.

कल्पलता is the wish-tree of heaven made a creeper, and लता is 34's vine, 107's lightning-creeper and 579's arms.

354. पशुपाशविमोचिनी → पशु-पाश-विमोचिनी

पशु = cattle, a beast; hence the bound soul; and per the readings, all beings from Brahmā to a tree, and — by Vararuci's numerals — fifty-two
पाश = a noose, a bond; and per the readings, hunger and thirst, Varuṇa's noose, dice, and the afflictions
विमोचिनी = she who wholly releases (वि + मुच् "to loose")
"She who releases the bound souls from their bonds."

Vigraha: पशूनां पाशान् विमोचयतीति।

index.html's body opens with the material displaced from 352 — "the three circles are the moon in the sahasrāra, the sun in the anāhata, and the fire in the mūlādhāra; this may mean also the three parts of the Pañcadaśī mantra" — and then the commentary proper begins.

**First, six readings of the compound.**

*Paśu as the undiscriminating.* "Paśus are those who are devoid of the conviction of non-separation." Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.10 is the authority: "now, he who worships another deity, thinking the deity is one and himself another individual, he does not know. He is like a Paśu." And then a pun on that verse's own wording — यो ऽन्यां देवताम्, "who worships another deity" — is read as योन्याम्, "in the yoni," meaning the triangular Śrīcakra, with the Taittirīya for support: "in that golden three-petalled bud the three-syllabled mantra is established." So the Upaniṣad's condemnation of dualistic worship is made to point at the triangle in which non-dual worship is done.

*Pāśa as hunger and thirst.* "Pa, thirst; aśa, hunger. These belong only to the ignorant, and she completely releases them. The ignorant are called Paśus because they possess the desire of eating and drinking only." The Śruti: "now the other paśus understand only hunger and thirst; they do not speak of the known, they do not see the known, they do not know the future, nor this nor the other world."

*Paśu as an indeclinable.* "Or Paśu means completely," on a Śruti usage.

*Pāśa as Varuṇa's noose*, "from which she frees her devotees."

*Pāśa as dice*, and this is the reading worth keeping: "Paśu, dice; vi, much; mocinī, throwing. The meaning is that in gambling with Śiva, while throwing the dice on the board, she conquered him."

So one reading of a nama about liberation is that She beat Śiva at dice. It belongs with 954 शंभुमोहिनी and 345's infant, as one more place where the relation between them is settled in Her favour.

*Paśupa as Śiva.* "The protector of paśus, that is the supreme Śiva; those who desire to obtain Śiva, such ones she emancipates entirely."

*Paśu as all beings.* "All things from Brahmā to a tree, because they have the quality of paśus; pāśa, avidyā, because it is the means of bondage." The Saura Saṃhitā: avidyā "is the cause of all bondage." The Liṅga Purāṇa: "from Brahmā to trees are the Paśus of the trident-bearer, because they all have the nature of beasts. The twenty-four categories, including Māyā, action and the guṇas, and the objects also, are called Paśus because they bind the Jīvas. Bound by these, all embodied souls are emancipated by devotion to Śiva alone."

**Then three enumerations of the afflictions, and their reconciliation.**

The Yoga Sūtra's five kleśas are given with definitions: "nescience is the absence of discrimination between the Self and the non-self. Egoism is the assumption that body and the rest, which are not Self, are Self. Desire is the craving after flowers, scents and the rest, which are the means of bodily enjoyment. Anger is aversion to whatever obstructs the attainment of them. Ardent attachment is not renouncing a thing even though one knows it is not beneficial."

The Devī Bhāgavata gives five under different names: "non-discrimination is darkness, Tamas; bewilderment of mind is confusion, Moha; desire of worldly pleasures is great confusion, Mahāmoha; death is deep indignation, Andhatāmisra; and anger is called indignation, Tāmisra. Thus nescience which sprang from the great Ātman is fivefold."

And the Liṅga Purāṇa maps the two lists onto each other term by term: "nescience is darkness; egoism is confusion; desire is great confusion; attachment to life is deep indignation; and hatred is indignation." Bhāskararāya notes the one adjustment needed: "death here corresponds to ardent attachment."

Then the subdivision, from the same Purāṇa: "there are eight kinds of darkness, eight of confusion, ten of great confusion, eighteen of deep indignation and eight of indignation." Eight plus eight plus ten plus eighteen plus eight is fifty-two — "these are in all fifty-two. Some say that indignation has ten more, making sixty-two in all."

And the Kulārṇava's quite different eight: **"the Pāśas are eight, viz. pity, doubt, fear, shame, disgust, family, custom and caste."**

Bhāskararāya's rule for holding them together is stated plainly: "the above enumerations of the afflictions are not contradictory; the larger are simply elaborations of the smaller."

**And then the fourth use of Vararuci's numeral system in the text, with a named precedent.**

"Thus in the text the word Pāśa, according to the rule of Vararuci's system, though it indicates the number fifty-one — श five and प one — is here taken, according to the rule of approximity, as fifty-two. Thus we see in the first verse of the Śāradātilaka, when the word for fifty occurs, explained as fifty-two by Harṣa Dīkṣita and others. Therefore Paśu means fifty-two; Pāśas, afflictions; vimocinī, remover."

Two things about that. It is the fourth Vararuci reading, after उप = 10 at 529, दारु = 28 at 749, and आदि = 80 at 296 — and it is the only one where the computed figure has to be adjusted, by "the rule of approximity," to match the doctrine.

And the precedent named is the same one 833 पञ्चाशत्पीठरूपिणी invokes. There Harṣadīkṣita was cited for reading the Śāradātilaka's "fifty" as fifty-one, because the pīṭhas run अ to क्ष; here he is cited for reading the same text's "fifty" as fifty-two. So one commentator on one verse is used twice in this Sahasranāma for two different corrections of the same round number.

The Śiva Rahasya closes the section: "he alone who binds the Paśus by the five afflictions and fifty-two Pāśas is able, being worshipped with much devotion, to free them." And Bhāskararāya marks the transition: "so much for the Paurāṇic interpretation."

**Then the Śaiva doctrine proper: the three malas.**

"Or, atoms, difference and action are the three Paśus." Each is then defined.

*Āṇava.* "Of these, ignorance is aṇu; this is of two kinds — the absence of the cognition of the nature of the Self which is Intelligence itself, and the erroneous cognition of the self in body and the rest. These two together are called the impurity of aṇu. Aṇu is so called because it limits the unlimited Self." The Saura Saṃhitā: "it is called aṇu because it causes the limitation of the Self; as it is impure it is called impurity."

*Māyīya.* "Bheda means division of the one self into many. Of this, the root cause is called Māyā, that is the sixth affliction to be added to the five. The group of the categories, the products of these six from the seventh to the thirty-sixth, is another. These two together are called the impurity of illusion."

*Kārma.* "Karma means the product of ordained or prohibited actions, capable of giving bodies, and invisible. This is of two kinds, good and bad; together these are called the impurity of action."

And the nesting: "thus in these three, the latter have the qualities of the former."

The Pratyabhijñā Śāstra is quoted, and then the Śaiva Sūtra Vārtika at length, which frames the whole thing as an objection and its answer: "if, of the waking soul as above described, intelligence is the body, how is it connected with bondage? To remove this doubt, the great Īśvara replies with the Sūtras treating of the contact and non-contact with the Pāśas." Śiva Sūtra 1.2 — "ignorance is the bondage" — is then explained, with the note that "the aṇu impurity is not the sole bond"; and Śiva Sūtra 1.3, "birth is the group," is unpacked with यonि as difference and वर्ग as the categories from time to earth.

**Then the three grades of soul, which is what 134 pointed here for.**

"The word paśu indicates the three kinds of Jīvas resulting from the three bonds. Though, by the combinations of all possible ways with the three bonds, there are seven kinds of Jīvas, yet in reality, as the second bond includes the first and the third the other two, there are only three kinds."

That is the argument 133 निरञ्जना states in one sentence — "in these three, the second has also the impurity of the first, and the third that of the second" — given its combinatorial form: seven subsets of three bonds, reduced to three by the nesting.

"These paśus in the Nityāhṛdaya are termed respectively pure, mixed, and impure. But in the Svacchanda Tantra and other works they are called respectively Vijñānakevala, Pralayākala and Sakala." Those are exactly 133–135's three, and the Svacchanda is quoted for their natures.

*Sakala*, bound by all three: "covered with impurity from the beginning, covered with illusion and action, though pure in himself, regarding the body as Self, ever tainted with separateness, weak, continually active, enjoying the fruits of his own actions, ever enamoured with pleasure — this is the Sakala Paśu."

Each grade is then divided by whether its impurities are burnt or unburnt, and **the burnt Sakalas are counted**: "of those who have burned the three impurities are the one hundred and eighteen sages; they, by power of the full grace of Śiva, obtained dominion over the mantras. Of these, a hundred are called Rudras, eight Śatamaṇḍalins, eight Krodhabhaṭṭāraka and others, one is Vīreśvara and the last is Śrīkaṇṭha."

A hundred plus eight plus eight plus one plus one is a hundred and eighteen, and the arithmetic checks. Krodhabhaṭṭāraka is Durvāsa, the twelfth of the twelve vidyā-holders at 238 and 812 and the author of the Lalitāstavaratna quoted at 305, 686 and 785.

The unburnt Sakalas "are appointed to different births in order to burn their impurities through fruition. That itself is a sign of graciousness to them."

*Pralayākala*, bound by aṇu and karma, have "the body of eight cities"; their burnt class "become the lords of the universe," of three kinds. *Vijñānakevala*, bound by aṇu alone: the burnt "become the lords of knowledge," and the unburnt "are the spirits of the seven crores of powerful mantras" — with a striking insistence that "these must not be considered inanimate sound; they, like ourselves, possess Caitanya."

The seven crores of mantras are 203's blood of Śiva and 204's सर्वमन्त्र.

**And then the closing argument, which is the best thing in the entry.**

"But if release is the work of Śiva, how does Devī become an agent? Without possessing the power of release Śiva can do nothing; therefore the agency of release should be acknowledged to belong to Śakti alone, by the rule of agreement and continuity."

The verse quoted for it: "I adore with all my heart that Śakti which is Intelligence, primeval, through whom Śiva is able to confer happiness and salvation on all Paśus."

**And then Pāṇini is made to settle it.** "Moreover the agency is independence, because Pāṇini 1.4.54 says: *the agency is independence*. That belongs to Śakti; so the Śakti Sūtra says, *the independent intelligence is the cause of the establishment of the Universe*."

Pāṇini 1.4.54 is स्वतन्त्रः कर्ता, the definition of the grammatical agent: the कर्तृ is whichever participant is independent. Bhāskararāya takes that as a definition of agency simply, observes that independence belongs to Śakti, and concludes that Śakti is the agent of liberation. A sūtra of grammar used to decide which of two deities acts — and the same word स्वतन्त्र is nama 723 स्वतन्त्रा, where three senses are got out of it and the third undercuts the first.

He then anticipates the objection from the other side: Śaiva Sūtra 1.1 says "intelligence is the self, Śiva," but "as there is no expression of independence there, and from the force of the neuter gender — the word Caitanya being neuter — Śiva has not the quality of agency." And the resolution is the standard one: the Śakti Sūtra and the Śiva Sūtra together, with "the saying of the wise that cit applies to Śiva as well as to Śakti, mean in such cases that Śiva and Śakti are inseparable. Such is the doctrine of the Śaiva schools."

That is 999 शिवशक्त्यैक्यरूपिणी's conclusion reached by a grammatical route.

355. संहृताशेषपाषण्डा → संहृत-अशेष-पाषण्डा

संहृत = destroyed, drawn together and away (सम् + हृ "to seize")
अशेष = without remainder, entire (अ + शेष)
पाषण्डा = a heretic, a heterodox sect
"She who has destroyed the heretics without remainder."

Vigraha: संहृताः अशेषाः पाषण्डाः यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: संहृत + अशेष → संहृताशेष (आ by 6.1.101).

The definition of heresy is procedural rather than doctrinal, and that is its interest. The Liṅga Purāṇa: "observers of vows not enjoined in the Vedas, and those who are excluded from the ceremonies enjoined by the Śrutis and Smṛtis, are called heretics; they are not to be spoken with by the twice-born."

Then the Brahmavaivarta supplies the fourteen seats of dharma against which heresy is measured: "Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstras, the six Aṅgas from Śikṣā to Jyotiṣa, and the four Vedas which are the source of knowledge — these fourteen are the seat of righteousness. These are the true; what is beyond these, imagined by men, is called heresy; this is created by the great confusion for the bewilderment of the Daityas."

So heresy is whatever falls outside a list of fourteen, and its purpose is stated: it exists to bewilder demons. That is 703 सर्वमोहिनी's bewildering put to a specific use.

And the etymology: "if the reading is Pākhaṇḍa, it gives the same meaning. The explanation of the word is: pa means the meaning of the Vedas, and khaṇḍa cutting off." So a heretic is one who cuts off the Veda's sense.

The fourteen are the "fourteen Vidyās" of 902 विज्ञानकलना and 943 विमानस्था's sixth reading, and 991's six paths.

356. सदाचारप्रवर्तिका → सत्-आचार-प्रवर्तिका

सत् = good, right
आचार = conduct, observance (आ + चर्)
प्रवर्तिका = she who sets in motion, who incites (प्र + वृत् "to turn," causative)
"She who sets right conduct in motion."

Vigraha: सदाचारं प्रवर्तयतीति।

Sandhi: सत् + आचार → सदाचार, the त् voicing before the vowel.

"Because she destroys the wicked, and she incites to right action" — so the nama follows 355 as its positive counterpart.

And the scope is then divided over both halves of the Veda: "she gives the inclination to observe the precepts enjoined in the Karmakāṇḍa, and the Advaita Brahman in the Jñānakāṇḍa, through the means laid down in the Purāṇas."

The Kūrma Purāṇa is then quoted in Her own voice, and it is a statement of textual authority: "the eighteen Purāṇas, O King, were promulgated by Vyāsa by the command of Brahman; in them righteousness is established. The other supplementary Purāṇas were promulgated by his pupils. In every age he, the knower of the science of righteousness, is the promulgator of all. Śikṣā, Kalpa, Grammar, Nirukta, Chandas and Jyotiṣa, and logic and the rest, and the four Vedas — thus the fourteen scriptures are the sources of knowledge. Righteousness is not to be found elsewhere. Thus the supreme Dharma, which has come down from the grandsire, Manu, Vyāsa and others, by my command, is established till the dissolution of the universe."

The same fourteen as 355, so the two namas share a canon: heresy is outside it and right conduct is inside it. And आचार is 194 दुराचारशमनी's word and 98 समयाचारतत्परा's. Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (78).

प्रवर्तिका is the causative of वृत्, as in 843 भवचक्रप्रवर्तिनी, where what She sets turning is the wheel of existence.

Note on the verse. Four namas, and 354 is a treatise.

What it settles is the doctrine 133–135 announced and 134 explicitly deferred: the three malas, the three grades of soul, and their nesting. And it adds what those namas had no room for — the combinatorial argument reducing seven possible bond-combinations to three, the division of each grade by burnt and unburnt impurity, and a census of the hundred and eighteen liberated Sakalas whose arithmetic checks.

Three other things in it are worth keeping on their own account. The Kulārṇava's eight pāśas — pity, doubt, fear, shame, disgust, family, custom, caste — are a wholly social list where every other enumeration is psychological. Vararuci's numerals make पाश fifty-one and the doctrine requires fifty-two, so Bhāskararāya adjusts by "the rule of approximity" and cites Harṣadīkṣita's parallel adjustment of the Śāradātilaka — the same commentator he used at 833 to correct the same round number in the other direction.

And the closing argument settles the agency of liberation on Śakti by way of Pāṇini 1.4.54, स्वतन्त्रः कर्ता: agency is independence, independence is Hers, therefore She acts and Śiva does not. It is the only place in the text where a grammatical sūtra decides a theological question.

353 also supplies the mechanism the leniency-namas assume: imperfect worship now produces perfect devotion in the next birth.

Textual note. 354's body opens with the three-circles material displaced from 352.

---

## तापत्रयाभिसंतप्तसमाह्लादनचन्द्रिका । तरुणी तापसाराध्या तनुमध्या तमोऽपहा

*tāpatrayābhisaṃtaptasamāhlādanacandrikā । taruṇī tāpasārādhyā tanumadhyā tamo'pahā*

Verse 79, namas 357–361.

357. तापत्रयाभिसंतप्तसमाह्लादनचन्द्रिका → ताप-त्रय-अभिसंतप्त-सम्-आह्लादन-चन्द्रिका

ताप = heat, burning, torment (from तप् "to burn")
त्रय = a triad
अभिसंतप्त = thoroughly scorched (अभि + सम् + तप्त)
सम् = fully
आह्लादन = gladdening, refreshing (आ + ह्लाद् "to be glad")
चन्द्रिका = moonlight (चन्द्र with the diminutive)
"She who is the moonlight refreshing those scorched by the three torments."

Vigraha: तापत्रयेण अभिसंतप्तानां समाह्लादनचन्द्रिका।

Sandhi at two joints: ताप + त्रय stands, त्रय + अभिसंतप्त → त्रयाभिसंतप्त and सम् + आह्लादन → समाह्लादन (आ by 6.1.101).

"The three miseries are that which belongs to body, to elements, and to deities" — the ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika and ādhidaivika of the standard classification, whose reverses are three of the eight siddhis at 224 and 296.

The figure is heat against coolness, and it is the same construction as 851 जन्ममृत्युजरातप्तजनविश्रान्तिदायिनी — there birth, death and age were the तप्त and what was given was विश्रान्ति, rest. Here the affliction is threefold and the relief is moonlight.

And moonlight-against-affliction is one of the eight similes at 742–749 which the commentary marks as rūpakālaṅkāra: 746 भाग्याब्धिचन्द्रिका uses the same चन्द्रिका, though there it raises good fortune rather than cooling misery. So the word appears twice in the text and inverts its figure.

The Śruti closes the entry: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.25, "without decay and immortal" — of the man freed from saṃsāra.

358. तरुणी → तरुणी

तरुणी = young, youthful; a young woman (from तर् "to cross"?)
"The Youthful."

Vigraha: तरुणी युवती।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

तरुण is the word of 922 तरुणादित्यपाटला, the young sun whose rose Bhāskararāya makes the colour of the śṛṅgāra aspect specifically — and where the whole entry becomes an argument that colour is a function of the meditation's purpose. Here the youth is Her own and unqualified.

359. तापसाराध्या → तापस-आराध्या

तापस = an ascetic — one who practises tapas (from तप्); and per the division, ताप misery with सार essence
आराध्या = to be worshipped (आ + राध्)
"She who is worshipped by ascetics."

Vigraha: तापसैः आराध्या।

Sandhi: तापस + आराध्या → तापसाराध्या (आ by 6.1.101).

The alternative divides the whole compound differently: "or, Tapa, saṃsāra the father of misery; sāra, essence; ā, deep; dhyā, meditation — that is, Devī is the essential object of meditation amidst the earthly misery."

So a nama about ascetics is re-divided into a claim about what to meditate on while suffering, and तप् is read as the misery rather than the discipline. That is continuous with 357's three torments two namas back.

आराध्या for the eleventh time in the text.

360. तनुमध्या → तनु-मध्या

तनु = thin, slender
मध्या = the waist, the middle
"She who is slender of waist."

Vigraha: तनुः मध्यः यस्याः सा।

Two readings besides, and both make the nama a proper name.

"Tanumadhyā is the deity worshipped in the country of Kāñcī; for it is said: *may Devī Tanumadhyā, the wife of Bilveśvara residing on the bank of the Nivā river, protect me.*" That is the twelfth located identification in the text, and Kāñcī is also where Brahmā's penance at 280 पद्मनाभसहोदरी takes place.

"Tanumadhyā is the name of a certain metre. The Piṅgalā Sūtra says: if there is one tagaṇa and yagaṇa in each foot it is called Tanumadhyā."

So this is the fourth nama the text identifies as a metre, after 829 प्रतिष्ठा the sixteen-syllabled, 660 सुप्रतिष्ठा the twenty-syllabled, and 673 बृहती the thirty-six-syllabled — and in every case the note is Bhāskararāya's addition to a nama whose plain sense is something else.

Her waist is 35's, which must be inferred; 36's, buckling under a weight; 130 शातोदरी's, which becomes Himavat's hundred caves; and 847 तलोदरी's, which becomes Atala-loka.

361. तमोऽपहा → तमस्-अपहा

तमस् = darkness; and per the gloss, ignorance
अपहा = removing, taking away (अप + हा "to abandon," or अप + हन्)
"The Remover of darkness."

Vigraha: तमः अपहन्तीति तमोऽपहा।

Sandhi: तमस् + अपहा → तमोऽपहा, the अस् becoming ओ and the following अ elided, marked by the avagraha. That avagraha is part of the nama's own sandhi and not a stray from the preceding word — so it is not an instance of the 50/537/554/642/729/828/926/972/985/988/815 class, all of which carry a mark belonging to the previous nama's joint. This is the only nama in the text whose avagraha is internal.

"Tamas, ignorance." Īśa 9: "they who worship ignorance enter blind darkness." And the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "the Āraṇyaka Śruti blames all worship except that of Vidyā."

Both citations are the ones 791 सत्यज्ञानानन्दरूपा uses for its inverted reading, where सती with अज्ञान and अनानन्द made the nama an account of what the ignorant receive — and where Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.11's joyless worlds were read as the nama's own आनन्द. So the same pair of authorities serves a privative here and a reversal there.

अपहा is 121 भयापहा's word, where what was removed was fear.

Note on the verse. Five namas, all on त, and the verse is built on तप्.

357 gives the three torments and answers them with moonlight; 359's second reading re-divides an ascetic's nama into a claim about meditating amid misery; and both rest on the same root. Against them 358's youth and 360's waist are the verse's only descriptive namas, and 360 turns out to be a place-name and a metre as well.

361's avagraha is worth marking because it is the text's only internal one — every other avagraha in the thousand carries the elision of a preceding nama's final vowel.

Textual note. 358 has no commentary body.

## चितिस्तत्पदलक्ष्यार्था चिदेकरसरूपिणी । स्वात्मानन्दलवीभूतब्रह्माद्यानन्दसंततिः

*citis tatpadalakṣyārthā cidekarasarūpiṇī । svātmānandalavībhūtabrahmādyānandasaṃtatiḥ*

Verse 80, namas 362–365.

> **These four namas are a continuous argument**, of the kind the text runs at 703–713: each answers an objection the previous one raises, and Bhāskararāya marks the moves. The question is how the conditioned and unconditioned Brahman can be the same thing.

362. चितिः → चितिः

चितिः = consciousness, intelligence (from चित् "to perceive")
"Consciousness."

Vigraha: चेतति इति चितिः।

The dev field reads चिति, the visarga lost — and the next nama has gained the स् it became before त् (चितिः + तत्पद → चितिस्तत्पद). The verse text carries it too, with the space in the wrong place: चिति स्तत्पदलक्ष्यार्था.

**That is the second instance in the text of the स्-form of this fault**, after 628 त्रिमूर्तिः and 629 त्रिदशेश्वरी. Every other instance produces र्, because the following sound is voiced; here and at 628 it is a voiceless dental, so the visarga becomes स्.

"Cit is wisdom opposed to avidyā." The Śakti Sūtra: "cit is independent and the cause of the establishment of the Universe" — which is the very sūtra 354 cited eight namas back to prove, with Pāṇini 1.4.54, that agency belongs to Śakti.

And the Mahāvāsiṣṭha: "she is called cit because she is the life of those who desire life."

363. तत्पदलक्ष्यार्था → तत्-पद-लक्ष्य-अर्था

तत् = "that" — the demonstrative of the mahāvākya
पद = a word, a term
लक्ष्य = to be indicated, denoted indirectly (from लक्ष् "to mark")
अर्था = meaning, sense
"She who is the meaning indicated by the word *tat*."

Vigraha: तत्पदस्य लक्ष्यः अर्थः यस्याः सा।

The dev field reads स्तत्पदलक्ष्यार्था, carrying the स् that belongs to 362's visarga.

**And the entry turns on the technical distinction between direct and indirect denotation.** "Tat, the word which occurs in the transcendental phrases, means the conditioned Brahman endowed with the work of creation and the rest. The same word tat also indicates, indirectly — lakṣya — the unconditioned Brahman, who is without attributes. The relation between the two Brahmans is sameness, tādātmya."

So तत् denotes the saguṇa Brahman by वाच्यार्थ, its literal sense, and the nirguṇa by लक्ष्यार्थ, what it points at — and the nama specifies the second. That is the standard Advaitin analysis of तत् त्वम् असि, and the nama is named for the indirect sense specifically.

908 तत्त्वमर्थस्वरूपिणी makes Her the meaning of both तत् and त्वम्, and the Paribhāṣā at 1000 prescribes dividing 907 तत्त्वमयी as तत् + त्वम् + अयि — so the mahāvākya is in the thousand three times, and this is the only one that separates तत् from त्वम् and treats it alone.

364. चिदेकरसरूपिणी → चित्-एक-रस-रूपिणी

चित् = consciousness
एक = one, sole
रस = essence, flavour
रूपिणी = having the form of, embodying
"She whose form is the one essence of consciousness."

Vigraha: चितः एकः रसः रूपं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: चित् + एक → चिदेक, the त् voicing before the vowel.

**And here two objections are raised and answered, which Bhāskararāya sets out explicitly.**

The first: "but even the unconditioned Brahman has the attributes of bliss and the rest." If the nirguṇa Brahman has bliss, it is not attributeless, and 363's identification fails. The answer is that the attributes are not separate from it: "bliss, consciousness and other attributes — the expression means that those attributes are inseparable from her." The Pañcapādikā of Padmapādācārya is quoted: "bliss, the perception of the objects and eternity are attributes which, although inseparable from consciousness, appear as different."

The second: "the unconditioned Brahman is not the real nature of Īśvara, because both are different; hence the relation just described at 363 is not possible." The answer is the nama itself: "Cidekarasarūpiṇī — she is ever non-separated from the cit. The relation of these two is possible as the two are one and the same. Though the two appear as different by attributes, yet at the same time they are one."

रस here is essence rather than flavour, and एकरस — of one taste throughout — is the same word सामरस्य is built on at 792 सामरस्यपरायणा, where the Śiva–Śakti coequality is named by shared flavour. So the unconditioned and conditioned Brahman are of one taste here as Śiva and Śakti are there.

365. स्वात्मानन्दलवीभूतब्रह्माद्यानन्दसंततिः → स्व-आत्म-आनन्द-लवी-भूत-ब्रह्म-आदि-आनन्द-संततिः

स्व = own
आत्म = self
आनन्द = bliss
लवी = a particle, a drop (लव with the feminine)
भूत = become
ब्रह्म = Brahmā
आदि = beginning with, and the rest
संततिः = a continuity, a whole succession, a totality (सम् + तन् "to stretch")
"She a mere drop of whose own bliss is the whole succession of the bliss of Brahmā and the rest."

Vigraha: स्वात्मानन्दस्य लवीभूता ब्रह्माद्यानन्दसंततिः यस्याः सा।

Sandhi at three joints: स्व + आत्म → स्वात्म, आत्म + आनन्द → आत्मानन्द, and आदि + आनन्द → आद्यानन्द (आ by 6.1.101, with य् by 6.1.77 at the last). The dev field and the verse text both read स्वात्मानम्द- for स्वात्मानन्द-, म् where न् belongs.

At nine members this is the longest nama in the batch and one of the longest in the thousand.

"The bliss of Indra and others is but a drop in the Ocean in comparison with the bliss of Devī. Brahmā and the rest: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, who possess the quality of creation, preservation and destruction."

Taittirīya 2.8 is the authority — "other beings live on a mere part of this bliss" — the same verse 729 आनन्दकलिका rests on, where She was "one portion of the bliss enjoyed by Jīvas." So the drop belongs to the jīvas there and to the gods here, and the direction of the comparison reverses.

Then Bhāskararāya explains how the Upaniṣad's ladder works and why it stops where it does: "the same Śruti, describing from man's bliss more and more in the higher grades, includes among the bliss of Devas the bliss of Prajāpati also — as it is limited, and as it is less than the bliss of unconditioned Brahman, and consequently unfit for human aspiration — and establishes that the bliss of Brahman alone is unlimited."

So the ānandamīmāṃsā's graded scale of blisses is read as an argument by exhaustion: every named grade including Prajāpati's is limited, and what remains unlimited is Brahman's.

**And then the argument of the four namas is closed by a Mīmāṃsā rule.** "The meaning is that the word *tat* at 363 indicates the unconditioned Brahman, in order to agree with the authorities which establish the meaning of them by the rule of beginning and the rest — Upakrama and the rest — as the knowledge which is the means of Puruṣārthas."

उपक्रमादि is the set of six criteria by which Mīmāṃsā determines a passage's purport: its opening and close, repetition, novelty, fruit, praise, and reasoning. Bhāskararāya invokes them to fix तत् on the unconditioned Brahman — so 363's choice of the indirect sense is justified not by the word but by the six marks of the passages it stands in.

That is the second time in eleven namas that a technical rule from another discipline settles a doctrinal point, after Pāṇini 1.4.54 at 354.

The Viśva is cited last for लव: "particle, and sport."

Note on the verse. Four namas, and they argue.

362 names consciousness. 363 makes Her the indirect sense of *tat*, distinguishing the conditioned Brahman that the word denotes from the unconditioned that it indicates, and asserting sameness between them. 364 meets two objections — that the unconditioned has attributes after all, and that Īśvara and Brahman are simply different — the first with Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā on attributes inseparable from consciousness, the second with the nama's own एकरस. And 365 closes by grounding the whole reading in the Mīmāṃsā rule of उपक्रमादि.

So a four-nama verse contains a compressed Advaita argument with its objections marked, and its two decisive moves are borrowed from grammar and from exegesis rather than from Vedānta.

Textual note. 362's dev and verse text have lost the visarga of चितिः and 363's have gained the resulting स् — the second instance of the स्-form of this fault, after 628–629, and here it appears in both arrays with the verse text putting a space before the stray स्. 365's dev and verse text both read स्वात्मानम्द- for स्वात्मानन्द-.

---

Textual note for verses 71–80.

**Nama 354 पशुपाशविमोचिनी carries the second-longest commentary in the Sahasranāma**, after 256, and it is where the cross-reference at 134 lands — "for more details, the commentator refers the readers to Lalitā Sahasranāma, name 354." It contains: six readings of the compound, one of which is that She beat Śiva at dice; the Yoga Sūtra's five kleśas mapped term by term onto the Devī Bhāgavata's five by the Liṅga Purāṇa; that Purāṇa's subdivision into 8+8+10+18+8 = 52 afflictions; the Kulārṇava's quite different eight — pity, doubt, fear, shame, disgust, family, custom, caste; the three malas defined and nested; the combinatorial argument reducing seven possible bond-combinations to three grades of soul; the identification of those three with 133–135's Vijñānakevala, Pralayākala and Sakala; and a census of the 118 liberated Sakalas (100 Rudras + 8 Śatamaṇḍalins + 8 Krodhabhaṭṭāraka and others + Vīreśvara + Śrīkaṇṭha), whose arithmetic checks.

**Vararuci's numerals for the fourth time, and the only time they need adjusting.** 354 reads पाश as fifty-one (श=5, प=1) where the doctrine requires fifty-two, and Bhāskararāya corrects by "the rule of approximity," citing Harṣadīkṣita's reading of the Śāradātilaka's "fifty" as fifty-two. That is the same commentator on the same verse whom 833 पञ्चाशत्पीठरूपिणी cites for reading it as fifty-one. One authority, one verse, two different corrections of the same round number. The other three uses are उप=10 at 529, दारु=28 at 749, आदि=80 at 296.

**Two technical rules from other disciplines settle doctrinal points, eleven namas apart.** At 354, Pāṇini 1.4.54 स्वतन्त्रः कर्ता — agency is independence — is used to prove that the agent of liberation is Śakti and not Śiva: "without possessing the power of release Śiva can do nothing." At 365, the Mīmāṃsā rule of उपक्रमादि fixes *tat* on the unconditioned Brahman. And at 322 the grammarians' *pratyāhāra* device explains why one name, Kāmakalā, covers four bindus — first member plus terminal marker.

**A fourth mantra-cipher, at 313–315.** Bhāskararāya says at 315: "Ramā indicates ī, rākenduvadanā the anusvāra. Thus the Kāmakalā Mantra is indicated here." So ईं is encoded across two namas, and 322 seven namas on gives that mantra's doctrine. The earlier ciphers are the three kūṭas in namas 1–3, the weapon-bījas at 8–11 (withheld), and the whole Pañcadaśī at 278–284.

**The four Vedas as the four gates of the Cintāmaṇi palace**, at 335 — so nama 57's architecture acquires doors — with the four quarters from the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa and four groups of goddesses, three of which are namas elsewhere: Śuddhavidyā (25, 840), Lopāmudrā (647), Turīyāmbā (262). And 338 supplies the chain from Her to scripture: the kuṇḍalinī's triangle produces the vowels and consonants, and the letters produce the Vedas.

**Sandhi mis-division: the second instance of the स्-form, and it is in both arrays.** 362 चितिः has lost its visarga and 363 has gained the resulting स् — the visarga becoming स् rather than र् because the following sound is a voiceless dental, exactly as at 628–629. That is the only other place in the text where this happens, and here the verse text carries it too, with a space before the stray स्.

**Letter faults, three, and all three in both arrays:** 318 राक्षसन्नी for राक्षसघ्नी, the third loss of the घ् of घ्नी after 842 and 173, and again corrected only by the gloss; 333 वारुणीमदविला for वारुणीमदाविह्वला, losing both the sandhi-आ and the ह्व; 365 स्वात्मानम्द- for स्वात्मानन्द-.

**An internal avagraha, the text's only one.** 361 तमोऽपहा carries an avagraha belonging to its own sandhi (तमस् + अपहा), where all eleven other avagraha-namas — 50, 537, 554, 642, 729, 815, 828, 926, 972, 985, 988 — carry the mark of the *preceding* nama's elision.

**Displaced and duplicated fields.** 341, 342 and 343 share one gloss and body, all three carrying 341's, with 342's heading stranded in 343's gloss — a three-nama duplication matching 184–186 and 997–999. 312 and 313 share one body, which is 313's. 305's body carries Sastry's footnote on *vyākulākṣara* verses, belonging to 301. 352's material on the three circles has been carried into 354's body. 332's body carries Bhāskararāya's footnote qualifying the five substances of 330 — dedicate to God first and taper the habit — which is the only moral note on the pañcamakāra in the thousand.

**Empty bodies, seven of sixty-one:** 307, 314, 316, 318, 323, 326, 348, 349, 358 — nine, and all short namas.

**The sixty-eight sacred places are invoked twice more**, at 346 (Kashmir) and 351 (Jaḍa), after 793's Chagalaṇḍa — against 833's fifty-one pīṭhas and 112's hundred and eight tīrthas. And three more located identifications: Kalyāṇī on the Malaya mountain (324), Vimalā at Puruṣottama (347), Tanumadhyā at Kāñcī (360).

**A fourth nama identified as a metre:** 360 तनुमध्या, on the Piṅgalā Sūtra, after 829 प्रतिष्ठा (sixteen syllables), 660 सुप्रतिष्ठा (twenty) and 673 बृहती (thirty-six). In every case the metrical note is Bhāskararāya's addition to a nama whose plain sense is something else.

## परा प्रत्यक्चितीरूपा पश्यन्ती परदेवता । मध्यमा वैखरीरूपा भक्तमानसहंसिका

*parā pratyakcitīrūpā paśyantī paradevatā । madhyamā vaikharīrūpā bhaktamānasahaṃsikā*

Verse 81, namas 366–372.

> **Nama 366 carries the third-longest commentary in the Sahasranāma**, after 256 and 354, and it is placed as the answer to a question the previous verse raised. At 363 तत्पदलक्ष्यार्था Bhāskararāya made Her the *indirect* sense of the word *tat*; this nama explains why the direct sense will not do, and to explain it it sets out the whole doctrine of the four stages of speech, the four-fold bindu-cosmogony, and the correspondences between them. And the four pīṭhas that scheme produces are namas 375–379, which follow immediately.

366. परा → परा

परा = supreme, highest; the first and unmanifest stage of speech
"Parā."

Vigraha: परा वाक्।

**The question first, and it is 363's continued.** "Since the power of expression depends upon the correspondence of the words and their meanings, and as the unconditioned Brahman is also included in the Śabdabrahman, why then is Brahman indirectly indicated by the words *existence* and the rest, as the Vedāntins say? Because the words which are the physical forms of speech, Vaikharī, only express the physical form of Brahman, the Virāṭ, and do not correspond to the pure unconditioned Brahman. Thus replying, he divides speech into four forms."

So the four stages are introduced to justify a Vedāntin's move: words reach only the Virāṭ, so *tat* can only point.

**Then the cosmogony of the bindu**, in three named states. "During Pralaya, when the actions of beings about to be manifested are not yet ripe, the Brahman, bound by Māyā and by those actions, is called Ghanībhūta, the congealed one. When in course of time the actions begin to ripen and the former state of unripeness disappears, that state is called Vicikīrṣā, longing for action. At the moment of ripeness, when the modification of Māyā appears, Brahman endowed with Māyā in the form of ripened actions is called Avyakta, unmanifested."

The Avyakta is then identified with the Kāraṇabindu — "as it is the sprouting root of the universe" — on the Prapañcasāra: "that Intelligence, the congealed one, desirous of action, attains the state of Kāraṇabindu." And from it the series: "from this Kāraṇabindu proceeds in order the Kāryabindu; from the latter Nāda; thence the Bīja; thus the three came into being."

The three are graded by their share of consciousness: "in their nature they partake respectively of cit, of cit-and-acit combined, and of acit." The Rahasyāgama: "that Bindu, when in course of time it sprouts, becomes three. Its three divisions are gross, subtle and supreme. These are called Bindu, Nāda and Bīja."

**And then the correspondence-table, which is the entry's most useful passage.** The four — Kāraṇabindu, Kāryabindu, Nāda, Bīja — are matched across three levels:

*Adhidaivata:* Avyakta, Īśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Virāṭ.
*Four Śaktis:* Śāntā, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī.
*And again:* Ambikā, Icchā, Jñāna, Kriyā.
*Adhibhūta, on the Nityāhṛdaya:* "these are the four seats — Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara and Oḍyāna."
*Adhyātma:* "the Kāraṇabindu resides in the Mūlādhāra and is known by the words Śaktipiṇḍa, Kuṇḍalinī and the rest."

**The four seats are the next four namas.** 375 कामपूजिता and 376 शृङ्गाररससंपूर्णा are read at 376 as Kāmarūpa and Pūrṇagiri; 378 जालन्धरस्थिता is Jālandhara; 379 ओड्याणपीठनिलया is Oḍyāṇa. So the text names all four pīṭhas in order across two verses, and this nama supplies the scheme they belong to — each seat being one of the four bindus at the elemental level.

Icchā, Jñāna and Kriyā are 658's triad, where the Saṅketapaddhati makes them Her head, trunk and feet; Ambikā is nama 295 and 976; and the Kuṇḍalinī of the Adhyātma level is 110, whose Laghustava verse is quoted here — "there is a Śakti called Kuṇḍalinī; having known her who is ever engaged in the work of the creation of the universe, a man never again enters his mother's womb as a child."

**Then the Śabdabrahman and its four stages.** "When it sprouts, in order to create the three, then the unmanifested sound called Śabdabrahman arises in it… This sound, since it is one with the Kāraṇabindu and is therefore all-pervading, yet first appears in the Mūlādhāra of persons by the power of air acted upon by the effort of manifestation."

And the four are then defined by position, faculty and degree of motion, which is the precision worth keeping:

*Parā* — "in the Kāraṇabindu, when it is manifested, remaining motionless in its own place."
*Paśyantī* — "produced by the same air proceeding as far as the navel, joined with the reasoning intellect, Manas, possessing the nature of the manifested Kāryabindu, with simple motion."
*Madhyamā* — "as far as the heart, joined with the determining understanding, Buddhi, in the manifested Nāda, endowed with special motion."
*Vaikharī* — "as far as the mouth, developed in the throat, in the form of articulation, capable of being heard by the ears of others, possessing the nature of the manifested Bīja, with the most manifest motion."

So each stage has a station, a mental faculty, a bindu-level and a grade of स्पन्द — motionless, simple, special, fully manifest. Two authorities are then quoted with slightly different cakra-assignments: the Ācārya gives mūlādhāra, then Paśyantī, then heart with buddhi, then full manifestation; the Nityā Tantra gives mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, anāhata, viśuddhi.

**Then the Vedic warrant**, and it is the classic verse. "Though there are four kinds of speech, gross-minded men who do not understand the first three think speech to be Vaikharī alone." The Śruti: "hence men think that alone to be speech which is imperfect" — imperfect, Bhāskararāya glosses, "by not possessing the first three forms." And Ṛgveda 1.164.45: "four are the definite grades of speech; those Brāhmaṇas who are wise know them. Three, deposited in secret, are motionless; men speak the fourth grade of speech."

The Sūta Saṃhitā 4.4.23 adds a formulation on पद: "Apada, the motionless Śabdabrahman, became pada, and pada may become apada. He who knows the distinction between pada and apada, he really sees."

**And then the grammarians are called in to count the four.** "The characteristic of the words, pada, according to Gautama Sūtra 2.2.50, is: *the pada is that which has a termination*. Pāṇini also, Sūtra 1.4.14: *that which ends in sup or tiṅ is called pada*. Again, the sup termination has four divisions."

So the four stages of speech are underwritten by the grammatical definition of a word — पद is what bears an ending, and the nominal ending has four kinds. That is the second time in thirteen namas that a sūtra of Pāṇini is made to carry a doctrinal point, after 1.4.54 at 354 settled the agency of liberation on Śakti.

**The conclusion returns to 363's question and answers it.** "Even the word Tat in the Parā form only denotes the unmanifested form, Avyakta, the cause of Parā and the rest, which has the three qualities, and does not indicate the unconditioned Brahman which is above that. How can the word Tat in the Vaikharī form indicate Brahman? It does not. But even if the word Tādātmya has the power to denote Brahman, yet the word Tat can only indicate it indirectly."

So the argument is complete: not even Parā-speech reaches past the Avyakta, so Vaikharī certainly does not, and 363's लक्ष्य is the only option.

Two further readings close the entry. "Or Parā, highest: she is called Parā because she is the highest of the three lower speeches." And the Tripurā Siddhānta's three: "as she is pleased with Parānandanātha, she is called Parā. As she is celebrated in the work called Parānanda, she is Parā. And as she is the supreme source of grace, she is Parā."

That is the third guru-etymology in the text, after Turīyānandanātha at 262 and Bhuvanānandanātha at 294 — and all three follow the same pattern of an initiatory name ending in -ānandanātha.

The four stages are set out with the sprouting-seed simile at 25 शुद्धविद्याङ्कुराकारद्विजपङ्क्तिद्वयोज्ज्वला, where the teeth resemble Vaikharī specifically because two leaves parted at the tip and joined at the root is the shape of two rows meeting; and Bhāskararāya glosses "all speech" at 290 as these four.

367. प्रत्यक्चितीरूपा → प्रत्यक्-चिति-रूपा

प्रत्यक् = turned inward, backward (प्रति + अञ्च् "to bend")
चिति = consciousness (from चित्)
रूपा = form
"She whose form is inward-turned consciousness."

Vigraha: प्रत्यक् चितिः रूपं यस्याः सा।

The gloss is one line: "Pratyak, inwardly, one who approaches the Self; rūpa, form — that is, the unmanifested Brahman as her form."

प्रत्यक् is 781 प्रत्यग्रूपा's word, where Bhāskararāya sets out the technical vocabulary — बहिर्मुखत्व and पराङ्मुखत्व for the senses turned out, अन्तर्मुखत्व and प्रत्यङ्मुखत्व for the turn inward, with Kaṭha 4.1 for why the turn is against the grain. So the two namas are 414 apart with the same first member, and this one adds चिति, which was nama 362 four namas back.

368. पश्यन्ती → पश्यन्ती

पश्यन्ती = seeing, beholding (present participle of दृश् "to see"); the second stage of speech; and per the commentary, also called Uttīrṇā
"Paśyantī."

Vigraha: पश्यतीति पश्यन्ती।

The Saubhāgyasudhodaya supplies both the etymology and a second name: "as she sees all in herself, and as she rises — Uttīrṇā — above the path of action, hence this Mother is called Paśyantī and Uttīrṇā."

So Paśyantī is named for seeing and Uttīrṇā for crossing, and what she has crossed is the karmamārga — which is 113 भावनागम्या's second reading, where the gerundive was reversed to make Her "unattainable by the path of action."

The stage is placed at the navel by 366's first account and at the svādhiṣṭhāna by its second, and it is where the Kāryabindu is manifested with "simple motion."

369. परदेवता → परा-देवता

परा = supreme, highest
देवता = a deity, a divinity
"The supreme Deity."

Vigraha: परा देवता।

The whole commentary is one clause: "she is to be worshipped as the Supreme deity."

The nama interrupts the four-speech sequence, which resumes at 370 — so the order runs Parā, the inward consciousness, Paśyantī, this, Madhyamā, Vaikharī. देवता is the word of 909's neighbourhood and of 391's sixteen Nityās.

370. मध्यमा → मध्यमा

मध्यमा = middle, intermediate; the third stage of speech
"Madhyamā."

Vigraha: मध्ये भवा मध्यमा।

index.html's gloss and body are duplicates, and the definition is entirely negative and positional: "because she abides in the midst. It is said: *she is neither like Paśyantī, nor does she proceed outwards like Vaikharī with articulation fully developed; but she is in the middle between these two.*"

So Madhyamā is defined by what it is between, which is what its name says. And 366 gives it the heart, the buddhi, the manifested Nāda and "special motion."

मध्यमा had stood at 35 as Her waist and at 366's citations; and Madhyamā is one of the four speeches Bhāskararāya names at 290 and 25.

371. वैखरीरूपा → वैखरी-रूपा

वैखरी = the articulate, uttered stage of speech; and per three etymologies, from वि + खर, from वै + ख + र, or from the Vikhara breath
रूपा = form
"She in the form of Vaikharī."

Vigraha: वैखरी रूपं यस्याः सा।

Three etymologies and no choice between them. "Vaikharī: vi, much; khara, hard — that is, speech in its physical form." Or, per the Saubhāgyasudhodaya: "vai, certainly; kha, the cavity of the ear; ra, to go or to enter" — so speech named by its arrival at a hearer. Or, per the Yoga Śāstras: "she is called Vaikharī because she was produced by the Prāṇa called Vikhara."

So the word is derived from hardness, from the ear, and from a named breath — and the second is the only one that makes speech relational.

Vaikharī is where 366 says the word *tat* certainly cannot reach Brahman, and 289 श्रुतिसीमन्तसिन्दूरीकृतपादाब्जधूलिका's whole argument is that scriptural language gets only the dust of Her feet.

372. भक्तमानसहंसिका → भक्त-मानस-हंसिका

भक्त = a devotee
मानस = the mind; and Lake Mānasa
हंसिका = a female swan (हंस with the diminutive)
"The swan on the Mānasa of her devotees' minds."

Vigraha: भक्तानां मानसे हंसिका।

index.html's body is Sastry's own gloss in brackets: "as the mythical swans live in the celestial lake called Mānasa, so she lives in the minds of her devotees."

**This nama is 816 मुनिमानसहंसिका with भक्त for मुनि**, and the two stand 444 apart with the same second and third members. At 816 the pun was the whole point — मानस being both mind and the swans' lake, so the figure needs no comparative particle — and there Bhāskararāya offered a second reading making सहंसिका "a dancer with bangles on the ankles." Here the compound is repeated with the sages exchanged for the devotees, and only Sastry glosses it.
