So the text uses one compound twice, and the difference is who owns the mind. Bhāskararāya marks the verse: (80).

Note on the verse. Seven namas, four of them the stages of speech, and 366 carries everything.

What that nama does is unusual even for this commentary: it answers a question raised two namas earlier in the previous verse, and to answer it constructs a complete apparatus — three states of the pralaya-Brahman, four bindus, four adhidaivata levels, four Śaktis, the Icchā-Jñāna-Kriyā triad, four pīṭhas, and the kuṇḍalinī — before locating the four speeches by station, faculty, bindu and grade of motion. Then it returns to the question and answers it: not even Parā reaches past the Avyakta, so *tat* can only indicate.

And the four pīṭhas that scheme yields are the four namas immediately following, in order — Kāmarūpa and Pūrṇagiri at 375–376, Jālandhara at 378, Oḍyāṇa at 379. So this nama is the key to the next verse and a half.

Textual note. 370's gloss and body are duplicates. 372's body is Sastry's bracketed gloss rather than Bhāskararāya's commentary.

---

## कामेश्वरप्राणनाडी कृतज्ञा कामपूजिता । शृङ्गाररससंपूर्णा जया जालन्धरस्थिता

*kāmeśvaraprāṇanāḍī kṛtajñā kāmapūjitā । śṛṅgārarasasaṃpūrṇā jayā jālandharasthitā*

Verse 82, namas 373–378.

373. कामेश्वरप्राणनाडी → कामेश्वर-प्राण-नाडी

कामेश्वर = Kāmeśvara
प्राण = breath, life
नाडी = a channel, a vessel, a duct
"She who is the life-channel of Kāmeśvara."

Vigraha: कामेश्वरस्य प्राणनाडी।

The whole commentary is Saundaryalaharī 28, and it is a claim about what kept Śiva alive: "when Śiva drank the virulent poison, his days did not end, owing, O mother, to the power of your ear-ornaments."

Sastry's footnote explains why the ornaments matter: "such ornaments are worn by a married woman only during her coverture." So Her tāṭaṅkas are the emblem of a living husband, and the verse argues backwards from the emblem — while she wears them he cannot die, so the poison did not kill him.

That joins two things the text has separately. Her ear-ornaments are nama 22 ताटङ्कयुगलीभूततपनोडुपमण्डला, where the pair of them are the orbs of the sun and the moon, and 864 कनत्कनकताटङ्का, where they are glittering gold. And nama 30's displaced footnote records that "the marriage emblem tied round the neck was not the Āryan custom and was not found referred to in any Vedic literature; earring was the emblem." So the earring is the older marriage-token, and this nama makes Śiva's survival depend on it.

The poison in his throat is also 392 श्रीकण्ठार्धशरीरिणी's etymology nineteen namas on, and nama 1's fifth reading of श्री.

नाडी is the word of 333's Vāruṇī nāḍī and of the three at 912.

374. कृतज्ञा → कृत-ज्ञा

कृत = done, an action performed; also the Kṛta age; also the winning cast at dice
ज्ञा = knowing (from ज्ञा)
"She who knows what is done."

Vigraha: कृतं जानातीति कृतज्ञा।

Four readings before the substantial one, and they take कृत four ways.

As actions: "kṛta, good and bad actions" — and then the nine witnesses: "the Sun, the moon, the god of death, time, and the five elements, these nine are the witnesses of good and bad actions; she is not separated from these, hence she is called Kṛtajñā." That makes Her the whole apparatus of moral bookkeeping, which is 288 पुण्यापुण्यफलप्रदा's function.

Or "kṛta, the actions done; jñā — she rewards them by imparting knowledge." Or "kṛtavat, already acquired; jña, knowledge — she possesses it." Or कृत as the golden age, "as then righteousness was perfectly established and knowledge also was perfect."

**And then the dice, which is where 354's reading gets its scriptural apparatus.**

"According to the science of dice there are four Dyūtas which are called Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, and numbered respectively four, three, two and one; but they count ten, six, three and one respectively, because in the higher number the lower ones are included."

Chāndogya 4.3.8 is cited for the arithmetic — "now these five and other five make ten, that is the Kṛta cast" — and Chāndogya 4.1.4 for the consequence: "as in the game of dice all the lower casts belong to him who has conquered with the Kṛta cast." So one who wins the Kṛta wins the other three, and Bhāskararāya draws the analogy: "the meaning is, like the all-pervading and all-Kṛta cast, her knowledge is all-embracing."

And then the last reading: "or she knows the Kṛta cast. The expression is that she always conquers when she casts the dice with Śiva."

At 354 पशुपाशविमोचिनी one of the six readings of पाश was "dice… the meaning is that in gambling with Śiva, while throwing the dice on the board, she conquered him." That was given without support. Here the game is explained — four casts numbered 4, 3, 2, 1 but counting 10, 6, 3, 1, with the highest containing the rest — and two Chāndogya verses are cited. So the two namas twenty apart make one claim, and this is the one that documents it.

375. कामपूजिता → काम-पूजिता

काम = Kāma — the bodiless son of Lakṣmī
पूजिता = worshipped (from पूज्)
"She who is worshipped by Kāma."

Vigraha: कामेन पूजिता।

**In 366's scheme this nama is the pīṭha Kāmarūpa**, per 376's commentary.

The Aruṇa Upaniṣad — Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.11 — is quoted: "there is a bodiless son of Lakṣmī; though he is without mind, he has life. He acquired that jewel" — the jewel being the Pañcadaśī mantra.

That is the passage 586 कामसेविता gives in full, where the bodiless Kāma "though without fingers worshipped; though without neck he adorned himself; though without tongue he tasted it," and is thereby made the Ṛṣi of the vidyā — with the ritual rule attached that the external cakra can be entered only by knowing him. So the same Upaniṣadic figure supplies two namas 211 apart, and here only its opening clause is given.

The burnt Kāma revived by Her is 84; Manmatha is fifth of the twelve holders at 238 and 812.

376. शृङ्गाररससंपूर्णा → शृङ्गार-रस-संपूर्णा

शृङ्गार = the erotic sentiment, the first of the rasas; and per the numeral reading, शृङ्ग two
रस = flavour, an aesthetic mode; and per the numeral reading, six
संपूर्णा = wholly filled, complete (सम् + पूर्)
"She who is filled with the essence of love."

Vigraha: शृङ्गाररसेन संपूर्णा।

**And here the pīṭha-identification is given, together with a numeral reading of the compound.**

"Or, as he refers below to the Jālandhara and Oḍyāṇa centres, these two — 375 and 376 — represent the pīṭhas called Kāmarūpa and Pūrṇagiri."

So the four seats of 366's Adhibhūta level are namas 375, 376, 378 and 379, in the order the Nityāhṛdaya gave them.

Then the numeral reading: "Śṛṅga, two — that is, two horns; rasa, six — that is, six flavours; so Śṛṅgārarasa means the centre called Anāhata, which has twice six petals. Sam, frequently; pūrṇa, remains — that is, she frequently remains in that centre."

शृङ्ग is two because horns come in pairs and रस is six because the flavours are six — the *bhūtasaṃkhyā* convention, as वह्नि was three at 352. Two times six is twelve, and the anāhata has twelve petals. So a compound about the erotic mode is read as a cakra by counting.

And then the placement of the four seats in the body: "according to the Tantras, the well-known four centres in the elements — Kāmarūpa and the rest — remain in the body in the Mūlādhāra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi and the Ājñā respectively. Hence this name indicates the Anāhata and Pūrṇagiri centres, in the body and in the world."

So the four pīṭhas are also four cakras, which completes 366's three-level table with a fourth column: bindu, deity, śakti, seat, and now cakra.

A last reading: "or Śṛṅga, chief; avara, covering — that is, the Avidyā which veils; sa with sampūrṇa, Brahmā — that is, she is both the conditioned and unconditioned Brahman."

377. जया → जया

जया = victory, victorious (from जि "to conquer")
"The Victorious."

Vigraha: जयः अस्याः अस्तीति जया।

The whole commentary is a placement: "according to the Padma Purāṇa, Jayā is the deity worshipped in the Varāha mountain."

जया is also one of the sixteen Nityās — the twelfth, as Vijayā — and one of the eleven house-names at 347; and 346 विजया is the same root with वि, where Bhāskararāya gave four readings including an hour of the day with a stated duration.

378. जालन्धरस्थिता → जालन्धर-स्थिता

जालन्धर = Jālandhara, the third of the four pīṭhas
स्थिता = abiding, seated
"She who abides in Jālandhara."

Vigraha: जालन्धरे स्थिता।

**The third pīṭha of 366's scheme.**

"According to the Padma Purāṇa, Jālandhara is a place where she is worshipped under the name of Viṣṇumukti." And by 376's placement, Jālandhara corresponds to the viśuddhi in the body.

Bhāskararāya marks the division: "17th verse divides 44 names."

Note on the verse. Six namas, and the verse begins the pīṭha-sequence 366 set up.

374 is the entry to keep. Its last reading — that She always wins when she throws dice with Śiva — is the same claim 354 made without support, and here the game is documented: four casts, numbered 4, 3, 2, 1 but counting 10, 6, 3, 1, the highest containing the rest, on two Chāndogya verses. So a throwaway line in the longest commentary in the text turns out to rest on the Upaniṣad's own account of dicing.

373 makes Śiva's survival of the poison depend on Her ear-ornaments, which are the emblem of a living husband — and nama 30's footnote records that the earring, not the neck-thread, is the older marriage-token.

And 376 reads its own compound by numerals to get the anāhata's twelve petals, then completes 366's correspondence-table with a column of cakras: Kāmarūpa in the mūlādhāra, Pūrṇagiri in the anāhata, Jālandhara in the viśuddhi, Oḍyāṇa in the ājñā.

---

## ओड्याणपीठनिलया बिन्दुमण्डलवासिनी । रहोयागक्रमाराध्या रहस्तर्पणतर्पिता

*oḍyāṇapīṭhanilayā bindumaṇḍalavāsinī । rahoyāgakramārādhyā rahastarpaṇatarpitā*

Verse 83, namas 379–382.

379. ओड्याणपीठनिलया → ओड्याण-पीठ-निलया

ओड्याण = Oḍyāṇa, the fourth of the four pīṭhas
पीठ = a seat, a sacred seat
निलया = abode, dwelling (नि + ली "to settle")
"She whose abode is the Oḍyāṇa seat."

Vigraha: ओड्याणपीठं निलयः यस्याः सा।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

**This closes the four-pīṭha sequence** — Kāmarūpa at 375, Pūrṇagiri at 376, Jālandhara at 378, Oḍyāṇa here — which 366 set out as the Adhibhūta aspect of the four bindus and 376 placed in the ājñā cakra.

Oḍḍiyāna is also where the Kālikā Purāṇa places Kātyāyanī at 556, and where 905 बैन्दवासना's neighbourhood puts the Bindu. पीठ is the word of 833 पञ्चाशत्पीठरूपिणी, where the fifty-one pīṭhas are Her form and are set in the places of the mātṛkās — a different and larger set than these four.

निलया for the eighth time in the text.

380. बिन्दुमण्डलवासिनी → बिन्दु-मण्डल-वासिनी

बिन्दु = a point, a drop — the Bindu at the Śrīcakra's centre
मण्डल = a circle, a disc
वासिनी = dwelling (from वस्)
"She who dwells in the circle of the Bindu."

Vigraha: बिन्दुमण्डले वासिनी।

"Bindumaṇḍala, the centre called Sarvānandamaya. Some explain that Bindu means white, Maṇḍala, circle — that is, the Brahmarandhra."

The Sarvānandamaya is the ninth and innermost enclosure, which 905 बैन्दवासना gives as one identification of the बैन्दव and 974 बिन्दुतर्पणसंतुष्टा makes the site of the libation. So the nama places Her at the diagram's centre, having just placed her at the four pīṭhas.

And the second reading relocates it into the skull, as 275 भानुमण्डलमध्यस्था relocated the sun's disc into the anāhata and 240 चन्द्रमण्डलमध्यगा made the moon's disc the Śrīcakra.

381. रहोयागक्रमाराध्या → रहः-याग-क्रम-आराध्या

रहः = a secret, a lonely place (रहस्)
याग = a sacrifice, an offering (from यज्)
क्रम = a method, a step
आराध्या = to be worshipped (आ + राध्)
"She who is worshipped by the method of the secret sacrifice."

Vigraha: रहोयागक्रमेण आराध्या।

Sandhi: क्रम + आराध्या → क्रमाराध्या (आ by 6.1.101).

**This is 230 महायागक्रमाराध्या with रहः for महा**, and the two namas are 151 apart with the same last three members. At 230 the Mahāyāga was "the worship of sixty-four yoginīs from Akṣobhya," or the rite of Bhāvanopaniṣad 84 "to be accomplished by Śivayogins alone."

Here the secret place is named: Saundaryalaharī 9 — "in the Sahasrāra lotus, in the secret place, you sport with your husband."

And the sacrifice is internal: "Raho, in the secret, that is in the Sahasrāra; yāga, the sacrifice of the eight oblations of good actions and the rest in the fire of cit supported by the golden Kuṇḍalinī; or Rahoyāga means the meeting of Śiva and Śakti in a lonely place; krama, stepping into that place; ārādhyā, to be attained."

The eight oblations are 919 चैतन्यकुसुमप्रिया's eight flowers — non-injury, restraint of the senses, pity, compassion, wisdom, penance, truth, meditation, of which not one is a thing. And the fire of cit is nama 4 चिदग्निकुण्डसंभूता's altar.

Then Āpastamba on solitude, and the list of what disqualifies is worth having: "salvation is not for him who confines himself to scriptural words alone, nor for him who delights in fine houses, or in rich food and clothes, or in worldly ideas; but the man of firm vow who leads a lonely life and has ceased from worldly pursuits attains salvation, and he who constantly rejoices in meditation on the Self and who never injures anything attains salvation."

That is the severe register against which the text's leniency-namas — 353, 736, 815, 167 — stand.

382. रहस्तर्पणतर्पिता → रहः-तर्पण-तर्पिता

रहः = secret, lonely (रहस्)
तर्पण = a satisfying libation (from तृप् "to be satisfied," causative)
तर्पिता = satisfied, gratified (from तृप्)
"She who is gratified by the secret libation."

Vigraha: रहस्तर्पणेन तर्पिता।

The compound doubles the root: तर्पण the offering that satisfies and तर्पिता the being satisfied — which is exactly 974 बिन्दुतर्पणसंतुष्टा's construction, where तर्पण was paired with तुष्टा from a second root, and where the substances were graded by class.

The Aruṇa Upaniṣad again: "if one would enter, let him enter, having practised lonely communion." And Bhāskararāya's gloss makes it a precondition: "according to the method of devotion to the Śrīvidyā, one should only adopt the path after having recognised the higher self."

**And then two mantras of the internal sacrifice, which are the fullest such formulae in the text.**

"Holding in both hands, representing brightness and darkness — Prakāśa and Vimarśa — the sacrificial ladle of Unmanī, pouring out the ghee of righteousness and unrighteousness and the senses in the fire of consciousness, I sacrifice."

So the two hands are the two poles of 548 विमर्शरूपिणी, the ladle is the transmental state of 207 मनोन्मनी, the ghee is dharma and adharma together, and the fire is cit. Every implement is a doctrine, and what is poured in is exactly what 255 धर्माधर्मविवर्जिता says She is free of.

"Another description is: I sacrifice the Universe from Earth to Śiva in the fire of saṃvit, ever burning without fuel, and ever-increasing, dispelling the darkness of illusion, the centre from which ever emanates beautiful rays."

"From Earth to Śiva" is the thirty-six tattvas, and "burning without fuel" is nama 4's own phrase for the cidagnikuṇḍa.

Note on the verse. Four namas, and they move from place to rite.

379 closes the four-pīṭha sequence and 380 places Her at the Bindu, so the verse begins by finishing the geography 366 laid out.

Then 381–382 give the internal sacrifice, and between them every part of it is named: the place is the sahasrāra, the oblations are the eight dispositions, the ladle is Unmanī, the hands are Prakāśa and Vimarśa, the ghee is merit and demerit, the fire is cit or saṃvit and burns without fuel, and what is offered is the whole tattva-series. That is 918 चैतन्यार्घ्यसमाराध्या's nirādhāra worship set out as a rubric rather than asserted.

Textual note. 379 has no commentary body.

---

## सद्यःप्रसादिनी विश्वसाक्षिणी साक्षिवर्जिता । षडङ्गदेवतायुक्ता षाड्गुण्यपरिपूरिता

*sadyaḥprasādinī viśvasākṣiṇī sākṣivarjitā । ṣaḍaṅgadevatāyuktā ṣāḍguṇyaparipūritā*

Verse 84, namas 383–387.

383. सद्यःप्रसादिनी → सद्यः-प्रसादिनी

सद्यः = at once, immediately
प्रसादिनी = she who is pleased, who shows favour (प्र + सद् "to settle, to grow clear")
"She who is pleased at once."

Vigraha: सद्यः प्रसीदतीति।

The whole commentary places the nama: "she is at once gratified by the sacrifice and oblation mentioned above" — that is 381 and 382. So the immediacy is a response to the internal rite specifically, and not a general claim.

The nama is 869 क्षिप्रप्रसादिनी with सद्यः for क्षिप्र — and there Bhāskararāya graded the speed into three, this birth, the third, or the next, according to the devotee. Here no grading is offered because the rite named is the highest.

384. विश्वसाक्षिणी → विश्व-साक्षिणी

विश्व = all, the universe
साक्षिणी = a witness — literally she who is with the eye (स + अक्षि, with इन् and ङीप्)
"The Witness of the universe."

Vigraha: विश्वस्य साक्षिणी।

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

साक्षिणी is 571 महाप्रलयसाक्षिणी's and 232's word, where the reason She alone can witness is that nothing else survives the dissolution. Here the object is the universe rather than the dance, and the next nama supplies the argument.

385. साक्षिवर्जिता → साक्षि-वर्जिता

साक्षि = a witness
वर्जिता = devoid of, excluding (from वृज्)
"She who has no witness."

Vigraha: साक्षिणा वर्जिता।

The whole commentary is one clause and it is the regress-argument in its shortest form: "there is no witness to the one who is the witness of all things."

That is 877 निरालम्बा's structure — "there is no support for that which supports all; otherwise we obtain regression to infinity" — and 132, 147 and 152's, each on a different stem. Here the stem is साक्षि, and 384–385 make the pair explicit: witness of all, witnessed by none.

386. षडङ्गदेवतायुक्ता → षट्-अङ्ग-देवता-युक्ता

षट् = six
अङ्ग = a limb, a member
देवता = a deity
युक्ता = joined with, accompanied by (from युज्)
"She who is accompanied by the deities of the six limbs."

Vigraha: षडङ्गदेवताभिः युक्ता।

Sandhi: षट् + अङ्ग → षडङ्ग, the ट् voicing before the vowel. The dev field reads षडङ्गदेवतायुक्त। — the final आ lost and a daṇḍa standing in its place — and the verse text carries the same.

Three readings, and they give three quite different sets of six.

*The ritual six.* "The aṅgas are heart, head, tuft of hair, eyes, armour and weapons. She is accompanied by the Śaktis belonging to these." And the Jñānārṇava on the practice: "next he should perform the consecration of the limbs which belong to the Śrīvidyā mantra. This one should perform externally in order; afterwards he should worship the surrounding deities, which are three in number. By these Āvaraṇa deities the number nine is completed."

So six aṅga-nyāsa deities plus three surrounding deities make nine, which is the number of the Śrīcakra's enclosures.

*The six divine attributes.* "Or Ṣaḍaṅga-devatā is Śiva who presides over the six aṅgas." The Devī Bhāgavata: "omniscience, contentment, non-original wisdom, independence, unfading power and infinity — these, say the learned, are the six aṅgas of the Lord Maheśvara."

*The six Vedāṅgas.* "Or Ṣaḍaṅgas are phonetics, ceremonial, grammar, lexicography, prosody and astronomy. Surrounded by the deities of these six means the Vedas are her form."

That third set is six of the fourteen seats of dharma listed at 355 संहृताशेषपाषण्डा and 356, where heresy is defined as whatever falls outside them.

387. षाड्गुण्यपरिपूरिता → षाड्गुण्य-परिपूरिता

षाड्गुण्य = the set of six qualities (vṛddhi abstract of षड्गुण)
परिपूरिता = wholly filled, complete (परि + पूर्)
"She who is filled with the six qualities."

Vigraha: षाड्गुण्येन परिपूरिता।

Two sets of six, and the first is political.

"The six guṇas, according to the Kāmandaka ethical code, are peace, war, marching, sitting encamped, dividing his forces, and allies."

Those are the ṣāḍguṇya of statecraft — sandhi, vigraha, yāna, āsana, dvaidhībhāva, samāśraya — the six courses open to a king. So this is the third nama in the text with a political reference, after 608 दण्डनीतिस्था, the science of chastisement, and 812 परमन्त्रविभेदिनी, where मन्त्र was the royal power of counsel and the three śaktis of a king were named.

"The Purāṇas give out the following: prosperity, righteousness, fame, wealth, wisdom and dispassion."

That second set is the six भग of 279 भगवती, where the Purāṇas gave "the full supremacy, righteousness, fame, prosperity, wisdom, discrimination." So the same six qualities are named twice in the text under two words, भग and गुण.

Note on the verse. Five namas, and two pairs.

383 makes the immediacy of Her grace a response to the internal rite of 381–382 rather than a general disposition — which is a narrowing 869 क्षिप्रप्रसादिनी did not make.

384–385 are the witness-pair, and 385's one clause is the regress-argument on its fifth stem in the text.

386 and 387 then give five sets of six between them — the ritual aṅgas, Śiva's six attributes, the six Vedāṅgas, the six courses of statecraft, and the six भग — and Bhāskararāya adjudicates none of them. That is his standing method with numbered sets: 946's six sets of five sacrifices, 250's five sets of five Brahmans, 343's five definitions of kṣetra.

Textual note. 386's dev and verse text both read षडङ्गदेवतायुक्त। — the final आ lost and a daṇḍa in its place. 384 has no commentary body.

---

## नित्यक्लिन्ना निरुपमा निर्वाणसुखदायिनी । नित्याषोडशिकारूपा श्रीकण्ठार्धशरीरिणी

*nityaklinnā nirupamā nirvāṇasukhadāyinī । nityāṣoḍaśikārūpā śrīkaṇṭhārdhaśarīriṇī*

Verse 85, namas 388–392.

388. नित्यक्लिन्ना → नित्य-क्लिन्ना

नित्य = ever, perpetual
क्लिन्ना = moist, wet — hence softened, compassionate (past participle of क्लिद् "to be wet")
"The Ever-moist — the ever-compassionate."

Vigraha: नित्यं क्लिन्ना।

क्लिन्न is literally wetted, so compassion is named by moisture — the melting of a hard thing. That is the same register as सान्द्र at 197 सान्द्रकरुणा, where compassion was given a thickness, and 326 करुणारससागरा, where it was an ocean.

"Or Nityaklinnā is the deity of the third day of the lunar fortnight." The Garuḍa Purāṇa is quoted: "next I describe Nityaklinnā; she is Tripurā herself, giving happiness and salvation."

**And Nityaklinnā is the third of the sixteen Nityās**, whose full list Sastry gives at 391 three namas on. So the nama is both a tithi-deity and a member of the set the next verse-group names — and several of the sixteen are namas of the thousand.

389. निरुपमा → निर्-उपमा

निर् = without
उपमा = a comparison, a likeness (उप + मा "to measure")
"The Incomparable."

Vigraha: उपमा यस्याः नास्ति सा।

Śvetāśvatara 4.19: "none is equal to him."

उपमा is उप + मा, a measuring-alongside — so incomparability is again named by the absence of a measure, as तुला was a balance at 184 निस्तुला and सादृश्य a reckonable likeness at 29. And 198 समानाधिकवर्जिता makes the same claim with both terms spelled out, on the same Śvetāśvatara chapter.

390. निर्वाणसुखदायिनी → निर्वाण-सुख-दायिनी

निर्वाण = extinction, final beatitude; and per the etymology, निर् without + वाण body
सुख = happiness
दायिनी = she who gives (दा + णिनि, feminine ङीप्)
"She who bestows the bliss of Nirvāṇa."

Vigraha: निर्वाणसुखं ददातीति।

**The etymology given is not the usual one and it is argued.** "Nirvāṇa: nir, freed; vāṇa or bāṇa, body — because in the Śruti, Praśna 2.2, *holding this bow*, and in the word *girvāṇa*, this word is explained by the Vedāntins and Mīmāṃsakas as body. The Amaraśeṣa also says, bāṇa means body and bow. So here Nirvāṇa means without body, that is, indescribable bliss."

So निर्वाण is derived from वाण, a body — not from वा, to blow out. That makes the word mean bodilessness rather than extinction, which is a substantially milder reading, and Bhāskararāya supports it with a Śruti usage, a compound, and a lexicon.

The Kūrma Purāṇa then has Devī tell Himavat what is required: "if you neglect me, O king of mountains, you cannot attain the pure rest of the supreme Nirvāṇa; therefore seek refuge in me, regarding me as one, as many, or as combined; thus worshipping me, O great king, you will attain that state."

"As one, as many, or as combined" is a threefold licence — the same generosity as 681 सुखाराध्या's freedom from rubric.

दायिनी for the ninth time in the text.

391. नित्याषोडशिकारूपा → नित्या-षोडशिका-रूपा

नित्या = a Nityā deity; and per the second reading, compulsory
षोडशिका = the set of sixteen; and per the second reading, a house where the graha sacrifice is performed
रूपा = form
"She in the form of the sixteen Nityās."

Vigraha: नित्याः षोडशिकाः रूपं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: नित्या + षोडशिका stands.

"The sixteen deities are from Kāmeśvarī to Tripurasundarī." And the Tantrarāja supplies the relation of the sixteenth to the fifteen: "the fifteen deities are the limbs of Lalitā, who is the first of the sixteen; as she is endowed with these limbs, she is the body of which they are parts."

**Sastry's footnote gives the whole list**, and it is worth having because so many of the sixteen are namas of this text: "(1) Kāmeśvarī, (2) Bhagamālinī, (3) Nityaklinnā, (4) Bheruṇḍā, (5) Vahnivāsinī, (6) Mahāvajreśvarī, (7) Śivadūtī, (8) Tvaritā, (9) Kulasundarī, (10) Nityā, (11) Nīlapatākinī, (12) Vijayā, (13) Sarvamaṅgalā, (14) Jvālāmālinī, (15) Citrā, and (16) Tripurasundarī."

Of those, Bhagamālinī is nama 277, Nityaklinnā 388, Śivadūtī 405, Nityā 136, Vijayā 346, Sarvamaṅgalā 200, Tripurasundarī 234 and 997 — eight of the sixteen, and Jvālāmālinī is the Jvālāmālinikā of nama 71 and Vahnivāsinī the वह्निमण्डलवासिनी of 352. So ten of the sixteen Nityās are named in the thousand, which is a higher proportion than any other set the text draws on.

The fifteen are also the tithis of 256's scheme and 610 प्रतिपन्मुख्यराकान्ततिथिमण्डलपूजिता's lunar round, and the sixteen the Meru Prastāra of 775.

Then the second reading, which changes the nama entirely: "or nitya, compulsory; ā, frequent; ṣoḍaśika, a house where the graha sacrifice is performed; rūpa, pleased — that is, she is pleased by the compulsory sacrifices." And the Śakti Rahasya on how cheaply: **"the mother is as much pleased by a single repetition of the Ṣoḍaśī as by crores of Vājapeya and of Ṣoḍaśī sacrifices."**

One repetition against crores of great sacrifices — which is the leniency-doctrine at its most extreme, and it belongs with 353's rule that imperfect worship yields perfect devotion next birth.

392. श्रीकण्ठार्धशरीरिणी → श्रीकण्ठ-अर्ध-शरीरिणी

श्रीकण्ठ = Śiva — the fair-throated, or, per the etymology, he in whose throat the poison is fixed (श्री poison + कण्ठ throat); and per the Mātṛkākośa, the letter अ
अर्ध = half
शरीरिणी = bodied, having a body (शरीर with इन् and ङीप्)
"She who is half the body of Śrīkaṇṭha."

Vigraha: श्रीकण्ठस्य अर्धं शरीरं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: श्रीकण्ठ + अर्ध → श्रीकण्ठार्ध (आ by 6.1.101).

**The etymology returns nama 1's fifth reading.** "Śrīkaṇṭha: śrī, poison; kaṇṭha, throat — as the poison is fixed in his throat, Śiva is called Śrīkaṇṭha."

At nama 1 श्रीमाता Bhāskararāya offered exactly that sense of श्री — "śrī is poison and mā *to fix*, referring to the poison fixed in Śiva's throat" — and noted the cost: "in these two last cases the name Śrīmātā is masculine, Śiva and Śakti being one and the same." So the poison-reading of श्री appears at the text's first nama and here, and nowhere else.

Then the Ardhanārīśvara. "She forms one body with Śiva." Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.1–3: "in the beginning this was Self alone… he then divided himself into two, and thence arose husband and wife" — the passage 878 स्वात्मारामा uses to explain how self-delight is possible for one who is alone.

And the Vāyu Purāṇa gives the division a colour-scheme: "that beneficent one, having the half of the body of Śaṃkara — the right half of her body is white and the left is blue; thus divide my body, said Brahmā to Devī. Thus of the two forms one became Gaurī, white, the other Kālī, blue."

So Gaurī at 635 and Kālī at 751 are the two halves of one body, and the text's difficulty about Her colour — reconciled at 922 by making colour a function of the meditation's purpose — here has an anatomical answer.

**Then the letter-reading, which is the entry's substance.** "According to the Mātṛkākośa, अ means Śrīkaṇṭha, Indra, forehead, and Viṣṇu. Thus Śrīkaṇṭha is अ. The letter अ is half the body of the other letters in speech."

The Śruti is cited for that: "अ is all the speech; that अ takes on different forms in combination with the different consonants." So every syllable contains अ, and अ is therefore half of each — which makes अर्धशरीरिणी literally true of the alphabet.

And Bhāskararāya draws the consequence for the four speeches: "the meaning is that अ, the first utterance, is the Parā form which becomes later on the Vaikharī." The Sūta Saṃhitā 4.47.59: "the supreme Śakti, Devī, the form of cit, arises as speech; that speech is called Parā. I ever bow down in devotion to that Śakti who is the half body of Śiva."

Then two further readings. "Or Devī who has only half a body, the other half is called Śrīkaṇṭha, that is the fulfiller of the half" — with the Sūta Saṃhitā again: "the Śakti called desire is filled in the belly of Śiva," which Bhāskararāya explains as a nyāsa: "in the performance of Nyāsa half the body is filled by the Pūrṇodarī and other Śaktis and the other half by Śrīkaṇṭha of Śiva."

**And a last reading which is graphical rather than semantic**: "or, when we write the letter अ, half of it is like the Kāmakalā."

So the shape of the written character is observed: the left portion of अ resembles the Kāmakalā figure. That is the only place in the text where an argument turns on how a letter looks on the page rather than on what it sounds or means, and the Kāmakalā it resembles is nama 712's single vowel and 322's pratyāhāra of four bindus.

Note on the verse. Five namas, and 391 and 392 carry it.

391 names the sixteen Nityās and Sastry lists them — ten of the sixteen are namas of the thousand, which is a closer overlap than the text has with any other set. And its second reading gives the leniency-doctrine its sharpest form: one repetition of the Ṣoḍaśī equals crores of great sacrifices.

392 is the denser entry. It derives Śrīkaṇṭha from the poison in the throat, which returns the reading nama 1 offered of श्री and nowhere else repeated; it makes Gaurī and Kālī the white and blue halves of one body; and then it identifies Śrīkaṇṭha with the letter अ and argues that अ is half of every syllable, so that "half the body of Śrīkaṇṭha" is a fact about the alphabet. Its last line observes that half the written अ looks like the Kāmakalā.

390's derivation of निर्वाण from वाण, a body, rather than from वा, to blow out, is also worth keeping: on that reading the word means bodilessness rather than extinction, and Bhāskararāya argues it from a Śruti usage, a compound and a lexicon.

---

## प्रभावती प्रभारूपा प्रसिद्धा परमेश्वरी । मूलप्रकृतिरव्यक्ता व्यक्ताव्यक्तस्वरूपिणी

*prabhāvatī prabhārūpā prasiddhā parameśvarī । mūlaprakṛtir avyaktā vyaktāvyaktasvarūpiṇī*

Verse 86, namas 393–399.

393. प्रभावती → प्रभा-वती

प्रभा = radiance, splendour (प्र + भा "to shine"); and per the commentary, the surrounding deities
वती = possessing (मतुप्, feminine ङीप्)
"She who possesses radiance."

Vigraha: प्रभा अस्याः अस्तीति प्रभावती।

"Prabhā, the surrounding Āvaraṇa Devatās, viz. Aṇimā and the rest, because there is a saying: *Devī is surrounded by Aṇimā and other luminaries.*" So the radiance is a retinue — the eight siddhis personified as the deities of an enclosure, which 224 महासिद्धिः names and gives a second set of eight for.

**And then a Jaina citation, which is rare in the text.** "Some learned Jains, Haribhadra and others, record in their works Dharmasaṅgrahiṇī and the rest: *the rays are the qualities, they are not the substratum; among these even, the quality of brightness is not the substratum.*"

So a Jaina position on the relation of quality to substrate is quoted at the head of a two-nama pair whose point is precisely to deny that distinction — 394 states "the identity of the quality and the possessor of it." The Jainas are named for a view and then contradicted, which is what 141 शान्ता does with the Digambaras and 149 नित्यबुद्धा reverses by making two Tīrthaṅkaras Her devotees.

394. प्रभारूपा → प्रभा-रूपा

प्रभा = radiance
रूपा = form
"She whose form is radiance."

Vigraha: प्रभा रूपं यस्याः सा।

"This indicates the identity of the quality and the possessor of it. Prabhā, Aṇimā and other Devatās."

So 393 makes Her possess the radiance and 394 makes Her be it, and the pair is the text's standing device — affirm the relation, then dissolve it. Chāndogya 3.14.2 is cited: "mind itself, brightness itself."

That is 906–907's move with the tattvas, 341–342's with the field, and 384–385's with the witness.

395. प्रसिद्धा → प्र-सिद्धा

प्र = forth, widely
सिद्धा = established, accomplished, celebrated (from सिध् "to succeed")
"The Celebrated."

Vigraha: प्रसिद्धा प्रख्याता।

**The reason given is that everyone already knows Her**, and it is the strongest form of that claim in the text: "because Devī is known by all in the shape of *I*. That Devī all men recognise under the form of *I*."

And the Devī Bhāgavata's opening verse: "we meditate upon the primeval Vidyā in the form of the Universal Caitanya."

That is 994 आबालगोपविदिता's Sūta Saṃhitā — "all beings recognise Him in the shape of the idea of *I*" — and 830 प्रकटाकृतिः's, where प्रकट means "experienced by all" and the same verse is quoted. So three namas make the claim, and it is the ground of 995's objection: if everyone knows he himself is Devī, will Her command not be held cheap?

396. परमेश्वरी → परम-ईश्वरी

परम = highest, supreme
ईश्वरी = mistress, sovereign lady
"The supreme Sovereign."

Vigraha: परमा ईश्वरी।

Sandhi: परम + ईश्वरी → परमेश्वरी (अ + ई → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87). index.html carries 395's gloss and body on this nama, so no commentary of its own survives.

ईश् for its eighteenth turn, and this is its widest form after 202 सर्वेश्वरी and 569 निखिलेश्वरी.

397. मूलप्रकृतिः → मूल-प्रकृतिः

मूल = a root; and per the readings, the Śrīvidyā mantra; and per the numeral reading, eight
प्रकृतिः = nature, origin, the primary matter (प्र + कृ "to make")
"The root Matter."

Vigraha: मूला प्रकृतिः।

The dev field reads मूलप्रकृति, the visarga lost — and the next nama has lost its initial अ to the same joint. See the textual note; the sense of 398 inverts as a result.

index.html carries 396's stranded heading in this nama's gloss field. And **the body is the fourth-longest commentary in the Sahasranāma**, after 256, 354 and 366.

**First, four identifications of the root.**

"Mūla, root — that is, the Śrīvidyā mantra; prakṛti, origin. She is in the form of two letters, Prakāśa अ, which is the origin of all other letters, and Vimarśa ह, the last letter." So the root is the alphabet's two ends, which is 392's अ five namas back and 2 श्रीमहाराज्ञी's pair.

"Or Mūlaprakṛti is the matter of the Sāṃkhya school," and Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Kārikā 3 is quoted — "the seven, Mahat and the rest, are productions and productive; Mūlaprakṛti is no production; the sixteen are the modifications; Puruṣa is neither Prakṛti nor its modifications." That is the same Kārikā 145 निर्विकारा quoted, where Bhāskararāya adopted the Sāṃkhya count and placed Her outside it.

"According to the Mṛgendra Saṃhitā, the Kuṇḍalinī is called Mūlaprakṛti with its seven productions; it is surrounded by Suṣumnā, which is in the form of the seven."

And the element-chain, which yields the argument for the name: "of the five elements from ether to earth, each is the Prakṛti of the succeeding one; of ether Brahman is the Prakṛti, for Taittirīya 2.1 says *from the Self arose ether*. That Brahman has no Prakṛti. So he is the root, the first cause."

The Pāñcarātra Āgama then has Śiva say it: "there is one mother of the Universe, the mother of the Scriptures, Sarasvatī, who has no origin; hence she is called Mūlaprakṛti. In her I took birth with the categories, Mahat and the rest."

**Then the prākṛta pralaya, with a dilemma worked out.**

"Amongst the actions which are to become ripe in a certain time, those that ripen are exhausted by fruition; the others which are not ripe and have not come to fruition — a new creation for their sake being useless — a Prākṛta pralaya takes place. Then Māyā, consuming all the world, is absorbed into the independent Paramaśiva, who is without attributes; it abides thus till the ripening of the remaining actions."

The Viṣṇu Purāṇa gives the sequence of absorptions: "the earth becomes dissolved into water, water is absorbed by fire, fire into air, air into ether, this into the unmanifested, and this is entirely absorbed in the unconditioned Puruṣa."

**And then the difficulty, which Bhāskararāya sets out in full.** "The dissolution of Māyā is not absolute annihilation as in Nirvāṇa, but like the mental modifications in the state of sleep, as there is no appearance of the modifications of Māyā during pralaya. Though at that time, by the power of the illumination of the unconditioned supreme Self, it receives light, yet it remains as if it has no light. If there is no light at all to Māyā, then there is no existence of it. If you accept this theory, there will be no succeeding creation."

So Māyā during the pralaya must be lit and unlit at once: unlit, or it would be manifest; lit, or it would not exist and nothing could follow. The sleep-analogy is offered as the model, and the argument for it is that a subsequent creation requires something to survive.

Then the awakening: "the modification of Māyā in the form of desire of creation arises in Paramaśiva for the sake of bestowing the fruit on those whose unripened actions are absorbed in Māyā; when their actions become ripe in course of time, that state of Māyā is variously named by the words *sight*, *desire*, *thought*, *desire of action*." Four Upaniṣads are cited for the four names — Aitareya 1.1 "he thought, let me create the worlds," Chāndogya 6.2.3 "it thought, let me become many," Taittirīya 2.6 "he desired, let me become many," Muṇḍaka 1.1.8 "by penance Brahman is increased."

**Then the six prākṛta creations, and a disagreement between two schools.**

*First*, the creation of darkness: "this manifestation of Māyā, characterised by objective distinctions, is the first creation, the creation of darkness, void of consciousness." Ṛgveda 10.129 is cited — "there was no being at that time, nor was there no being… in the beginning darkness was hidden by intelligence."

*Second*, Mahat: "from this creation called Tamas, in which the three qualities were differentiated, arose the creation of the partially manifested, Mahat."

*Third*, Ahaṃkāra: "in which the three guṇas are manifested objectively" — and threefold, "Vaikārika, Taijasa and Tāmasa, which last is the origin of the elements."

*Fourth*, the five tanmātras, from the Tāmasa egoism with the aid of Rajas.

*Fifth*, the eleven senses, from the Vaikārika egoism with the aid of Rajas.

*Sixth*, the presiding deities — "Dik, Vāta, Arka, Pracetas, the Aśvins and the rest, who are the deities of the above two" — from the Rājasa egoism.

Īśvarakṛṣṇa 25 is quoted for that assignment: "from the pure egoism arose the eleven sāttvic creation; from the Bhūtādi the subtle elements; and from Rajas egoism the deities presiding over both."

**And then the Śaiva school is said to differ**, and the difference is stated precisely: "but in the Śaiva school it is said, from pure egoism comes mind, from passional egoism the ten senses; thus there is a difference. For the Śaivas say: *from Taijasa mind comes, from Vaikārika senses, from Bhūtādi the subtle elements.*"

So Sāṃkhya derives all eleven senses from the sāttvika ahaṃkāra and the deities from the rājasa; the Śaivas split the eleven, giving manas to the taijasa and the ten senses to the vaikārika. Bhāskararāya records both, and here states the difference as a disagreement rather than as alternatives.

The Viṣṇu Bhāgavata's own list of six is then given, and Bhāskararāya notes an ordering problem in it: "here the creation of Tamas called Avyakta is the sixth in the order, but according to its meaning it should be taken as first."

And the further creations: "the Vaikṛta creation comprises trees and the rest, whose life-current tends upwards; animals, whose life-current is horizontal; and Bhūtas, Pretas and the rest, whose life-current tends downwards. These Prākṛta and Vaikṛta creations, taken together, are called the Kaumāra creation."

Kaṭha 3.10–11 closes the doctrinal part with the ascending series: "beyond the senses there are the objects; beyond the Mahat the Avyakta; beyond Avyakta there is the Person. Beyond the Person there is nothing. This is the goal and the supreme abode."

**And then a fifth numeral reading, and it works differently from the other four.**

"Or, ma, five — that is, the five subtle elements — and la, three — that is, Avyakta, Mahat and Ahaṃkāra — therefore Mūla, eight; Prakṛti, causes. The Sāṃkhya Sūtra says: *there are eight Prakṛtis*."

म is five and ल is three by the letter-numeral scheme, but the two are **added** rather than read positionally: five plus three is eight, and the eight prakṛtis are the Sāṃkhya set. The other four numeral readings in the text — उप = 10 at 529, दारु = 28 at 749, आदि = 80 at 296, पाश = 51 at 354 — all take the digits in place. This one sums them, and it is the only instance of that operation.

398. अव्यक्ता → अ-व्यक्ता

अ = not (नञ्)
व्यक्ता = manifest, evident (वि + अञ्ज् "to make clear")
"The Unmanifested."

Vigraha: व्यक्ता न भवति इति अव्यक्ता।

The dev field reads व्यक्ता, the initial अ lost to the sandhi with 397's visarga (मूलप्रकृतिः + अव्यक्ता → मूलप्रकृतिरव्यक्ता), and with no avagraha to mark it. **So the recorded form says the opposite of what the nama means** — and the gloss preserves the reading, "Undeveloped," while the whole body expounds Avyakta.

That is the same damage as 993 अज्ञानध्वान्तदीपिका and 616 अमेया, where the lost अ inverted the sense; and 616 stood in a chain of three exactly like this one.

Bhāskararāya opens by marking a new sequence: "he now proceeds to praise Devī under the form of the creations in order." So 398–401 follow the six creations 397 has just enumerated.

Then the definitions. "Avyakta is the manifestation of Māyā. According to the Sāṃkhya school it is expressed by the words Pradhāna, Prakṛti and other words." The Sāṃkhyasaptati: "that is the Avyakta which is subtle, without characteristics, inanimate, without beginning or end, capable of production, without parts, one and universal." Pañcaśikhācārya: "Pradhāna, say the wise, is the Avyakta, which is without beginning or middle, beyond Mahat, and permanent."

"It is the collective form of the three qualities." And Sāṃkhya Sūtra 6.39 is cited to keep the guṇas off Brahman: "Sattva and the rest are not qualities of that Brahman, because they are the qualities of that Avyakta."

Then two other referents. "Or Avyakta means Brahman, for at Vedānta Sūtra 3.2.23 it is said, *that Brahman is Avyakta, for the scriptures say so*," with Muṇḍaka: "he is not to be felt by the eyes, nor by the speech, nor by the other senses, nor by penance, nor by action." Or "Avyakta means Viṣṇu," on the Liṅga Purāṇa: "the names of Viṣṇu, who is ever capable of creation, are Pradhāna, Avyaya, Yoni, Avyakta, Prakṛti and Tamas."

399. व्यक्ताव्यक्तस्वरूपिणी → व्यक्त-अव्यक्त-स्व-रूपिणी

व्यक्त = manifest — and per the readings, Mahat; the perishable; the individual
अव्यक्त = unmanifest — and per the readings, egoism; the imperishable; the collective
स्व = own
रूपिणी = having the form of
"She whose very form is the manifest and the unmanifest."

Vigraha: व्यक्तम् अव्यक्तं च स्वरूपं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: व्यक्त + अव्यक्त → व्यक्ताव्यक्त (आ by 6.1.101).

Seven readings, which is the most any nama in this batch receives.

*As Mahat and Ahaṃkāra.* "Vyakta, the category Mahat, called so because it was first manifested and also from its greatness. Avyakta: ā, on all sides; vyakta, manifested — that is, egoism, the product of the above." So both members are creations from 397's list, and the privative अ is read as आ, "on all sides," to make the second manifest rather than unmanifest.

*As two namas.* "This name may be taken as two names, if the name Brahmajananī, 822 and 823, is taken as one." So the text's nama-count is elastic at exactly the two points the Paribhāṣā at 1000 legislates about — and Bhāskararāya notes the trade-off explicitly: split this one and join those, or the reverse.

*As Parāhantā.* "According to this view, vyakta is the supreme egoism, for supreme egoism is in the form of Tripurasundarī, because she is manifested in the category of egoism." Parāhantā is 711's inherent quality of Hers, and 854, 856 and 576's word.

*As subject and not subject to modification.* The Liṅga Purāṇa: "Vyakta is called Sat, as it is the second modification of the elements; Avyakta is called Asat because it is devoid of that."

*As perishable and imperishable.* The Matsya Purāṇa.

*As individual and collective.* The Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa: "the Avyakta is known as collective, and vyakta is individual." And the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "the wise say the seventy-three categories are meant by the word Vyakta, and by the word Avyakta the supreme Prakṛti."

**And then the three kinds of liṅga**, which is the unexpected reading: "or vyakta, avyakta and vyaktāvyakta — thus there are three kinds of Liṅgas. She is in all the forms." The Brahmavaivarta: "there are three Liṅgas, Svāyambhuva, Bāṇaliṅga and Śailaliṅga; these are respectively called Vyakta, Avyakta and Vyaktāvyakta. Vyakta, they say, gives salvation; the Avyakta gives worldly happiness; and Vyaktāvyakta gives both. The Bāṇaliṅga is said to be that which outweighs even two or three Tulās. The rest are called Śaila, mere stone, by the learned."

So the nama's own compound is the name of a class of liṅga, and the three classes are graded by what they confer.

*And as manifest to some and not to others.* "She is manifested in those whose deeds are ripened and is not manifested in those who are bound by the noose of Māyā." The Śaktirahasya then raises an objection about the descent of Śakti and answers it: "how do you say that the supreme Śakti which is all-pervading descends? The descent is from above downwards; only that which has form and is not all-pervading can descend. True — she is all-pervading, eternal, coexistent with Śiva; yet she is hidden in those who are bound by the noose of impurity and action, and manifested in them whose sins are burned out. In this way she is said to descend."

That is 354's burnt and unburnt impurities used to explain a technical term: śaktipāta is not motion but the difference between the concealed and the manifest.

Note on the verse. Seven namas, and 397 is a treatise.

What it contains is the whole cosmogony the text presupposes elsewhere: four identifications of the root, the prākṛta pralaya with its worked dilemma about whether Māyā is lit during the dissolution, the four Upaniṣadic names for the creative impulse, the six prākṛta creations, the Sāṃkhya and Śaiva disagreement about which egoism yields the senses, and the Vaikṛta and Kaumāra creations. And it closes with a numeral reading that sums म and ल to eight rather than reading them in place — the only one of the text's five such readings that adds.

399 then gives seven readings of one compound, including its own possible division into two namas — with the observation that doing so requires joining 822–823, which is exactly what the Paribhāṣā at 1000 rules on.

393's Jaina citation is worth marking: Haribhadra is named for the view that "the rays are the qualities, they are not the substratum," and the next nama asserts "the identity of the quality and the possessor of it." Named, then contradicted.

Textual note. 397's dev has lost the visarga of मूलप्रकृतिः and 398's has lost the initial अ of अव्यक्ता at that joint — so the recorded 398 reads व्यक्ता, the exact opposite of the nama, and only the gloss and body preserve it. The verse text carries the same, with a space in the wrong place: मूलप्रकृति व्यक्ता. 396 carries 395's gloss and body, and 397's gloss field holds 396's stranded heading.

---

## व्यापिनी विविधाकारा विद्याविद्यास्वरूपिणी । महाकामेशनयनकुमुदाह्लादकौमुदी

*vyāpinī vividhākārā vidyāvidyāsvarūpiṇī । mahākāmeśanayanakumudāhlādakaumudī*

Verse 87, namas 400–403.

400. व्यापिनी → व्यापिनी

व्यापिनी = pervading, extending through (वि + आप् "to reach")
"The All-pervading."

Vigraha: व्याप्नोतीति व्यापिनी।

"She is called all-pervading because she assumes the forms of the three creations of the threefold egoism." So the pervasion is specified from 397's list: the tanmātras from the tāmasa, the senses from the vaikārika, and the deities from the rājasa — the fourth, fifth and sixth creations.

**And this nama closes the fourth hundred, with the colophon in its body**: "thus ends the fifth Kālī, called Jvālinī, with the fourth hundred in the Saubhāgyabhāskara composed by Bhāskararāya," followed by "The Fifth Hundred."

**That is the seventh of the text's colophons, and the third consecutive one.** With 200's third Kalā closing the second hundred and 300's fourth closing the third, the run 200–300–400 is unbroken, and the rule holds at every surviving point: third/second, fourth/third, fifth/fourth, eighth/seventh, ninth/eighth, tenth/ninth, eleventh/tenth. Seven of the ten division-points survive; only 100, 500 and 600 are missing.

And eight of the eleven kalā-names are known: the second Tāpinī (in the colophon at nama 100), the third Dhāmrika, fourth Marīci, fifth Jvālinī, eighth Bhogadā, ninth Viśva, tenth Bodhinī, eleventh Dhāriṇī. The first, sixth and seventh have not appeared.

Also worth noting: this colophon names the author as Bhāskararāya where 200, 300, 700, 800, 900 name him by his initiatory name Bhāsurānanda. So the two names alternate across the colophons.

व्यापिनी is also the sixth of the eight stations above the brow at 207 and 299, where it is Vyāpinī or Vyāpikā.

401. विविधाकारा → विविध-आकारा

विविध = manifold, of various kinds (वि + विध)
आकारा = form, shape (आ + कृ)
"She of manifold forms."

Vigraha: विविधाः आकाराः यस्याः सन्ति सा।

Sandhi: विविध + आकारा → विविधाकारा (आ by 6.1.101).

"The different forms of the Vaikṛta creation, or of the Kaumāra creation" — with a cross-reference to 397, where those were the trees, animals and Bhūtas whose life-currents tend up, across and down.

So 400 covered the three prākṛta creations from egoism and 401 covers the vaikṛta, which completes the sequence 398 announced: "he now proceeds to praise Devī under the form of the creations in order."

आकार is denied of Her at 137 निराकारा, where it means "the form to which the qualities are attributed"; here the forms are the creations themselves.

402. विद्याविद्यास्वरूपिणी → विद्या-अविद्या-स्व-रूपिणी

विद्या = knowledge; and per the readings, knowledge of the Self, and the last modification before realisation
अविद्या = ignorance; and per the readings, the confused knowledge of separateness
स्व = own; and per the third reading, the knowledge belonging to supreme Brahman
रूपिणी = having the form of
"She whose form is knowledge and ignorance."

Vigraha: विद्या अविद्या च स्वरूपं यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: विद्या + अविद्या → विद्याविद्या (आ by 6.1.101).

Īśa 11 opens it, and it is the verse that makes both necessary: "one who knows both knowledge and ignorance, having crossed over death by ignorance, attains immortality by knowledge."

Then a technical division: "Vidyā, knowledge of the Self; Avidyā, the knowledge in the form of the last modification of duality — that is, just before realisation." So अविद्या is not error but the final penultimate state, which is 661 सदसद्रूपधारिणी's second reading of सत् and असत्.

The Bṛhannāradīya: "the supreme Śakti of that Viṣṇu, capable of absorbing the universe, in the form of existence and non-existence, is sung as Vidyā and Avidyā." And the Devī Bhāgavata twice: "she is Brahman himself, very difficult to attain, and in the form of Vidyā and Avidyā"; and "O King, know that Vidyā and Avidyā are two forms of Devī; by one men are freed, by the other they are bound."

That is 644 ज्ञानविग्रहा's Viṣṇu Purāṇa citation — "know that Jñāna is both Vidyā and Avidyā" — which resolved 643 ज्ञानदा's reversal by refusing the distinction. Here it is the nama itself.

**And then स्व is made a third term.** "Or, Vidyā, the knowledge in the form of the last modification of duality; Avidyā, confused knowledge of separateness; Sva, the knowledge belonging to supreme Brahman — because according to a lexicon Sva means relations and Self. Rūpa: these three are her form."

So the compound is read as three states rather than two, and the Liṅga Purāṇa supplies the same three under other names: "Śiva has three forms, Bhrānti, Vidyā and Parā. The knowledge of different objects is called Bhrānti, confused, by the learned. Knowledge in the form of Self is called Vidyā. Knowledge concerning Brahman without ambiguity is called Parā."

403. महाकामेशनयनकुमुदाह्लादकौमुदी → महा-कामेश-नयन-कुमुद-आह्लाद-कौमुदी

महा = great
कामेश = Kāmeśa, Kāmeśvara
नयन = an eye (from नी "to lead")
कुमुद = a white water-lily, which opens at moonrise; and per the second reading, कु inferior + मुद् pleasure
आह्लाद = gladdening, delighting (आ + ह्लाद्)
कौमुदी = moonlight, especially of the month Kārtika (vṛddhi derivative of कुमुद)
"She who is the moonlight gladdening the water-lilies that are Mahākāmeśa's eyes."

Vigraha: महाकामेशस्य नयनकुमुदानाम् आह्लादकौमुदी।

Sandhi: कुमुद + आह्लाद → कुमुदाह्लाद (आ by 6.1.101).

The figure depends on the flower: the कुमुद opens at moonrise, so his eyes open at the sight of Her. And कौमुदी is derived from कुमुद, so the moonlight is named after the flower it opens — which makes the compound circular by design.

The Yādava is cited for the range: "kumuda in the neuter means water-lily and red lotus, and in the masculine an ape. Kaumuda means the month Kārtika, and Kaumudī the moon of that month."

**Then the whole compound is re-divided into a claim about the wretched.** "Or, ku, inferior; mud, pleasure — Kaumuda are those who long for worldly pleasures. They are called inferior because their pleasures are mixed with pain and for other reasons. So Kaumuda means a miserable one." The Śāśvata and Viśva are cited: "kumut means inferior men and water-lily."

"Ā, full; hlāda, joy — that is, salvation. A man attains that stage by being led — nayana — to Mahākāmeśa. Kaumudī, light. The meaning is she becomes, out of pity, light as it were to them who are blind in worldly pursuits."

So नयन is read not as an eye but as a leading — which its root नी allows and which 247 पद्मनयना's etymology depends on — and the nama becomes: she is light to the worldly-blind, whom she leads to Śiva. A compound about His eyes becomes a compound about their blindness.

Note on the verse. Four namas closing the creation-sequence and then turning.

400 and 401 finish what 398 announced, covering the three creations from egoism and then the vaikṛta and kaumāra; and 400 carries the seventh colophon, which makes the kalā-run unbroken from 200 to 400.

402 makes Her both knowledge and ignorance on Īśa 11, and then re-reads the compound as three states with स्व for the third — matching the Liṅga Purāṇa's Bhrānti, Vidyā and Parā.

403 is the verse's ornament and its second reading dismantles it: a compound about the water-lilies of Śiva's eyes becomes a compound about men blind in worldly pursuit, with नयन read as leading rather than as an eye.

---

## भक्ताहार्दतमोभेदभानुमद्भानुसंततिः । शिवदूती शिवाराध्या शिवमूर्तिः शिवंकरी

*bhaktāhārdatamobhedabhānumadbhānusaṃtatiḥ । śivadūtī śivārādhyā śivamūrtiḥ śivaṃkarī*

Verse 88, namas 404–408.

404. भक्ताहार्दतमोभेदभानुमद्भानुसंततिः → भक्त-आहार्द-तमः-भेद-भानुमत्-भानु-संततिः

भक्त = a devotee
आहार्द = of the heart (vṛddhi derivative of हृद्)
तमः = darkness (तमस्)
भेद = splitting, dispelling (from भिद्)
भानुमत् = possessing light, the sun (भानु + मतुप्)
भानु = a ray of light
संततिः = a continuity, a succession (सम् + तन्)
"She who is the sun's unbroken succession of rays, dispelling the darkness in her devotees' hearts."

Vigraha: भक्तानाम् आहार्दतमोभेदे भानुमतः भानुसंततिः।

Sandhi at two joints: भक्त + आहार्द → भक्ताहार्द (आ by 6.1.101), and भानुमत् + भानु → भानुमद्भानु, the त् voicing before भ्.

index.html has no commentary for this nama.

At seven members this is the longest nama in the batch. It is 993 अज्ञानध्वान्तदीपिका's figure with a sun for a lamp and hearts for the world — there Gītā 10.11 supplied both compassion and lamp for two adjacent namas, and here the light is a continuous stream rather than a single flame.

संतति is also the last member of 365 स्वात्मानन्दलवीभूतब्रह्माद्यानन्दसंततिः, where what was a whole succession was the gods' bliss.

405. शिवदूती → शिव-दूती

शिव = Śiva
दूती = a female messenger (from दू "to go"); and here the one who *has* Śiva as messenger
"She whose messenger is Śiva."

Vigraha: शिवः दूतः यस्याः सा।

**And here Bhāskararāya rejects a rival reading outright, which he does rarely.**

The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "as Śiva himself was made a messenger by that Devī, she was known in the world as Śivadūtī." Then: **"some commentators think that she was made a messenger by Śiva. But this interpretation is without authority."**

The compound is genuinely ambiguous — शिवदूती could be "Śiva's messenger" or "she who has Śiva for messenger" — and Bhāskararāya settles it on the Purāṇa's testimony in the direction that subordinates Śiva. That is the same direction as 410 शिवपरा five namas on, 954 शंभुमोहिनी, 947's couch, and 354's Pāṇinian argument.

Explicit rejections of other readings occur elsewhere at 814 अमूर्ता, where the Naiyāyika definition of मूर्त is dismissed "as it has no foundation," and at 833, where the Sundarīmahodaya's count of fifty pīṭhas is rejected.

Then the placement: "this is the deity of the Puṣkaratīrtha," on the Padma Purāṇa — "she who lives in the Puṣkara, ever conferring happiness."

Puṣkara is where 699 सावित्री and 804 पुष्करा are also placed, and where 420 गायत्री's story happens fifteen namas on. And Śivadūtī is the seventh of the sixteen Nityās listed at 391.

406. शिवाराध्या → शिव-आराध्या

शिव = Śiva
आराध्या = to be worshipped (आ + राध्)
"She who is worshipped by Śiva."

Vigraha: शिवेन आराध्या।

Sandhi: शिव + आराध्या → शिवाराध्या (आ by 6.1.101).

**And the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa makes his androgyny the fruit of worshipping Her**: "even Śiva, by worshipping whom, by meditation, by the power of Yoga, becomes the lord of all Siddhis, and becomes half-female."

So Ardhanārīśvara is not a given but an attainment — the reward of Śiva's own worship of Her — which is a considerable claim and it makes 392 श्रीकण्ठार्धशरीरिणी fourteen namas back a consequence rather than a fact.

That is the same relation 558 कमलाक्षनिषेविता asserts of Viṣṇu, where the Padma Purāṇa says "Viṣṇu ever worships the sapphire Devī, hence he attained his own state."

"Śivadūtī is a certain mantra of four parts worshipped by Śiva" — the body carries that back-reference to 405, together with 407's stranded heading.

आराध्या for the twelfth time in the text.

407. शिवमूर्तिः → शिव-मूर्तिः

शिव = Śiva; also auspicious; also salvation
मूर्तिः = form, embodiment
"She whose form is Śiva."

Vigraha: शिवः मूर्तिः यस्याः सा।

index.html's gloss and body are duplicates, and the reason is stated first: "because there is no separation between Śiva and Śakti."

The Śruti: "one Rudra hidden in all beings; he is with Māyā, with parts and without parts. He is Devī himself, and is not separated from her. By knowing this one attains immortality."

Then two further senses of शिव: "or Śiva, beneficent; mūrti, form. Or Śiva, salvation; mūrti, form — because salvation is the realisation of the very Self." The Saura Saṃhitā: "the supreme salvation is the realisation of the Self; those who were bound by Avidyā are freed by Vidyā."

So शिव is the god, the auspicious, and liberation — three senses in one nama, and the third makes शिवमूर्तिः mean "she whose form is release," which is 737 मुक्तिरूपिणी.

मूर्ति for the seventh time in the text.

408. शिवंकरी → शिवम्-करी

शिवम् = auspiciousness, welfare (accusative of शिव)
करी = she who makes (from कृ)
"She who makes welfare."

Vigraha: शिवं करोतीति शिवंकरी।

The formation is the accusative with करी, as in वशंकरी at 697 and 978 and प्रियंकरी at 731.

"She makes her devotees happy by removing the noose of Avidyā and leads them to Brahman, which is to be attained by liberated souls. Or Śiva means auspiciousness and karī, giver."

The noose of avidyā is 354's पाश, and this nama is 126 शांकरी in a fuller form — there शम् with कर gave "she who makes happiness," and the Kālikā Purāṇa made Her birth from Dakṣa a per-kalpa recurrence.

Note on the verse. Five namas, four of them on शिव, and the group is about the relation between the two of them.

405 settles an ambiguous compound in the direction that makes Śiva Her messenger, and rejects the reverse reading as unauthorised. 406 makes his half-female form the fruit of worshipping Her. 407 then denies any separation at all, and 408 makes what he *is* — auspiciousness — what She does.

So the four namas move from subordination to identity in four steps, and 410 in the next verse states the first plainly: "the position of Śiva depends upon Śakti."

Textual note. 404 has no commentary body. 406's body carries 407's stranded heading. 407's gloss and body are duplicates.

---

## शिवप्रिया शिवपरा शिष्टेष्टा शिष्टपूजिता । अप्रमेया स्वप्रकाशा मनोवाचामगोचरा

*śivapriyā śivaparā śiṣṭeṣṭā śiṣṭapūjitā । aprameyā svaprakāśā manovācāmagocarā*

Verse 89, namas 409–415.

409. शिवप्रिया → शिव-प्रिया

शिव = Śiva
प्रिया = dear to; a beloved
"Beloved of Śiva." — or, "She to whom Śiva is dear."

Vigraha: शिवस्य प्रिया। or शिवः प्रियः यस्याः सा।

The commentary is four words and it gives the second reading: "or Śiva is loved by her."

So the compound is left ambiguous on purpose, as शिवदूती was at 405 and settled there. प्रिया for its fourteenth turn.

410. शिवपरा → शिव-परा

शिव = Śiva
परा = beyond, superior; and per the second reading, the supreme
"She who is beyond Śiva."

Vigraha: शिवात् परा।

**And the reason is stated in eight words, which is the plainest form of the claim in the thousand**: "because the position of Śiva depends upon Śakti."

Then two alternatives which soften it: "or, to whom Śiva is the supreme; or she reveals Śiva to her devotees."

The claim is made elsewhere at 354 by grammatical argument, at 947 by furniture, at 406 by making his androgyny an attainment, at 954 by bewilderment, at 995 by the chain of command ending at Her eyebrows, and at 373 by making Her ear-ornaments the cause of his surviving the poison. Here it is simply asserted.

411. शिष्टेष्टा → शिष्ट-इष्टा

शिष्ट = taught, ordained; also the learned, the well-conducted (past participle of शास् "to teach")
इष्टा = desired, wished; also a sacrifice (from इष् "to desire," or from यज्)
"She who is desired by the wise." — or, "She to whom the ordained rites are dear."

Vigraha: शिष्टैः इष्टा। or शिष्टानि इष्टानि यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: शिष्ट + इष्टा → शिष्टेष्टा (अ + इ → ए by guṇa, 6.1.87).

Two readings, and the first is about rites rather than people: "Śiṣṭa, ordained ceremonies which are dear to her. Śiṣṭa: she is worshipped by the ordained ceremonies." And the rule quoted is severe: **"the Lord should be worshipped by means of ceremonies according to one's caste and order, and not by mere offering of scent, flower and the rest."**

That is the strictest statement in the text about what worship requires, and it stands against 950 पञ्चसङ्ख्योपचारिणी's five domestic services — scent, flowers, incense, lamp, food — which are exactly what this rule dismisses. And against 681 सुखाराध्या's freedom from restriction.

Then the Mahābhārata and Bṛhannāradīya: "righteousness arises from conduct; the lord of righteousness is Viṣṇu."

**And the Vasiṣṭha Sūtras define the शिष्ट, which is worth having**: "the Śiṣṭas are those who always control their limbs, eyes, speech and whole body; who receive the Vedas with their supplements by tradition; who are devotees to Brahman; and whose every motive directly depends on the scriptures."

Or simply "she is worshipped by the wise."

शास् is the root of शास्त्र at 845 and 705, and of शासना at 995.

412. शिष्टपूजिता → शिष्ट-पूजिता

शिष्ट = the wise, the well-conducted
पूजिता = worshipped (from पूज्)
"She who is worshipped by the wise."

Vigraha: शिष्टैः पूजिता।

The whole commentary is one clause of self-reference: "this name clearly sums up the meaning of the previous one."

So 412 exists to disambiguate 411 — the previous nama admitted both the rites-reading and the persons-reading, and this one settles on persons. The text does the same at 405, where an ambiguous compound is fixed by authority, and at 384–385, where a claim is followed by its argument.

पूजिता for the fourth time, and the wise are the worshippers at 825 बुधार्चिता and 917 धीरसमर्चिता too.

413. अप्रमेया → अ-प्रमेया

अ = not (नञ्); and per the readings, Brahmā and Viṣṇu; also अप्, water
प्रमेया = measurable, knowable (प्र + मा "to measure," gerundive)
"The Immeasurable."

Vigraha: प्रमातुं न शक्या इति अप्रमेया।

Three readings, and the second and third both take अ as something rather than as a negative.

"Or, A, Brahmā, Viṣṇu and the rest; prameya, to be known or measured — that is, she is to be known by them only." So the privative becomes a restriction on who can know.

"Or, ap, water; prameya, abiding in." The Śruti: "my origin is in the water of ocean." That is 298 नारायणी's water-derivation and 837 वियत्प्रसूः's neighbourhood.

प्रमेय is the third term of the epistemic triad — pramātṛ, pramāṇa, prameya — which 234 महात्रिपुरसुन्दरी makes the three cities of Tripurā: "the measurer, the measuring, and the thing measured." So the nama denies of Her the very term that nama makes her.

And 616 अमेया is the same claim on the simpler gerundive, where the lost अ inverted the sense; 642 अपरिच्छेद्या and 701 देशकालापरिच्छिन्ना make it with छिद्.

414. स्वप्रकाशा → स्व-प्रकाशा

स्व = own; and per the second reading, सु much
प्रकाशा = light, illumination, manifestation (प्र + काश् "to shine")
"The Self-luminous."

Vigraha: स्वयं प्रकाशते इति स्वप्रकाशा।

Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.9: "here this Person becomes self-illuminated." That is the dream-passage, which 258 स्वपन्ती's Pratyabhijñā definition depends on — dream being the objectifying of what is already in the mind, so the light in it is the sleeper's own.

"Or, su, much; ap, water; prakāśa, manifested" — the same अप् as the previous nama's third reading, so two consecutive namas are given a water-division.

प्रकाश is the pole opposite Vimarśa at 548 विमर्शरूपिणी, where Vimarśa is "the inherent vibration of Parabrahman who is in the Prakāśa aspect"; and 382's two hands are the two of them.

415. मनोवाचामगोचरा → मनस्-वाचाम्-अगोचरा

मनस् = mind
वाचाम् = of speech (genitive plural of वाच्)
अगोचरा = not within range, not attainable (अ + गोचर, "cow-pasture," hence range or reach)
"She who is beyond the range of mind and speech."

Vigraha: मनसः वाचां च अगोचरा।

Sandhi: मनस् + वाचाम् → मनोवाचाम्, the अस् becoming ओ.

गोचर is literally a cow-range, the ground a cow goes over — so what is अगोचर is outside the pasture, beyond where a thing can graze. It is a good word for a limit.

Taittirīya 2.9.1: "from whence speech and mind turn away, unable to reach it." And the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's Prahlāda: "I bow down to the Supreme Īśvarī who transcends speech and mind, and who can be grasped by the wisdom of the wise alone."

Then a re-division: "or, A is to be prefixed to the name: then manas, mind; vāc, speech; ama, not purified — literally unbaked, as a clay vessel; a, not. She is beyond those whose mind and speech are not purified, and therefore cannot be known by them."

So the नञ् is moved and अम is read as "unbaked," giving a claim about who cannot know rather than about what cannot be known. The clay-vessel figure is the same one 169 क्रोधशमनी's Āpastamba uses: worship performed in anger is "like water in a vessel of unbaked clay."

**And then a scriptural contradiction is raised and settled by a named commentator.** "How is it that the Śruti in one place says *the mind turns away*, and again at Kaṭha 4.11 *by mind alone it should be perceived*? This contradiction is removed in the Bhāmatī — the commentary on Śaṅkara's commentary on the Vedānta Sūtra by Vācaspati Miśra — by adding *not purified* and *purified* respectively to the word mind."

So the two verses speak of two minds, and the qualifier the nama's own re-division supplied is what resolves them. The Bhāmatī is cited once elsewhere, at 845 शास्त्रसारा, for the widest definition of śāstra — "that by which, whether revealed texts or otherwise, men are instructed to act or to refrain."

Note on the verse. Seven namas, four on शिव and three of inaccessibility.

410's eight words are the plainest statement in the text of the claim the whole शिव-run has been making: "the position of Śiva depends upon Śakti."

411–412 then pair as ambiguity and its resolution, and 411's rule — that the Lord is to be worshipped by the ceremonies of one's caste and order "and not by mere offering of scent, flower and the rest" — is the strictest thing the text says about worship, dismissing exactly what 950 prescribes.

And 415 closes by resolving a real scriptural conflict with a named authority: Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī distinguishes the purified mind from the unpurified, so Taittirīya's "mind turns away" and Kaṭha's "by mind alone" both stand.

---

## चिच्छक्तिश्चेतनारूपा जडशक्तिर्जडात्मिका । गायत्री व्याहृतिः सन्ध्या द्विजबृन्दनिषेविता

*cicchaktiś cetanārūpā jaḍaśaktir jaḍātmikā । gāyatrī vyāhṛtiḥ sandhyā dvijabṛndaniṣevitā*

Verse 90, namas 416–423.

416. चिच्छक्तिः → चित्-शक्तिः

चित् = consciousness (from चित् "to perceive"); and per Pāṇini, comparison
शक्तिः = power, energy
"The Power of consciousness."

Vigraha: चितः शक्तिः।

Sandhi: चित् + शक्ति → चिच्छक्ति, the त् assimilating to च् before श् and the श् becoming छ् (Pāṇini 8.4.40 and 8.4.63). The dev field reads चिच्छक्ति, the visarga lost, and the verse text carries the same with a space.

**index.html's gloss opens with a Pāṇinian note**: "Cit, according to the Yāska Smṛti and Pāṇini 8.2.101, means comparison."

Pāṇini 8.2.101 is चित्ते चित् — the particle चित् used in comparison — so the sūtra is about an indeclinable homonym and not about consciousness at all. It is the third Pāṇini citation in this stretch, after 1.4.54 at 354 and 1.4.14 at 366, and the only one where the grammatical point is lexical rather than doctrinal.

Then the substantial reading: "or Citśakti, the power of removing Avidyā, also termed Caitanya." Śvetāśvatara 5.1 is quoted: "in the imperishable and infinite highest Brahman, wherein the two, Vidyā and Avidyā, are hidden — one is imperishable and the other is perishable; he who rules these two is different from either." That is 402 विद्याविद्यास्वरूपिणी's pair fourteen namas back, now with a ruler above both.

And the Devī Bhāgavata Book 5: "O king, in all beings there is the Śakti with all its power; any being devoid of that Śakti becomes like a corpse. That Citśakti is in all beings; that is but her form."

**"Any being devoid of that Śakti becomes like a corpse" is 249 पञ्चप्रेतासनासीना's argument** — where the five gods deprived of their śaktis are corpses because "activity belongs to Śakti" — stated as a general principle rather than of the five in particular.

Sastry notes an omission here: "the commentator discusses in this place the division of some names according to the Chchalākṣara Sūtras" — a discussion the translation drops, as it drops the division-discussion at 925.

417. चेतनारूपा → चेतना-रूपा

चेतना = consciousness, sentience (from चित्)
रूपा = form
"She whose form is consciousness."

Vigraha: चेतना रूपं यस्याः सा।

Saṅkṣepaśārīraka: "the pure Citśakti of the supreme Lord is called Caitanya" — the same line 572 पराशक्तिः cites. The Gauḍapāda Sūtra 3: "Śakti is Caitanya itself."

Then the Devī Bhāgavata, and Bhāskararāya identifies what it is quoting: "we meditate upon that primeval Vidyā which is in the form of Caitanya of all, and which guides our senses. **This means the tripartite Gāyatrī.**" And the Matsya Purāṇa is added: "they know the Bhāgavata which begins with Gāyatrī."

So the verse is the Gāyatrī with Vidyā for Savitṛ, which places this nama three before 420 गायत्री and explains why the two stand close.

And Taittirīya 2.8.1's "that of bliss is to be discussed" is glossed as "the energy in the form of consciousness," on Śaṅkarāraṇya's commentary the Vidyāratna — "as the Vimarśa form." Śaṅkarāraṇya is cited elsewhere at 895 for the senses of पुर.

418. जडशक्तिः → जड-शक्तिः

जड = inert, insentient, dull
शक्तिः = power, energy
"The power of the inert."

Vigraha: जडस्य शक्तिः।

The dev field reads जडशक्ति, the visarga lost, and the next nama has gained the र् it became. The verse text carries both, with a space before the stray र्.

"A certain modification of Māyā which is correlative to the power which creates the animate world — that is, this name simply denotes the creative energy."

So जडशक्ति is the counterpart of 416's चिच्छक्ति, and the pair is consciousness-power against matter-power. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa is quoted at length for how the two causes relate, and the last clause is the interesting one: "the energies of all beings are not to be grasped by our intellects. The creative energies of Brahman are a hundred times more difficult to grasp; they are in him like heat is in fire, O best of ascetics. **He, Brahman, is only the instrumental cause of the creation of the world. The creative energies are the material cause.** Except the instrumental cause, the creative energies depend on nothing. An object becomes itself by its own energy."

So Brahman is the निमित्तकारण and the śaktis are the उपादानकारण — the material cause is Hers. That is a strong technical claim and it is the material counterpart of 354's argument that agency belongs to Śakti.

The heat-in-fire simile is 711's, where Parāhantā is Her inherent quality "as we see burning to be the inherent quality of fire only."

419. जडात्मिका → जड-आत्मिका

जड = inert, insentient
आत्मिका = having the nature of, being the very self of
"She whose nature is the inert."

Vigraha: जडः आत्मा यस्याः सा।

Sandhi: जड + आत्मिका → जडात्मिका (आ by 6.1.101). The dev field reads र्जडात्मिका, carrying the र् of 418's visarga.

index.html has no commentary for this nama; the gloss is "the objective world."

416–419 are two pairs on one pattern: the power of consciousness and consciousness itself, then the power of the inert and the inert itself. So the same relation — śakti and what it is the śakti of — is asserted twice, once on each side of the sentient divide, and both times She is both terms.

आत्मिका for the seventh time in the text.

420. गायत्री → गायत्री

गायत्री = the Gāyatrī — the twenty-four-syllable metre and its verse; and per the etymologies, she who protects the singer, or she who is sung and approached
"Gāyatrī."

Vigraha: गायन्तं त्रायते इति गायत्री।

"The metre consisting of twenty-four syllables is called Gāyatrī." The Kūrma Purāṇa: "I am Gāyatrī among the metres," with Gītā 10.35.

**That makes this the fifth nama the text identifies as a metre**, after 829 प्रतिष्ठा (sixteen syllables), 660 सुप्रतिष्ठा (twenty), 673 बृहती (thirty-six) and 360 तनुमध्या. And at 673 Bhāskararāya had to reconcile Bṛhatī with the Kūrma Purāṇa's "I am the Gāyatrī among the metres" — answering that "Devī is both the metres." So the conflict he settled there is settled again here by the same citation from the other side.

**Then a Purāṇic story that separates Gāyatrī from Sāvitrī, and it is a domestic scene.** "Or a cowherd's daughter is called Gāyatrī, who is the younger wife of Brahmā. This story occurs in the Padma Purāṇa. Once in the Puṣkara, when Brahmā was performing a sacrifice and called Sāvitrī, who was with Lakṣmī and others, she did not come but replied, *I will come with the others*. Enraged at this speech, he substituted a cowherd's daughter bestowed by the hand of Indra, and thus addressed Viṣṇu: *let us hasten for the sacrifice; there is here, O Lord, a very virtuous woman called Gāyatrī.* Thus addressed, Viṣṇu replied to Brahmā: *do you wed this woman by the Gāndharva form of marriage. I give her to you, O Lord; do not hesitate. Take the hand of this cowherd's daughter.* And thus the grandsire wedded her by the Gāndharva marriage."

So Gāyatrī is Brahmā's second wife, married in haste because Sāvitrī was late for his own sacrifice, with Viṣṇu giving her away. The Puṣkara of the story is where 405 Śivadūtī, 699 सावित्री and 804 पुष्करा are all placed — and 699 is Sāvitrī herself, so the two wives are two namas of the thousand.

Then four etymologies, all of them from गै or गा. The Bharadvāja Smṛti: "because she protects — trā — the singer — ga — she is called Gāyatrī." The Padma Purāṇa in Her own voice: "after bathing in the Puṣkara one should repeat me, the mother of the Vedas. Though I abide in the eight syllables of each part, yet this universe is pervaded by me." The Devī Purāṇa: "as everyone sings her and approaches her, she is called Gāyatrī." And Chāndogya 3.12.1: "sings forth and protects."

"Or Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas" — which is nama 338 वेदजननी, where the Devī Purāṇa derived the Vedas from the letters and the letters from the kuṇḍalinī's triangle.

421. व्याहृतिः → वि-आहृतिः

वि = apart, forth
आहृतिः = an utterance, a pronouncement (आ + हृ "to bring forth")
"The Utterance."

Vigraha: व्याहरणं व्याहृतिः।

index.html's gloss and body are duplicates, and the gloss carries 420's tail: "Gāyatrī, because she is in the form of Vyāhṛti. The utterance, or a certain Mantra."

व्याहृति is the technical term for the three great utterances भूर्भुवः स्वः prefixed to the Gāyatrī, so the nama stands where it does because those precede the verse in recitation.

The Vāyu Purāṇa gives a derivation from the story: "addressed by me — vyāharaṇa — you approached; hence you are known by the name Vyāhṛti."

**And 423 will read 421–423 as the three states**, with Vyāhṛti for waking.

422. सन्ध्या → सम्-ध्या

सम् = together
ध्या = meditation; and the word also means junction, twilight (सम् + धा or ध्यै)
"Sandhyā — the junction, and the meditation."

Vigraha: संधीयते अत्र इति संध्या। or सम्यक् ध्यायन्ति एनाम् इति संध्या।

index.html's gloss and body are duplicates and the gloss is cut mid-sentence.

The definition holds both senses of the word: "Sandhyā means junction, also meditation — that is, the idea of the non-separation of ourselves and that of the Caitanya which is in the sun. The explanation of the word is: men meditate wholly — sam — on her; she is called Sandhyā."

So the twilight-word is derived from meditation rather than from the joining of day and night, and the object of that meditation is identity: "the aspirant should think, *I am the servant of that Brahman who is existence and consciousness, and I am He*." The Vyāsa Smṛti presses it: "do not distinguish Gāyatrī from Brahman; in any case one should worship her saying *I am She*."

The Mahābhārata: "Sandhyā means the Brahman which abides in the Sun, and she is meditated as one by Brahmā and all beings who are his rays." The Bharadvāja Smṛti: "she who is differentiated as Brahman, the witness of action, radiant, the Śakti of Īśvara, is called by the wise Sandhyā." And a verse of the great men ties her to the mantra's parts: "Gāyatrī with her head and with the fourth part is described in the Vedas as Sandhyā. O Tripurā, thou alone dost decree the result of even great actions."
